*The Cooperative Publishing Union, in beginning its work with the present publication, feels it a duty to express its gratitude to all those who, by assisting with advice and aid, allowed it to undertake its first endeavor with confidence.*

*The benevolence and encouragement of His Excellency Deputy F. Mariotti, Undersecretary of State for Public Instruction, who was pleased to suggest the printing of this Treatise; the kind condescension of the illustrious Senator M. Tabarrini, who, by composing the elaborate Preface, allowed it to be presented to the public under the auspices of his renowned name; the zealous, friendly, and affectionate work of the Honorable Deputy A. Maffi, who facilitated the task undertaken by the Cooperative; the welcome services rendered by the Honorable Deputy V. Armirotti; the precious suggestions of the most distinguished gentlemen G. Bobbio, G. Chiarini, G. Cugnoni, R. De Cesare, A. Fantoni, G. Mazzoni, D. Melegari, G. Mestica, and E. Monaci; the promise of the Honorable Senator A. Messedaglia, of the Honorable Deputies R. Bonghi and F. Martini, and of the most distinguished gentlemen C. Calisse, I. Giorgi, D. Gnoli, E. Novelli, G. Tomassetti, and O. Tommasini, to contribute to the works that will follow this one, constitute a collection of support that makes the Cooperative Publishing Union hesitant <note>The publishers are expressing a modest concern that their work might not fully live up to the high level of support they received.</note> as to whether it has responded adequately to them.*

*And the gratitude of the publishers is also due to the firm of G. C. Sansoni of Florence, which, through Professor G. Biagi and Mr. G. Ceccherini, contributed to making this volume even more valuable by authorizing the inclusion of the Life of Da Vinci <note>This refers to the biography of Leonardo written by Giorgio Vasari in the 16th century.</note> taken from its highly accurate edition of Vasari's works, accompanied by new notes and the Commentary of Professor G. Milanesi <note>Gaetano Milanesi (1813–1895) was a famous art historian known for his definitive annotated editions of Vasari.</note>.*

*To all these collaborators, the Cooperative Publishing Union gives thanks.*

*Rome, January 1890.*

# PREFACE

<note>original: "PREFAZIONE"</note>

<column-break/>

The work presented here represents more than a mere technical manual; it is the intellectual legacy of a man who viewed painting as a science of the natural world. In this edition, we have sought to reconcile the various manuscript fragments to provide a cohesive narrative of the Master's theories on light, shadow, and the "motions of the mind."

<margin>The 1651 edition served as our primary structural guide.</margin>

It is essential for the reader to understand that Leonardo did not organize these notes into a finished book during his lifetime. Instead, they were gathered by his pupil, Francesco Melzi, who inherited the chaotic mass of drawings and reflections. <insert>Melzi's devotion preserved these insights for posterity.</insert>

## ON THE NATURE OF THE PAINTER

The painter who draws by practice and judgment of the eye, without the use of reason, is like a mirror that reproduces all the objects placed before it, without knowing them. <note>This is a foundational concept in Leonardo's philosophy: the artist must be a "philosopher-scientist" rather than a mere craftsman.</note>

<column-break/>

->**THE UNIVERSAL PRINCIPLES**<-

| Principle | Description |
|:---|:---|
| <term>Perspective</term> <note>The mathematical representation of three-dimensional space on a flat surface.</note> | The bridle and rudder of painting. |
| <term>Chiaroscuro</term> <note>The treatment of light and shade in drawing and painting.</note> | The art of giving relief to figures. |
| <term>Sfumato</term> <note>The technique of blending colors and tones so subtly that there is no perceptible transition.</note> | The smoky blurring of edges to create depth. |

As the Master wrote: *The mind of the painter should be like a mirror, which always takes the color of the thing it reflects, and is filled by as many images as there are objects placed before it.* <note>original: "La mente del pittore si debbe trasmutare in tante similitudini, quante sono le figure degli oggetti che gli si parano dinanzi."</note>

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>This page marks the beginning of the main text of the "Treatise on Painting," following the blank divider noted on the previous page. It introduces a specific 19th-century edition produced by a workers' cooperative.</meta>

->[Decorative header: A frieze featuring classical acanthus leaf scrolls flanking a central panel with two sketched male profiles—one elderly and bearded, one younger—reminiscent of Leonardo’s studies of human ages.]<-

THIS reprint of the *Treatise on Painting* by Leonardo da Vinci is the first attempt by a Cooperative Society of Printers <note>Società cooperativa di tipografi: These were 19th-century labor associations where workers shared ownership and profits.</note>, who, working in their spare time on their own account, intend to bring to light books that are easy to sell and of proven utility. This act by intelligent and industrious workers—associating to produce and market the products of their own craft—seems to us to deserve encouragement, more for its moral value than for its economic consequences, which we do not wish to debate here. And the moral value of this act lies in combining capital (the fruit of savings) with labor directed by harmonious and well-disposed wills, for the purpose of doing something useful for the associates and beneficial to the public. Indeed, they do not intend to exploit the unhealthy curiosity of our time by using the press to spread novels and short stories where both modesty and the most noble sentiments of nature are offended.

[An engraving appears here depicting a man with thick, curly hair and a stern, downward expression, a classic example of Leonardo’s physiognomic studies <note>Physiognomy: The historical practice of judging a person's character from their facial features, a subject Leonardo studied extensively.</note>.]

<summary>This page introduces a new edition of Leonardo da Vinci's "Treatise on Painting," highlighting that it was produced by a cooperative of printers as a moral and educational alternative to the popular "unhealthy" literature of the era.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the new edition of Leonardo da Vinci's "Treatise on Painting," shifting focus from the printers' cooperative to the specific editorial choices made for this volume, such as modernizing the language for accessibility.</meta>

<page-num>XIV</page-num>
<header>M. TABARRINI</header>

humanity—things ignored by famous printers rich in capital and equipment—but they wish to choose books that honor literature and aim to improve rather than corrupt.

The promise of these laudable intentions is meanwhile found in this first volume, which they offer to their fellow citizens; and from which they hope for an honest profit as well as the approval of all those who see in the humble beginnings of things the importance of the effects that may derive from them in the future.

This reprint of Leonardo’s work, although conducted accurately based on the best editions produced in Italy and compared against the Vatican Codex <note>original: "codice Vaticano." This refers to the Codex Urbinas Latinus 1270, the primary source for Leonardo's Treatise on Painting.</note>, does not have the ambition of providing a genuine text supported by all the aids of modern criticism. The goal proposed by the editors—to make Leonardo’s book accessible to the greatest number of readers, even those with a modest education, and especially to artists—led to the necessity of modernizing the spelling and punctuation, and of removing archaisms <note>Archaisms: Outdated words or expressions that are no longer in common use.</note> that made understanding the text exceedingly difficult. In this, they mostly followed the reading adopted by De Romanis in the edition published in Rome in 1817. By conducting the printing in this manner, they did neither more nor less than what previous Italian editors had done. However, they studied the collation of the Vatican Codex with greater accuracy, correcting the other editions wherever they had strayed from it, and placing in their proper positions the additions that are found confusedly within it. Anyone who looks at the edition of the codex produced with a great display of scholarship by Heinrich Ludwig in Vienna in 1882 will be easily persuaded that the text, if left in that antiquated and incorrect form, might have satisfied critics—who today demand, not without reason, the faithful reproduction of texts—but it certainly would not have increased the number of readers for this new reprint. And of this opinion were Commander Filippo Mariotti and Professor Giovanni Mestica,

<summary>The author explains the editorial decision to modernize Leonardo's text for the benefit of artists and general readers, rather than producing a strictly academic or archaic reproduction. It acknowledges the influence of previous editors like De Romanis and Heinrich Ludwig while prioritizing accessibility.</summary>

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface by Marco Tabarrini, transitioning from the editorial philosophy of the publishing cooperative to the historical context and scientific nature of Leonardo da Vinci's treatise.</meta>

<page-num>XV</page-num>
<header>PREFACE</header>

who first encouraged the Cooperative Publishing Union, and advised them on the reproduction of Leonardo’s book on painting.

   These things regarding the intentions of the publishers needed to be said at the very beginning, so that this reprint may be judged for what it is, and not for what others might perhaps have wished it to be.

   Leonardo wrote this book on painting around 1498 for the school that Lodovico Sforza <note>Ludovico "Il Moro" Sforza (1452–1508), the Duke of Milan and Leonardo's major patron.</note> had founded in Milan, from which emerged that beautiful group of painters and sculptors who flourished for a long time in Lombardy, always maintaining a character that shares both in the Tuscan school of the fifteenth century <note>original: "quattrocento"</note> and the Roman school of Raphael and his imitators. Anyone who wished, moreover, to compare Leonardo’s school to the Academy founded later by the Carracci in Bologna <note>The Accademia degli Incamminati, founded around 1582, which sought to revitalize Italian art through a systematic curriculum.</note>, would find in the comparison that the differences are far greater than the similarities. The Carracci intended to delay the decline of art with conventional rules; whereas Leonardo aimed to give the subsidy of science to a flourishing art. And a scientist, in the sense that could be given to that word at the time, Leonardo truly was; with the inventive genius with which he was endowed, he anticipated some modern discoveries in his observations of natural facts. This book on painting, like the others on perspective and on light and shadows, are collections of practical precepts deduced with great sharpness from the theorems of geometry, optics, and mechanics—sciences not yet formed into a body of doctrine in his time, but which he glimpsed in embryo with the eyes of his mind.

   It will perhaps be said that all these precepts concern the technical part rather than the concept of art; but it is precisely the technical part that can form the subject of teaching, while everything that is ideality and sentiment—if the artist does not have it within himself—no master will be capable of teaching it to him. Leonardo applied to his works the teach—

<summary>The author explains that Leonardo's treatise was intended as a scientific foundation for art, written for the Sforza court in Milan, and argues that while technique can be taught, artistic "sentiment" must come from within.</summary>
<keywords>Leonardo da Vinci, Ludovico Sforza, Milan, Lombardy, Raphael, Carracci, Bologna, perspective, optics, mechanics, art education, science and art</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues Marco Tabarrini's preface, moving from the scientific foundations of Leonardo's teachings to a defense of his meticulous methods and a broader celebration of the Italian Renaissance.</meta>

<page-num>XVI</page-num>
<header>M. TABARRINI</header>

teachings that he gave to his pupils; and what effects he knew how to derive from them is told by his divine paintings, which in all times have formed the wonder of the world. It is also told by the contempt in which those teachings are held today by those who clutter the halls of public exhibitions with paintings dashed off haphazardly <note>original: "alla brava," meaning done with a superficial boldness or lack of care</note> without study and without concept, which are outrages to nature and to art. Despite all the progress that the sciences applied to the arts have made in our day, we believe that Leonardo’s precepts always possess a very great value; and although some could today be demonstrated with a greater rigor of scientific principles, the observation of the fact from which they are deduced remains nonetheless true. And it is not to be wondered at that this master of art studied his paintings in such minute detail that he seemed to his contemporaries to be wasting time trifling with unproductive preparations; for it is only with this study and with these scrupulous precautions that one can make of a portrait of a woman, such as the *Mona Lisa* <note>original: "Gioconda"</note>, a masterpiece to stand on par with paintings of grand composition.

Leonardo is truly one of the greatest and most brilliant figures of the Renaissance, one of the most universal and original minds that Italy has ever had. In that singular era, which has no parallel other than in the most beautiful century of ancient Greece, Italy possessed a portentous fertility of men of genius who ensured her primacy in letters and the arts, while the rest of Europe struggled to emerge from the darkness of the Middle Ages. The character of that era was the beauty and elegance that sprang from all manifestations of life. The ugly and the deformed were not only not represented, they were not even conceived. It was a spontaneous flowering of intellects who felt all the harmonies of beauty and knew how to represent it in all its forms.

Art was the luxury of those times, and the Courts of the Medici <note>The ruling family of Florence</note>, the Este <note>original: "Estensi," the rulers of Ferrara</note>, the Sforza <note>The ruling family of Milan</note>, and the Gonzaga <note>original: "Gonzaghi," the rulers of Mantua</note> were schools of refined manners

<summary>Tabarrini defends Leonardo's meticulous scientific approach to painting against modern superficiality and frames Leonardo as the quintessential genius of the Italian Renaissance.</summary>
<keywords>Leonardo da Vinci, Mona Lisa, Renaissance, Italian Art, Medici, Sforza, Este, Gonzaga, Artistic Theory</keywords>

--- Page 19 ---
<meta>This page continues Marco Tabarrini’s preface, transitioning from the description of the Renaissance as a "portentous fertility of men of genius" to a specific analysis of the social and political atmosphere of the Italian courts and the eventual decline of the era's influence.</meta>

<page-num>XVII</page-num>
<header>PREFACE</header>

and a brilliant gathering of artists and poets. The fantasies of Pulci and Ariosto <note>Luigi Pulci (1432–1484) and Ludovico Ariosto (1474–1533) were famous epic poets whose works reflected the courtly culture of the Renaissance.</note> reflected the carefree life of those Courts, which had nothing of the feudal about them, unlike the Courts of France and Germany <note>original: "Alemagna"</note>; but, having arisen in the cities from the more or less consented-to supremacy of powerful citizens, they had preserved a civil <note>The author uses "civile" to imply both "civic" and "refined," contrasting it with the martial nature of Northern European feudalism.</note> character and were open to all men of talent without privileges of caste, without the dominance of the sword. Even Christianity seemed to have relaxed its austerity and its terrors, and the Court of the Popes was entirely filled with the spirit of the age. And this spirit was so civil and so innovative that it does not seem reckless to think that perhaps, if it were not for the theological reform of Martin Luther, many claims of liberty in Italy could have been achieved solely through the effect of universally diffused culture, and of the power of talent universally recognized.

But why did the Renaissance, with such a splendor of efforts, beyond the miracles of art, produce nothing great in political institutions? Why did it consume itself without leaving behind anything but poems, paintings, and statues? Why did Italy emerge from it more miserable, more enslaved, and more corrupt?

Among the many reasons that could be brought forward for this most capital fact in our history, we stop at this one alone which encompasses many others. The Renaissance lacked a high moral idea that would make the work of so many geniuses aim at a worthy goal; it lacked the concept of a great homeland <note>The author refers to the lack of a unified Italian state or national identity at the time.</note> that would make operative in the field of facts the forces that were lost in vain speculations.

Those generations educated in elegance did not have the feeling of the strength that produces action, nor a high goal to reach that would ennoble the products of genius. Michelangelo was a solitary giant in the midst of ruins, pensive on the destinies of the world; Torquato Tasso, perhaps the only true poet of the Renaissance, sang in earnest

<summary>Tabarrini argues that the Italian Renaissance failed to produce lasting political institutions or liberty because it lacked a unified moral purpose and national identity, despite its artistic brilliance.</summary>
<keywords>Renaissance courts, Pulci, Ariosto, Martin Luther, political decline, Italian identity, Michelangelo, Torquato Tasso</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Marco Tabarrini’s preface, moving from the political failings of the Renaissance to a specific focus on Leonardo da Vinci as a bridge to the modern scientific era, while lamenting the personal instability of even the greatest geniuses of that age.</meta>

<page-num>XVIII</page-num>
<header>M. TABARRINI</header>

the prowess of chivalry—already reduced to a fairy tale by Ariosto—and the enthusiasms of faith in the midst of a people who no longer thought of the Sepulcher of Christ <note>Ariosto’s *Orlando Furioso* treated chivalry with irony, while the "enthusiasms of faith" refers to the religious themes of Torquato Tasso, whose *Jerusalem Delivered* reflected a late Renaissance attempt to revive crusading ideals.</note>. All others appear as mere decorators of that great banquet, in which neither was paganism truly reborn, nor was Christianity purified. Thus, in politics, cunning was held to be the "science of State," and Italy, facing the powerful monarchies of Europe that made her the field for their ambitions, responded not with united arms, but with the subterfuge of leagues and treaties concluded today and renounced tomorrow; but all these tricks and clever maneuvers were not enough, and she fell prey to the victor.

Leonardo da Vinci is perhaps the only great man who links the Renaissance to modern times. His universal genius, which joined within itself the most exquisite aspects of art and the most practical applications of science, foresaw the great scientific movement that would awaken in the near future. He invoked *experience as the interpreter of the secrets of nature, which he held as the teacher of superior intellects.* Through these intuitions, which abound in his treatises and notes—where he placed, almost without knowing it, the seeds of <term>optics</term> <note>The study of light and vision.</note>, <term>hydraulics</term> <note>The study of the movement of liquids.</note>, and mechanics—Leonardo can be said to reach out and shake hands with Galileo.

But how he too must have felt the misery of his time! Ignored by the Medici in Florence, unwelcome to Leo X in Rome, he had to settle for Ludovico "the Moor" in Milan, who did not even possess the prowess and courage that were the virtues of his lineage. Once the Moor fell, he found no better course than to place himself in the service of Cesare Borgia <note>A ruthless Italian nobleman and condottiero, famous for the political schemes described by Machiavelli in *The Prince*.</note>, another scoundrel of the same stripe as the Sforzas; and he followed him, as a military engineer, in the campaign of the Romagna. Failing even there, he was reduced to hiring himself out to Francis I, who aspired to bring Italian culture to France, and he died in a foreign land, at Cloux near Amboise, in 1519.

<summary>Tabarrini characterizes the late Renaissance as a period of political decay and "cunning" that failed Italy, while highlighting Leonardo da Vinci as a singular figure whose scientific intuition bridged the gap between the Renaissance and the age of Galileo.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marco Tabarrini’s preface, expanding on the moral and political critiques of the Renaissance. It contrasts the "pagan" focus of the Italian Renaissance with the "Christian" foundation of the Reformation, ultimately positioning Leonardo da Vinci as a figure who transcended the moral failings of his era through his prophetic genius.</meta>

<page-num>XIX</page-num>
<header>PREFACE XIX</header>

From these considerations on the Renaissance, of which Leonardo was one of the most original figures, it will not be useless to draw some consequences. And the most evident is this: that men of talent are not enough to save nations when the guiding moral principle of human actions is lost. "**We have lost the true names of things** <note>original Latin: "Vera rerum nomina amisimus." A famous lament from Cato the Younger, as recorded by the historian Sallust, regarding the breakdown of Roman civic morality.</note>," cried Cato in the Roman Senate when Catiline was finding apologists; and the same could be said of 16th-century Italy, when a savior was hoped for in Cesare Borgia <note>The Machiavellian prince and son of Pope Alexander VI, known for his ruthless attempts to carve out a state in central Italy.</note>. When the notions of good and evil are corrupted, the anarchy of minds paves the way for the anarchy of facts. And to this anarchy of facts, the sword of Charles V <note>The Holy Roman Emperor whose troops famously sacked Rome in 1527, marking the end of the High Renaissance's political independence.</note> put an end. — One can also deduce this: that a civilization does not regain its strength except by returning to the principle that generated it. The Renaissance sought to evoke, at least in its forms, pagan civilization while forgetting Christianity; for this reason, its work proved fruitless in producing great effects, nor was it defended against the uncivilized force that oppressed it. The nations that embraced the Reformation emerged from the struggle more tempered and stronger than we Latins, because the civilization they established was fundamentally Christian. It is useless to quibble over facts; our civilization, founded on Christianity, can do nothing but flourish or perish with it.

Returning now to the principle from which our words began, we observe that Leonardo da Vinci, within the Renaissance, represents the divination of the future; in this sense, he is perhaps the greatest genius of that marvelous century. For even if he, too, had to bend to the moral miseries of the time—painting portraits of the women loved by Sforza <note>Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan and Leonardo's long-time patron.</note> and assisting the enterprises of "Il Valentino" <note>Cesare Borgia, who employed Leonardo as a military engineer.</note>—he preserved in his soul a virtue that raised him above the greater part of his contemporaries.

If the renaissance <note>The original uses the word "risorgimento," which here refers generally to the cultural "rebirth" of the era rather than the 19th-century political movement.</note>, at least in its outward form, presents itself to us as a joyous carnival of princes, politicians, poets, and artists,

<summary>Tabarrini argues that the Italian Renaissance failed politically because it abandoned Christian morality for pagan forms, whereas Leonardo da Vinci’s genius allowed him to transcend these failings and foresee the future.</summary>
<keywords>Leonardo da Vinci, moral philosophy, Cesare Borgia, Charles V, Reformation, Christian civilization, Ludovico Sforza, Italian Renaissance</keywords>

# LEONARDO DA VINCI

## FLORENTINE PAINTER AND SCULPTOR. <gloss>1</gloss>

THE GREATEST gifts are seen to rain down from celestial influences upon human bodies, many times naturally, and sometimes even supernaturally; an abundance of beauty, grace, and virtue may gather in a single body in such a manner that wherever such a person turns, every action is so divine that, leaving all other men behind, he manifests himself as something—as he truly is—bestowed by God and not acquired by human art. Men saw this in Leonardo da Vinci, in whom, besides a physical beauty that could never be sufficiently praised, there was a grace more than infinite in every one of his actions; and his virtue was of such a kind that wherever his mind turned toward difficult things, he resolved them with ease. His strength was great, and joined with dexterity; his spirit and courage were always royal and magnanimous; and the fame of his name spread so far that he was not only held in high esteem during his own time, but his reputation grew even more among posterity after his death. <gloss>2</gloss>

Vinci; <margin>1</margin> and in erudition and the principles of letters he would have made great profit, had he not been so varied and unstable. For he set himself to learn many things; and once begun, he then abandoned them. Behold, in arithmetic <note>original: "abbaco," referring to the study of calculation and commercial mathematics</note>, in the few months that he attended to it, he made such progress that by continually raising doubts and difficulties for the master who was teaching him, he very often confounded him. He gave some effort to music; but soon he resolved to learn to play the lyre, as one who by nature possessed a most elevated spirit and one full of grace, wherefore he sang divinely upon it extemporaneously. <margin>2</margin> Nonetheless, although he attended to such varied things, he never left off drawing and working in relief, as things that appealed to his fancy more than any other. Seeing this, Ser Piero, and considering the elevation of that intellect, took some of his drawings one day and carried them to Andrea del Verrocchio, who was a great friend of his, and strictly entreated him to say whether Leonardo, by attending to drawing, would make any profit. Andrea was amazed to see the grand beginnings of Leonardo, and encouraged Ser Piero to make him attend to it; wherefore he arranged with Leonardo that he should go to the workshop <note>original: "bottega"</note> of Andrea: which Leonardo did most willingly. And he not only practiced one profession, but all those in which drawing was involved; and having an intellect so divine and marvelous that, being an excellent geometer, he not only worked in sculpture, making in his youth some heads of women in clay who are laughing, which are cast in finished form by the art—

<margin>1</margin> He was the natural son of Ser Piero d’Antonio di Ser Piero di Ser Guido da Vinci, born to him of a certain Caterina, woman of Cattabriga or Accattabriga, of Piero di Luca of the same place. <margin>2</margin> Of his poetry, nothing remains to us but the following sonnet, preserved for us by Lomazzo and reprinted several times:

> He who cannot do what he wills, let him will what he can;
> For to will what cannot be done is folly.
> Therefore the man is to be held wise,
> Who withdraws his will from what he cannot do.
> Because all our delight and sorrow
> Lies in knowing, willing, and being able to say yes and no.
> Therefore he alone can do, who with duty
> Draws reason out from its threshold.
> Nor is it always to be willed what a man is able to do;
> Often that which turns bitter seems sweet.
> I already wept for what I wanted, after I had it.
> Therefore you, reader of these notes,
> If you wish to be good to yourself and dear to others,
> Will always to be able to do what you ought.

† Regarding this sonnet, see in the Roman journal *Il Buonarroti*, issues of June and August 1875, an article by GUSTAVO UZIELLI entitled *Upon a sonnet attributed to Leonardo da Vinci*. It is not by Leonardo, but by Antonio di Matteo di Meglio, herald of the Signoria of Florence from 1418 to 1446, in which year he died, to whom it is assigned by the majority of the 15th-century codices in the Florentine libraries.

And every day he made models and drawings to be able to level mountains with ease and pierce them to pass from one plain to another, and by means of levers and cranes and screws he showed how to lift and pull great weights: and ways to empty harbors, and pumps <note>original: "trombe," literally trumpets or siphons</note> to draw water from low places, for that brain never stopped fantasizing <note>original: "ghiribizzare," to dream up whimsical or complex inventions</note>; of which thoughts and labors many drawings are seen scattered through our art, and I have seen many of them. <margin>5</margin> Besides which he wasted time even drawing knots of cords made in order, so that from one end the rest followed all the way to the other, until they filled a circle; of which there is seen a very difficult and beautiful one in print, and in the middle are these words: *Leonardo Vinci Academy* <note>original: "Leonardus Vinci Accademia"</note>. <margin>6</margin> And among these models and drawings there was one, with which many times to many ingenious citizens who then governed Florence he showed his desire to

to raise the temple of San Giovanni in Florence <note>The Baptistery of Florence</note>, and to place the steps beneath it without ruining it; and he persuaded people with such strong reasons that it seemed possible, although everyone, after he had departed, recognized for themselves the impossibility of such an enterprise.

He was so pleasant in conversation that he drew the souls of people to him; and having, one might say, nothing, and working little, he constantly kept servants and horses, in which he took great delight, and particularly in all other animals, which he managed with the greatest love and patience: and he showed this, for often passing by places where birds were sold, taking them out of the cage with his own hand and having paid the seller the price that was asked, he let them fly into the air, restoring to them their lost liberty. Wherefore nature wished to favor him so much, that wherever he turned his thought, brain, and soul, he showed such divinity in his works that in giving the perfection of readiness, vivacity, goodness, beauty, and grace, no one else was ever his equal. It is well seen that Leonardo, through his understanding of art, began many things and never finished any of them, it seeming to him that the hand could not add to the perfection of art in the things he imagined: since he formed in his idea some subtle and so marvelous difficulties that with his hands, even though they were most excellent, they would never have been expressed. And so many were his caprices, that philosophizing about natural things he attended to understanding the properties of herbs, continuing and observing the movement of the heavens, the course of the moon, and the paths of the sun.¹

He settled himself therefore, as has been said, by means of Ser Piero <note>Leonardo's father</note>, in his childhood to the art with Andrea del Verrocchio, who, while making a panel where Saint John was baptizing Christ, Leonardo worked on an angel who was holding some garments; and although he was a youth, he executed it in such a manner that Leonardo's angel stood much better than the figures of Andrea; which was the reason that Andrea never again wished to touch colors, being indignant that a child knew more than he.² There was commissioned to him for a—

This conjecture of ours could become certainty if it were given to us to assign the precise time of that painting. But Vasari's account calls us to other considerations; that is, in the first place whether it is to be believed so easily that Verrocchio made such great marvels seeing the angel painted by Leonardo in the panel of the *Baptism*, when he should not have had experience of what Da Vinci was worth in his art then for the first time; and in the second place whether it is likely that Verrocchio, seeing himself overcome by the disciple, took such indignation as to no longer want to touch brushes; being very certain that he still kept his painter's shop open even in 1476, that is, some years after that in which it can be conjectured that the said panel was painted.

<meta>This page continues Vasari's narrative of Leonardo's early career, specifically detailing his meticulous draftsmanship and his inventive, sometimes macabre, imagination during his youth in Florence.</meta>

door-curtain, which was to be made in Flanders of gold and woven silk to be sent to the King of Portugal, a cartoon <note>A full-scale preparatory drawing for a tapestry or painting</note> of Adam and Eve when they sin in the Earthly Paradise. In this, Leonardo used a brush to create in chiaroscuro <note>original: "chiaro e scuro"; the use of light and shadow to create three-dimensional volume</note> highlighted with white lead a meadow of infinite grasses with some animals; in truth, it can be said that in diligence and naturalism, no divine intellect in the world could produce anything so similar. Here is a fig tree, where besides the foreshortening of the leaves and the views of the branches, it is executed with so much love that the mind is bewildered just thinking how a man could have such patience. There is also a palm tree which has the roundness of the palm-dates worked with such great and marvelous art, that nothing but the patience and intellect of Leonardo could have done it. This work was not carried out any further, so the cartoon is today in Florence in the fortunate house of the magnificent Ottaviano de' Medici, given to him not long ago by Leonardo's uncle. <margin>I</margin>

It is said that Ser Piero da Vinci, being at his villa, was asked as a favor by one of his peasants—who had with his own hand made a buckler <note>original: "rotella"; a small round shield</note> from a fig tree he had cut down on the farm—to have it painted for him in Florence. Ser Piero did this most gladly, as the countryman was very skilled at catching birds and fishing, and Ser Piero made great use of him in these pursuits. Therefore, having had it brought to Florence, without saying anything to Leonardo about whose it was, he asked him to paint something upon it. Leonardo, taking this buckler into his hands one day and seeing it warped, poorly made, and clumsy, straightened it with fire; and giving it to a turner, he had it transformed from the rough and clumsy thing it was into something delicate and even. Then, having primed it with plaster <note>original: "ingessatala"; prepared with gesso</note> and prepared it in his own way, he began to think what might be painted on it that would terrify anyone who came across it, representing the same effect as the head of Medusa. For this purpose, Leonardo carried to a room of his, where no one entered but himself, lizards, green lizards, crickets, snakes, butterflies, locusts, bats, and other strange species of similar animals. From the multitude of these, variously adapted together, he derived a very horrible and terrifying monster, which poisoned with its breath and turned the air to fire. He depicted it emerging from a dark and broken rock, belching poison from its open throat, fire from its eyes, and smoke from its nostrils so strangely that it seemed a truly monstrous and horrible thing. He labored so long in doing it that the stench of the dead animals in that room was most cruel, but it was not noticed by Leonardo because of the great love he bore for art. When this work was finished—which was no longer sought after by either the peasant or his father—Leonardo told him that he might send for the buckler at his convenience, for as far as he was concerned, it was finished. Ser Piero having gone one morning to the room for the buckler, and having knocked at the door, Leonardo opened it, telling him to wait a little; and returning into the room, he arranged the buckler in the light on the easel, and adjusted the window so that it made a dimmed light; then he let him come in to see it. Ser Piero, at the first glance, not thinking of the thing, was suddenly shaken, not believing that it was a buckler,

This seemed more than miraculous to Ser Piero, and he greatly praised the whimsical invention of Leonardo; then, having quietly bought from a peddler another shield painted with a heart pierced by an arrow, he gave it to the peasant, who remained indebted to him for as long as he lived. Afterward, Ser Piero sold Leonardo’s shield secretly in Florence to certain merchants for one hundred ducats, and in a short time it came into the hands of the Duke of Milan, sold to him for three hundred ducats by the said merchants. <margin>I</margin> <note>This famous shield, painted with a terrifying Medusa-like monster, is now lost.</note>

Leonardo then painted a most excellent Our Lady <note>The Virgin Mary</note> in a painting that was owned by Pope Clement VII; and among other things done therein, he counterfeited a carafe full of water with some flowers inside, where, beyond the marvel of their lifelike quality, he had imitated the dew-drops on top, so that it appeared more real than reality itself.² To Antonio Segni, his very dear friend, he made on a sheet of paper a Neptune, executed in drawing with such diligence that it seemed entirely alive. One could see the turbulent sea and his chariot pulled by sea-horses with phantoms, orcas, and the winds <note>original: "noti"; the South Winds</note>, and some most beautiful heads of sea gods; which drawing was given by his son Fabio to Master Giovanni Gaddi, with this epigram:

> ->Virgil painted Neptune, Homer painted him;<-
> ->While he guided his horses through the depths of the sounding sea.<-
> ->Both poets beheld him with the mind indeed,<-
> ->But Da Vinci with his eyes; and by right he conquers them.³<-
> <note>original Latin: "Pinxit Virgilius Neptunum..." This poem praises Leonardo for seeing with his eyes what poets could only imagine.</note>

The fancy took him to paint in an oil picture the head of a Medusa, with a head-dress of a cluster of serpents, the strangest and most extravagant invention that could ever be imagined; but as a work that required time, and as happens with almost all his things, it remained unfinished. This is among the excellent things in the palace of Duke Cosimo,⁴ together with a head of an angel, who raises one arm in the air, which is foreshortened <note>original: "scorta"; a technique to show an object receding in space</note> from the shoulder to the elbow as it comes forward, and the other hand goes to the breast.⁵ It is a marvelous thing that this genius, having the desire to give the highest relief to the things he made, went so far with dark shadows to find the deepest backgrounds, seeking blacks that would shade and be darker than other blacks, to make the highlights, by means of them, more lucid; and

ultimately this method turned out so dark that, with no light remaining, the works had more the appearance of things made to mimic a night scene than the refinement of daylight; but all this was in pursuit of giving greater relief <note>The 3D effect of figures standing out from the background</note>, and finding the end and perfection of art. It pleased him so much when he saw certain bizarre heads, whether with natural beards or hair, that he would follow someone who had caught his fancy for an entire day; and he would fix them so firmly in his mind that, upon arriving home, he would draw them as if he had them present before him. Of this sort one sees many heads, both of women and men, and I myself have several drawn by his hand with a pen in our *Book of Drawings* so often cited; $^1$ such as that of Amerigo Vespucci, which is a most beautiful head of an old man drawn in charcoal, and likewise that of Scaramuccia, captain of the Gypsies, which later belonged to $^2$ Master Donato Valdambrini of Arezzo, canon of San Lorenzo, left to him by Giambullari. $^3$ He began a panel of the *Adoration of the Magi*, which contains many beautiful things, especially heads; this was in the house of Amerigo Benci, opposite the Loggia of the Peruzzi, which also remained unfinished like his other works. $^4$

Whereupon he, most diligently observing all their gestures and those ridiculous things they did, impressed them upon his mind; and then, after they had departed, he retired to his room, and there perfectly drew them, in such a way that they moved the viewers to laughter no less than Leonardo's stories had moved them at the feast."

Leonardo was brought to the Duke <note>Ludovico Sforza, known as "Il Moro"</note>, who took great delight in the sound of the lyre, so that he might play; $^1$ and Leonardo brought that instrument which he had manufactured with his own hand, largely of silver, in the shape of a horse's skull—a bizarre and novel thing—so that the harmony might be produced with greater volume and a more sonorous tone; $^2$ whereby he surpassed all the musicians who had gathered there to play. Besides this, he was the best improviser of rhymes of his time. Hearing Leonardo’s discourse to be so admirable, the Duke became so enamored of his virtues that it was an incredible thing. And having requested it of him, he had him paint an altar panel of a Nativity, which was sent by the Duke to the Emperor. $^3$ He also created in Milan, for the friars of Saint Dominic at Santa Maria delle Grazie, a *Last Supper* <note>original: "Cenacolo"</note>, a most beautiful and marvelous thing; $^4$ and to the heads of the apostles he gave such majesty and beauty, that he left the head of Christ unfinished, not thinking he could give it that celestial divinity which is required for the image of Christ. $^5$ Which—

<meta>This page continues Vasari's account of Leonardo da Vinci's work on "The Last Supper" in Milan, specifically detailing his creative process, his conflict with the Prior of Santa Maria delle Grazie, and the later history of his preparatory sketches.</meta>

<page-num>xi</page-num>
<header>LIFE OF LEONARDO DA VINCI</header>

The work, remaining thus as finished, has been held by the Milanese in the greatest veneration continually, and by foreigners as well; seeing that Leonardo imagined, and succeeded in expressing, that suspicion which had entered the apostles, of wanting to know who was betraying their master. Because of this, one sees in the faces of all of them love, fear, and indignation, or rather the grief of not being able to understand the mind of Christ: a thing which brings no less wonder than the recognition, by contrast, of the obstinacy, hatred, and treachery in Judas; besides which, every smallest part of the work shows an incredible diligence; since even in the tablecloth, the weave of the fabric is imitated in a manner that the actual linen <note>original: "rensa," a fine linen cloth from Reims</note> does not show the truth any better.

It is said that the Prior of that place urged Leonardo very importunately to finish the work, it appearing strange to him to see Leonardo sometimes stay for half a day at a time lost in contemplation; and he would have liked him—as he did with those who hoed in the garden—never to have stopped his brush; and this not being enough, he complained to the Duke, and so inflamed him that he was forced to send for Leonardo and tactfully urge him to the work; showing in a kind way that he did it all because of the importunity of the Prior. Leonardo, knowing the intellect of that prince to be sharp and discerning, wished (which he had never done with that Prior) to discuss with the Duke at length regarding this: he spoke much to him of art, and made him understand that elevated geniuses sometimes work the most when they labor the least; searching with the mind for inventions, and forming those perfect ideas which the hands then express and portray from those already conceived in the intellect. And he added that he still lacked two heads to do: that of Christ, for which he did not wish to search on earth and could not think so much that in his imagination he felt able to conceive that beauty and celestial grace which must have belonged to the incarnate divinity. He then lacked that of Judas, which also caused him thought, not believing he could imagine a form to express the face of him who, after receiving so many benefits, had a soul so fierce that he could resolve to betray his lord and the creator of the world; yet, that he would search for this second one, but that in the end, finding nothing better, he would not lack that of that Prior who was so

---

of those perfections which he conceived in his mind, but which it was not given to the hand to reach. — * And Leonardo, says Lomazzo <note>Giovanni Paolo Lomazzo, a 16th-century painter and writer on art</note>, could not penetrate so far with his intellect as to achieve this *deity* in the Christ of the *Last Supper* <note>original: "Cenacolo"</note>. It is false that the drawings of the thirteen heads of the apostles were once in the Ambrosiana <note>The Biblioteca Ambrosiana in Milan</note>. Pino says that from Count Arconati they passed to Marquis Gasnedi. Then the Sagredo family of Venice had them, from whom the English consul Udny bought them. It seems that he bequeathed them to two English painters, whereby they were divided into two parts: one of ten, the other of three, which went into the hands of an English lady. Sir Thomas Lawrence bought the others; and at his death they were acquired by the art dealer Woodburn. Finally, they passed into the collection of the King of Holland at The Hague; and in the sale of that gallery which was made by public auction in August 1850, they were released for 17,200 francs. These cartoons <note>Full-scale preparatory drawings</note> are made in pastel; which agrees with what Lomazzo writes in chapter V of book III of his *Treatise on Painting*, where he says: "..... [pastel coloring] was much used by Leonardo Vinci, who made the heads of Christ and the apostles in this manner, excellent and miraculous, on paper." The apostles are: 1st Saint Andrew, 2nd Saint Matthew, 3rd Saint James, 4th Saint Philip and Saint Jude Thaddeus, 5th Saint Peter and Judas, 6th Saint John the Evangelist, 7th Saint Bartholomew and Saint Thomas, 8th Judas Iscariot. The original drawing of the entire painting is seen in the collection of the museum in Paris <note>The Louvre</note>. The first and light sketches are possessed by the Academy of Venice.

Bottari relates that in 1726 it was cleaned by one Michelangelo Bellotti; but he does not say what means he used to revive the colors; wherefore it is to be feared that, together with the other known causes of destruction, such as humidity, military license, etc., these also contributed to reducing it to its deplorable present state.</gloss> In the same refectory <note>The dining hall of a monastery.</note>, while he was working on the *Last Supper*, on the end wall, where there is a...

---

<gloss>
\* Here too we use, with liberty, the notes placed in the German edition of Vasari, willingly taking from them the following beautiful considerations on Vinci's *Last Supper*. No other painting can better than this provide a standard to measure the height to which art had risen in those times, and to establish a comparison with the preceding periods of painting. If one compares Leonardo's creation with the *Last Supper* executed by Giotto, or by one of his disciples, in the refectory of Santa Croce in Florence, or with that of Domenico del Ghirlandaio in the small refectory of San Marco (and, we shall add, with the other by the same painter in the refectory of Ognissanti), one sees clearly how the painting of mere symbolic representations progressed to the most expressive and characteristic ones, and from defective to the most perfect beauty. In Giotto, the apostles appear in their dignity as preachers of the divine word; they sit next to one another almost without any passionate expression, and do not seem moved by the words of the Redeemer, except as much as is granted to them by the consciousness of their own mission; they are typical characters arranged symmetrically side by side. In Ghirlandaio, the apostles appear now as most noble men of profound affection, whose dignity is not placed in the feeling of consciousness, but in their very nature: nevertheless, although Ghirlandaio's inventions have some traits of expression in common with Leonardo's, those figures still seem separate; they lack the beautiful unity and the delicate communication of affections, and the graceful grouping and movement; the narrow and rectilinear symmetry of Giotto still shines through. Leonardo alone knew how to reach the most perfect and living beauty both in expressing affections and in the movements of bodies; he knew how to manifest all the feelings of the human heart; he knew how to draw the most charming groups and the most charming forms; and while his predecessors arranged figures with symmetry, he ordered the groups with eurythmy <note>Harmonious proportion or rhythm.</note>, that is to say, with the freest movement joined to the most regular order. Here the servility of the type or the portrait no longer appears, but instead an ideal reality is created, as true and living as it is noble and most spiritual. Here painting has reached the pinnacle of perfection; and it is to be regretted that the versatility of subsequent efforts in art prevented Leonardo's figures of the apostles from being regarded as typical.
</gloss>

# LIFE OF LEONARDO DA VINCI
<page-num>xiii</page-num>

In the old manner,<sup>1</sup> <note>The "old manner" refers to the traditional fresco style of the late 15th century, contrasting with Leonardo's experimental techniques.</note> he portrayed the said Ludovico with Maximilian, his firstborn son, and on the other side the Duchess Beatrice with Francesco, his other son, who both later became Dukes of Milan; these are portrayed divinely.<sup>2</sup>

While he was attending to this work, he proposed to the Duke to make a bronze horse of marvelous size,<sup>3</sup> to place there the image of the Duke in memory;<sup>4</sup> and he began it so large and it turned out so great, that it could never be completed.<sup>5</sup> <note>The Italian "condurre" here means to bring to completion or finish.</note> There are those who have held the opinion (as human judgments are varied, and often malicious through envy), that Leonardo, as with his other things, began it so that it would not be finished; because being of such great size, an incredible difficulty was seen in wanting to cast it in one piece; and one could also believe that many have made this judgment based on the result, since many of his works have remained imperfect. But, in truth, it can be believed that his most grand and excellent mind, by being too purposeful, was hindered, and that the desire to always seek excellence upon excellence and perfection upon perfection was the cause; so that the work was delayed by the desire, as our Petrarch said.<sup>6</sup> And in truth, those who see the model—

which Leonardo made of clay, large as it was, judge that they have never seen anything more beautiful or more magnificent; it lasted until the French came to Milan with Louis, King of France, when they broke it all to pieces. Also lost is a small model in wax, which was considered perfect, together with a book on the anatomy of horses made by him for his own study. He then attended, but with greater care, to the anatomy of men, helped by and mutually helping in this Master Marcantonio della Torre, an excellent philosopher <note>In this period, "philosopher" often referred to a man of science or a professor of medicine.</note>, who was then lecturing in Pavia and writing on this subject: and he was among the first (as I hear tell) who began to illustrate the matters of medicine with the doctrine of Galen <note>Galen was a 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medical science for over a thousand years.</note>, and to give true light to anatomy, which until that time had been involved in much and very great darkness of ignorance; $^1$ and in this he made marvelous use of the genius, labor, and hand of Leonardo, who made a book of it drawn in red chalk and hatched with a pen, $^2$ which he flayed and portrayed with his own hand with the greatest diligence; wherein he made all the bone structures, and to those he then joined in order all the nerves and covered them with muscles; the first attached to the bone, the second that hold the stability, and the third that move; and in those, part by part, he wrote notes in awkward characters, which are made with the left hand in reverse; and he who has no practice in reading them does not understand them, because they cannot be read except with a mirror. Of these papers on the anatomy of men, a great part is in the hands of Master Francesco da Melzo, a Milanese gentleman, who in the time of Leonardo was a very beautiful boy $^3$ and much loved by him, just as today he is a beautiful and noble old man,

beauty, having beautiful curly and ringed hair, in which Leonardo took great delight; and he taught him many things concerning art; and certain works, which in Milan are said to be by Salai <note>Gian Giacomo Caprotti, Leonardo’s pupil and companion</note>, were retouched by Leonardo.

He returned to Florence,¹ where he found that the Servite friars had commissioned Filippino <note>Filippino Lippi</note> with the work for the altarpiece of the high altar of the Nunziata: because of which it was said by Leonardo that he would have willingly done such a thing. Whereupon Filippino, having heard this, being the noble person that he was, withdrew himself from it: and the friars, so that Leonardo might paint it, took him into their house, providing expenses for him and all his household: and thus he kept them waiting a long time, and never began anything. Finally he made a cartoon <note>A full-scale preparatory drawing for a painting</note> containing a Madonna and a Saint Anne with a Christ child, which not only made all the artists marvel, but when it was finished, for two days men and women, young and old, continued to go to the room to see it, as one goes to solemn festivals; to see the wonders of Leonardo, which made all those people amazed; because one saw in the face of that Madonna all that is simple and beautiful which can, with simplicity and beauty, give grace to a mother of Christ, wishing to show that modesty and that humility which is in a virgin, most content with gladness at seeing the beauty of her son whom she tenderly supported in her lap, and while she with a most honest gaze downward perceived a young Saint John, who was playing with a little lamb, not without a smile from a Saint Anne, who filled with joy saw her earthly progeny become celestial: considerations truly from the intellect and genius of Leonardo. This cartoon, as will be said below, later went to France.² He portrayed Ginevra d’Amerigo Benci, a most beautiful thing:³ and he abandoned the work for the friars, who

By then pointing out its provenance from the Niccolini house, from where the *nun* emerged, and where in 1472 Ginevra entered as a bride, and by noting the *purity* and *mastery* of the painting, Rosini strives to convince readers that he is the fortunate possessor of the questioned portrait.

<page-num>xvii</page-num>

# LIFE OF LEONARDO DA VINCI

They returned the commission to Filippino <note>Filippino Lippi</note>, who, also being overtaken by death, was unable to finish it. <gloss>1</gloss> Leonardo undertook to paint the portrait of Mona Lisa, his wife, for Francesco del Giocondo; <gloss>2</gloss> and after toiling over it for four years, he left it unfinished; which work is today with King Francis of France at Fontainebleau. In this head, whoever wished to see how far art could imitate nature could easily understand it, because therein were reproduced all the minutiae that can be painted with subtlety. For the eyes had those glimmers and watery moisture that are continually seen in life, and around them were all those reddish tones and the hairs, which cannot be rendered without the greatest subtlety. The eyelashes, through the manner in which the hairs spring from the flesh, here thicker and there thinner, and curving according to the pores of the skin, could not be more natural. The nose, with all those beautiful reddish and tender openings, appeared to be alive. The mouth, with its opening, and its ends joined by the red of the lips to the flesh-tints of the face, seemed not colors, but truly flesh. In the pit of the throat, whoever looked most intently saw the beating of the pulse; and in truth, it can be said that this was painted in a manner to make every brave craftsman tremble and fear, whoever he may be. He also employed this artifice: that since Madonna Lisa was very beautiful, he had someone play music or sing while he was painting her, and continually kept jesters to make her stay merry, in order to remove that melancholy that painting often gives to the portraits being made; and in this work of Leonardo’s, there was a smile <note>original: "ghigno"</note> so pleasant that it was a thing more divine than human to behold, and it was held a marvelous thing, for it was no different than life itself. <gloss>3</gloss>

Because of the excellence of the works of this most divine craftsman, his fame had grown so much that all persons who delighted in art—indeed, the entire city—desired that he should leave them some memorial; and there was talk everywhere of having him do some notable and great work, whereby the public might be adorned and honored by such genius, grace, and judgment as was recognized in Leonardo’s things. And among the Gonfaloniers <note>The high-ranking magistrates of the Florentine Republic</note> and the great citizens, it was discussed that, since the Great Hall of the Council had been newly built—the architecture of which was arranged with his judgment and advice, and that of Giuliano da Sangallo, and Simone Pollaiuoli, called Cronaca, and—

---

<gloss>1</gloss> It was finished by Perugino.

<gloss>2 *</gloss> Francesco di Bartolommeo di Zanobi del Giocondo was born in 1460. He was one of the Twelve Good Men <note>Twelve Buonomini: a civic advisory board</note> in 1499, and one of the Priors in 1512. He was approved in the scrutiny <note>An eligibility check for office</note> of 1524. He died of the plague in 1528. He had three wives, namely Camilla di Mariotto Rucellai, married in 1491; Tommasa di Mariotto Villani, in 1493; and Lisa di Anton Maria di Noldo Gherardini, in 1495; and this is the "Beautiful Gioconda" portrayed by Leonardo.

<gloss>3 *</gloss> Today this portrait is preserved in the Louvre Museum, but greatly faded <note>original: "sfiorato," meaning touched or grazed, here implying the loss of top layers</note> by a poor restoration. It is a young woman in half-figure, seen from the front, with loose hair, a veil on her head, and with her breast somewhat uncovered. She sits in an armchair, on one of the arms of which she rests her right arm and hand, and places her left hand over it. Behind her is a stone parapet, from which one sees a desolate and mountainous landscape. Francis I paid 4,000 gold scudi for this panel, which is equivalent to 45,000 francs. Many copies of this portrait are known, some excellent: such as in Florence in the Mozzi house; in the Madrid museum; in the Villa Sommariva on Lake Como; at the Torlonia in Rome; in London with Abraham Hume and with Woodburn; and in the Hermitage in Petersburg, having come from Houghton Hall; and finally, there is another copy in the Munich Gallery, of which a lithograph can be seen in Vol. II of the work: *The Munich Gallery Illustrated, 1817-21* (in German).

<page-num>xviii</page-num>
<header>GIORGIO VASARI</header>

by Michelangelo Buonarroti and Baccio d'Agnolo (as will be discussed more distinctly in their respective places); which being finished with great speed, it was ordained by public decree that Leonardo should be given some beautiful work to paint; and so by Piero Soderini, then the Gonfalonier of Justice <note>The highest magistrate in the Florentine Republic.</note>, the said hall was assigned to him. For which reason, wishing to carry it out, Leonardo began a <term>cartoon</term> <note>A full-scale preparatory drawing for a fresco or painting.</note> in the Pope’s Hall, a place in Santa Maria Novella, depicting therein the story of Niccolò Piccinino, captain of Duke Filippo of Milan, in which he drew a group of horses fighting for a banner: a thing that was held to be most excellent and of great mastery, because of the most wonderful considerations he had in depicting that flight; for in it, one recognizes no less the rage, disdain, and revenge in the men than in the horses; among which two, having their front legs intertwined, wage war with their teeth no less than those who ride them do in fighting for the said banner; where a soldier, having hooked his hands upon it, with the strength of his shoulders, while he puts his horse to flight, turned with his body, has grasped the shafts of the standard to wrench it by force from the hands of four others; two of whom defend it with one hand each, and with the other in the air with their swords they attempt to cut the shafts, while an old soldier, with a red cap, shouting, holds one hand on the shaft, and with the other, having raised a <term>scimitar</term> <note>original: "storta" — a curved, short sword.</note>, deals a blow in anger to cut off both the hands of those who, gnashing their teeth with force, attempt with a most fierce attitude to defend their banner. Besides which, on the ground, between the legs of the horses, there are two figures in <term>foreshortening</term> <note>original: "iscorto" — a technique used to create the illusion of an object receding strongly into the distance.</note> who, fighting together, while one on the ground has a soldier over him who, having raised his arm as high as he can, with the greatest force plunges a dagger into his throat to end his life, and the other, with his legs and arms flailing, does what he can to avoid death. Nor can one express the design that Leonardo made in the garments of the soldiers, variously varied by him; likewise the crests and other ornaments, without mentioning the incredible mastery he showed in the forms and lineaments of the horses, which Leonardo, better than any other master, rendered with muscular bravery and graceful beauty. ^1

1 * The <term>cartoon</term> by Da Vinci, made in competition with Buonarroti for the Council Hall, after having served as a study for the greatest artists of that age, was dispersed, and its memory was only preserved by some engravings. The group, as described by Vasari, leaves it in doubt whether Leonardo's <term>cartoon</term> represented the battle fought in 1440 near Anghiari between the Florentines and Niccolò Piccinino, commander of the forces of Filippo Maria Visconti, Duke of Milan, of which Leonardo left the entire composition written in a note (AMORETTI, *Memories cited*, page 95); or rather an episode of it, that is to say, the combat of knights around a banner. It is probable that, as Vasari mentions no other group, and even Benvenuto Cellini makes particular mention of this one alone in his *Life*, Leonardo represented only an episode of that battle. The copies of this group known today are the following: 1st One, unfinished, painted on a panel, is recorded in the inventory of the Florence gallery made in 1635 and subsequent ones as a work by Leonardo himself; but we, having found this panel in the deposits of the Royal Wardrobe in the Palazzo Vecchio, are persuaded that it is not by his hand. 2nd An engraving on a transverse sheet that seems made from this panel, with the inscription: *taken from a painting on a panel by Leonardo da Vinci's own hand, a work produced by Lorenzo Zacchia of Lucca and now printed by the same, 1558* <note>original: "ex tabella propria Leonardi Vincii manu picta opus sumptum a Laurentio Zacchia Lucensi ab eodemque nunc excussum 1558"</note>. 3rd Another <term>engraving</term> <note>original: "intaglio"</note> by Edelinck, which is said to be made after a very free drawing by Rubens; which is the most beautiful, and most responsive to Vasari's description. 4th A weak <term>engraving</term> in plate XXIX of the *Etruria Pittrice*, taken from an old drawing existing in the Rucellai house, which is said to be a copy of the original <term>cartoon</term>; and this corresponds to the unfinished panel we mentioned above. 5th A lithograph...

It is said that while going to the bank for the stipend he used to receive every month from Piero Soderini, the cashier wanted to give him certain packets of copper coins; and he did not want to take them, answering him: "I am not a painter for small change." Being accused of having cheated, Piero Soderini murmured against him: because of this, Leonardo did so much with his friends that he gathered the money and brought it back to be returned; but Piero did not want to accept it.

It is curious to note that to make the <term>cartoon</term> <note>A full-scale preparatory drawing for a mural.</note> there were used one ream and 29 quires of "royal" sheets of paper; to paste it, 88 pounds of flour; and to edge it, a sheet made of three lengths of linen. For the painting itself, 663 pounds of gypsum were consumed, 89 of Greek pitch, 223 of linseed oil, 48 of Alexandrian white lead, 36 of "soda" white, only 11 ounces of walnut oil, and some sheets of gold leaf. But while Leonardo was working on the said painting, it appears that in May of 1506 he was requested to go to Milan by Charles d'Amboise, Lord of Chaumont, governor of 그hat city for Louis XII, King of France. And the Signoria <note>The governing body of the Republic of Florence.</note>, to grant him this, required Leonardo to promise by a contract dated the 30th of that month, notarized by Ser Niccolò Nelli, a Florentine notary, that after three months he would present himself personally in Florence before the Signoria, under penalty, if not observed, of 150 <term>gold florins</term> <note>Large gold coins of Florence; the penalty was "in oro larghi," meaning high-quality, full-weight gold.</note>, with Master Leonardo Bonafè, the <term>hospital director</term> <note>Italian: "spedalingo," the head of the Hospital of Santa Maria Nuova.</note> of Santa Maria Nuova, acting as his guarantor for this sum. Those three months were about to end when Chaumont, still having need of Leonardo to finish a certain work commissioned from him, wrote on August 18 to the Signoria of Florence, begging them that, notwithstanding the promise made, they would extend Leonardo's time of absence at least through the entire month of September, as is more extensively detailed in another letter addressed to the Signoria on the 19th of the same month by the vice-chancellor Jafredo Caroli (and not Kardi, as printed in Gaye). In the closing of this letter, the Signoria uses, with some reason, rather resentful words against Leonardo, but says something contrary to the truth when it asserts that he had not even begun the work, because from the entries in the aforementioned books of the Officials of the Works of the Palace, it appears clearly that Leonardo had already completed the <term>cartoon</term>, and had set his hand since February 1504—that is, for 17 months—to the painting of the hall. From the letter of Piero Soderini on October 9 of the same year to the said Jafredo Caroli, in response to one from Chaumont on August 18, who was then away from Milan, it would seem that Leonardo had not at that time returned to Florence. In it, the words of the perpetual <term>gonfalonier</term> <note>The highest magistrate of the Florentine Republic.</note> regarding Leonardo are even more resentful than those read in the letter reported above. Only when King Louis, both through Francesco Pandolfini, ambassador of the Republic in France, and with his own letter of January 18, 1507, requested the Signoria to be satisfied that Leonardo should not depart from Milan until his arrival in Italy—intending to make use of him for a certain work of his, which we know to have been the painting of a panel—the response of the Signoria on January 22 to the aforementioned Pandolfini and the letter to Leonardo on the same day were in different terms and of great benevolence toward the artist. Thus, in the letter to the former, they charge him to let His Majesty understand that the Signoria could have no greater pleasure than to do something pleasing to him, and that not only Leonardo, but any other of their men, they would wish to serve him in his desires and needs. And in the other to Leonardo, they say it is always most pleasing to them that he serve His Majesty, considering that it would result in his convenience and honor. After this time, no other record is found in the public books regarding either Leonardo or the painting of the hall, except that already cited from March 1, 1513, which records the expense of "wooden framing for the painting Leonardo da Vinci made, so that it would not be spoiled." Nevertheless, it was spoiled, and for several centuries both the painting and the <term>cartoon</term> have been miserably lost: the work of Leonardo meeting the same fate that befell the other by Michelangelo, made at the same time for the same place. <page-num>xxi</page-num>
# THE LIFE OF LEONARDO DA VINCI

He went to Rome with Duke Giuliano de' Medici upon the election of Pope Leo <note>Pope Leo X, born Giovanni de' Medici, elected in 1513</note>, who was very much devoted to philosophical matters, and especially to alchemy. There, forming a paste out of wax, while he walked he would create extremely delicate animals filled with air, which, by blowing into them, he made fly through the sky; but when the wind ceased, they fell to the ground. On a lizard, found by the vine-dresser of the Belvedere, which was most bizarre, he attached wings made from the scales of other lizards flayed for the purpose, using a mixture of quicksilver <note>mercury</note> so that they trembled as it moved when it walked; and having given it eyes, horns, and a beard, he tamed it and kept it in a box, and all the friends to whom he showed it would flee out of fear. He used to often have the intestines of a ram thoroughly cleaned of fat and purged until they became so thin that they could be held in the palm of one's hand; and he had placed in another room a pair of blacksmith's bellows, to which he attached one end of the said intestines, and by inflating them he filled the room, which was very large; so that whoever was there was forced to retreat into a corner, showing how those transparent things filled with wind, which had taken up little space at the start, had come to occupy a great deal, comparing them to virtue. He performed infinite numbers of these follies, and occupied himself with mirrors, and attempted most strange methods in searching for oils for painting, and varnish to preserve the finished works. He made during this time for Master Baldassarri Turini of Pescia, who was the Datary <note>an official of the Roman Curia</note> to Leo, a small picture of Our Lady with the Child in her arms, with infinite diligence and art. But, whether it be the fault of whoever prepared the plaster ground, or perhaps because of his many and capricious mixtures of primers and colors, it is today much ruined. And in another small picture he portrayed a little boy, who is marvelously beautiful and graceful: both of which are today in Pescia in the possession of Master Giulio Turini. <margin>Of these two paintings, one is believed lost, the other is said to be in the gallery of Düsseldorf.</margin> It is said that when a work was commissioned from him by the Pope, he immediately began to distill oils and herbs to make the varnish; for which it was said by Pope Leo: "Alas! This man is not destined to do anything, since he begins to think about the end before the beginning of the work." <margin>Regarding a Holy Family, believed to have been made for Pope Leo, see the Commentary.</margin> There was a very great disdain between Michelangelo Buonarroti and him: because of which Michelangelo left Florence due to the competition, with the excuse of Duke Giuliano, having been called by the Pope for the facade of San Lorenzo. Leonardo, hearing of this, departed and went to France, <margin>Vasari hints here very obscurely at a certain rivalry born between Michelangelo and Leonardo during the final times the latter lived in Florence.</margin> where the King, having

having possessed works of his, was very fond of him, and desired that he should color the cartoon of Saint Anne; but he, according to his custom, kept him a long time with words. Finally, having become old, he remained ill for many months; and seeing himself near death, he turned diligently to inform himself about Catholic matters¹ and about our good and holy Christian religion, and then with much weeping, confessed and contrite,² although he could not stand on his feet, supporting himself in the arms of his friends and servants, he wished devoutly to receive the most holy Sacrament out of his bed. Whereupon there came upon him a paroxysm, the messenger of death; for which reason the King having risen and taken his head to help him and offer him favor, so that the illness might be eased; his spirit, which was most divine, knowing it could have no greater honor, expired in the arms of that King, in the seventy-fifth year of his age.³

the loss of Leonardo grieved beyond measure all those who had known him, for there was never a person who brought such honor to the art of painting. With the radiance of his presence, which was most beautiful, he cheered every sorrowful soul, and with his words, he could turn any hardened intention toward "yes" or "no." With his physical strength, he could restrain any violent fury; with his right hand, he could twist the iron ring of a wall-bell or a horseshoe as if it were lead. With his generosity, he welcomed and fed every friend, whether poor or rich, provided they possessed talent and virtue. He adorned and honored even the most humble and bare room with his every action. For this reason, Florence truly received a magnificent gift in the birth of Leonardo, and suffered a loss more than infinite in his death. In the art of painting, he added a certain darkness to the method of oil coloring, from which modern painters have derived great strength and relief <note>The quality of appearing three-dimensional</note> for their figures.<gloss>1</gloss> In sculpture, he gave proof of his skill in the three bronze figures that stand above the North door <note>original: "tramontana"</note> of the Baptistery of San Giovanni; these were made by Giovanni Francesco Rustici but arranged with Leonardo's counsel. They are the most beautiful examples of casting, design, and perfection that have yet been seen in modern times.<gloss>2</gloss> From Leonardo, we have the anatomy of horses, and that of men which is far more perfect. Therefore, because of his many divine qualities—even though he achieved much more through his words than through his finished deeds—his name and fame shall never be extinguished.<gloss>3</gloss>

† To trace the records and documents of Leonardo's stay and to find his tomb, some research was conducted in 1863, commissioned by the French Government, by Mr. Arsène Houssaye. In his report to the Minister of Fine Arts and in his *History of Leonardo da Vinci* <note>original: "Histoire de Léonard de Vinci"</note>, Paris, 1869, he recounts that after the conspiracy of Amboise in 1560, tradition held that the tombs in the church of Saint-Florentin, where Leonardo was buried, were broken open and the bones of those interred were scattered. When the church was demolished in 1808 by order of Roger Ducos, the tombstones were sold and the lead coffins from the burials were melted down. Other memorials of Leonardo gradually disappeared, and the few that still remain are seen only in the manor of Cloux, today called Clos-Lucé. In the small chapel attached to the manor are paintings attributed to Leonardo; Houssaye believes he sees the head of an angel by Melzi's hand, or at least in the Milanese style, in a painting of the Madonna that has been heavily retouched. According to the evidence that has reached us regarding Leonardo's tomb, it appears it was in the choir of the aforementioned church of Saint-Florentin in Amboise. Following the indications gathered, Houssaye began excavations in June 1863 at the site where the church was said to have stood. From these excavations, beneath a pile of stones belonging to the demolished church, a skeleton was discovered along with various objects. At a certain distance from the skeleton, two pieces of stone were found: on one was carved "LEO" and on the other "INC," and after further searching, a third fragment was found inscribed "EO DUS VINC." These letters constitute the elements to partially form the name *Leonardus Vinci* <note>The Latin form of Leonardo da Vinci</note>. However, we do not know what became of these investigations and discoveries in the end. (See G. Uzielli, *op. cit.*, page 44 and following.)

<gloss>1</gloss> * Leonardo's merit in oil painting has not yet been sufficiently appreciated. From his *Treatise on Painting*, one learns how many minute observations he made on the gradation of shadows and tones, on aerial perspective, and on the fluidity of contours. His paintings were the first to show that *sfumato* <note>A technique of blending colors and tones so subtly that there is no perceptible transition</note>—that soft and rounded quality—which later became a law in oil coloring. His style of coloring served as a school for Correggio, who knew how to express all the enchantment of which this genre of painting is capable. Leonardo used to sketch out his work with dark or gray shadows and finish the flesh tones with glazes <note>thin, transparent layers of paint</note>. One cannot, however, deny that it was precisely because of his method of coloring that his paintings became so dark, especially in the shadows.

That vast and profound genius wanted equal—
