For which reason it was said in his praise by Master Giovan Batista Strozzi thus:

->He alone surpasses<-
->All others, and surpasses Phidias and surpasses Apelles,<-
->And all their victorious host. $^1$<- <note>original: "Vince costui pur solo / Tutti altri, e vince Fidia e vince Apelle, / E tutto il lor vittorioso stuolo." Phidias was the most celebrated sculptor of Ancient Greece, and Apelles was its most famous painter.</note>

<term>Giovanantonio Boltraffio</term> <note>also known as Giovanni Antonio Beltraffio (1467–1516)</note> of Milan was a disciple of Leonardo, $^2$ a very practical and knowledgeable person, who in the year 1500 painted a panel in oil with great diligence in the church of the Misericordia outside Bologna. It depicted Our Lady with the Child in her arms, Saint John the Baptist, and a nude Saint Sebastian, along with the patron who commissioned it, a portrait from life in a kneeling position; $^3$ a truly beautiful work; and upon it, he wrote his name and that he was a disciple of Leonardo. He produced other works both in Milan and elsewhere, but let it suffice to have named this one here, which is the best. $^4$ And likewise <term>Marco Uggioni</term> <note>commonly known as Marco d'Oggiono (c. 1470–1524)</note>, $^5$ who in Santa Maria della Pace made the *Passing of Our Lady* and the *Wedding at Cana in Galilee*. $^6$

---

...truly ruling both over the forces of the spirit, from which the imagination creates new life and informs thought, and over material forces, through which man governs nature at his will. If in the first aspect he is honored as one who reached the greatest perfection in his age, in the second he is regarded as the precursor to the science of our modern times. See part three of the Commentary that follows.

<page-num>XXV</page-num>
<header>LIFE OF LEONARDO DA VINCI</header>

Regarding Leonardo, in addition to Salaì of Milan and Ferrando the Spaniard—who worked with him in the hall of the Palace of the Lords <note>The Palazzo Vecchio in Florence</note>—there are also remembered a certain Zoroastro from Peretola, and Riccio the Florentine from the Gate at the Cross. We have not succeeded in discovering who this latter figure was: perhaps he was Raffaello di Biagio, a painter who assisted Leonardo in the aforementioned hall, or perhaps Lorenzo del Faina, who ground colors for him. We have no doubt that this is the same Lorenzo named by Leonardo along with Salaì, Melzi, and Fanfoia in a memorandum from 1514, whom others have erroneously believed to be the Bergamasque painter Lotto. As for Zoroastro, whose proper name was Tommaso di Giovanni Masini, a gardener from Peretola—though he claimed to be the son of Bernardo Rucellai, brother-in-law of Lorenzo the Magnificent—AMMIRATO speaks of him in volume II, page 242 of his *Opuscules*. He says that he joined Leonardo, who made him a garment covered in oak galls <note>original: "gallozzole"; small growths on trees used for making ink</note>; for a long time afterward, he was nicknamed *Gallozzola*. He was later taken by Leonardo to Milan, where he was called *the Soothsayer*, as he practiced the magical arts. Later he went to Rome and entered the service of Giovanni Rucellai, the author of *The Bees*, then with Viseo, the Portuguese ambassador (who later became a cardinal), and finally with Ridolfi, acquiring the nickname *Zoroastro*. He was a very strange man. He would become enraged with the village folk because they mangled his name Zoroastro into *Chialabastro* or *Alabastro*; he would not have killed a flea for anything in the world; nor would he ever wear wool, so as not to carry anything dead upon his person. When Leonardo was painting in the Council Hall, Zoroastro was his apprentice and color-grinder. Some years later we find him working as a goldsmith and dressing semi-precious stones. Lasca also speaks of Zoroastro in the fourth and sixth novellas of the *Second Supper*, recounting several pranks played by him and his companions Pilucca, Scheggia, and Monaco. He finally died in Rome and was buried in Saint Agatha between Trissino and Giovanni Lascari. Another of his disciples was Atalante, who we know was born in 1466, the illegitimate son of Manetto Migliorotti. Under Leonardo's discipline, he became an excellent lyre player; at about sixteen years of age, he was taken by Leonardo to Milan when he entered the service of Ludovico the Moor. In 1490, he was called to Mantua to play the lead role in the performance of Poliziano’s *Orpheus*. After this time, we lose sight of him until 1507, in which year he was in Rome, intending to bring a lawsuit against the commune of Castelnuovo in Val di Cecina regarding certain boundaries. In 1513, he was an overseer of the building projects for Pope Leo, and remained so for three years. The last record we have of him, in which he is called an architect, dates to 1535.

# COMMENTARY.

## PART ONE.

### CONCERNING THE AUTHENTIC PAINTINGS BY LEONARDO NOT MENTIONED BY VASARI, AND OTHERS ATTRIBUTED TO HIM.

---

It would be a long, difficult, and deceptive task if one wished to record all the paintings that are, or are claimed to be, by Da Vinci. The reader will be well persuaded that it is not possible to compile a complete catalog. However, those who desire one may see the lists in the works of writers who have spoken of Leonardo, of whom there are several; among these, besides those already cited by us in the first note and elsewhere, are Piacenza (*Additions to Baldinucci*), Della Valle (Sienese edition of Vasari), Lanzi, etc. Nevertheless, we shall make mention of some which, if nothing else, carry with them the credit of a now-recognized celebrity.

ROME. Convent of the Hermits of Saint Onophrius. — In the upper cloister is a lunette <note>A half-moon shaped architectural space</note>, inside which is painted in fresco Our Lady seated with the naked Child in her lap, and to the left the figure of the patron <note>Likely St. Onophrius or the donor</note> in a devout posture with his cap in hand. Of this fresco, one can see engravings of the heads traced from the original, and a small engraving of the composition in plate CLXXIV of D'Agincourt (*Painting*); a larger engraving is in the *Ape Italiana*, a Roman fine arts journal. — <margin>† There have been those in modern times who wished to see in this painting the hand of Lorenzo di Credi <note>A fellow pupil of Leonardo in Verrocchio's workshop</note> rather than that of Leonardo.</margin>

— Barberini Gallery. — Vanity and Modesty, half-length figures of natural size, painted on panel. — <margin>† Others attribute them to Luini and others to Salai <note>Leonardo's pupil and companion</note>.</margin>

— Aldobrandini Gallery. — Christ disputing with the Doctors of the Law. A composition of five half-length figures, life-size, on panel. Of this, as well as the other painting, there is a small engraving in plate CLXXV of D'Agincourt.

MILAN. Palazzo Belgioioso. — A small painting on panel with Our Lady, a half-length figure, nursing the Child. Prince Belgioioso bought it for 300 zecchini <note>Gold coins</note> from the church of the Madonna di Campagna near Piacenza; and it is claimed that this is the same Madonna that the Anonymous Morellian <note>The pseudonym of Marcantonio Michiel, a 16th-century art connoisseur</note> (pages 83-84) saw in the house of Michele Contarini.

<margin>† VENICE. In the Civic Museum <note>The Museo Correr</note> is the portrait of Duke Valentino <note>Cesare Borgia, for whom Leonardo worked as a military engineer</note> donated by General Pepe. It is on panel, one-third life size, showing little of the torso; besides many drawings formerly belonging to the painter Bossi, which mostly came from De Pagave; and among these a portrait of Da Vinci.</margin>

PARIS. National Museum of the Louvre. — Saint John the Baptist, a half-length figure with a cross in one hand, while pointing to heaven with the other. He wears a lambskin that leaves the upper part of his body uncovered. — Perhaps this is the same panel cited by Father Dan (*Treasury of the Wonders of Fontainebleau*, 1642), which was part of the collection of Francis I. Louis XIII commissioned...

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

Upon the death of Charles I, it was sold for 140 pounds sterling to the banker Jabach, who later ceded it to Louis XIV. — It was engraved by Boulanger when it belonged to Jabach.

— Panel with Our Lady, the Child Jesus, and Saint Anne. The Virgin, seated on her mother’s lap, leans down to take the child, who is on the ground caressing a lamb. The background is a mountainous landscape. It was engraved by J. N. Laugier. <gloss>I</gloss> The authenticity of this painting has been vigorously contested by notable critics, who, although they admired its beauty, nevertheless sought to demonstrate that it could not be by Leonardo’s hand. To properly summarize this controversy, which forms the subject of more than one volume, would exceed the limits assigned to our work. Let the following indications suffice. The Louvre painting was brought back from Italy to France by Cardinal Richelieu, when in December 1629 he personally commanded the siege of Casale. It adorned the Cardinal’s gallery, and upon his death passed into that of the King. Messrs. Dufresne, Félibien, Mariette, and Lepicié attribute this painting to Leonardo. Later, Landon, Lorenzo, and Rabilliardo Peronville, editors of the *French Museum*, had doubts about the truth of this attribution, and thought it might instead be by Bernardino Luini <note>A prominent North Italian painter and follower of Leonardo</note>. Waagen regards it as the work of a pupil of Da Vinci: and of this opinion is also the Abbot Aimé-Guillon, who wrote a work on the many repetitions of this composition. Delécluze believes it was painted by Salaì <note>Gian Giacomo Caprotti, Leonardo's pupil and companion</note> or by Luini under Leonardo’s eyes, and perhaps even retouched by him. Passavant sees in this painting only the brush of the master; and a great number of connoisseurs are of the same opinion. The composition of the cartoon <note>A full-scale preparatory drawing</note>, which, as we noted, is still in existence (see above on page xvi, note 2), differs from that of the Louvre painting. Several copies or repetitions of this painting are known: that of the Leuchtenberg gallery in Munich, formerly in the church of San Celso in Milan, is generally held to be the work of Salaì: and an engraving of it can be seen in the *School of Leonardo da Vinci in Lombardy*, published by Fumagalli, Milan, 1811. Also by Salaì is held to be the one in the Florence gallery. In Milan, one by Bernardino Luini can be seen in the Ambrosiana. Returning to the Louvre painting, we shall conclude with Mündler

> “that, despite the many authorities cited above, some of whom are quite respectable, it can never be admitted that anyone other than Leonardo would have succeeded in painting this masterpiece, one of the jewels of the Louvre, one of the wonders of art. The accessories are neglected, the garments unfinished; but the heads! how to describe the eloquence of those lips, the ineffable enchantment of that smile, the fascination of that gaze, from which love overflows like from a vessel too full? And of the execution, what can ever be said? Is there in painting an example of greater power and equal fineness of modeling? And how can one imagine, in a work executed upon a cartoon by the master, that intimate harmony between the thought and its realization, when Leonardo himself would have been incapable of rendering the concepts of others with such perfection?”

(*Essay on a critical Analysis of the Notice of Italian Paintings in the Louvre*, etc. [by Frédéric Villot], by Otto Mündler, Paris, Didot, 1850).

— The Virgin of the Rocks (*La Vierge aux Rochers*). The Child Jesus sitting, and supported by an angel, blesses the little Saint John presented to him by the Madonna. In the background, a grotto, a landscape, and rocks of bizarre shape, from which the painting takes the name *The Virgin of the Rocks*. There is an engraving of it by Boucher Desnoyers. — The painting was in the collection of Francis I. — Waagen does not believe it is authentic. Passavant thinks it is a copy of the one made by Leonardo for the Chapel of the Conception in the Franciscan church in Milan, cited by Lomazzo in Book II, chapter XVII of his *Treatise on Painting*. Two Angels of great beauty that were at the sides of the main painting are currently in the gallery of Duke Melzi. Several very fine repetitions of this painting also exist, including one in the museum of Nantes. — The Louvre painting, originally painted on panel, was transferred to canvas after the restoration of 1815.

— The Madonna known as *of the Scales*. The Virgin is seated holding the Divine Infant on her knees, to whom the archangel Saint Michael, kneeling, presents a pair of scales, a symbol of eternal Justice. Near the Virgin, Saint Elizabeth supports the little Saint John, who is seated with a lamb. This canvas was part of the collection of Louis XIV. It is attributed by Waagen to Marco d’Oggiono, by Passavant to Salaino, and by Mündler to Cesare da Sesto. <note>These are all prominent "Leonardeschi," or followers of Leonardo's style.</note>

— A panel representing Jesus who, seated upon a cushion and supported by His Mother, receives a reed cross presented to him by Saint John. Belonging to the old collection. Passavant and Waagen believe that this panel derives from the Roman school. The latter critic regards it as a fine work by Pierin del Vaga. Mündler believes it to be by Bernardino Luini; not from his finest period, but from his old age, when, striving to graft Raphael-esque motifs and elements of the Roman school onto his old style, he disturbed, so to speak, the source of his inspiration and became inferior to himself.

— Bacchus seated upon a stone, crowned with vine leaves, leaning on a thyrsus <note>A staff tipped with a pine cone, associated with Bacchus</note>. It comes from the collection of Louis XIV. The inventory of the Restoration assigns this canvas only to some pupil of Leonardo. Waagen likewise attributes it to one of his scholars, and the landscape seems to him to be painted by Bernazzano. Passavant judges this painting to be an original, and thinks that it primarily represented a Saint John in the Desert, to which the vine leaves and clusters were later added. An ancient copy with the appearance of Saint John was seen in the church of Sant’Eustorgio in Milan. — † It is known that Leonardo painted a Bacchus, sold in 1505 by Antonio Pallavicino, which then passed into France. (See an article by Marquis Giuseppe Campori in the *Acts of Parmesan and Modenese National History, 1865*).

— Portrait of Charles d’Amboise, Marshal of Chaumont (Ciamonte). He wears a cap on his head adorned with a medal and a gold necklace around his neck. This portrait was also believed to be that of Louis XII; but it is now proven to be that of Ciamonte, <gloss>I</gloss> and as such it was engraved by Thevet. Passavant considers it a work by Beltraffio; Mündler, with good reason, by Andrea Solario.

— Portrait of a woman on panel; the head is seen in three-quarters view; the hair is smooth; the forehead is encircled by a small black cord fastened by a diamond; her neck is adorned by a cord, and she wears a red embroidered dress. This portrait was likely part of the collection of Francis I, and is indicated by Father Dan (*Treasury of the Wonders of Fontainebleau, 1642*) as representing the Duchess of Mantua. It has been engraved several times as the "Beautiful Féronnière" (beloved of Francis I). It is presumed that it offers the likeness of Lucrezia Crivelli, whom Leonardo painted in Milan around 1497, if it is true that Ludovico the Moor only after the death of Beatrice had by Lucrezia that Giovan Paolo who was the progenitor of the Marquises of Caravaggio. Waagen holds this painting to be one of the most beautiful and authentic by Leonardo. <note>This painting is now widely known as "La Belle Ferronnière" in the Louvre.</note>

† From a letter by Father Don Pietro da Nuvolara to the Marchioness Isabella Gonzaga, written from Florence on April 4, 1501, it is noted that Leonardo at that time, being in Florence, was attending to his mathematical experiments, perhaps regarding the course of the Arno, and that he had undertaken to paint for Florimond Robertet, secretary to the King of France, a small picture with a seated Madonna <note>original: "come volesse inaspare fusi e il Bambino posto il piede nel canestrino de’ fusi ha preso l’aspo e mira attentamente"</note> *as if she wished to wind yarn on spindles, and the Child, having placed his foot in the basket of spindles, has taken the yarn-winder and looks at it attentively.*

The letter, the original of which is in the archive of San Fedele in Milan, was published by Calvi in the *Notes on Leonardo da Vinci*. Leonardo, having departed from Milan together with Pacioli, seems to have visited Venice before returning to Florence, taking with him the portrait of the Marchioness of Mantua: which is proven by a letter from Lorenzo da Pavia, written on March 13, 1500, to the same Gonzaga lady.

**VIENNA. Imperial Gallery of the Belvedere.** — Herodias commanding the executioner to place the head of Saint John in the basin, in full-length figures nearly life-size. By some, however, it is attributed to Cesare da Sesto. There is an engraving of it in volume IV of the work *Imperial and Royal Gallery of the Belvedere in Vienna, Vienna and Prague, 1821-28*. — In the illustration, it is said that this panel was once the ornament of Cardinal Mazarin's palace in Paris; that a certain Ficini, an Italian, having made an exact copy of it, placed it in the location of the original, which he took to Florence, from whence it passed into the aforementioned gallery; and that the Ambrosian Library of Milan possesses the red chalk studies for this painting.

**DRESDEN. Royal Gallery.** — Portrait on panel of a man in mature age, with a beard, a cap on his head adorned with gems, richly dressed and covered by an ample fur. He has his right hand covered by a glove, and with his left he holds a sheathed dagger. Various are the opinions on the person portrayed in this panel. There are those who believe him to be Francis I of France; others, Francesco Sforza, Duke of Milan. In modern times, the authenticity of the painting has been cast into doubt by attributing it to the younger Holbein, and it has been believed to be the portrait of Morett, jeweler to Henry VIII. But the illustrators of the magnificent work *The Dresden Gallery* (with French and German text), published in Dresden with stupendous lithographic plates, believe they have strong reasons to doubt that it is the portrait of Francesco Sforza, and hold it rather to be that of Ludovico Sforza his son, called "the Moor" <note>Ludovico "Il Moro" Sforza, Leonardo's great patron in Milan</note>, reflecting that his father was already dead sixteen years before Ludovico invited Leonardo to Milan. — † To us, it does not even seem probable that this portrait is of "the Moor," because being bearded it contradicts the custom of those times, which was to go clean-shaven and with a long bob <note>original: "zazzera"</note>, as can be known from many portraits of men of that time.

**MUNICH. Royal Gallery.** — A Saint Cecilia, a figure shown to the knees, on panel; and another panel with Our Lady seated beneath a grotto, who holds with her right arm the Infant Jesus stretched out at her side on her mantle, with a cross in his hand. Figures smaller than half life-size.

**HANOVER.** — A nude Leda, with two toddlers, Cupid and the Swan. In the background, a pergola of mulberry trees is seen. The *Lower Saxony Gazette*, announcing this discovery, says that this is the famous painting commissioned from Leonardo by Ludovico the Moor to solemnize the birth of his two twin sons. (See the *Universal Gazette* <note>original: "Allgemeine Zeitung"</note>, no. 41, February 6, 1851). We shall note, however, that this Leda does not seem to be the one mentioned by Lomazzo in book II, chapter xv, of his *Treatise on Painting*, with these words:

> "and Leonardo Vinci observed it (the act of modesty) by making Leda entirely nude with the swan in her lap, who modestly lowers her eyes."

**THE HAGUE. Gallery of William II, King of Holland.** — Panel with Leda. The beloved of Jove, holding one knee to the ground, makes the gesture of lifting a child whom she supports with her right arm, while with her left hand she points to Pollux and Helen, born from one and the same egg. On the opposite side is seen a child crouching near a broken egg, from which he seems to have just emerged. In the background is a landscape with a river surrounded by buildings with small towers, and mountainous distances, in the midst of which two knights and an amazon ride at full speed. — This panel was in the Royal Gallery of Hesse-Kassel; from whence it passed into that of Napoleon at Malmaison, and then into that of the King of Holland. It was sold at public auction for 31,175 francs in August 1850.

Upon his death, his heirs brought it to Moris, their homeland in the Trentino region. — † Amoretti says that this panel later passed into the Hermitage gallery, but Calvi asserts that it is still in Moris.

Professor Raffaello Tosoni of Cetona, residing in Florence, a devoted owner of various precious art objects, possesses two drawings by Leonardo. The first is a head of a woman, life-sized, seen from the front, with curly and loose hair, a string of pearls at the neck, and with the sleeves of her dress slashed and tied with ribbons. The second, of unquestionable authenticity, contains various beautiful pen sketches. One sees a warrior in the act of hurling an arrow *passed through a hole in the middle of a shield that acts as a bow*. Below is written from right to left: " *this shield should be long* " (sic). Two other figures of warriors likewise in the act of discharging bolts through shields that act as bows, and are braced on the ground by a kind of foot or stand, with the inscription: " *here it would be well if the small round shield were made of steel and in bending it performed the duty of the crossbow* ". A ball, or grenade, which rolls along spitting fire, as the words say: " *Ball that runs by itself throwing fire to a distance of 6 braccia* ". <note>A 'braccio' (plural 'braccia') was a historical Italian unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 centimeters.</note> Then two warriors running with crossbows in hand; then two others aiming their shield which acts as a crossbow; and finally the cross-section of said ball, where one sees the manner in which the tubes of combustible material are arranged. This drawing was part of the distinguished collection of Thomas Lawrence. — † Since the death of Prof. Tosoni, these drawings were sold outside of Italy two years ago.

† Giuseppe Vallardi of Milan sold in 1856 to the Louvre Museum for 35 thousand francs a large folio volume containing drawings by Leonardo, partly in black chalk and partly red, in watercolor and heightened with white, and partly in pen on a white background. Vallardi purchased it in 1829, while traveling to Rome, from an ancient illustrious family, enlarging it with several other drawings that belonged to the Calderara gallery and the Sannazzaro collection. In 1855, he printed an illustrated description of it in only 100 copies, which are not for sale, to give to friends. Regarding those that were or still are in the Ambrosiana <note>The Biblioteca Ambrosiana in Milan.</note>, one can read the Memoir by Giovanni Dozio, printed in Milan in 1871. Also in the Royal Castle of Windsor and in the British Museum are drawings by Vinci.

## PART THREE.

### ON THE SCIENTIFIC WORKS OF LEONARDO DA VINCI.<sup>I</sup>

Leonardo da Vinci is one of those men who, by the power of genius, knew how to overcome adverse fortune. He did not have much to praise her for from birth, since it is certain that he was not the son of any of his father's four wives; nor much later, seeing as the works of art of Leonardo...

---

<note>I Vasari's Life of Leonardo, while it portrays well the excellence of that divine genius in painting, is equally insufficient in accounting for the universality of his learning and the formidable manifestation of his intellect in physical and mathematical speculations. Thus, it appearing to us that a discourse intended to briefly outline the investigations he made in the physical and mathematical sciences, and his merits toward them, would not be considered a useless addition to the illustrations of this Life; we have requested and obtained that this subject, unfamiliar to us, be discussed in the present Commentary by our esteemed friend Prof. Girolamo Buonazia of Siena, to whom we here publicly express singular gratitude.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Leonardo da Vinci’s life, transitioning from a list of specific drawings to a broader overview of his lost scientific writings and his move from Florence to the court of Milan.</meta>

<page-num>xxxiv</page-num>
->COMMENTARY<-

and the writings have suffered very serious damage from both time and men, and the vast majority have been lost. The *Treatise on Painting*, published after his death, and the *Hydraulics*, printed for the first time in 1828 in Bologna, are nothing but fragments arranged in an order different from that intended by the author. The treatise on anatomy, that of local motion and impact, researches in mechanics, studies in optics, writings on the Martesana canal, on botany, geology, and the flight of birds—forgotten immediately after Leonardo's death—remained unknown for a long time. It would be extremely difficult now to reconstruct them from the fragments remaining in his manuscripts and from the notes he took when experience and reasoning led him to the discovery of difficult truths. Furthermore, these notes—in which contemporaries sought Leonardo's secret arts, while he instead delighted in covering everything he did in mystery—have been ransacked and dispersed by ignorant hands, transported from one library to another, divided among many, and remain only to bear witness to a genius who perhaps has had no equal in the world. He lived for himself and for science, without finding anyone to gather the precious heritage he left behind; so much so that more than a century was then necessary to retrace the path he had traveled, and posterity is forced to admire him without his contemporaries having known how to understand him. Thus he lived in Florence, his homeland, for thirty years, practicing the art of painting in his early youth and applying his mind to the study of mechanics. He was easily the first among painters; among engineers, he was such that he could only be compared to the ancients, whose long-abandoned studies and research he resumed. Yet those who governed the city, including <term>Lorenzo de' Medici, called the Magnificent</term><note>The de facto ruler of the Florentine Republic and a famous patron of the arts, though he apparently did not fully appreciate Leonardo's scientific leanings.</note>, did not make use of his work as either an engineer or a painter.

Since his studies of mechanics and hydraulics were not received with much favor, he attempted studies of military art, in which the use of artillery had brought about a complete revolution. He alone, along with Giuliano da Sangallo, then understood the modern art of fortifying and attacking places defended by regular fortifications. With this skill, he hoped to make himself welcome at the court of <term>Lodovico il Moro</term><note>Ludovico Sforza (1452–1508), the Duke of Milan, known as "the Moor."</note>, regent and nearly the lord of the Duchy of Milan in the name of his nephew Gian Galeazzo. Leonardo offered himself to him as a military engineer, hydraulic engineer, architect, painter, and sculptor in the letter we report here. ^I^ This letter refers to the early times of Leonardo's arrival in Milan; and it would be...

---

> ^I^ Here is Leonardo's letter as reported by AMORETTI, *Historical Memoirs of Leonardo da Vinci* (Milan, 1804) on page 24, and reproduced in facsimile also in the cited *Essay on the Works of Leonardo da Vinci, etc.*, published in Milan in 1872 for the inauguration of the monument erected in that city to Leonardo:
> 
> "Having, my Most Illustrious Lord, now sufficiently seen and considered the proofs of all those who count themselves masters and composers of instruments of war; and that the invention and operation of said instruments are in no way different from common use: I shall exert myself, without detracting from anyone else, to make myself understood by Your Excellency, opening to You my secrets, and afterwards offering them at your every pleasure, to work with effect at opportune times concerning all those things which shall be briefly noted in part below.
> 
> "1. I have methods for very light and strong bridges, fit to be carried very easily, with which to pursue and sometimes flee the enemy; and others secure and indestructible by fire and battle, easy and convenient to lift and place. And methods to burn and destroy those of the enemy.
> 
> "2. I know how, in the siege of a territory, to take away the water from the moats, and to make infinite bridges, <term>ghatti</term> <note>original: "ghatti". These were "cats," or mobile covered sheds used to protect soldiers as they approached defensive walls.</note>, and ladders, and other instruments pertaining to said expedition.
> 
> "3. Item, if by height of the bank or by strength of the place and site it were not possible in the siege of a territory to use the office of <term>bombards</term> <note>original: "bombarde". Early forms of cannons.</note>; I have methods for ruining every rock-fortress or other stronghold, unless it be founded upon the rock itself, etc.
> 
> "4. I have also methods for bombards most convenient and easy to carry, and with them to hurl a storm of small stones (he had written and then erased 'to hurl small stones in the likeness almost of a storm'); with the smoke of which giving great terror to the enemy, to his grave injury and confusion, etc.
> 
> "5. Item, I have methods for mines and secret, winding ways made without any noise, to reach a designated point even if it were necessary to pass under moats or any river.
> 
> "6. Item, I will make covered chariots, secure and unassailable, which entering among the enemy with their artillery, there is no multitude of men-at-arms so great that they would not break through; and behind these, infantry will be able to follow quite unharmed and without any impediment.
> 
> "7. Item, occurring the need, I will make bombards, mortars, and <term>passavolanti</term> <note>original: "passavolanti". A type of small-caliber, long-range light artillery.</note> of most beautiful and useful forms, outside of common use.
> 
> "8. Where the operation of bombards might fail,

it is important to trace the date. "Il Moro" <note>Ludovico Sforza (1452–1508), Duke of Milan, nicknamed "the Moor" due to his dark complexion.</note> proposed to make the Martesana canal navigable; in 1483 he had issued an edict for work to begin by going up the Adda river as far as Trezzo: and he later had in mind its continuation, the studies for which he entrusted to Giuliano Vascone, and which was prevented by the disasters of 1499. The occasion was favorable to Leonardo, if he truly came here in '83, as Amoretti maintains, based on the authority of Cavalier Giovan Sabba da Castiglione, who asserts that he worked for sixteen years on the colossus <note>The "Great Horse," a massive bronze equestrian monument intended to honor Francesco Sforza.</note> destroyed in 1499. Would he—young, eager for glory, provided with science, aware of his own strength, he who had written to Ludovico the letter we have reported in such a confident tone—have found a work to which he could give his name, and with which to overcome envy? However, we must say that the first records in Leonardo's own hand referring to hydraulic works do not go back further than March 20, 1492;<sup>I</sup> and these contain criticism of existing works and the corrections necessary for the work to meet its intended purpose. These things, and the name of Giuliano Vascone mentioned above, make us doubt whether Sforza employed the work and advice of Leonardo at that time for the management of the canal waters, and whether he came into credit at the court of Ludovico for such works. In another record from one of his notebooks entitled *On Light and Shade* one reads: "On the 23rd day of April 1490 I began this book, and restarted the horse." He was therefore occupied with the *Treatise on Painting* as early as 1490, and had already begun the studies of the horse; we must therefore refer the institution of the Vincian Academy and the studies of equine anatomy to these times, about which he wrote a treatise that Lomazzo saw at the home of Francesco Melzi <note>Leonardo's pupil and heir to his manuscripts.</note>, divinely drawn by Leonardo's hand. Perhaps from the same years or slightly later are the studies of human anatomy, which he performed in Pavia, helped by and mutually helping Marcantonio della Torre. We have no other date in Leonardo's hand prior to 1490; and this must cause us wonder, considering that he was accustomed to always carry small books with him, in which he noted everything of importance that occurred to him: how then did he spend the seven years running from 1483 to 1490? Some rhymes by Bellincioni, which refer to the period between 1487 and 1489, show us Leonardo occupied in directing the festivities for the wedding of Gian Galeazzo with Isabella of Aragon, and in painting the portraits of Cecilia Gallerani and Lucrezia Crivelli, beloved by Ludovico il Moro. These women were so powerful, and their portraits so celebrated by all those who wished to gain favor with Ludovico, that it must be believed they were the cause of favor for him, who arrived as a stranger and without fortune in a court where the power of intellect and greatness of soul were sometimes prized, but much more so the beauty of the body and the exercise of all the arts that join with civil customs and a soft and happy life. However it may be, to earn a living, he must have abandoned Florence between 1483 and 1487 and made his way to Milan, where

<meta>This page continues the account of Leonardo da Vinci’s tenure at the court of Ludovico "il Moro" Sforza in Milan, shifting from his arrival to his specific artistic, scientific, and personal struggles during this period.</meta>

<page-num>xxxvi</page-num>
<header>COMMENTARY</header>

Leonardo was received with favor by Ludovico il Moro. It would be useless to investigate whether the Duke retained him because he took great delight in the sound of an instrument that Leonardo had fashioned with his own hand—largely of silver and in the shape of a horse's skull (as Vasari <note>Giorgio Vasari (1511–1574), the famous biographer of Renaissance artists.</note> asserts)—or because he wanted him to execute the bronze equestrian statue of Francesco I Sforza, his father. Vasari's assertion has been contested by those saying the first work he undertook was the horse; nevertheless, it is well known that the princes of that time took more pleasure in musicians and courtesans than in works of art and science. Poets, artists, and scientists were welcomed at the Moor's court provided they were not ashamed to use their talent and labor to commend his scandalous love affairs, for he brazenly prostituted noble and respectable young women to his pleasures. <gloss>I</gloss> Thus, it is enough for us to have seen that not the least of Leonardo's works in Milan were the portraits of Ludovico's two concubines. <note>These are likely the famous paintings "The Lady with an Ermine" (Cecilia Gallerani) and "La Belle Ferronnière" (Lucrezia Crivelli).</note> Let us hasten rather to remember how, from such small beginnings, Leonardo knew how to surround himself with pupils by whom he was admired and who constituted a great part of his glory, and how he counted among his intimates the most distinguished people of Milan and the most learned men of his time. Among these we have spoken of Marcantonio della Torre, and we shall speak of Friar Luca Pacioli, who shared his life and studies with Leonardo and worthily represented the flower of Tuscan science in that city. The former received from Leonardo's hand the drawings for *Anatomy*; the latter those for the *Treatise on Divine Proportion*. Pacioli was perhaps the only one who could understand the mind of that divine man in speculations pertaining to natural philosophy and assist him with profound knowledge in more rigorous studies. To this period we owe the fragments reported by Venturi on the fall of heavy bodies combined with the rotation of the earth, on the oscillation of various parts of a system around a center of attraction, on the respective resistance of solids, on friction, the theory of the inclined plane and of forces applied obliquely to a lever, and the principle of virtual velocities. Of these mechanical studies, Pacioli speaks with admiration and exalts Leonardo above all those who frequented Ludovico's court.

The Duke, however, does not seem to have rewarded him generously. After fifteen years of work on the colossus <note>The "Great Horse" monument.</note>; after the institution of the Vincian Academy, for which he had written the *Treatise on Painting*; after having corrected the works on the Canal; after having labored on the treatise of local motion, on studies of mechanics and comparative anatomy; Leonardo writes to the Duke <gloss>2</gloss> that he wishes to change his profession because he has no commissions; he asks to be given some clothing and complains of being left with two years of unpaid salary; he notes that from his works he has only had enough to pay his workmen; and that, after expenses, he finds himself with a profit of about fifteen lire for his labor. Perhaps these laments moved the Duke to honest shame, for on April 26, 1499, he gave Leonardo sixteen perches of a vineyard <gloss>3</gloss> purchased from the monastery of San Vittore near the Vercellina gate. He was not able to enjoy this peacefully for long. For in that same year, Milan being invaded by the French, the Duke lost his state, and Leonardo saw the model of the horse made into a target for the Gascon crossbowmen and destroyed. At the age of forty, after having spent the flower of his life conducting works of art and public utility, and composing great treatises by which the sciences and arts were to be entirely renewed, he was reduced—

<page-num>xxxvii</page-num>
<header>THE LIFE OF LEONARDO DA VINCI</header>

...to flee from his adopted homeland, having lost all the fruit of his labors and being constrained to begin again that manner of life of which he was already weary since his early youth, when he first left Florence. It seems he remained for a long while uncertain of what he should do with himself, deeply moved by the events that had unfolded before his eyes, and not without grave personal loss. We have, from 1502, the patent from the <term>Valentino</term> <note>Cesare Borgia (1475–1507), Duke of Valentinois, who employed Leonardo as a military engineer.</note> appointing him as his architect and general engineer. In his service, Leonardo traveled through the Emilia region, visiting fortified towns and noting everything encountered on the journey pertaining to mechanics and the natural sciences. 1

Having returned to Florence in 1503, he proposed a canal that would branch off from the Arno, crossing the countryside of Prato, Pistoia, and Serravalle, and the Lake of Sesto. He spoke of the construction costs, the waters to be introduced into the canal, and the rivers that would have to cross it. He had cherished this thought since he was a young man; and after his work on the canals of the Milanese territory, for which the Moor <note>Ludovico "Il Moro" Sforza.</note> had often required Leonardo’s counsel, he could hope to be easily believed. He went to the camp outside Pisa to consult on a work to be undertaken against that city, and he drew the cartoon of the <term>Battle of Anghiari</term> <note>A famous lost fresco commissioned for the Hall of the Five Hundred in Florence; Leonardo experimented with a mural technique that ultimately failed to set.</note>. But between the rivalry with Michelangelo, the resentment that his studies of mechanics and hydraulics regarding the channeling of the Arno were poorly received, the sorrow of seeing his new attempt at oil painting on a wall fail, and the annoyance of being scolded by Soderini <note>Piero Soderini, the chief magistrate (Gonfalonier) of Florence.</note> for not attending to the completion of the work commissioned to him, he remained there only until 1506, 2 leaving the work unfinished. Meanwhile, in Milan, affairs had settled into some order; and there Leonardo found in Louis of France <note>King Louis XII.</note> less impudence than in Soderini and greater liberality than in the Moor. He dwelt in Vaprio for a long time at the home of his friend Melzi and made corrections for the continuation of the <term>Martesana canal</term> <note>A major canal in Lombardy connecting the Adda river to Milan.</note>, traveling up the Adda from Trezzo to Brivio. 3 In 1509, he executed a <term>discharge outlet</term> <note>An engineering structure used to manage water levels.</note> on the <term>Naviglio Grande</term> <note>The oldest and most important canal in the Milanese system.</note> near San Cristoforo. 4 For these services, he received as a reward from Louis of France <term>twelve ounces of water</term> <note>A legal grant of water rights, allowing the diversion of a specific volume of water from a canal for private use.</note> to be drawn from the said Canal, just as since 1507 he had held the title and salary of painter to the King. He recalls these things with satisfaction some time later, writing from Florence, where he had come in 1511 to collect part of the inheritance of his uncle, who died perhaps in 1507. His letters are addressed to the King’s lieutenant, to the president, and to Master Francesco Melzi; 5 to whom he promises that he will know how to make good use of the twelve ounces of water and that he will bring with him, upon his return, two paintings of <term>Our Ladies</term> <note>Paintings of the Virgin Mary.</note> made for the <term>Most Christian King</term> <note>The traditional title of the Kings of France.</note>. He kept his promise shortly thereafter by returning to Milan, where his residency was made dear to him by his standing with the King of France, the friendship of Melzi, the memories of his youth, and the glory by which he saw himself surrounded in that city—a city he had embellished with his paintings and benefited with his art by regulating the flow of the waters of the Ticino and the Adda. These thoughts, which carry great weight in all human minds, have even more power over the soul of an old man who has now completed sixty years, who knows he has done much for glory and feels his strength failing for new endeavors; and these things made that residence so dear to him that he found rest in no other place.

But the reconquest of the Milanese territory, undertaken against the French to restore the Sforza to the throne, removed him from there against his will; or perhaps the old man’s soul was moved by thinking of the outcry raised by Michelangelo and Raphael, whose fame, even from a distance, seemed to him to harm his own. And since he felt himself so much greater than them in the divine intelligence of art, just as they were greater than him in practice, he departed for Rome on September 24, 1514. 6 But fortune loves the young; and he,

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Leonardo da Vinci’s life, transitioning from his time in Florence and Milan to his final years. It highlights his difficult relationship with the Roman court under Pope Leo X, his rivalry with Michelangelo, and his eventual move to the French court of Francis I. It also begins an analysis of Leonardo’s intellectual philosophy, emphasizing his reliance on "experience" over the rigid scholasticism of his peers.</meta>

<page-num>xxxviii</page-num>
<header>COMMENTARY</header>

Leonardo, who never had much reason to be pleased with his fellow citizens <note>Leonardo often felt undervalued by the Florentine authorities compared to the support he found elsewhere.</note>, found in Rome under Leo X the same reception that the young Leonardo had once received from Lorenzo the Magnificent, and later from Soderini—the hydraulic engineer who had directed the canal works, and the painter who had painted the *Last Supper*. Vasari relates that, upon being commissioned for a work by the Pope, Leonardo immediately began distilling oils and herbs to make a varnish; and that the Pope, hearing of this, said: "Alas! This man is intended to do nothing, since he begins thinking about the finish before the start of the work." Indignant at this, and all the more because he knew that Buonarroti <note>Michelangelo Buonarroti, who was a fierce rival of Leonardo.</note>, who was no friend of his, had been called to Rome, Leonardo departed. The prosperous successes of the French in Lombardia soon drew Leonardo back, as he had placed all his hopes in the French court and looked favorably upon the noble principles of Lodovico’s successor. ¹ To him, triumphing at Pavia, Leonardo presented the mechanical lion that walked forward and opened its chest to reveal it was full of lilies <note>The fleur-de-lis, the heraldic symbol of the French monarchy.</note>; he followed him to Bologna for the congress with Leo X—of whose arrogant spite he perhaps then remembered with satisfaction, seeing the Pope defeated and forced to seek peace. He followed the King to France in 1515, although already heavy with years and worn by his labors; and if he did not breathe his last in the King's arms, ² as Vasari relates and as was believed for nearly three centuries, it is no less true that the hospitality and honors received at the French court made his death in a foreign land less heavy. Thus, Francis I deserved—if he did not share it with Leonardo’s disciples—the honor of receiving the last sigh of that great man and of supporting that weary and honored head with his own arms.

What we know of the early studies of the young Leonardo can be deduced almost entirely from some of his manuscript fragments, where he speaks of himself and the controversies raised against him by the learned men of the time. Born in a century of scholars for whom everything ancient was good, and everything that the ancient philosophers—chief among them Aristotle—had asserted about natural things was true, he soon began to show little respect for this erudition. These scholars wished to remake nature so that it would obey the precepts of the then-accepted philosophical systems; Leonardo called this race of philosophers "trumpeters and reciters of the works of others." But more than with words, he showed through his studies that he did not wish to hold them in any regard; for in his works, he never cites the authors from whom he might have drawn knowledge of the natural phenomena he describes; rather, he protests that he does not know them and has observed things for himself. ³

> "If I could not, like them, cite authors, I shall cite something much greater and more worthy by citing experience, the mistress of their masters. These men go about puffed up and pompous, dressed and adorned not in their own labors, but in the labors of others, and they will not even grant me my own. They despise me as an inventor; how much more should they, who are not inventors but trumpeters and reciters of the works of others, be blamed?"

->« PREFACE.<-

> "Men who are inventors and interpreters between nature and men are to be judged and esteemed no differently, in comparison to the reciters and trumpeters of others' works, than an object outside a mirror is to the likeness of the object appearing in the mirror—which is in itself... nothing. These are people little indebted to nature, for they are dressed in accidental qualities, and without these, I could count them among the herds of beasts."

Nor should we believe because of this that he held all the ancient masters in the same regard as he did their learned commentators; for in the rigorous studies of geometry and mechanics, he wished to learn as a youth everything that was known. Where teachers were not enough—whom he often confounded with his questions and soon abandoned—he provided for himself with his own genius. The first among the moderns, he resumed the research of Archimedes on the center of gravity of figures and on the equilibrium of fluids, beginning from where the ancient geometer had finished; designing machines moved by water, air, and steam, among which we shall mention only the idea of applying the pendulum to the measurement of time. ⁴

<meta>This page continues the biographical account of Leonardo da Vinci’s scientific and engineering pursuits, specifically focusing on his transition from Florence to Milan and his early work on hydraulic systems.</meta>

<page-num>xxxix</page-num>
<header>ON THE LIFE OF LEONARDO DA VINCI</header>

and the force of steam to artillery; <gloss>¹ <note>original: "e la forza del vapore alle artiglierie"</note></gloss> he dictated, more than a century and a half before Castelli <note>Benedetto Castelli (1578–1643), a mathematician and student of Galileo known for his work on water in motion.</note>, the most complete and exact theories of hydraulics.

Daring a century before Galileo to preach experience as the sole mistress in the study of natural phenomena; admitting hypotheses on the physical constitution of the globe deduced from the laws of mechanical physics and hydraulics, while fighting against "occult qualities" <note>A reference to the medieval scholastic belief in hidden forces that could not be explained by physical laws.</note>: he renewed all of natural philosophy in his mind; and alone, without teachers and without books, he explored a field still untouched, of which he nevertheless measured the entire extent and difficulties with his prodigious intellect. But as a young man of thirty, reasoning at great length before very grave persons upon the first true and known principles (as he himself expresses it), and deducing consequences beyond common understanding, he caused all his friends and those to whom he communicated the fruit of his studies to admire his discourse, but to receive it rather as a vain speculation of a great genius than as the expression of one who has sweated while walking in search of the truth along a path hitherto untrodden. Such a reception was given to the plan to channel the Arno from Pisa to Florence, and the other by which he several times showed many ingenious citizens who then governed Florence that he wished to raise the temple of San Giovanni <note>The Baptistery of Florence.</note> and place steps beneath it without ruining it. These facts narrated by Vasari <note>Giorgio Vasari, the 16th-century biographer of Italian artists.</note>, who in the very manner of his narrative shows that he does not sufficiently understand Leonardo's mind, bear witness that those studies were not much believed in, because those who were considered wise were not accustomed to studying in that way. Wherefore he, tired by now of their learned annoyances, and tired of passing his life without having put his hand to almost anything great, abandoned Florence. Fortune had denied him the chance to spend his work for the benefit of his homeland, but it could not take from him the consciousness of his own strength. Having barely arrived in Milan, he wrote to the Duke the letter that we have reported.

Where he had learned all that he relates, we do not know. We know well that he could maintain much more than he promised, and that the fruit of his studies appeared very soon. Having founded the Vincian Academy in Milan, he wrote for it the *Treatise on Painting* and continued on the Martesana canal the hydraulic studies he had begun on the Arno. Twice he was occupied with the canals of that province: in 1492 by order of Ludovico il Moro, and from 1507 to 1510, called by Louis of France. The works of the second time seem more important than those of the first. Let us say meanwhile that the works of the Martesana canal, directed by the engineer Bertolino da Novara from 1457 to 1460, diverted the waters of the Adda below the fort of Trezzo and led them near Milan. The waters of this canal were sold for irrigation. In 1480, the walls and the ground having given way, they fell back into the river, whereby it was necessary to dig 200 cubits <term>braccia<note>An Italian unit of measurement, literally "arms," roughly 23 inches.</note></term> of the canal again into the rock. A lock had been built near San Marco with the aim of providing for the navigation of the canal, which meanwhile could not be achieved. Ludovico il Moro, recalled from exile, suggested to his nephew Gian Galeazzo the thought of making the Martesana canal navigable, and in his name issued the decree to execute this on May 16, 1483. <gloss>²</gloss> Although Leonardo's arrival is meant to refer to this time, it is not quite certain that the direction of the Martesana works was entrusted to Leonardo, nor is it certain when they were conducted. It seems, however, it must be argued that at first they were not undertaken with too much success. Because in some fragments of notes taken by Leonardo during an inspection made in 1492 of the canals of Lombardy by order of the Moor, one finds a critical examination of the works built and the corrections to be made. He demonstrates that the waters of the canal would not have been sufficient to carry ships if the canal were not narrowed by almost half, and that by diverting a greater quantity of water from the Adda, irrigation could also be provided for, by digging veins of water alongside the Naviglio from which the surplus would be poured. The excavation of the Naviglio and the relative expertise are noted in Leonardo's codices. He likewise designed the lock of San Marco, an already existing building; he made a critical analysis of all

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Leonardo da Vinci’s hydraulic engineering projects in Lombardy, specifically his work on the canals of Milan and the Adda river, following the mention of his early proposals in Florence.</meta>

its parts; <gloss>1</gloss> he wrote about the motion of water when opening sluice gates from above, in the middle, or from below; the differences in level when lowering or moving the surface of falls, eddies, and the curving of waves, as seen in the canal locks <note>original: "conche" — the chambers of a canal lock system used to raise and lower boats.</note> of Milan; <gloss>2</gloss> he identified the defects of existing locks and proposed repairs for them. All of this should lead us to believe that he intended for the canals of the Milanese region to be largely rebuilt, though we cannot assert or deny whether the care of them was officially entrusted to him at that time. It is certain that the proposed corrections were later made, probably between 1506 and 1510, a time when Leonardo remained for a long period in Lombardy, occupied with nothing other than hydraulic works. We know that in the Vincian codices <note>The various notebooks and manuscripts left by Leonardo.</note> there is a chapter titled *On the Martesana Canal*, in which he expresses his opinion on lessening the damage that would result to the Lodi region due to water being diverted from the irrigation of meadows in favor of navigation, and that this chapter was written in 1508.

Oltrocchi <note>Baldassarre Oltrocchi (1714–1797), a scholar who studied Leonardo's manuscripts in the Ambrosian Library.</note> saw in the *Codex Atlanticus* the design of the upper and lower gates of the locks, the leveling performed by Leonardo, the way he provided for the diversion of the Lambro river which crossed the canal, and the locations where he planned the locks. With three of these locks, he brought the Adda river to the level of the city ditch <note>The "Fossa Interna" or inner ring of canals in Milan.</note>, where the waters had not yet been brought due to their excessive height; and with two other locks, he gave them an outlet into the old navigable ditch to encircle the entire city, after having ensured a perpetual equal level with a suitable spillway <term>scaricatoio: a channel or structure designed to release excess water</term> before the water entered it. <gloss>3</gloss>

The letters from Louis of France <note>King Louis XII, who occupied Milan and became a patron of Leonardo.</note> recalling da Vinci from Florence, reported by Gaye, are from 1506.

On July 5, 1507, he wrote from the rectory of Vaprio, where he had resumed his studies for the navigation of the Adda, intending to ascend it as far as Brivio. He drew the course of the Adda, and alongside the drawing, he noted the measurements of the work to be done and the computation of the expenses: the drawing begins at Brivio and extends to the mouth of the Naviglio below Trezzo. <gloss>4</gloss> Many of Leonardo's manuscripts remained forgotten for a long time at Vaprio in the Villa Melzi, <gloss>5</gloss> and these are perhaps the ones in which he had recorded his most detailed studies on the course of the Adda. From this, we must conclude that Il Moro <note>Ludovico Sforza (1452–1508), the Duke of Milan.</note> had only achieved the navigation of the Adda to the detriment of private individuals, from whom he had taken all the water used for irrigation; Leonardo narrowed the canal and opened small outlets <term>bocchelli: small apertures or nozzles used to regulate water flow</term> in its walls above a certain level, which he speaks of in letters written from Florence in 1511, distributing and regulating the "inch of water" <note>An "oncia d'acqua" was a historical unit of water flow measurement used in Lombardy.</note> according to the theories he explains in his treatise *Hydraulics*.

The last four books of Leonardo's *Hydraulics* contain the results of his observations on the motion of waters; the first five contain the theories and the most subtle speculations of the science. We must believe that the four were those Leonardo wrote during the time he directed hydraulic works in Lombardy, or are at least derived largely from the notes he took as cases worthy of observation presented themselves. In the sixth and seventh books, concerning breaches made by water and things carried by water, he considers the damage caused by water against embankments—where it creates greater or lesser concavity or breaches due to the narrowing of the banks, the increase in velocity, the rebounding of water against an obstacle, the increase in the slope of the bed, or the unevenness of that bed; where the bottom is scoured and where the bank is eroded by two meeting currents; what happens where two rivers enter one another; where the riverbed rises and where it lowers; how soil should be restored to places exposed and stripped by the course of the waters; and how running water should be used to carry soil from the mountains to marshy valleys to make them fertile and heal the surrounding air.

Everything that Benedetto Castelli first discussed regarding the measurement of running waters had already been recorded by Leonardo in the eighth book of *Hydraulics*, speaking of the "inch of water" and of the—

The questions regarding the quantity of water to be extracted from the canals of Lombardy for irrigation, and its fair distribution and sale, drew Leonardo's attention toward determining the true quantity of the "water-inch" <note>original: "oncia di acqua" — a historical unit of water flow used in Italy to measure the volume of water delivered through an opening.</note> that exits from a given opening. We have seen that he concerned himself with this especially in the chapter on the Martesana canal, and he returns to this same subject when writing from Florence to Melzi <note>Francesco Melzi (c. 1491–1570), Leonardo’s favorite pupil and the heir to his manuscripts.</note> in 1511 regarding the regulation of the outlets of the Naviglio <note>The system of navigable canals in and around Milan.</note>. The question is considered from the most varied perspectives, and it can be said that this book is one of the most important in Leonardo’s *Treatise on Hydraulics*: to this belong several fragments taken from Leonardo's manuscripts, reported by Venturi in his *Essay on Leonardo da Vinci*. The experiments proposed for the resolution of all the cases that occur to his mind are simple and decisive; they form excellent models for anyone who devotes themselves to the study of the causes of phenomena in an as-yet unexplored field. In these, he was able to separate what is owed to each individual cause within complex effects; for each, he was able to find that experiment which makes the theory more perceptible and best helps the mind form the truest and most accurate concept of what occurs in nature. While in the first books the experiments are included with strict parsimony, in this book—where it was a matter of making truths that affect the interests of so many people perceptible to all—they are multiplied. Although we must generally judge that Leonardo had a more vast and speculative genius, though less practical than Castelli <note>Benedetto Castelli (1578–1643), a mathematician and student of Galileo who is often considered the founder of modern hydrodynamics.</note>, it seems to us, in reviewing this book, that he wished to make himself accessible to everyone. He did this to provide a splendid proof that he knew how to create and overturn systems with the genius of a philosopher—that he knew, as a man of science, how to apply reasoning and lead from abstract principles and bold hypotheses to their ultimate consequences; but that he equally knew how to serve the public utility, as well as any other person (be they who they may), in the administration of such an important branch of public and private wealth. In this, he considers the quantity of water that pours from different openings, taking into account the height of the water above each when the level remains constant, the variation in velocity as the level drops, and the measurement of the "inches" delivered at the water outlets, which are greater or lesser according to the greater or lesser velocity of the water passing through said outlet; <note>1</note> the different quantity of water provided by the same openings placed on the surface of the same canal, according to the conditions of the canal; <note>2</note> and he does not neglect the more subtle speculations on the shape of the water's surface...

---

> ¹ "The measurements of the inches <note>original: "once"</note> given at the water outlets are greater or lesser according to the greater or lesser velocities of the water passing through that outlet. Double velocity gives double water in the same amount of time, and thus triple velocity will give a triple quantity of water in the same time, and so it would continue successively to infinity." (LEONARDO, *Hydraulics*, page 424).

> ² "The motion of every river, in equal time, gives an equal weight of water at every part of its length. And this happens because, if the river, in its discharge, pours out a certain weight of water in a certain time, necessity dictates that an equal weight of water in the same time must succeed the discharged water, moving from the part immediately preceding it; and thus, successively, another weight of water succeeds this one, until reaching the first part of the river’s length. Otherwise, if a greater sum of water were discharged at the outlet than what is found at the start of the river, it would follow that in the middle of the canal the water would continually decrease; and conversely, if a smaller sum of water passed through the same discharge than what enters at its birth, the water in the middle would grow continually: but both are manifestly false. Therefore, the motion of every river in equal time gives an equal weight of water in every part of its length. Two equal and similar outlets placed in the bank of a river with equal slope of the bottom: one will pour out more or less water according to whether you increase or decrease the width of that river..., and just as much as you increase or decrease the width of the river, so much will you decrease or increase the velocity of its motion. A river of equal depth will have so much more 'fleeing' <note>i.e., speed or flow</note> in the narrower width as the greater width exceeds the smaller... if there is a place that has three different widths which are connected, and the first smaller width fits into the second four times, and the second fits twice into the third; I say that the men who fill said places with their bodies, being in continuous motion, when the men in the largest space take one step, those in the second smaller space will take two." (Loc. cit., pages 427, 428, 429).

The first five books, as we have already noted, contain only the theory, and are derived from these latter ones. Besides Leonardo's habit of always making experience precede theory, we have one more reason to believe what we have asserted, observing that in the first books of the treatise he very often refers back to the propositions or experiments of the last ones. They were therefore written later.

The physical constitution of water and earth, the formation of clouds, $^2$ the way they remain suspended in the highest regions of the atmosphere, $^3$ the laws of equilibrium of water and air, and of fluids in general, the search for the center of gravity of the earth and water, form the subject of the first book of Leonardo's *Hydraulics*. A most acute observer of the way the different forces of nature operate, he separates and classifies them with a unique power of analysis, and with rigor of deduction establishes the principles of natural philosophy and pushes them to their ultimate consequences.

In the second book, he takes up more generally the theory and experiments proposed in the eighth, applying to the motion of waters in a channel the principles that served for the solution of problems regarding the measurement of water exiting from a given opening. The variation of the speed of water in the different sections of a channel, at different depths from the surface, having regard to the nature and the obliquity <note>The slope or angle</note> of the bottom, $^4$ the friction on the bottom $^5$ and on the walls of the channel, the experiments to be established to recognize if

> $^1$ "Water is given an exit near its surface, and it is asked which part of the water's surface will take on faster or slower motion in providing water to such an exit. And to make a rule, you shall place particles of things that float, which are equal, such as some tiny seeds of herbs, and place them in a circle equidistant from the exit. And note the first that reaches the mouth, stop the water, look at the circle, and thus you will make a rule. To see which water in the vessel is that which moves to the exit at the bottom of said vessel, take two square glass plates, a quarter of a cubit <note>original: "braccio," a Renaissance measure of length</note> in size, and place them near each other at a distance of two knife-edges with uniform space, and seal the edges on three sides with wax; then through the fourth side at the top fill it with clear water, in which small seeds are scattered, which are floating throughout the height of such water; then you will make a small hole in the bottom, and give an exit to such water, and keep your eye steady on the face of the vessel. And thus the motion of the said seeds will give you knowledge of which water it is that runs with the greatest speed to the exit." (Loc. cit., pages 413, 418).
>
> $^2$ "The heat of the element of fire always draws to itself moist vapors, and thick mists, and dense clouds, which it detaches from the seas and other marshes, and rivers and moist valleys, and drawing those little by little up to the cold region, that first part stops, because the heat and moisture do not mix with the cold and dry; wherefore the first part having stopped there, the other parts settle there; and thus adding part to part, thick and dark clouds are made, and often they are moved and carried by the winds from one region to another, where by their density they create such heavy weight that they fall in thick rain. And if the heat of the sun increases the power of the element, the clouds will be drawn higher and find more cold, in which they freeze, and cause stormy hailstorms." (Loc. cit., page 289).

The water that falls from the cloud sometimes resolves into such lightness by the friction it has with the air, that it cannot divide the air.... and often it is converted into such minute particles, that it cannot descend, and thus it remains within the air." (Loc. cit., page 291).

That river is of faster course which has less contact with the bottom, the bottom being firm and of uniform width, and, conversely, that one is slower which has more contact with the bottom." (Loc. cit., pages 301, 303).

to the treatise on local motion and to anatomy, on which he worked simultaneously. He describes how the functions of the various limbs and muscles of the human body behave, and how their movements are executed according to the laws of mechanics; how they must be arranged around the center of gravity so that the action the painter wishes to represent shows its effect. <gloss>1</gloss> In the simplicity and exactness of his expressions, one easily recognizes the scientist in the painter—the first, after Archimedes, to occupy himself in mechanics with the search for the center of gravity of figures. He discovered, before Maurolico and Commandino <note>Francesco Maurolico and Federico Commandino were 16th-century mathematicians who later formalized these principles.</note>, the center of gravity of the pyramid; he knew the theory of the inclined plane and of forces applied obliquely to the lever. If we still possessed the treatise on local motion and percussions—an inestimable work, according to Paciolo <note>Luca Pacioli, a contemporary of Leonardo and famous mathematician.</note>—we would see that after having begun in the science of equilibrium where the ancient masters had finished, he perhaps laid the foundations of dynamics before Galileo. And if he, occupied in so many and such varied studies, sometimes lacked the time to reduce his concept to a rigorous demonstration, he did not lack the mind to discern the cause of every phenomenon. The sixth book, on trees and greenery, is a treatise on plant physiology as perfect as the knowledge of that time allowed. <gloss>2</gloss> When he speaks of colors, aerial perspective, and vision, he shows that no one knew the theory better than he; he indicates that, since the image of an object forms in two different ways for the two eyes of an observer, for a painting to show the same relief as reality, the two images would need to overlap. Not long ago, experience confirmed Leonardo's assertions; and this is a new praise due to him who, before Porta <note>Giambattista della Porta, often credited with the invention of the camera obscura.</note>, described the optical chamber <term>camera ottica: the camera obscura, a device that projects an image of its surroundings onto a screen</term>. Since everyone is familiar with the *Treatise on Painting*, and in any case it would be impossible to analyze it fully, it will suffice to mention that from the general rules, in which he summarizes his entire concept, to the minute details which he investigates with a power of analysis beyond any comparison, he shows such superiority of ideas and such power of intellect that one cannot hope there will ever be anyone to equal him in the sentiment of art.

# CHRONOLOGICAL PROSPECTUS

### *OF THE LIFE AND WORKS OF LEONARDO DA VINCI.*

---

1452. Leonardo is born in Vinci.
1472. He is recorded in the *Red Book of debtors and creditors* of the Company of Painters of Florence <note>The "Compagnia di San Luca," the professional guild for artists.</note>.
1476. He was still working in the workshop of Verrocchio <note>Andrea del Verrocchio, the renowned master who trained Leonardo.</note>.
1478, January 1st. He is commissioned to paint the altarpiece for the chapel of the Signoria <note>The government palace of Florence, now known as the Palazzo Vecchio.</note>.
1478, March 16th. He receives 25 gold florins as a down payment for the aforementioned painting.
1480, March. The friars of San Donato at Scopeto commission him to create the altarpiece or <term>ancona</term> <note>A large, framed altarpiece, often consisting of multiple panels.</note> for the high altar of their church.
1483. Until approximately this year, Leonardo remains in his homeland, occupied with painting. The *Rotella* <note>A painted shield; "rotella" means small wheel or round shield.</note>, the *Medusa*, the *Neptune* for Antonio Segni, and the cartoon <note>A full-scale preparatory drawing for a fresco or painting.</note> of *Adam and Eve* were made during this time.
1483 (?). Leonardo goes to seek his fortune with Lodovico Sforza, known as "the Moor" <note>original: "il Moro"</note>, regent of the Duchy of Milan.
1483-1489, and likewise during the first years of his stay in Milan. He paints the portraits of Cecilia Gallerani and Lucrezia Crivelli, mistresses of Lodovico the Moor. <gloss>I</gloss>
1487. He creates a model for the dome of the Milan Cathedral.
1489 (?). He constructs a mechanism of pulleys and ropes to transport the sacred relic of the Holy Nail <note>original: "santo Chiodo"; believed to be one of the nails from the True Cross.</note> to a more venerable and secure location—specifically, the final arch of the central nave of the Milan Cathedral.
1489. He directs the spectacles given for the wedding of Duke Gian Galeazzo to Isabella of Aragon.
1490. He prepares the apparatus for the spectacles for the wedding of Lodovico the Moor to Beatrice d’Este.
1490, April 23rd. He begins the book *On Light and Shadow* <note>original: "Della luce e delle ombre"</note>, and restarts the model of the horse, namely the equestrian statue of Francesco I Sforza.
1491. He organizes the tournament festival for Galeazzo Sanseverino.
1492. He conducts studies to make the Martesana canal navigable from Trezzo to Milan.
1492. He is occupied with directing the decorations and painting the rooms of the fortress <note>original: "rôcca"</note> where Lodovico the Moor resided.
1492. He builds the bath for Duchess Beatrice in the castle park.

1496. He creates the figures, sixty in number, for the treatise *On Divine Proportion* <note>original: "De divina proportione"</note> by Friar Luca Pacioli, which was later published in 1509.
1496 (?). A panel with the Nativity of Our Lady, sent by the Duke of Milan as a gift to the Emperor.
1496. He paints the *Last Supper* <note>original: "Cenacolo"</note> in the refectory of the Grazie in Milan.
1498. He was still among the number of virtuous men who frequented the court of Lodovico the Moor. $^2$
1499. He receives as a gift from Duke Lodovico sixteen <term>pertiche</term> <note>A traditional Italian unit of land measurement.</note> of a vineyard, recently purchased from the monastery of San Vittore near the Vercellina gate.
1499-1500. He departs with Luca Pacioli for Florence.
1500 (?). The mold of the equestrian statue of Francesco I Sforza, upon which Leonardo had spent sixteen continuous years, is ruined, used as a target by Gascon crossbowmen when the French entered Milan.
1500. He goes to Venice.
1500 (?). Having returned to Florence, he paints the portraits of Lady Lisa del Giocondo <note>The world-famous "Mona Lisa."</note> and Amerigo Benci. He studies the method of making the Arno navigable from Florence to Pisa.
1501. He paints a small panel with the Madonna for the secretary Robertet.
1501, July 29. Leonardo, by a legal instrument made in Florence where he is called painter and sculptor, declares he has received from Pietro di messer Giovanni di Oreno, a Milanese, one year's rent for a piece of land located near the Vercellina gate of Milan.
1502. He receives from Duke Valentino <note>Cesare Borgia.</note> the patent of his architect and general engineer in Romagna.
1502, July 30. He was in Urbino, where he designed a dovecote, a staircase with various entrances, and the fortress.
1502, August 1. He is in Pesaro.
1502, August 8. In Rimini.
1502, August 11. In Cesena.
1502, September 6. At Cesenatico, and designs its port. From Emilia he returns to his homeland; then he travels in the southern part of Tuscany.
1503, January 25. He is among the artists called to give their opinion on the most convenient place to position Michelangelo's *David*.
1503, July 23. He is in the camp below Pisa, to consult on the design of a work to be made to divert the course of the Arno.
1503-1504. His name is found written on folio 93 verso of the *Red Book of debtors and creditors* of the Company of Painters, cited above.
1503-1505. The cartoon of the *Battle of Anghiari* and the beginning of the painting in the Hall of the Great Council.
