1504, July 9. Ser Piero da Vinci, his father, dies.

1505. He is still in Florence.

1506. In the company of other architects, he gives his opinion on the church of San Salvadore, which was in danger of collapsing, and on the method for rebuilding the bell tower of San Miniato al Monte.

1506, May 30. Leonardo, *distinguished painter and Florentine citizen*, promises that within three months from that day he would present himself personally in Florence before the Magnificent Priors <note>The high-ranking officials of the Florentine government.</note>, under penalty, if failing, of 150 gold florins.

1507. His uncle Francesco dies. He returns to Florence. Two paintings of Our Lady <note>The Virgin Mary.</note>, begun in Florence, are brought to a very advanced stage.

1507, April 27. Chaumont <note>Charles d'Amboise, the French governor of Milan.</note> orders that the vineyard given to Leonardo by Lodovico the Moor be restored to him.

1507, August 15. A letter from Chaumont to the Signoria of Florence, recommending Leonardo who had departed for Florence, so that they might expedite the dispatch of his lawsuit against his brothers.

1507, September 18. Leonardo writes from Florence to Cardinal Ippolito d'Este for this same reason.

1507, October. He had returned to Milan. His hydraulic works.

1508. He writes a chapter titled: *On the Martesana Canal*.

1509. He completes the lock-gate of the San Cristoforo Canal in Milan.

1509. He receives as a gift from the King of France twelve <term>once</term> <note>A unit of water flow measurement used in historical irrigation and engineering.</note> of water to be drawn from the Naviglio Grande in the vicinity of San Cristoforo.

1509. He likely creates the decorations for the triumphal entry of Louis XII into Milan. Perhaps in this same year, he paints the portrait of Giangiacomo Trivulzio, cited by Lomazzo: *Treatise on Painting*, book VII, chapter xxv.

1510, October 21. He participates with various architects in a council to examine the improvements that could be made to the construction of the dome of the Milan Cathedral.

1511. He is in Florence because of the litigation with his brothers over the inheritance of his uncle Francesco.

1512. He returns to Milan.

1513. In October, he is found again in Florence.

1514, September 24. He departs from Milan for Rome with Giovanni (Beltraffio?), Francesco Melzi, Lorenzo (del Faina?), and Fanfoia.

1514. He goes to Rome with Giuliano de' Medici to attend the coronation of Leo X. He paints two small pictures there for Baldassarre Turini of Pescia, the <term>datary</term> <note>A high-ranking official in the Roman Curia.</note> of Leo X. One of these is said to be in the Düsseldorf gallery.

1514. He is in Parma.

1514, in December. He is in Florence once more.

1515. To this year Amoretti attributes the figure of the lion made in Pavia by Leonardo, which walked through the hall, stopped before Francis I of France, and opening its chest, showed it to be full of lilies.

1515, in December. He is in Bologna on the occasion of the concordat made in that city between Francis I and Leo X.

1515. There he draws the portrait of Artus, the king's master of the chamber.

1516, at the end of January. He goes to France with Francis I, in the capacity of painter to the king, with a salary of 700 crowns per year.

1518, April 22. He makes his will at Cloux near Amboise.

1519, May 2. He dies.

<meta>Following the initial sketches and faint impressions on the preceding page, this section marks the beginning of the formal text of Leonardo da Vinci’s "Treatise on Painting." Here, the author shifts from visual practice to theoretical foundation, establishing the intellectual framework for painting as a rigorous discipline.</meta>

## PART ONE.

1. Whether painting is a science or not.

**SCIENCE** is the name given to that <term>mental discourse<note>original: "discorso mentale"; refers to the process of logical reasoning and intellectual inquiry that takes place in the mind before or during physical action.</note></term> which originates from its ultimate principles, beyond which nothing else can be found in nature that is part of that science. Take, for example, the science of <term>continuous quantity<note>original: "quantità continua"; a mathematical concept referring to things that are not made of separate parts, such as a line, a surface, or time itself.</note></term>—that is, the science of geometry. Geometry begins with the surfaces of bodies and finds its origin in the line, which is the boundary of that surface. Yet, we are not fully satisfied by this, because we know that the line ends in a **point**, and the point is that thing which nothing else can be smaller than. Therefore, the point is the first principle of geometry; and nothing else can exist, either in nature or in the human mind, that can give rise to the point.

Because if you say that the contact made upon a surface by the extreme sharpness of the tip of a stylus is the creation of a point, this is not true; rather, we would say that such a contact is a surface that

<column-break/>

<note>The following text continues Leonardo's argument that what we perceive as a physical point is actually a tiny surface, emphasizing the distinction between mathematical theory and physical reality.</note>

<note>The accompanying engraving depicts a group of five men in a lively debate. A youthful figure with long curls—often interpreted as a young Christ among the doctors—gestures with his fingers as if counting off points of an argument. Four older, bearded men surround him, their faces etched with deep concentration, skepticism, and wonder. This visualizes the "mental discourse" mentioned in the text.</note>

<note>In the lower margin, a sketch of a nude male figure demonstrates Leonardo's application of "science" to the human form. By understanding the "principles" of anatomy and geometry, the artist can accurately reconstruct the human body in space.</note>

<summary>In this opening chapter, Leonardo defines science as a form of rigorous mental reasoning and argues that painting, like geometry, is built upon fundamental, indivisible principles starting with the mathematical point.</summary>
<keywords>science, geometry, mental discourse, mathematical point, first principles, artistic theory, anatomy</keywords>

# LEONARDO DA VINCI

[§ 1

surrounds its center, and in that center is the residence of the point. Such a point is not of the matter of that surface; neither it, nor all the points of the universe, possess any power <note>original: "in potenza"; here meaning physical magnitude or dimension</note> even if they were joined together. Given that they could be united, they would not compose any part of a surface. And if you were to imagine a whole being composed of a thousand points, by dividing any part from this quantity of a thousand, one could very well say that such a part is equal to its whole. This is proven with the zero or "nothing"—that is, the tenth figure of arithmetic, which is represented by an O for that nothingness. When placed after a unit, it makes it ten; if you place two after such a unit, it says one hundred; and thus infinitely it will always increase the number ten times wherever it is added. Yet, in itself, it is worth nothing more than nothing, and all the "nothings" of the universe are equal to a single nothing in terms of their substance and value. No human investigation can be called true science if it does not pass through mathematical demonstrations. And if you say that the sciences which begin and end in the mind have truth, this is not conceded, but denied for many reasons; first, because in such mental discourses experience <note>Leonardo uses "esperienza" to mean empirical observation and physical testing</note> does not occur, without which nothing gives certainty of itself.

### 2. Example and difference between painting and poetry.

Such proportion exists from the imagination to the effect as exists from the shadow to the shaded body; and the same proportion exists from poetry to painting. This is because poetry places its subjects in the imagination through letters <note>meaning written words</note>, while painting presents them realistically outside the eye. From this eye, the mind receives the likenesses no differently than if they were natural objects. Poetry provides them without this likeness, and they do not pass to the "impressive" faculty <note>term: impressiva; the part of the brain Leonardo believed received sensory impressions</note> by way of the visual power as painting does.

### 3. Which science is more useful, and in what its utility consists.

That science is more useful whose fruit is more communicable, and conversely, that which is less communicable is less useful. Painting has its end communicable to all the generations of the universe, because its end is a subject of the visual power, and it does not pass through the ear to the common sense <note>term: senso comune; the traditional philosophical concept of a central faculty that coordinates the five senses</note> in the same way that it passes through sight. Therefore, this [painting] has no need of interpreters of different languages, as letters do, and it immediately satisfies the human species no differently than things produced by nature do. And not only the human species, but other animals as well; as was shown in a painting imitated from a father of a family, which was caressed by small children who were still in swaddling clothes, and similarly by the dog and the cat of the same house—it was a marvelous thing to consider such a sight.

Painting represents the works of nature to the senses with more truth and certainty than words or letters do, but letters represent with more truth

<summary>Leonardo argues that true science must be mathematically and empirically proven, asserting that painting is superior to poetry because it communicates directly and universally through sight.</summary>

words to the senses, which painting does not do. But we said that the science which represents the works of nature is more admirable than that which represents the works of the operator—that is, the works of men, which are words, such as poetry and the like, which pass through the human tongue.

### 4. Of the imitable sciences, and how painting is inimitable, and therefore it is a science.

The sciences that are imitable are of such a kind that through them the disciple becomes equal to the author, and similarly produces his own fruit; these are useful to the imitator, but they are not of such excellence as those which cannot be left as an inheritance, like other substances. Among these, painting is the first; this cannot be taught to one to whom nature does not grant it, unlike mathematics, of which the disciple takes as much as the master reads to him. This cannot be copied like letters, where the copy is worth as much as the original. This cannot be cast from a mold like sculpture, where the impression is the same as the original in terms of the virtue of the work. This does not produce infinite offspring as printed books do; this alone remains noble, this alone honors its author and remains precious and unique, and never gives birth to children equal to itself. And such singularity makes it more excellent than those sciences which are published everywhere. Now, do we not see the great kings of the East go about veiled and covered, believing they would diminish their fame by publishing and revealing their presence? Now, is it not seen that paintings representing the images of divine deities are continually kept covered with coverings of great price? And when they are uncovered, first great ecclesiastical solemnities are performed with various songs and diverse sounds. And at the uncovering, the great multitude of people who gather there immediately throw themselves to the ground, adoring and praying to the one for whom such a painting is depicted, for the recovery of lost health and for eternal salvation, no differently than if such an idea <note>original: "idea"; here referring to the divine prototype or the saintly figure itself</note> were there present and alive. This does not happen in any other science or other human work, and if you say this is not the virtue of the painter, but the specific virtue of the thing imitated, the answer is that in this case the minds of men could be satisfied by staying in bed, and not going to laborious and dangerous places on pilgrimages, as we continually see happen. But if such pilgrimages are continually in existence, who moves them without necessity? Certainly, you will confess that it is such an image <note>original: "simulacro"; a physical representation that stands in for the divine</note>, which all the writings that could depict such an idea in form and virtue could not do. Therefore, it appears that the idea itself loves such a painting, and loves those who love and revere it, and delights in being adored more in that than in any other figure imitated from it, and through it grants graces and gifts of health, according to the belief of those who gather in such a place.

<summary>Leonardo argues that painting is the highest science because it is "inimitable" and unique to the artist's genius, unlike text or mathematics. He highlights the spiritual power of painting, noting how religious icons command more devotion and pilgrimage than written descriptions.</summary>
<keywords>inimitability of art, divinity in painting, religious icons, pilgrimage, superiority of visual over verbal, artistic genius, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s argument by defining painting as a form of natural philosophy. He transitions from the idea of painting as an "inimitable science" (from page 5) to its technical role in capturing the physical world through the mechanics of vision and perspective.</meta>

<page-num>6</page-num>
<header>LEONARDO DA VINCI [§ 5]</header>

### 5. How painting embraces all the surfaces of bodies, and extends into them.

Painting only extends to the surface of bodies, and its <term>perspective</term> <note>Leonardo refers to "linear perspective," the mathematical system for creating the illusion of space on a flat surface.</note> extends to the increase and decrease of bodies and of their colors; for an object that moves away from the eye loses as much in size and color as it gains in distance. Therefore, painting is **philosophy**, because philosophy treats of the motion of increase and decrease <note>original: "moto aumentativo e diminutivo." In Leonardo’s time, "philosophy" often meant "natural philosophy," or what we now call science. He is linking the visual change in size to the Aristotelian concept of motion.</note>, which is found in the aforementioned proposition; of which we will state the converse, and say: an object seen by the eye gains as much in size, clarity, and color as the space between it and the eye seeing it decreases.

Whoever blames painting blames nature, because the works of the painter represent the works of nature itself, and for this reason, such a critic suffers from a *poverty of feeling*.

Painting is proven to be philosophy because it deals with the motion of bodies in the readiness of their actions, and philosophy likewise extends into motion. All sciences that end in words have as quick a death as they have a life, except for their manual part—that is, writing—which is a mechanical part.

---

### 6. How painting embraces the surfaces, shapes, and colors of natural bodies, and philosophy only extends into their natural virtues.

Painting extends into the surfaces, colors, and shapes of whatever thing is created by nature, and philosophy penetrates inside those same bodies, considering within them their own inherent virtues <note>In this context, "virtues" refers to the internal properties or "powers" of an object, rather than moral goodness.</note>. But philosophy does not remain satisfied with that truth achieved by the painter, who embraces within himself the **first truth** of such bodies, because the eye is less easily deceived.

---

### 7. How the eye is less deceived in its exercises than any other sense, in luminous, or transparent, and uniform mediums.

The eye, at proper distances and through proper mediums, is less deceived in its duty than any other sense, because it sees only by straight lines, which compose the **pyramid** <note>The "visual pyramid" was a fundamental concept in Renaissance optics; Leonardo imagined lines of light traveling from an object to a point in the eye, forming a pyramid shape.</note> that takes the object as its base and leads it to the eye, as I intend to prove. But the ear is greatly deceived regarding the positions and distances of its objects, because the <term>species</term> <note>original: "specie." In medieval and Renaissance science, "species" were the sensory images or "likenesses" emitted by objects that traveled through the air to reach the senses.</note> do not come to it by straight lines, as those of the eye do, but by winding and reflected lines; and many are the times that distant things appear closer than those nearby, by means of the paths of such species; although the voice of an **echo** returns to the sense only by straight lines. The sense of smell is even less certain of the site from which an odor originates; but taste and touch, which physically contact the object, alone have knowledge of that contact.

<summary>Leonardo argues that painting is a superior form of science (philosophy) because it accurately captures the "first truth" of nature—the surface and form of things—using the reliable mechanics of the eye and the visual pyramid.</summary>
<keywords>perspective, philosophy, natural philosophy, optics, visual pyramid, senses, anatomy of vision, Leonardo da Vinci, mechanics of art</keywords>

### 8. How he who despises painting loves neither philosophy nor nature.

If you despise painting, which is the sole imitator of all the visible works of nature, you certainly despise a subtle invention which, with philosophical and subtle speculation, considers all the qualities of forms: the sea, landscapes, plants, animals, grasses, and flowers, all of which are enveloped in shadow and light. Truly, this is a science and the legitimate daughter of nature, because painting is born of nature itself; but to be more precise, we shall call it the granddaughter of nature, because all visible things have been born from nature, and from these things painting is born. Therefore, we may rightly call it the granddaughter of nature and a relative of God. <note>Leonardo argues that because God created Nature, and Nature creates the world the artist copies, the artist is participating in a divine lineage of creation.</note>

### 9. How the painter is lord of every kind of people and of all things.

The painter is master of all things that can pass through the human mind, for if he has a desire to see beauties that would make him fall in love, he is the lord who can generate them; and if he wishes to see monstrous things that terrify, or those that are buffoonish and laughable, or truly pitiable, he is their lord and creator. And if he wishes to generate desert sites, or shady or cool places in times of heat, he depicts them, and likewise warm places in cold weather. If he wants valleys, it is the same; if he wants to discover a great countryside from high mountain peaks, and if he wants to see the horizon of the sea after them, he is the lord of it; and so too if from low valleys he wants to see high mountains, or from high mountains the low valleys and beaches. And in effect, whatever exists in the universe through essence, presence, or imagination, he has it first in his mind and then in his hands; and these works are of such excellence that they generate a proportionate harmony in a single glance, just as real things do. <note>Leonardo emphasizes that unlike a story told over time, a painting reveals its "harmony"—its total composition—all at once to the eye.</note>

### 10. Of the poet and the painter.

Painting serves a worthier sense than poetry <note>Leonardo considered sight the "prince of senses" and superior to hearing or reading.</note>, and represents the figures of nature's works with more truth than the poet. The works of nature are much worthier than words, which are the works of man; for the same proportion exists between the works of men and those of nature as exists between man and God. Therefore, it is a worthier thing to imitate the things of nature, which are the true likenesses in fact, than to imitate with words the deeds and words of men. And if you, poet, wish to describe the works of nature through your simple profession, imagining various sites and the forms of diverse things, you are overcome by the painter with an infinite proportion of power. But if you wish to clothe yourself in other sciences separate from poetry itself, they are not yours—such as astrology, rhetoric, theology, philosophy, geometry, arithmetic, and the like; then you are no longer a poet, you transform yourself, and are no longer the one we are discussing here. Do you not see that if you wish to go to nature,

<summary>Leonardo argues that painting is a divine "granddaughter of nature" and a superior science because it can instantly manifest anything the mind imagines, surpassing the descriptive power of poetry.</summary>

<page-num>8</page-num>

You <note>Leonardo is addressing the "poet" or the "theorist" in this rhetorical debate.</note> proceed there with the tools of sciences made by others based on the effects of nature, whereas the painter, by himself and without the help of science or other means, goes immediately to the imitation of these works of nature. By this [painting], lovers are moved toward the images of the beloved to speak with the imitated paintings; by this, nations are moved with fervent vows to seek out the images of the gods, rather than to see the works of poets, who represent those same gods with words. By this, animals are deceived: once I saw a painting that deceived a dog through its resemblance to its master, at which the dog rejoiced greatly; and similarly, I have seen dogs bark and try to bite painted dogs, and a monkey do infinite follies against another painted monkey. I have seen a swallow fly and land upon the painted iron bars that project from the windows of buildings; all these are the most marvelous operations of the painter.

## 11. Example between poetry and painting.

The imagination does not see such excellence as the eye sees, because the eye receives the <term>species</term> <note>original: "specie." In Renaissance psychology, "species" were the invisible "likenesses" or "forms" that traveled from an object to the eye.</note> or likenesses of objects, and gives them to the <term>impressiva</term> <note>The "impressiva" was thought to be a faculty in the brain that received sensory impressions before they reached the "common sense."</note>, and from this "impressiva" they go to the <term>common sense</term> <note>original: "senso comune." This was the internal sense that coordinated all five external senses into a single perception.</note>, and there they are judged. But the imagination does not go outside that same common sense, except when it goes to the memory, and there it stops and there it dies, if the thing imagined is not of great excellence. And in this case, poetry finds itself in the mind or the "imaginative" of the poet, who feigns the same things as the painter; by which fictions he wishes to equal himself to the painter, but in truth he is very far from it, as has been shown above. Therefore, in such a case of fiction, we will say with truth that the relationship between the science of painting and poetry is the same as that between a body and its <term>derivative shadow</term> <note>A "derivative shadow" refers to the shadow cast by an object in space, as opposed to the "primary shadow" on the object itself.</note>, and there is even a greater difference; for the shadow of such a body at least enters through the eye into the common sense, but the imagination of such a body does not enter that sense, but is born there in the dark eye. Oh, what a difference there is between imagining such light in the dark eye and seeing it in reality outside of the darkness!

If you, poet, describe a bloody battle, with the dark and gloomy air, by means of the smoke from the terrifying and mortal machines, mixed with the thick dust that makes the air turbid, and the fearful flight of the wretched ones frightened by a horrible death—in this case, the painter surpasses you, because your pen will be worn out before you describe in full what the painter represents to you in an instant with his science. And your tongue will be parched with thirst, and your body overcome by sleep and hunger, before you can demonstrate with words what the painter demonstrates to you in a heartbeat. In which painting nothing is missing except the soul of the things depicted, and in each body is the integrity of that part which can be shown from a single perspective. It would be a long and most tedious thing for poetry to retell all the movements of the participants in such a war, and the parts of their limbs and their ornaments; things which painting, finished with great brevity and truth, places before you. And from this demonstration, there does not—

<summary>Leonardo argues that painting is superior to poetry because it communicates directly and instantaneously to the eye, even deceiving animals, whereas poetry relies on the "dark eye" of the imagination. He uses the vivid example of a battle scene to show how a painter captures in a moment what a poet would take volumes to describe.</summary>

nothing is missing except the noise of the machines, the shouts of the terrifying victors, and the screams and laments of the terrified. These things, too, the poet cannot represent to the sense of hearing. We shall say, therefore, that poetry is a science that operates chiefly for the blind, and painting does the same for the deaf; but painting is so much more worthy insofar as it serves a better sense.

The only true office of the poet is to feign the words of people speaking together, and only these does he represent to the sense of hearing as if they were natural, because in themselves they are natural, created by the human voice; but in all other consequences, he is surpassed by the painter.

But the varieties to which painting extends are much more numerous, beyond comparison, than those to which words extend; for the painter will create infinite things that words cannot name, for lack of appropriate terms for them. Now, do you not see that if the painter wishes to feign animals, or devils in hell, with what abundance of invention he ranges?

Who is there who would not rather lose hearing, smell, and touch, than sight? For he who loses sight is like one who is cast out of the world, because he no longer sees it, nor any of its things; and this life is the sister of death.

## 12. Which is of greater harm to the human species: to lose the eye or the ear.

Animals receive greater harm from the loss of sight than of hearing, for several reasons. First, because by means of sight, food is found, by which one must be nourished, which is necessary to all animals. Second, because through sight one understands the beauty of created things, especially those things that induce love; which the man born blind cannot grasp through hearing, because he never had knowledge of what the beauty of any thing was. There remains to him hearing, through which alone he understands voices and human speech, in which are the names of all things to which a proper name is given. Without the knowledge of these names, one can indeed live happily, as is seen in those born deaf—that is, the mute—by means of <term>drawing</term> <note>original: "disegno"; in Leonardo's time, this encompassed both drawing and the underlying conceptual design or structure of art</note>, in which most mutes take delight. 

And if you should say that sight hinders the fixed and subtle mental cognition with which one penetrates the divine sciences, and that such an impediment led a philosopher to deprive himself of sight <note>Leonardo likely refers to Democritus, who was legendarily said to have blinded himself to think more clearly</note>, to this I reply that such an eye, as lord of the senses, does its duty in providing an impediment to confused and lying "discourses"—not sciences—through which men always dispute with great shouting and waving of hands. And the same should be done by hearing, which is more offended by this, because it desires harmony, in which all the senses are entwined. And if such a philosopher plucked out his eyes to remove the impediment to his discourses, consider that such an act was a companion to his brain and his arguments, for the whole thing was madness. Now, could he not have closed his eyes when he entered into such a frenzy, and kept them closed until such fury consumed itself? But the man was mad, and the discourse mad, and the plucking out of the eyes most foolish.

<summary>Leonardo argues for the superiority of painting over poetry and sight over hearing, claiming that sight is essential for experiencing beauty and finding sustenance, while dismissing the idea that blindness aids philosophical thought.</summary>

### 13. How the science of astronomy <note>original: "astrologia" — in Leonardo's time, the terms for astronomy and astrology were often used interchangeably to describe the study of celestial bodies</note> is born from the eye, because it is generated through it.

There is no part of astronomy that is not the function of visual lines and perspective, the daughter of painting; for the painter is the one who, by the necessity of his art, has given birth to this perspective. It cannot be achieved by itself without lines, and within these lines are enclosed all the various figures of bodies generated by nature, without which the art of the geometer is blind. And if the geometer reduces every surface surrounded by lines to the figure of a square, and every body to the figure of a cube; and arithmetic does the same with its square and cube roots; these two sciences extend only to the knowledge of continuous and discontinuous quantity <note>A classical distinction: continuous quantity refers to geometry (magnitudes), while discontinuous quantity refers to arithmetic (numbers)</note>. But they do not concern themselves with quality, which is the beauty of nature’s works and the ornament of the world.

### 14. The painter who disputes with the poet.

What poet, O lover, will set before you the true image of your idea with as much truth as the painter will do with words? Who will be the one to show you the sites of rivers, woods, valleys, and fields, where your past pleasures are represented, with more truth than the painter? And if you say that painting is a "mute poetry" in itself, unless there is someone to say or speak for it what it represents, do you not see that your book is in a worse state? For even though it has a man to speak for it, nothing is seen of the thing being spoken of, as will be seen of the one who speaks for paintings. These paintings—if the actions are well-proportioned to their mental states <note>original: "accidenti mentali" — Leonardo's term for the outward physical expression of internal thoughts and emotions</note>—will be understood as if they were speaking.

### 15. How painting surpasses all human works by the subtle speculations belonging to it.

The eye, which is called the window of the soul, is the principal way through which the common sense <note>A philosophical concept of the time: a central faculty of the mind that processes and integrates data from all five senses</note> can most copiously and magnificently consider the infinite works of nature; and the ear is the second, which becomes noble through the things recounted that the eye has seen. If you, historians, or poets, or other mathematicians, had not seen things with the eye, you could poorly report them in writing. And if you, poet, depict a history with the "painting" of the pen, the painter with the brush will make it with easier satisfaction, and less tedious to be understood. If you call painting "mute poetry," the painter may also call poetry "blind painting." Now look which is the more harmful monster: the blind man or the mute? If the poet is as free as the painter in his inventions, his fictions do not give as much satisfaction to men as paintings do; for if poetry extends itself with words to depict forms, actions, and places,

<summary>Leonardo argues that painting is the foundation of astronomy and geometry because it masters visual perspective, and he asserts painting's superiority over poetry by labeling the latter "blind painting."</summary>

->The painter moves with the very likenesses of forms to imitate those forms. Now consider: which is closer to man, the name of "man" or the likeness of that man? The name of a man varies in different countries, but the form is not changed except by death. And if the poet serves the senses by way of the ear, the painter does so by way of the eye, which is the worthier sense. But I ask nothing more of such people than that a good painter depict the fury of a battle, and that a poet write of another, and that both be placed before the public together. You will see where the viewers stop more often, where they contemplate more, where more praise is given, and which satisfies better. Certainly painting, being by far more useful and beautiful, will please more. Write the name of God in one place and place His image opposite it, and you will see which will be more revered. If painting embraces within itself all the forms of nature, you have nothing but names, which are not universal like forms; if you have the effects of demonstrations, we have the demonstrations of the effects.<-

Let a poet be chosen to describe the beauties of a woman to her lover, and let a painter be chosen to depict her; it will be seen where nature will more strongly turn the enamored judge. Certainly, the trial of things should allow experience to give the verdict. You have placed painting among the mechanical arts <note>In the Renaissance, "mechanical arts" were seen as manual labor, inferior to the "liberal arts" like rhetoric or music which were seen as purely intellectual.</note>. Certainly, if painters were as capable as you are of praising their own works in writing, I believe painting would not lie under such a lowly title. If you call it mechanical because it is first manual—since the hands represent what they find in the imagination—you writers draw manually with the pen what is found in your intellect. And if you say it is mechanical because it is done for a price, who falls into this error (if error it can be called) more than you? If you read for the sake of studies, do you not go to whoever rewards you most? Do you perform any work without some reward? Though I do not say this to blame such opinions, for every labor expects a reward; and a poet might say: "I will create a fiction that signifies great things." The painter will do the same, as *Apelles* did with *Calumny* <note>A reference to a famous lost painting by the ancient Greek artist Apelles, described by Lucian, which became a standard for allegorical painting in the Renaissance.</note>. If you say that poetry is more eternal, for this I will say that the works of a coppersmith are more eternal, since time preserves them longer than your works or ours; nonetheless, it possesses little imagination, and painting can, by painting upon copper with glass colors <note>Likely referring to enamel painting or "vetrificazione," which Leonardo admired for its durability.</note>, be made much more eternal. *By our art, we may be called the grandchildren of God.* If poetry extends into moral philosophy, painting extends into natural philosophy; if the former describes the operations of the mind that considers it, the latter considers what the mind operates through movements; if the former terrifies peoples with hellish fictions, the latter does the same with those same things in action. Let the poet set himself to depict a beauty, a ferocity, a foul and ugly thing, or a monstrous one, alongside the painter; let him make transformations of forms in his own way as he wishes, and the painter will still satisfy more. Have we not seen paintings possess such conformity with the thing imitated that they have deceived both men and animals?

<sig>[§ 16</sig>

## 16. The difference between painting and poetry.

Painting is a poetry that is seen and not heard, and poetry is a painting that is heard and not seen. Therefore, these two poetries—or, if you prefer, two paintings—have exchanged the senses through which they must penetrate the intellect. For if both are painting, they must pass to the common sense <note>The "common sense" (sensus communis) was believed in Renaissance psychology to be the part of the brain where all sensory inputs were coordinated.</note> through the most noble sense, which is the eye; and if both are poetry, they must pass through the less noble sense, which is hearing. Therefore, we shall submit painting to the judgment of one born deaf, and poetry shall be judged by one born blind. If a painting depicts movements appropriate to the mental accidents <note>Leonardo uses "mental accidents" to mean the internal emotions or thoughts that cause a person to move or change their facial expression.</note> of the figures acting in any given situation, the one born deaf will undoubtedly understand the actions and intentions of the actors; but the one born blind will never understand anything shown by the poet that might bring honor to that poetry. This is because among its noble parts is the depiction of gestures and the composition of stories, and ornate and delightful places with transparent waters through which one sees the green depths of their courses, the waves playing over meadows and tiny pebbles, with the plants that mingle with them alongside darting fish, and similar descriptions. Such things might as well be told to a stone as to one born blind, because he has never seen any of the things that compose the beauty of the world: namely light, darkness, color, body, figure, location, distance, proximity, motion, and rest—which are the ten ornaments of nature. But the deaf person, having lost the less noble sense, even though he has also lost speech (because having never heard anyone speak, he could never learn a language), will nevertheless understand every "accident" of the human body better than one who speaks and hears; and similarly, he will know the works of painters and what is represented in them, and for what purpose such figures are intended.

## 17. What the difference is from painting to poetry.

Painting is a mute poetry, and poetry is a blind painting, and both go about imitating nature as much as is possible for their powers; and through both, one can demonstrate many moral customs, as Apelles <note>Apelles was the most celebrated painter of ancient Greece; his lost painting "Calumny" was famously described in ancient texts and recreated by Renaissance artists like Botticelli.</note> did with his *Calumny*. But from painting—because it serves the eye, a sense more noble than the ear (the object of poetry)—there results a harmonic proportion. That is to say, just as from many and various voices joined together at the same time there results a harmonic proportion which so pleases the sense of hearing that the listeners remain in stunned admiration, almost half-alive; so much more will the proportional beauties of an angelic face placed in a painting do. From this proportionality there results a harmonic concord, which serves the eye in the same moment that music serves the ear. And if such harmony of beauties is shown to the lover of the one whose beauties are imitated, he will undoubtedly remain in stupendous admiration and joy.

...incomparable and superior to all other senses. But from poetry—which must extend itself to the representation of a perfect beauty, through the particular representation of each part from which the aforementioned harmony in painting is composed—no other grace results than what would happen in music if each voice were heard by itself at different times, from which no <term>concord<note>Leonardo uses the term "concento," referring to the harmonious sounding together of multiple musical parts.</note></term> would be composed. It is as if we wanted to show a face part by part, always covering those that were shown first; in such demonstrations, forgetfulness does not allow for the composition of any proportionality of harmony, because the eye does not embrace them with its <term>visual faculty<note>The "virtù visiva" was considered an active power of the eye to perceive the world.</note></term> at one and the same time. The same happens with the beauties of any thing imagined by the poet: because their parts are spoken separately at separate times, the memory receives no harmony from them.

### 18. The difference between poetry and painting.

Painting represents itself to you immediately with that demonstration for which its creator has generated it, and gives that pleasure to the highest sense which anything created by nature can give. And in this case the poet, who sends the same things to the <term>common sense<note>The "sensus communis," the mental faculty where all sensory inputs are integrated.</note></term> through the path of hearing (a lesser sense), gives no more pleasure to the eye than if one were to hear a thing being told. Now see what a difference there is between hearing a thing told that gives pleasure to the eye over a long duration of time, or seeing it with that swiftness with which natural things are seen. And even though the works of poets are read over a long interval of time, many are the times they are not understood, and it is necessary to make various commentaries upon them—in which such commentators very rarely understand what the poet’s mind was; and many times readers read only a small part of their works due to lack of time. But the work of the painter is immediately understood by its viewers.

### 19. On the difference and also the similarity that painting has with poetry.

Painting represents its essence to you in an instant in the visual faculty, and through the very medium by which the <term>receptive faculty<note>The "impressiva," the mental stage where sensory data is first imprinted before being processed by the common sense.</note></term> receives natural objects—and also at the same time in which the harmonic proportionality of the parts that compose the whole (which satisfies the sense) is formed. Poetry reports the same, but through a medium less worthy than the eye, which carries the representations of the named things into the receptive faculty more confusedly and with more slowness than the eye does. The eye is the true medium between the object and the receptive faculty, which immediately conveys with supreme truth the true surfaces and figures of what is presented before it. From these arises the proportionality called harmony, which satisfies the sense with sweet concord, no differently than the proportions of different voices do for the sense of hearing; which is still less worthy than [the eye]...

<summary>Leonardo argues that painting is superior to poetry because it provides an immediate, harmonious "totality" to the eye, whereas poetry and music must be experienced part-by-part over time, which causes the viewer to forget the harmony of the whole.</summary>

<page-num>14</page-num>
<header>LEONARDO DA VINCI [§ 19</header>

...than that of the eye, because as much as is born <note>Referring to the notes of music or the sounds of words.</note>, so much dies; and it is as swift in dying as it is in being born. This cannot happen with the sense of sight, because if you represent to the eye a human beauty composed of the proportionality of beautiful limbs, that beauty is not so mortal, nor does it destroy itself so quickly as music does. Instead, it has great permanence and allows itself to be seen and considered. It is not reborn, as music is through repeated playing, nor does it cause you weariness; rather, it makes you fall in love. It is the reason why all the senses, together with the eye, wish to possess it, and it seems they want to compete with the eye. It seems that the mouth would like it for itself within the body; the ear takes pleasure in hearing its beauties; the sense of touch would like to penetrate it through all its <term>pores<note>Original: "meati." This refers to the channels or passages of the body through which the senses were thought to operate.</note></term>; the nose also would like to receive the air that it continually breathes out.

But the beauty of such [living] harmony is destroyed by time in a few years; this does not happen to such beauty when imitated by the painter, because time preserves it for a long duration. And the eye, in performing its duty, takes the same true pleasure from such a painted beauty as it would from living beauty. It lacks only touch, which acts as an <term>elder brother<note>Leonardo uses "maggior fratello" to describe touch. In his hierarchy of the senses, touch is more primal and physically immediate ("older"), but sight is more intellectual and "noble."</note></term> at that same time; touch, once it has achieved its aim, does not prevent reason from considering the divine beauty. And in this case, the painting imitated from that beauty largely compensates for the loss, which a poet’s description cannot do. The poet, in this instance, wishes to be made equal to the painter, but he does not realize that his words, in mentioning the limbs of such a beauty, are divided from one another by time. Forgetfulness intervenes and divides the proportions, which he cannot name without great long-windedness. And because he cannot name them [all at once], he cannot compose that harmonic proportionality, which is made of divine proportions.

For this reason, the same moment of time that encompasses the contemplation of a painted beauty cannot provide a described beauty. He who tries to put into the ear what should be put before the eye commits a sin against nature. Let the office of music enter there, and do not put there the science of painting, the true imitator of the natural forms of all things.

What moves you, O man, to abandon your own homes in the city, to leave parents and friends, and to go into rural places over mountains and valleys, if not the natural beauty of the world? If you consider it well, you enjoy this beauty only through the sense of sight. And if the poet wishes to call himself a painter in this case as well, why do you not take the places described by the poet and stay at home without feeling the excessive heat of the sun? Would this not be more useful and less tiring for you, because it is done in the cool shade without movement or the danger of illness? But your soul could not enjoy the benefit of the eyes, the **windows of its habitations**, and it could not receive the <term>species<note>In Renaissance optics, "specie" (species) were the visual forms or "images" that objects were thought to transmit through the air to the eye.</note></term> of cheerful places; it could not see the shaded valleys striped by the play of winding rivers; it could not see the various flowers which, with their colors, create a harmony for the eye; nor could it see all the other things that can be represented to the eye.

But if the painter, in the cold and rigid times of winter, places before you those same painted landscapes—and others where you have taken your pleasures near some spring—where you can see yourself again as a lover with your beloved in flowery meadows, under the sweet shadows of greening plants, would you not receive far greater pleasure than from hearing such an effect described?

<page-num>15</page-num>

...from the poet? Here the poet responds, and while yielding to the aforementioned reasons, he claims that he surpasses the painter because he makes men speak and reason through various fictions, in which he feigns things that do not exist; and that he can incite men to take up arms, and will describe the heavens, the stars, nature, the arts, and everything else. To which it is answered: that none of these things of which he speaks is his own proper profession. If he wishes to speak and orate, he must be convinced that in this he is defeated by the orator; if he speaks of astrology, he has stolen it from the astrologer; and of philosophy, from the philosopher. In effect, poetry has no proper seat of its own, nor does it deserve one any more than a peddler <note>original: "merciaio," a traveling merchant or huckster</note> who gathers together merchandise made by various different craftsmen. 

But the divinity of the science of painting considers works both human and divine, which are bounded by their surfaces—that is, the lines of the limits of bodies—with which she commands the sculptor toward the perfection of his statues. This science, through its fundamental principle, which is drawing <note>original: "disegno," which in the Renaissance implied both the physical act of drawing and the intellectual concept of design</note>, teaches the architect how to make his building pleasing to the eye; it teaches the makers of various vessels, the goldsmiths, weavers, and embroiderers. It discovered the characters with which different languages are expressed; it gave numerals to the mathematicians; it taught the figures to geometry; and it teaches the masters of perspective, the astronomers, the toolmakers <note>original: "macchinatori," those who design machines or engines</note>, and the engineers.

### 20. Of the eye.

The eye, through which the beauty of the universe is mirrored by those who contemplate it, is of such excellence that whoever consents to its loss deprives himself of the representation of all the works of nature. It is through the sight of these things that the soul remains content within its human prison <note>A common Neoplatonic metaphor suggesting the body is a temporary jail for the soul</note>, by means of the eyes, through which the soul represents to itself all the various things of nature. But he who loses them leaves that soul in a dark prison, where all hope of seeing the sun—the light of the whole world—is lost. And how many are those to whom the darkness of night is utterly hateful, even though it is of short duration! Oh, what would they do if such darkness were the companion of their entire lives? Certainly, there is no one who would not rather lose his sense of hearing and smell than his sight; for though the loss of hearing entails the loss of all sciences that consist of words, one consents to this only so as not to lose the beauty of the world, which consists of the surfaces of bodies, both accidental and natural, which are reflected in the human eye.

### 21. Dispute of the poet with the painter, and the difference between poetry and painting.

The poet says that his science is invention and measure; and this is the simple body of poetry: the invention of subject matter and the measure of the verses, and that it then clothes itself in all the other sciences. To which the painter responds that he has the same obligations in the science of painting—namely, invention and measure: invention in the subject matter which he...

<note>Leonardo continues his rebuttal against the poet from the previous page.</note>
...he must feign, and use measure in painted things so that they are not disproportionate; but he does not clothe himself in those three sciences <note>Likely referring to the quadrivium sciences like music or geometry mentioned previously.</note>; rather, the others largely clothe themselves in painting. Take astrology, for example, which can do nothing without perspective—and perspective is a principal member of painting itself. I speak here of mathematical astrology <note>original: "astrologia matematica"; in Leonardo's time, this referred to what we now call astronomy.</note>, and not of that fallacious judicial astrology <note>original: "fallace giudiciale"; the practice of predicting the future or character through horoscopes, which Leonardo despised.</note>—may those who make a living from it by deceiving fools forgive me. The poet says that he describes one thing that represents another, full of beautiful maxims. The painter says he has the authority to do the same, and in this regard, he too is a poet. And if the poet says he can inflame men to love—which is the primary drive of all animal species—the painter has the power to do the same, all the more so because he places before the lover the very likeness of the beloved. The lover often interacts with this image, kissing it and speaking to it, which he would never do with the same beauties if they were merely set before him by a writer. And painting so far surpasses the wits of men <note>The Vienna edition of 1882 adds the words: "that it induces them" here.</note> to love and fall in love with a painting that does not even represent a living woman. 

It once happened to me that I made a painting representing a divine subject, which was bought by someone who loved it; he wished to have the symbols of its divinity removed so that he could kiss it without suspicion. But in the end, his conscience overcame his sighs and lust, and he was forced to remove it from his house. Now you, poet, try to describe a beauty without representing a living thing, and see if you can rouse men to such desires with it. If you say: "I will describe hell to you, or paradise, and other delights or terrors," the painter surpasses you, because he will place before you things that, while remaining silent, will speak of such delights or will terrify you and move your soul to flight. Painting moves the senses more readily than poetry. And if you say that with words you can move a people to tears or laughter, I tell you it is not you who moves them, but the orator—and that is a science that is not poetry. But the painter will move people to laughter, though not easily to tears, because weeping is a more profound affliction than laughter. A painter once made a picture that caused anyone who saw it to immediately yawn, and this accident was repeated as long as they kept their eyes on the painting, which itself was depicted as yawning. Others have painted libidinous acts, so lustful that they incited the viewers to the same "party"; poetry will not do this. And if you write down the description of certain gods, such writing will not be held in the same veneration as the painted image, because vows and various prayers will be continually offered to such a painting. Various generations from different provinces and from across the eastern seas will flock to it, and they will ask for help from the painting, not from the writing.

## 22. The poet's argument against the painter.

You say, O painter, that your art is adored, but do not credit yourself with such virtue; credit the subject that such a painting represents. Here the painter responds: O you, poet,

...that you still make yourself an imitator <note>Addressing the poet</note>, why do you not represent with your words things such that your letters—the containers of those words—might also be adored? But let us praise the one of words so much the less, insofar as words are accidental and created by a lesser author than the works of nature, of which the painter is an imitator; which nature is defined within the figures of their surfaces.

### 23. Response of King Matthias to a poet who competed with a painter.

On the birthday of King Matthias <note>King Matthias Corvinus of Hungary (1443–1490), a famous patron of the arts and sciences whom Leonardo likely knew of through the Sforza court.</note>, a poet brought him a work written in praise of the day on which the King was born for the benefit of the world; and a painter presented him with a portrait of his beloved. Immediately the King closed the poet's book and turned to the painting, fixing his gaze upon it with great admiration. Then the poet, deeply indignant, said: "O King, read, read, and you will hear something of greater substance than a mute painting." Then the King, feeling himself reproached for looking at mute things, said: "O poet, be silent, for you know not what you say; this painting serves a better sense than yours, which is for the blind. Give me something that I can see and touch, and not only that I can hear; and do not blame my choice for having placed your work under my elbow, while I hold this of the painter with both hands, offering it to my eyes. For the hands have taken it upon themselves to serve a worthier sense than hearing. And I for my part judge that such proportion exists from the science of the painter to that of the poet, as exists between the senses from which these objects are made."

"Do you not know that our soul is composed of harmony, and harmony is not generated except in instants in which the proportionalities of objects are made to be seen or heard? Do you not see that in your science there is no proportionality created in an instant? Rather, one part is born from another successively, and the succeeding part is not born if the preceding one does not die. For this reason, I judge your invention to be far inferior to that of the painter, solely because from it no harmonic proportionality is composed. It does not satisfy the mind of the listener or viewer as does the proportionality of the beautiful limbs composing the divine beauties of this face before me, which, joined all together at the same time, give me so much pleasure with their divine proportion that I judge no other thing made by man upon the earth can give greater."

There is no judgment so senseless that, if proposed which is more to be chosen—to stay in perpetual darkness or to lose one's hearing—would not immediately say he would rather lose his hearing, along with his sense of smell, before remaining blind. Because he who loses his sight loses the beauty of the world with all the forms of created things, and the deaf man only loses the sound made by the movement of struck air, which is the smallest thing in the world.

...is for the deaf. You who say that a science is more noble in proportion to the dignity of the subject it treats, and that for this reason a false imagination of the essence of God is worth more than the imagination of a less worthy thing; for this reason we shall say that painting—which extends only to the works of God—is more worthy than poetry, which extends only to the lying fictions of human works. With rightful lamentation, painting grieves for being cast out from the number of the liberal arts <note>The "Liberal Arts" traditionally included the Trivium (grammar, logic, rhetoric) and Quadrivium (arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy); Leonardo fought to have painting recognized among them due to its basis in geometry and optics.</note>; seeing as she is the true daughter of nature, and operated by the most worthy sense. Therefore, O writers, you have wrongly left her out of the number of said liberal arts, seeing as this art attends not only to the works of nature, but to infinite things that nature never created.

### 24. Conclusion between the poet and the painter.

Since we have concluded that poetry is, in the highest degree, a means of comprehension for the blind, and that painting does the same for the deaf, we shall say that painting is worth so much more than poetry as painting serves a better and more noble sense than poetry. This nobility is proven to be triple the nobility of the three other senses, because it has been chosen to rather lose hearing, smell, and touch than the sense of sight. For he who loses sight loses the view and beauty of the universe, and remains like one who is enclosed alive in a tomb in which he has motion and life. Now, do you not see that the eye embraces the beauty of the whole world? It is the head of astrology <note>In Leonardo's time, "astrology" often encompassed what we now call astronomy.</note>; it creates cosmography; it counsels and corrects all human arts; it moves man to diverse parts of the world. This is the prince of mathematics; its sciences are most certain. This has measured the heights and sizes of the stars; this has found the elements and their locations; this has enabled the prediction of future things by means of the course of the stars. This has generated architecture and perspective, and this has generated divine painting. 

O most excellent thing above all others created by God! What praises can express your nobility? What peoples, what languages can fully describe your true operation? This is the window of the human body, through which its way (?) <note>The original Italian "via" is followed by a question mark in the transcription, suggesting a possible error in the source manuscript; it likely refers to the soul's path or perception.</note> contemplates and enjoys the beauty of the world. Because of this, the soul is content in its human prison, and without this, that human prison is its torment. For this reason, human industry has discovered fire, by means of which the eye regains what darkness previously took away. This has adorned nature with agriculture and delightful gardens. But why must I extend myself in such a high and long discourse? What thing is there that is not done through the eye? It moves men from the East to the West; it discovered navigation. And in this, it surpasses nature, because simple natural things are finite, but the works that the eye commands of the hands are infinite, as the painter demonstrates in the fictions of infinite forms of animals and herbs, plants and places.

<summary>Leonardo argues for the superiority of painting over poetry by exalting the eye as the most noble sense organ and the source of all sciences and arts. He characterizes the eye as the "window of the soul" that makes life within the body bearable through the appreciation of the universe's beauty.</summary>

### 25. How music should be called the sister and the junior of painting.

Music is not to be called anything other than the sister of painting, considering that she is the subject of hearing—the second sense after the eye—and composes harmony through the conjunction of her proportional parts operated at the same time. These parts are forced to be born and to die in one or more harmonic intervals <note>original: "tempi armonici"</note>, which intervals surround the proportionality of the members of which such harmony is composed, not otherwise than the circumferential line does for the members from which human beauty is generated. But painting excels and reigns over music because she does not die immediately after her creation, as does the unfortunate music; rather, she remains in being, and demonstrates to you as living that which in fact is a single surface. O marvelous science, you preserve in life the fleeting beauties of mortals, which have more permanence than the works of nature, which are continually changed by time, leading them to their inevitable old age; and such a science has such a proportion with divine nature as its works have with the works of nature itself, and for this reason, it is adored.

### 26. The musician speaks with the painter.

The musician says that his science is to be equated to that of the painter, because it composes a body of many members, of which the observer contemplates all the grace in as many harmonic intervals as there are moments in which it is born and dies; and with those intervals, it gracefully entertains the soul that resides in the body of the contemplator. But the painter responds and says that the body composed of human members does not give pleasure through harmonic intervals in which beauty must vary itself to give form to another, nor that it must be born and die in those moments; instead, he makes it permanent for many, many years, and it is of such excellence that it preserves in life that harmony of proportioned members which nature, with all her strength, could not preserve. How many paintings have preserved the image <note>original: "simulacro"</note> of a divine beauty of which time or death has briefly destroyed the natural example, and the work of the painter has remained more worthy than that of nature, his mistress!

### 27. The painter gives the degrees of things opposite the eye, just as the musician gives those of the voices opposite the ear.

Although things opposite the eye touch one another step by step, nonetheless I will make my rule from twenty to twenty cubits <term>braccia: a Florentine measure of length, roughly 23 inches</term>, just as the musician has done among voices; for although the voice is united and joined together, he has nonetheless established few degrees from voice to voice, calling them first, second, third, fourth, and fifth, and so from degree to degree he has given names to the variety of the rising and falling of the voice.

<summary>Leonardo argues that painting is superior to music because it is permanent rather than fleeting, and he compares the mathematical proportions of visual perspective to the intervals of musical scales.</summary>

If you, O musician, say that painting is mechanical because it is performed with the exercise of the hands, and music is performed with the mouth—which is a human organ, though not used here for the sense of taste, just as the hand <gloss>I</gloss> <note>The hand is the organ for the sense of touch.</note> is for the sense of touch—then words are even less worthy than deeds. But you, writer of sciences, do you not copy with your hand, writing down what is in your mind, just as the painter does? And if you were to say that music is composed of proportion, I have followed that same path with painting, as you shall better see.

That thing is more worthy which satisfies a better sense. Therefore, painting, which satisfies the sense of sight, is nobler than music, which only satisfies hearing. That thing is nobler which has more eternity; therefore music, which goes on consuming itself even as it is born, is less worthy than painting, which is made eternal with glazes <note>original: "vetri," likely referring to glass-like glazes or enamels that preserve color.</note>. That thing which contains within itself more universality and variety of things shall be called of greater excellence. Therefore, painting is to be preferred above all other operations, because it contains all the forms that exist, and even those that do not exist in nature; it is more to be magnified and exalted than music, which only attends to the voice. With painting, the likenesses of the gods are made; around it, divine worship is conducted, which is adorned by music serving it; with this, lovers are given the likeness of the cause of their loves; with this, beauties are preserved which time and nature make fleeting; with this, we preserve the likenesses of famous men. And if you should say: music is made eternal by writing it down, we do the same here with letters. Therefore, since you have placed music among the <term>liberal arts</term> <note>The traditional medieval curriculum of "higher" subjects like grammar, logic, and music, which Leonardo argues should include painting.</note>, you must either place painting there as well, or remove music. And if you should say: base men practice it, so too is music spoiled by those who do not know it. If you say that the non-mechanical sciences are those of the mind, I tell you that painting is of the mind, and that she—just as music and geometry consider the proportions of continuous quantities, and arithmetic those of discontinuous ones—considers all continuous quantities, and the qualities of the proportions of shadows, lights, and distances within her perspective.

### 28. Conclusion of the poet, the painter, and the musician.

There is as much difference in the representation of bodily things between the painter and the poet as there is between bodies that are dismembered and those that are whole. This is because the poet, in describing the beauty or ugliness of any body, demonstrates it to you member by member and at different times, whereas the painter lets you see it all at once. The poet cannot set down with words the true figure of the limbs of which a whole is composed in the way a painter can, who places it before you with that truth which is possible in nature. And the same happens to the poet as to the musician, who sings alone a song composed for four singers, and sings first the soprano, then the tenor, then follows the contralto, and then the bass; from this, the grace of harmonic proportionality does not result,

<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s argument from page 20, where he asserts the superiority of painting over music and poetry. Having just argued that painting is "more eternal" than music, he now focuses on how poetry fails to capture the "divine harmony" of a whole composition because it must describe things one by one over time, rather than all at once.</meta>

<header>a 29 ] TREATISE ON PAINTING — PART ONE</header>

which [poetry] unfolds in harmonic intervals of time. The poet acts like someone showing you a beautiful face member by member; doing so, you would never be satisfied by its beauty, which consists solely of the **divine proportionality** <note>Leonardo uses this term to describe the mathematical relationship between parts that creates a beautiful whole.</note> of the aforementioned limbs composed together. Only in a single moment do these parts compose that divine harmony of the joined members, which often robs those who see them of their very liberty. Music, too, creates sweet melodies in its harmonic time, composed of its various voices—yet the poet is deprived of such harmonic description. And although poetry enters through the sense of hearing to the seat of judgment, just as music does, the poet cannot describe the harmony of music because he does not have the power to say different things at the same time. This is unlike the harmonic proportionality of painting, which is composed of different members at one and the same time; the sweetness of these parts is judged simultaneously, both in general and in particular. In general, regarding the intent of the whole composition; in particular, regarding the intent of the components from which the whole is made. 

For this reason, the poet lags far behind the painter in the representation of bodily things, and behind the musician in the representation of invisible things. But if the poet borrows help from other sciences, he can appear at the fairs like other merchants who carry various things made by many inventors. The poet does this when he borrows the science of others, such as that of the orator, philosopher, astrologer, cosmographer, and the like—sciences which are entirely separate from the poet’s own craft. Therefore, the poet is a broker who brings different people together to conclude a bargain. And if you wish to find the poet’s own proper office, you will find it is nothing other than being a gatherer of things stolen from various sciences, with which he makes a "lying composition," or, to put it more honestly, <gloss>1</gloss> a "fictional composition." In this free fiction, the poet makes himself equal to the painter—yet this fiction is the weakest part of painting.

## 29. Which science is mechanical, and which is not.

They say that knowledge is **mechanical** <term>mechanical: In Leonardo's time, "mechanical" arts were often looked down upon as mere manual labor, as opposed to the "liberal" arts of the mind.</term> when it is born from experience, and **scientific** when it begins and ends in the mind, and **semi-mechanical** when it is born from science and ends in manual operation. But to me, it seems that those sciences are vain and full of errors which are not born from **experience**, the mother of all certainty, and which do not end in a known experience—that is, those whose origin, middle, or end does not pass through any of the five senses. And if we doubt the certainty of everything that passes through the senses, how much more should we doubt things that rebel against those senses, such as the essence of God and the soul and similar matters, <gloss>2</gloss> over which people are always disputing and contending. And it truly happens that always—

---

# LEONARDO DA VINCI [§ 29]

Where reason is lacking, shouting takes its place, which does not happen in certain things. For this reason, we shall say that where there is shouting, there is no true science, because truth has a single conclusion; once this is published, the dispute is destroyed forever, and if the dispute arises again, it is a lying and confused science, and not a reborn certainty. But true sciences are those which experience <note>original: "speranza" (hope), though contextually Leonardo often implies "sperienza" (experience)</note> has caused to penetrate through the senses, imposing silence on the tongues of litigants. These do not feed their investigators on dreams, but always proceed successively from the first true and known principles, with true sequences until the end. This is seen in the primary mathematics—that is, number and measure, called arithmetic and geometry—which treat with ultimate truth the discontinuous and continuous quantity. Here, no one will argue that two threes make more or less than six, nor that a triangle has angles smaller than two right angles; rather, with eternal silence, every argument is destroyed, and they are enjoyed <gloss>I</gloss> in peace by their devotees, which the lying mental sciences cannot do. 

And if you should say that such true and known sciences are of a mechanical species because they cannot be completed except manually, I will say the same of all the arts that pass through the hands of writers, which are a species of drawing, a member of painting. Astrology and the others also pass through manual operations, but first they are mental, just as painting is; it exists first in the mind of its observer <note>speculatore: one who contemplates or investigates</note>, and cannot reach its perfection without manual operation. Regarding the scientific and true principles of painting: first, one establishes what a shaded body is, what is primary shadow and derivative shadow, and what is light—that is, darkness, light, color, body, figure, location, distance, proximity, motion, and rest. These are understood by the mind alone without manual labor; and this is the science of painting, which remains in the mind of those who contemplate it, from which the operation is then born, which is far more worthy than the aforementioned contemplation or science.

After this comes sculpture, a most worthy art, but not practiced with such excellence of genius, seeing as in two principal cases it is less difficult than the methods the painter uses in his own art. Sculpture is aided by nature—namely, by perspective, shadows, and lights. Furthermore, it does not imitate colors, for which the painter toils to ensure that the shadows are companions to the lights.

### 30. Why painting is not numbered among the sciences.

Because writers have had no knowledge of the science of painting, they have been unable to describe its degrees and parts. And since painting does not demonstrate its end through words, it has remained, through ignorance, behind the aforementioned sciences.

sciences, without losing its divinity because of this. And truly, it is not without reason that they have not ennobled it, because it ennobles itself by its own merit without the aid of others' tongues, no differently than the excellent works of nature do. And if painters have not described it in writing and reduced it to a formal science, it is not the fault of painting. Because few painters make a profession of letters, as their lives are not long enough to understand them, should we therefore say that painting is less noble? Should we say that the virtues of herbs, stones, and plants do not exist because men have not known them? Certainly not; we shall say that these herbs remain noble in themselves without the aid of human tongues or letters.

### 31. Begins concerning sculpture, and whether it is a science or not.

Sculpture is not a <term>science</term> <note>Leonardo uses "science" to mean a body of knowledge based on universal principles and mental reasoning</note> but a <term>most mechanical art</term>, because it produces sweat and bodily fatigue for its practitioner, and the simple measurements of the limbs and the nature of movements and poses are sufficient for such an artist. Thus it ends in itself, demonstrating to the eye what the object is, and it provides no wonder to its contemplator, as does painting, which on a flat surface, by force of science, demonstrates vast landscapes with distant horizons.

### 32. Difference between painting and sculpture.

Between painting and sculpture I find no other difference except that the sculptor carries out his works with greater physical fatigue than the painter, and the painter carries out his works with greater mental fatigue. This is proved to be true, since the sculptor, in making his work, uses the strength of his arms and percussion to wear away the marble or other surplus stone that exceeds the figure enclosed within it. This is a most mechanical exercise, often accompanied by great sweat composed of dust and turned into mud, with his face smeared and entirely floured with marble dust so that he looks like a baker, and covered with tiny chips, so that he appears to have been snowed upon; and his dwelling is filthy and full of stone chips and dust. The exact opposite happens to the painter—speaking of excellent painters and sculptors—for the painter sits with great ease before his work, well-dressed, and moves the lightest brush with beautiful colors, adorned with garments as he pleases. His dwelling is full of beautiful paintings and is clean, often accompanied by music or readers of various and fine works, which are heard with great pleasure without the din of hammers or other mixed noises. Furthermore, the sculptor, in bringing his works to completion, must make for each figure in the round many <term>outlines</term> <note>original: "dintorni" - the profiles or contours of a 3D object viewed from different angles</note>, so that the figure results in grace from every aspect; and these outlines are only created by the balance of high and low relief, which he cannot place truthfully unless he moves to the side to see it in profile,

<summary>Leonardo argues that painting is inherently noble despite a lack of written theory and contrasts it with sculpture, which he dismisses as a "mechanical" and messy labor compared to the intellectual and refined practice of painting.</summary>
