<meta>This page continues Leonardo’s "Paragone" (comparison of the arts), specifically addressing the sculptor's claim that their work requires more mental effort and the painter's rebuttal regarding the complexity of their respective sciences.</meta>

<page-num>24</page-num>
<header>LEONARDO DA VINCI [§ 32</header>

...that is, that the boundaries of the concavities and reliefs are seen to have borders with the air that touches them. But in truth, this adds no labor to the artist, considering that he, like the painter, has true knowledge of all the boundaries of things seen from every direction; which knowledge is always potentially available to the painter as much as to the sculptor. 

But the sculptor, having to carve out where he wishes to make the intervals between muscles, and to leave material where he wishes to make the reliefs of those muscles, cannot generate them with their proper shape—beyond having established their length and width—unless he moves sideways, bending or raising himself in such a way that he sees the true height of the muscles and the true depth of their intervals. These are judged by the sculptor from such a position, and through this method of checking the outlines <note>original: "dintorni"</note> they are corrected; otherwise, he will never properly place the boundaries or the true figures of his sculptures. 

And this method, they say, is a mental labor for the sculptor, whereas he actually gains nothing but bodily fatigue; because as for the mind, or rather the judgment, he has nothing to do but correct the outlines of the limbs in such a profile where the muscles are too high; and this is the sculptor's ordinary task in bringing his works to completion. This ordinary task is guided by the true knowledge of all the boundaries of the figures of bodies from every direction. 

The sculptor says that if he removes too much, he can no longer add to it, unlike the painter. To which one responds: if his art were perfect, he would have removed only what was sufficient through the knowledge of measurements, and not too much. This over-carving arises from his ignorance, which makes him remove more or less than he should. But I do not speak of these men, for they are not masters, but <term>wasters of marble</term> <note>original: "guastatori di marmi"</note>; true masters do not trust the judgment of the eye, because it always deceives, as is proven by anyone who tries to divide a line into two equal parts by eye alone, for experience often proves the judgment wrong. 

Therefore, out of such suspicion, good judges always fear, which the ignorant do not; and for this reason, they constantly govern themselves with the knowledge of the measurement of each length, thickness, and width of the limbs, and by doing so, they do not remove more than they ought. 

The painter has ten various discourses <note>or "modes of reasoning"</note> with which he brings his works to completion: namely, light, darkness, color, body, figure, location, distance, proximity, motion, and rest. The sculptor only has to consider body, figure, location, motion, and rest. He does not trouble himself with darkness or light, because nature generates them by itself in his sculptures; nothing of color; of distance or proximity he troubles himself only moderately—that is, he uses nothing but <term>linear perspective</term>, but not the perspective of colors, which vary at different distances from the eye in their hue and in the clarity of their boundaries and shapes. Therefore, sculpture requires less discourse, and consequently involves less mental labor than painting.

### 33. The painter and the sculptor.

The sculptor says his art is more worthy than painting, insofar as it is more eternal because it fears moisture, fire, heat, and cold less than painting does. To him, one responds that such a thing does not grant more dignity to the sculptor, because...

# TREATISE ON PAINTING — PART ONE

<meta>a 33]</meta>
->4<-
<meta>L. DA VINCI — Treatise on Painting.</meta>

Such permanence <note>Referring to the physical durability of the artwork.</note> arises from the material and not from the artist; this same dignity can also belong to painting, by painting with glass colors <note>Enamels or glazes.</note> upon metals or terracotta, and then making them flow in a furnace and later polishing them with various instruments to create a flat and lustrous surface. This is seen in our own day in various places in France and Italy, and especially in Florence within the family of the <term>Robbia</term> <note>The della Robbia family, famous for their innovative glazed terracotta sculptures and reliefs.</note>, who have found a way to execute every great work of painting upon terracotta covered in glass. It is true that this is subject to impact and breakage, just like marble sculpture, but it is not immune to the damage of destroyers <note>original: "ma non è a' distruttori come le figure di bronzo" — The manuscript suggests that while bronze might be melted down, glazed clay is simply smashed.</note> in the way that bronze figures are; however, in terms of eternity it joins with sculpture, and in beauty it surpasses it beyond comparison, because in painting the two perspectives are joined <note>Leonardo refers to linear perspective (the geometry of space) and atmospheric perspective (the way colors change with distance).</note>, while in sculpture in the round there is none that is not created by nature itself. The sculptor, in making a figure in the round, makes only two figures, and not an infinite number for the infinite viewpoints from which it can be seen; of these two figures, one is seen from the front and the other from behind. This is proven to be the case, because if you make a figure in mid-relief viewed from the front, you will never say you have done more work in your demonstration than the painter does in a figure made from the same viewpoint; and the same happens for a figure facing backward. But <term>basso rilievo</term> <note>low relief: sculpture that projects only slightly from the background.</note> requires incomparably more intellectual study than <term>tutto rilievo</term> <note>sculpture in the round.</note>, and it approaches the greatness of the study required for painting because it is bound to <term>prospettiva</term> <note>perspective.</note>. Sculpture in the round does not concern itself at all with such knowledge, because it uses the simple measurements as it finds them in the living model; and for this reason, in this regard, the painter learns sculpture more quickly than the sculptor learns painting. 

But to return to the subject of what was said about low relief, I say that it requires less physical labor than sculpture in the round, but much greater investigation, since in relief one must consider the proportion of the distances between the front parts of the bodies and the second parts, and from the second to the third successively. If you, as a master of perspective, consider these, you will find no work in low relief that is not full of errors regarding the cases of more or less relief required for the parts of bodies that are more or less near the eye. This will never happen in sculpture in the round, because nature helps the sculptor; and for this reason, what is done in the round lacks such great difficulty. There follows a capital enemy of the sculptor in both high and low relief: their works are worth nothing if they do not have the proper lighting similar to that under which they were worked. For if they have light from below, their works will appear quite distorted, <note>Others add: "monstrous."</note> especially low relief, which in such opposing judgments almost erases its own clarity. This cannot happen to the painter, who, in addition to having placed the limbs of his subjects, has transformed himself into the two offices of nature, which are very great: these are the two perspectives, and the third involving the greatest intellectual discourse, which is the <term>chiaro scuro</term> <note>chiaroscuro: the treatment of light and shade in drawing and painting.</note> of shadows and lights.

### 34. How sculpture requires less intellectual effort than painting, and lacks many natural elements.

Since I practice sculpture no less than painting, and have exercised both to the same degree, I believe I can—with little fear of reproach—give judgment on which of the two requires greater genius, presents more difficulty, and reaches higher perfection. First, sculpture is subject to specific lighting, namely from above, whereas painting carries its own light and shadow everywhere with it. Light and shadow are, therefore, the essential core of sculpture; in this case, the sculptor is aided by the nature of the <term>relief</term> <note>The physical depth or projection of the carved material.</note>, which it generates by itself. The painter, however, through the art of the "accidental" <note>In Leonardo’s time, "accidental" referred to effects created by the artist’s skill—like light and shadow—rather than those inherent to the physical object.</note>, creates these in the places where nature would reasonably do so. Furthermore, the sculptor cannot represent the diverse natures of the colors of things; painting lacks nothing in this regard. The perspectives of sculptors do not appear true at all; those of the painter appear to reach hundreds of miles beyond the work itself. <term>Aerial perspective</term> <note>The technique of depicting distance by making objects appear paler, bluer, or less distinct to simulate the effect of the atmosphere.</note> is entirely absent from the sculptor's work. They cannot represent transparent bodies, nor luminous ones; they cannot depict reflected lines, nor shiny bodies like mirrors and similar gleaming things; they cannot show mists, nor dark weather, nor infinite other things that I will not mention so as not to be tedious. What sculpture does have is that it is more resistant to time; although a similar resistance is found in painting done upon thick copper covered with white enamel, then painted with enamel colors and returned to the furnace to be baked. This form of painting surpasses sculpture for eternity. The sculptor might argue that when they make an error, it is not easy to repair it. This is a weak argument to prove that an irremediable lapse of memory makes the work more worthy; I would say instead that the intellect of the master who makes such errors will be harder to repair than the work he has ruined. We know well that a skilled master will not make such mistakes; rather, by following sound rules, he will remove so little material at a time that he will bring his work to a good conclusion. Furthermore, if the sculptor works in clay or wax, he can add and remove material, and once the work is finished, it is easily cast in bronze; this is the final and most permanent form of sculpture. For while marble is subject to decay and ruin, bronze is not. Therefore, that painting on copper—which can, as has been said of painting, be added to and removed just like the wax model for a bronze—is equal to bronze in durability. If that is bronze sculpture, then this <gloss>2: Other editions read: "this painting"</gloss> of copper and glass is even more eternal. While bronze remains black and dark, this painting is full of various and beautiful colors and infinite variety, as described above; <gloss>3: The Vienna edition adds: "as was said above, it is not mentioned so as not to be tedious"</gloss> if one only wanted to say...

Regarding panel painting, I would agree with sculpture on this point, saying: just as painting is more beautiful, more imaginative, and more abundant, sculpture is more durable, possessing nothing else. Sculpture, with little effort, displays what in painting appears miraculous: namely, making impalpable things seem palpable, flat things appear in relief, and near things appear distant. In effect, painting is adorned with infinite intellectual speculations <note>The term "speculazioni" here refers to deep theoretical study and mental observation.</note> that sculpture does not employ. There is no comparison between the genius, artifice, and discourse of painting and that of sculpture, for the latter does not concern itself with anything but the perspective caused by the quality of the material, and not by the craftsman. 

And if the sculptor says he cannot repair the material once too much has been removed from his work, whereas the painter can, the answer is this: he who removes too much understands little and is no master; for if he has mastery over measurements, he will not remove what he should not. Therefore, we shall say such a defect belongs to the operator and not to the material. But painting is of marvelous artifice, entirely composed of the most subtle speculations, of which sculpture is entirely deprived, being of very brief discourse. One answers the sculptor, who says his science is more permanent than painting, that such permanence is a virtue of the sculpted material and not of the sculptor; in this regard, the sculptor should not attribute it to his own glory, but leave it to nature, the creator of such material.

## 35. Of the sculptor and the painter.

The sculptor’s art involves greater bodily labor than the painter’s—that is, it is more mechanical—and less mental labor, meaning it requires little discourse compared to painting. This is because the sculptor only removes, while the painter always adds; the sculptor always removes from a single material, while the painter always adds various materials. The sculptor only seeks the outlines that surround the sculpted material, whereas the painter seeks those same outlines, and beyond those, he seeks shadow and light, color and foreshortening <term>scorto: the technique of depicting an object as having less depth or distance than it actually has, to create the illusion of three-dimensionality</term>. Nature continually assists the sculptor with these things—namely with shadow, light, and perspective—whereas the painter must acquire these parts by force of genius and transform himself into nature itself, while the sculptor finds them already made. 

And if you say: there is some sculptor who understands what the painter understands, I answer you that where the sculptor understands the parts of the painter, he is a painter; and where he does not understand them, he is a simple sculptor. But the painter always needs to understand sculpture—that is, the natural world, which has the relief that of itself generates light, dark, and foreshortening. Because of this, many return to nature because they are not learned in such discourse of shadows, light, and perspective; they portray the natural world simply because such portrayal has become a habit, without any other science or discourse of nature on the subject. And among these, there are some who look at things made by nature through glass, papers, or transparent veils, and there on the surface of the transparency they trace the profiles, and surrounding those profiles with the rules of proportionality, sometimes enlarging them within such profiles, they fill them with light and dark, noting the...

location, the quantity and shape of shadows and lights. But this <note>Referring to the use of mechanical aids or strict measurements mentioned at the end of the previous page.</note> is to be praised in those who know how to create from their imagination following the effects of nature, but only use such methods to relieve themselves of some labor and to ensure they do not fail in any small detail of the true imitation of that thing, which must be made to look precisely like the original. However, such an invention is to be condemned in those who do not know how to draw for themselves, nor how to reason with their own intellect, because through such laziness they are the destroyers of their own genius, and can never produce anything good without such help; and these people are always poor and wretched in every invention or composition of narratives <note>original: "storie" — in Renaissance art theory, the "historia" or narrative scene was considered the highest form of painting.</note>, which is the ultimate goal of this science, as will be demonstrated in its proper place.

### 36. Comparison of painting to sculpture.

Painting involves more mental discourse and greater artifice and wonder than sculpture, since necessity compels the mind of the painter to transform itself into the very mind of nature, and to become an interpreter between nature and art, explaining with art the causes of nature's demonstrations as governed by its laws. It explains how the likenesses of objects surrounding the eye converge with true images upon the pupil of the eye; and among objects equal in size, which will appear larger to that eye; and among equal colors, which will appear more or less dark, or more or less bright; and among things of equal depth, which will appear more or less low; and of those placed at an equal height, which will appear more or less high; and of equal objects placed at various distances, why one will appear less distinct than the other. 

And such an art embraces and contains within itself all visible things, which the poverty of sculpture cannot do—namely, the colors of all things and their diminutions <note>The fading of color and clarity over distance, known as atmospheric perspective.</note>. Painting represents transparent things, whereas the sculptor will show you natural ones without his own artifice; the painter will show you various distances by varying the color of the air interposed between the objects and the eye; he shows the mists, through which the forms of objects penetrate with difficulty; he shows the rains, which reveal behind them the clouds with mountains and valleys; he shows the dust that reveals within and behind itself the combatants who stir it up; he shows smoke, more or less dense; he will show you fish playing between the surface of the water and its bottom; he shows the polished pebbles of various colors resting upon the washed sands of the riverbed, surrounded by green plants beneath the water's surface; he shows the stars at different heights above us, and thus countless other effects to which sculpture cannot reach. 

The sculptor says that low relief is a species of painting; this could be accepted in part regarding the drawing, because it participates in perspective; but regarding shadows and lights, it is false in both sculpture and painting, because the shadows of such low relief are not of the nature of full relief, such as the shadows of foreshortenings <note>original: "scorti"</note>, which do not have the darkness of painting or sculpture in the round; rather, this art <note>Low relief.</note> is a mixture of painting and sculpture.

<meta>This page continues the "Paragone" or comparison between the arts, specifically focusing on the technical and intellectual deficiencies of sculpture compared to the atmospheric and optical mastery of painting.</meta>

Sculpture lacks the beauty of colors, it lacks the perspective of colors, and it lacks the perspective and the blurring of the boundaries of things remote from the eye; for it represents the boundaries of nearby things just as it does those of distant ones. It does not make the air interposed between the remote object and the eye occupy <note>In this context, "occupy" refers to the way atmosphere obscures or veils the clarity of distant objects.</note> that object more than the nearby one. It cannot represent lustrous and transparent bodies, such as veiled figures that show the naked flesh beneath the veils placed before it; nor can it represent the tiny pebbles of various colors beneath the surface of transparent waters.

Painting requires greater mental discourse than sculpture, and greater artifice; for sculpture is nothing other than what it appears to be—that is, a body in relief, surrounded by air, and clothed in dark and light surfaces, just like other natural bodies. Its artifice is guided by two operators: nature and man. But nature's contribution is much greater; for if nature did not assist such a work with shadows more or less dark, and with lights more or less bright, such a work would be entirely of a single light or dark color, similar to a flat surface. And to this is added the aid of perspective, which with its foreshortenings <term>scorti: the technique of depicting an object as having less depth or distance than it actually does to create an illusion of projection</term> helps to turn the muscular surfaces of bodies toward different aspects, with one muscle overlapping another to a greater or lesser degree. Here the sculptor responds and says: "If I did not create such muscles, perspective would not foreshorten them for me." To whom it is answered: "If it were not for the help of light and shadow <term>chiaro e scuro: the use of strong contrasts between light and dark to give the illusion of three-dimensional volume</term>, you could not make such muscles, because you could not see them." The sculptor says that it is he who gives birth to light and shadow by his removal of the sculpted material; the answer is that not he, but nature creates the shadow, and not art. If he were to sculpt in the darkness, he would see nothing, because there is no variety; even in a fog surrounding the sculpted material with equal brightness, one would see nothing but the edges of the sculpted material against the edges of the fog that borders it. And I ask you, sculptor, why do you not bring works to that same perfection in the open country, surrounded by the uniform, universal light of the air, as you do with a particular light that descends from above to illuminate your work? And if you give birth to shadow at your own pleasure by removing material, why do you not likewise make it appear in the sculpted material under universal light as you do under particular light? Certainly you deceive yourself, for it is another master who creates those shadows and lights, to whom you are but a servant, preparing the material where he imprints those effects <note>original: "accidenti" — in Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are properties like color or shadow that are not essential to the substance itself.</note>. So do not glory in the works of others; for you, the lengths and thicknesses of the limbs of any body and their proportions are enough, and this is your art; the rest, which is everything, is done by nature, a greater master than you. The sculptor says he will work in low relief, and will show by means of perspective what is not actually there; the answer is that perspective is a member of painting, and in this case the sculptor becomes a painter, as has been demonstrated before.

<summary>Leonardo argues that sculpture is intellectually inferior to painting because it relies on natural light to create depth, whereas painting creates the illusion of light, atmosphere, and transparency through pure intellect. He asserts that the sculptor is merely a "servant" to nature's light, while the painter masters the laws of optics.</summary>

<header>LEONARDO DA VINCI [§ 37</header>

### 37. The Sculptor’s Excuse.

The sculptor says that if he removes more marble than he ought to, he cannot correct his error as the painter does. To this, one responds that he who removes more than he should is no master, for one is called a master who possesses the true science <note>original: "scienza" — here meaning systematic knowledge or mastery of a craft</note> of his operation. The sculptor responds that while working the marble, a fracture might be discovered that was the cause of the error, and not the master himself. To this it is replied that such a sculptor is in the same position as the painter whose wooden panel breaks or is damaged while he is painting upon it.

The sculptor says that he cannot create one figure without creating infinite ones, due to the infinite boundaries <note>original: "termini" — referring to the infinite number of contours or profiles visible from every possible angle</note> possessed by continuous quantities. To this it is replied that the infinite boundaries of such a figure are reduced to two half-figures—that is, one half from the middle backward, and the other half from the middle forward. These, being well-proportioned, compose a round figure; and these halves, having their proper reliefs in all their parts, will respond of their own accord, without any further mastery, to all the infinite figures that such a sculptor claims to have made. The same could be said by one who makes a vase on a potter's wheel, for he too can show his vase from infinite aspects.

But what can the sculptor do if natural accidents do not continually assist him in all necessary and opportune cases, an aid which is free from deception? This aid is <term>chiaroscuro: the treatment of light and shade in drawing and painting</term>, which painters call light and shadow. The painter generates these within himself through great intellectual speculation, helping himself with the same quantities, qualities, and proportions that nature (without the sculptor’s own wit) provides to help sculpture. Nature also assists such a craftsman with the proper diminutions, which perspective produces naturally on its own without the sculptor’s reasoning; this is a science that the painter must acquire through his own intellect.

The sculptor will say that his works are more eternal than those of the painter; here one responds that this is a virtue of the sculpted material and not of the sculptor who carves it. If the painter paints on terracotta with glazes <note>original: "co’ vetri" — referring to the process of glazing or enameling ceramics</note>, his work will be even more eternal than sculpture.

### 38. On the obligation that sculpture has toward light, and not painting.

If a sculpture is lit from below, it will appear monstrous and strange; this does not happen to painting, which carries all its parts <note>i.e., its own internal lighting and shadows</note> with it.

### 39. Difference between painting and sculpture.

The first wonder that appears in painting is the appearance of being detached from the wall or other flat surface, deceiving subtle judgments with something that is not actually separated from the surface of the wall. In this case, the sculptor makes his works so that they appear exactly as they are. This is the reason why the painter must perform the duty...

<summary>Leonardo refutes the sculptor’s claims regarding the difficulty and durability of their medium, arguing that sculpture relies on nature for light and perspective, whereas the painter must recreate these through intellectual mastery.</summary>
<keywords>sculpture vs painting, mastery, chiaroscuro, perspective, durability, glazed terracotta, illusionism, Paragone</keywords>

<page-num>31</page-num>
->TREATISE ON PAINTING — PART ONE<-

...of the knowledge of shadows, which must be companions to the lights. The sculptor does not require such science, because nature assists his works, just as she does for all other physical objects; when light is removed from them, they are of a single color, and when light is restored to them, they appear in various tones, namely light and dark <note>original: "chiaro e scuro"</note>. The second thing that the painter requires through great reasoning is that, with subtle investigation, he must place the true qualities and quantities of shadows and lights; here, nature places them by herself into the works of the sculptor. The third is perspective, a most subtle investigation and invention of mathematical studies, which by the power of lines makes that which is near appear remote, and that which is small appear large; here, sculpture is aided by nature in this regard, and it occurs without any invention by the sculptor.

## 40. On painting and poetry.

In the representation of words, poetry surpasses painting, but in the representation of facts <note>The term "fatti" (facts/deeds) refers to the physical reality and actions that can be seen</note>, painting surpasses poetry. The same proportion that exists between facts and words exists between painting and poetry itself; because facts are the subject of the eye, and words are the subject of the ear. Thus, the senses have the same proportion among themselves as their objects have among each other, and for this reason, I judge painting to be superior to poetry. But because its practitioners have not known how to articulate its reasoning, it has remained for a long time without advocates; for painting does not speak, but demonstrates itself through its own merit and ends in facts; whereas poetry ends in words, with which, like a boastful person, it praises itself. <insert>I</insert>

<header>L. DA VINCI — *Treatise on Painting.*</header>

## SECOND PART.

### 41. On the first principle of the science of painting.

The principle of the <term>science of painting</term> <note>Leonardo viewed painting not just as a craft, but as a rigorous "science" based on mathematical laws of optics and geometry.</note> is the point; the second is the line; the third is the surface; the fourth is the body which is clothed by that surface. And this is as far as what is represented—that is, the body itself being represented—because in truth, painting does not extend further than the surface, through which is represented the body or figure of any evident thing.

### 42. Principle of the science of painting.

A flat surface has its entire <term>image</term> <note>original: "simulacro"; in this context, it refers to the optical projection or "likeness" of an object as it travels through space to another surface.</note> in all the other flat surface that stands before it as an object. This is proven: let *rs* be the first flat surface, and let *oq* be the second flat surface placed opposite the first; I say: that the first surface *rs* is entirely in surface *oq*, and entirely in *o*, and entirely in *q*, and entirely in *p*, because *rs* is seen from angle *o* and from angle *p*, and thus from infinite angles made in *oq*.

### 43. On the second principle of painting.

The second principle of painting is the shadow of the body, which is represented by it; and of this shadow we shall give the principles, and with those we shall proceed in <term>sculpting</term> <note>original: "isculpire"; Leonardo uses this metaphorically to describe how a painter uses light and shadow to "carve" a three-dimensional form out of a flat two-dimensional surface.</note> the aforementioned surface.

<summary>Leonardo defines the geometric foundations of painting—point, line, and surface—and introduces the optical theory that surfaces project their images across space. He identifies shadow as the essential tool for creating the illusion of three-dimensional depth on a flat plane.</summary>
<keywords>science of painting, geometry, optics, perspective, shadow, surface, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

<header>LEONARDO DA VINCI [§ 44</header>

### 44. On the scope of the science of painting.

The science of painting extends to all the colors of the surfaces and the shapes of the bodies covered by them, and to their proximity and distance with the proper degrees of diminution according to the levels of distance; and this science is the mother of **perspective**, that is, the visual lines. This perspective is divided into three parts, and of these the first contains only the **lineaments** <note>The outlines or structural contours of a form.</note> of bodies; the second treats the diminution of colors at various distances; the third, the loss of the definition <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: "congiunzione"; some editions read "cognizioni" (recognition/knowledge).</note> of bodies at various distances. But the first, which only extends to the lineaments and boundaries of bodies, is called **drawing**, that is, the figuration of any body. From this emerges another science that extends into shadow and light, or if you prefer, **chiaroscuro** <note>The technique of using strong contrasts between light and dark to give the illusion of three-dimensional volume.</note>; which science is of great discourse; but that of the visual lines has given birth to the science of **astronomy**, which is simple perspective, because they are all visual lines and intersected pyramids. <note>Leonardo conceptualized vision as a "pyramid" of light rays with the apex at the eye and the base at the object; "intersected" refers to the picture plane cutting through that pyramid.</note>

### 45. What the young student must learn first.

The youth must first learn perspective; then the measurements of every thing; then from the hand of a good master, to accustom himself to good limbs; then from nature, to confirm the reasoning of the things learned; then to look for a time at the works of the hands of various masters; then to form the habit of putting into practice and operating the art.

### 46. What the study of the youth should be.

The study of the youth, who desire to become professional <gloss>2</gloss> <note>original: "professionarsi"; other editions read "perfezionarsi" (to perfect themselves).</note> in the sciences that imitate all the figures of the works of nature, must be concerning drawing accompanied by the shadows and lights appropriate to the site where such figures are placed.

### 47. What rule should be given to child painters.

We clearly know that sight is among the fastest operations that exist, and in one point it sees infinite forms; nevertheless, it does not comprehend more than one thing at a time. Let us take the case: you, reader, look at this whole written page in one glance, and you will immediately judge it to be full of various letters; but you will not know in that time what letters they are, nor what they mean; therefore you must go word by word, line by line, if you wish to have knowledge of these letters. Again, if you wish to climb to the top of a building, you must ascend step by step, otherwise it will be impossible to reach its height. And so I say to you whom nature turns toward this art: if you wish

<sig>a 51 ]</sig>

To have true knowledge of the forms of things, you shall begin with their smallest parts, and do not move on to the second part until you have the first well-fixed in your memory and in practice. If you do otherwise, you will throw away your time, or truly, you will greatly lengthen your studies. And remember to learn diligence before speed <note>original: "prestezza"; Leonardo emphasizes that mastery of technique must precede the rapid execution often prized by amateurs.</note>.

### 48. On the life of the painter in his studio.

So that the prosperity of the body does not spoil that of the intellect <note>original: "ingegno"; refers to the creative and analytical faculty of the mind.</note>, the painter or draftsman should be solitary, and especially when he is intent on those speculations and considerations which, continually appearing before his eyes, provide material for the memory to be well-preserved. If you are alone, you will belong entirely to yourself; and if you are accompanied by even a single companion, you will belong only half to yourself, and even less so in proportion to the indiscretion of his conduct. And if you are with many, you will fall further into such inconvenience. If you should say: "I will do it my way, I will withdraw to one side so as to better speculate on the forms of natural things," I say this is difficult to do, because you could not help but often lend an ear to their chatter. One cannot serve two masters; you would perform the duties of a companion poorly, and the effect of your artistic speculation even worse. And if you say: "I will withdraw so far that their words will not reach me and will not hinder me," I tell you that in this case you would be considered a madman—but see, by doing so, would you not still be alone?

### 49. Recognition of the youth disposed toward painting.

There are many men who have a desire and love for drawing, but no disposition for it; and this will be recognized in boys who lack diligence and never finish their works with shadows <note>Leonardo views the mastery of "ombre" (shadows) as the true test of a painter's dedication to three-dimensional reality.</note>.

### 50. Precept.

That painter is not praiseworthy who does only one thing well, such as a nude, a head, draperies, animals, landscapes, or similar particulars; for there is no intellect so dull that, having turned itself to a single thing and practicing it constantly, it would not do it well.

### 51. How the youth should proceed in his study.

The mind of the painter must continuously transform itself into as many discourses as there are figures of notable objects appearing before him; he should pause at these, note them, and create rules based upon them, considering the location, the circumstances, the lights, and the shadows.

<summary>Leonardo advises students to master small details before progressing and argues that solitude is essential for the mental focus required for artistic speculation. He also warns against specializing in only one subject, urging the painter to be a universal master of all natural forms.</summary>
<keywords>artistic education, solitude, diligence, versatility, shadows and light, observation of nature, studio habits</keywords>

<sig>[§ 52]</sig>

## 52. On the method of study.

Study the science first, and then follow the practice born from that science. The painter must study with a system, and leave nothing that is not committed to memory, and observe what difference exists between the limbs of animals and their joints. <note>Leonardo uses "science" (scienza) to mean the underlying principles of nature, such as anatomy and optics, which must govern artistic practice.</note>

## 53. To what likeness the painter’s mind should be.

The painter’s mind <note>original: "ingegno"; the creative and intellectual faculty.</note> should be like a mirror, which always transforms into the color of the thing it has as its object, and is filled with as many likenesses as there are things placed before it. Therefore, knowing that you, the painter, cannot be good unless you are a universal master of imitating with your art all the qualities of forms produced by nature—which you will not know how to do unless you see them and portray them in your mind—whenever you go through the countryside, let your judgment turn to various objects. From one moment to the next, look now at this thing, now at that, making a bundle of various things chosen and selected from among the less good. And do not act like some painters who, tired in their imagination, set aside their work and take exercise by going for a walk, retaining a weariness in their minds; not only do they not wish to pay attention to various things, but often, when meeting friends and relatives and being greeted by them, they neither see nor hear them, and are no more recognized than if they had not encountered them at all.

## 54. On the painter’s judgment.

Wretched is that master whose work surpasses his judgment. But he whose work is surpassed by his judgment is directed toward the perfection of art. <note>Leonardo suggests that if an artist is satisfied with his work, his critical faculty has failed; a great artist always envisions something better than what he has physically achieved.</note>

## 55. Discourse on the precepts of the painter.

I have observed universally in all those who make a profession of portraying faces from life, that he who achieves the best likeness is a poorer composer of narrative scenes <note>original: "istorie"; refers to "history painting," the complex arrangement of multiple figures in a narrative, considered the highest form of art.</note> than any other painter. This happens because he who does one thing best clearly shows that nature has disposed him more toward that specific thing than another; because of this, he has had more love for it, and this greater love has made him more diligent. However, all the love placed in a part is missing from the whole, because all his delight is united in that single thing, abandoning the universal for the particular. Since the power of such a mind is reduced to a small space, it has no power in expansion. Such a mind acts like a concave mirror, which, catching the rays of the sun, when it reflects that quantity of rays into a greater area of expansion, it will reflect them

<summary>Leonardo advises the painter to maintain a "universal" mind like a mirror and warns that over-specialization in portraits can diminish one's ability to compose complex narrative scenes.</summary>
<keywords>method of study, universal mind, mirror metaphor, artistic judgment, portraiture vs. history painting, observation of nature</keywords>

with more lukewarm warmth; and when it reflects them all into a smaller space, then such rays possess immense heat, but operate in a small area. Such is the way of those painters who love no other part of painting than the human face alone; and what is worse is that they recognize no other part of the art which they hold in esteem or upon which they have judgment. Because their own works are without movement—being themselves lazy and of little motion—they criticize those things that have greater and more ready movements than those made by them, saying that such figures appear possessed <note>original: "spiritati"; literally "full of spirits," implying frantic or unnatural movement.</note> and like masters of the Morris dance <note>original: "moresche"; a lively, rhythmic folk dance often involving exaggerated gestures.</note>. It is true that one must observe **decorum** <term>decorum: the classical principle that a figure's actions and appearance must suit their character, status, and the situation.</term>, that is, that the movements are announcers of the motion of the soul of the mover. For instance, if one is to represent someone demonstrating a fearful reverence, it should not be made with such audacity and presumption that the effect appears as desperation, or as if giving a command <note>In the original manuscript, the word "commandment" is followed by "of the" and then a brief gap.</note>, as I saw in recent days an angel who, in his Annunciation, seemed as if he wanted to chase Our Lady out of her room, with movements that demonstrated as much insult as could be done to a most vile enemy. And Our Lady appeared as if she wanted, in desperation, to throw herself out of a window. So, keep it in mind not to fall into such defects.

Regarding this matter, I will make no excuse to anyone, because if someone believes I am speaking to him, it is because everyone who acts in his own way condemns himself and thinks he is doing well. You will recognize this in those who practice without ever taking counsel from the works of nature, and are only turned toward doing much; for a penny more of daily profit, they would sooner sew shoes than paint. But I will not extend my discourse further on these people, because I do not accept them into the art, which is the daughter of nature. But to speak of painters and their judgments, I say that to the one who moves his figures too much, it seems that he who moves them as much as is appropriate makes sleeping figures; and to the one who moves them little, it seems that he who makes the dutiful and convenient movement is making figures that are possessed. And for this reason, the painter must consider the ways of those men who speak together coldly or warmly, and understand the matter of which they speak, and see if the actions are appropriate to their subject matter.

The painter must be solitary and consider what he sees and speak with himself, choosing the most excellent parts of the species of whatever thing he sees; acting in the likeness of a mirror, which changes into as many colors as there are those of the things placed before it; and doing so, he will seem to be a second nature.

If you, painter, strive to please the leading painters, you will do your painting well, because they alone are the ones who can judge you with truth. But if you wish...

pleasing to those who are not masters, your paintings will have few foreshortenings <term>foreshortening: the technique of depicting an object or figure in a picture in depth, making it appear shorter than it actually is to create the illusion of three-dimensional space.</term>, and little relief, or ready movement. For this reason, you will fail in that part for which painting is held to be an excellent art: namely, making that which is nothing appear to be in relief <note>Leonardo argues that the greatest miracle of painting is creating the illusion of 3D depth on a flat 2D surface.</note>. And here the painter surpasses the sculptor, who does not cause wonder through such relief, since that which the painter acquires through his art is already provided to the sculptor by nature.

### 57. Precepts of the painter.

He will not be universal who does not equally love all things contained in painting; as if one does not like landscapes, he deems them to be a matter of brief and simple investigation. As our Botticella <note>original: "Botticella"; a diminutive or colloquial reference to Sandro Botticelli.</note> said, such study was vain, because by merely throwing a sponge full of various colors against a wall, it leaves a stain on that wall where a beautiful landscape can be seen. It is indeed true that in such a stain one sees various inventions of what man wishes to seek within it—namely, heads of men, diverse animals, battles, rocks, seas, clouds, and woods, and other similar things. It acts like the sound of bells, in which you can hear them saying whatever you imagine. But even though these stains give you invention, they do not teach you how to finish any particular detail. And this same painter <note>Referring back to Botticelli.</note> made very dismal landscapes.

### 58. On being universal in one's works.

You, painter, to be universal and to please diverse judgments, shall ensure that in the same composition there are things of great darkness and of great sweetness of shadows, making known, however, the causes of such shadows and sweetness.

### 59. Precept.

That painter who does not doubt, acquires little. When the work surpasses the judgment of the practitioner, that practitioner acquires little. And when the judgment surpasses the work, that work never ceases to improve, unless avarice <note>Greed or the desire to finish quickly for payment.</note> prevents it.

### 60. Precepts of the painter.

The painter must first accustom his hand by copying drawings by the hands of good masters; and having achieved this habituation under the judgment of his teacher, he must then accustom himself to portraying things in relief <note>Drawing from three-dimensional models or sculptures rather than flat images.</note> of good quality, following those rules of drawing from relief which shall be discussed.

<summary>Leonardo argues that a painter's true skill lies in creating the illusion of 3D relief and criticizes Botticelli's dismissive attitude toward landscape painting. He emphasizes that a master must be "universal," constantly doubting their own work to ensure their artistic judgment remains superior to their current output.</summary>
<keywords>relief, universal painter, Botticelli, landscape painting, artistic judgment, shadows, apprenticeship, imitation of masters</keywords>

### 61. Precept concerning the sketching of narrative scenes and figures.

The sketching of narrative scenes <note>original: "storie"; in Renaissance art theory, this refers to complex compositions depicting a story or historical event.</note> should be quick, and the rendering of the limbs should not be too finished; be content only with the positions of these limbs, which you can then finish at your leisure as it pleases you.

### 62. On the practitioner of painting and his precepts.

I remind you, painter, that when by your own judgment or the advice of others you discover errors in your works, you should correct them, so that in publishing such a work you do not also publish your own failings along with it. Do not excuse yourself by persuading yourself that you will redeem your reputation in your next work, because painting does not die immediately after its creation as music does; rather, it will bear witness to your ignorance for a long time. 

And if you say that correcting takes time—time which, if spent on another work, would earn you much more—you must understand that <term>money</term> <note>original: "pecunia," a Latin term for money or wealth.</note> earned in excess of what is necessary for our daily life is of little value. If you desire it in abundance, you will never finish using it, and thus it is not truly yours; all treasure that is not put to use belongs to us only in name, and what you earn that does not serve your life is in the hands of others without your benefit. 

But if you study and carefully polish your works with the logic of the two <term>perspectives</term> <note>Leonardo refers to "linear perspective" (the geometry of space) and "aerial perspective" (the way atmosphere affects color and clarity at a distance).</note>, you will leave behind works that give you more honor than <term>money</term>; for wealth is honored for its own sake and not for the one who possesses it, who often becomes a magnet for envy and a box for thieves. The fame of the rich man vanishes with his life; the fame of the treasure remains, but not that of the hoarder. 

The glory of the virtue of mortals is much greater than that of their treasures. How many emperors and how many princes have passed away leaving no memory, because they only sought power and riches to leave a name for themselves? How many were those who lived in poverty of coin to enrich themselves with virtue? This desire has succeeded much more for the virtuous man than for the rich one, in as much as virtue exceeds wealth. Do you not see that treasure by itself does not praise its accumulator after his life as knowledge does? Knowledge is always a witness and a trumpet for its creator, because she is the daughter of the one who generates her, and not a stepdaughter like <term>money</term>. 

And if you say you can better satisfy your desires for gluttony and lust through such treasure rather than through virtue, consider those others who have served only the foul desires of the body, like other base animals; what fame remains of them? And if you excuse yourself by saying you must struggle with necessity and have no time to study and make yourself truly noble, blame no one but yourself; for only the study of virtue is food for the soul and the body. How many philosophers were born rich and gave away their treasures so as not to be corrupted by them! And if you excuse yourself because of children you must nourish—a small thing suffices for them, but see to it that their nourishment is virtue, which is a faithful wealth, for it does not leave us except with life itself. And if you say that...

<summary>Leonardo advises artists to prioritize quick, gestural sketching before finishing details and argues that a painter should value the lasting "virtue" and "knowledge" of their art over the pursuit of temporary financial wealth.</summary>

...if you wish first to make a capital of money, which may be the dowry of your old age, this study will always be lacking, and it will not let you grow old <note>Leonardo suggests that the pursuit of wealth over art prevents the true maturation of the soul</note>, and the receptacle of your virtues will be full of dreams and vain hopes.

There is nothing that deceives us more than our own judgment if it is used to pass sentence on our own works; it is good for judging the things of enemies, but not of friends, because hate and friendship are two of the most powerful accidents <term>accidents: in Renaissance philosophy, these are external qualities or emotions that affect the mind</term> that exist among animals. And for this reason you, O painter, should be eager to hear no less willingly what your adversaries say of your works than what your friends say; for hate is more powerful than love, because hate ruins and destroys love. If he who judges you is a true friend, he is another version of yourself. You find the opposite in the enemy, and the friend might be deceived. There is then a third kind of judgment, which, moved by envy, gives birth to flattery that praises the beginning of good works so that the lie may blind the worker.

---

## 63. A way to increase and awaken the intellect to various inventions.

I will not refrain from including among these precepts a new speculative invention which, although it may seem small and almost worthy of laughter, is nonetheless of great utility in awakening the intellect to various inventions. And this is: if you look at certain walls smeared with various stains, or at stones of various mixtures. If you have to invent some setting, you will be able to see there similarities to various landscapes, adorned with mountains, rivers, rocks, trees, great plains, valleys, and hills in diverse ways; furthermore, you will be able to see there various battles and the lively actions of strange figures, expressions of faces, and costumes, and infinite things, which you can then reduce into complete and good forms. It happens with such walls and mixtures as it does with the sound of bells: in their tolling, you will find every name and word that you imagine.

Do not despise this opinion of mine, in which you are reminded that it should not be burdensome for you to stop sometimes to look at the stains on walls, or in the ashes of the fire, or clouds, or mud, or other similar places; in which, if they are well considered by you, you will find most marvelous inventions. These awaken the painter's intellect to new inventions, such as compositions of battles, animals, and men, as well as various compositions of landscapes and monstrous things, such as devils and similar things, because they will be the cause of bringing you honor; for in confused things, the intellect is awakened to new inventions. But first, be sure you know well how to make all the members <note>original: "membra" - referring to the parts or components</note> of those things you wish to represent, both the limbs of animals and the components of landscapes, namely rocks, plants, and the like.

---

I have also found it to be of no small utility, when you find yourself in the dark in bed, to go over in the imagination, repeating the superficial outlines of the forms...

## 65. The pleasure of the painter.

The divinity inherent in the <term>science of the painter</term> <note>Leonardo argues that painting is a "science" because it is based on mathematical principles of perspective and optics</note> causes the painter's mind to be transformed into a likeness of the divine mind; for with free power, it discourses upon the generation of diverse essences of various animals, plants, fruits, landscapes, countrysides, ruins of mountains, fearful and frightening places that strike terror into those who behold them, and also pleasant places—sweet and delightful with flowered meadows of various colors, bent by gentle waves of the soft motions of the winds, looking back at the wind as it flees from them; rivers descending from high mountains with the impetus of great <term>floods¹</term> <note>original: "diluvi"</note>, which drive before them uprooted plants mixed with stones, roots, earth, and foam, sweeping away whatever opposes their ruin; and the sea with its tempests contends and battles with the winds that fight against it, rising high with proud waves, and falling, and crashing down upon the wind that strikes its base; and enclosing and imprisoning the wind beneath itself, it tears and divides it, mixing it with its turbid foam, and through this vents its enraged anger; and sometimes, overcome by the winds, it flees from the sea, scouring the high cliffs of nearby promontories where, having surmounted the mountain peaks, it descends into the opposite valleys; and part of it mixes into the air, preyed upon by the fury of the winds, and part of it flees from the winds, falling back as rain upon the sea, and part of it descends ruinously from the high promontories, driving before it whatever opposes its ruin, and often encounters an oncoming wave, and clashing with it, rises to the sky, filling the air with a confused and foamy mist, which, struck back by the winds against the shores of the promontories, generates dark clouds that become prey to the victorious wind.

## 66. Of the games that draftsmen should play.

When you, O <term>draftsmen</term>, wish to take some useful pleasure from games, you should always use things relevant to your profession—that is, in making a good <term>judgment of the eye</term>, in knowing how to judge the truth of the widths and lengths of things. To accustom the intellect to such things, let one of you draw a straight line at random on a wall, and let each of you hold a thin <term>stalk</term> <note>original: "festuca" - a small piece of straw or reed</note> or straw in your hand, and let each cut his to the length that he thinks the first line has, standing at a distance of ten <term>braccia</term> <note>a Renaissance unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 cm; literally "arms"</note>; and then let each go to the example to measure his judged measurement against it; and he who comes closest with his measure to the length of the example shall be the superior and the winner, and shall receive from all the prize which was previously...

was ordered for you. Furthermore, one should take measurements in <term>foreshortening</term> <note>original: "scortate"; the technique of depicting an object as having less depth or distance than it actually has to create the illusion of three-dimensional space</note>, that is, take a dart or a rod and look at a certain distance in front of it, and let each person judge by their own estimation how many times that measure fits into that distance; and also see who can best draw a line of one <term>cubit</term> <note>original: "braccio"; a traditional unit of length roughly equal to the length of an arm</note>, and let it be tested with a pulled thread. Such games are the cause of developing a good judgment of the eye, which is the principal act of painting.

### 67. That one must first learn diligence rather than rapid practice.

When you, the draftsman, wish to undertake a good and useful study, make a habit in your drawing of working slowly; and judge among the lights which ones and how many hold the first degree of brightness, and similarly among the shadows, which are those that are darker than the others, and in what manner they blend together, and their proportions; and compare one with the other, and see toward which direction the outlines are aimed, and in the lines, how much of them twists in one direction or the other, and where they are more or less evident, and whether wide or thin; and finally, let your shadows and lights be united without strokes or marks, in the manner of <term>smoke</term> <note>original: "fumo"; referring to Leonardo's famous "sfumato" technique, where colors and tones blend into one another without perceptible transitions</note>. And when you have trained your hand and your judgment to this diligence, the rapid practice will come to you so quickly that you will not even notice it.

### 68. Whether it is better to draw in company or not.

I say and confirm that drawing in company is much better than alone, for many reasons. The first is that you will be ashamed to be seen among the number of draftsmen if you are insufficient, and this shame will be the cause of good study; secondly, a healthy envy will stimulate you to be among those more praised than yourself, for the praise of others will spur you on; another is that you will learn from the gestures of those who do better than you; and if you are better than the others, you will profit by avoiding their faults, and the praise of others will increase your virtue.

### 69. A way to learn well by heart.

When you wish to know a thing you have studied well by heart, follow this method: that is, when you have drawn the same thing so many times that you seem to have it in mind, try to do it without the model; and have the model traced upon a thin and flat piece of glass, and place it over the thing you have done without the model; and note well where the tracing does not match your drawing; and where you find you have erred, there keep it in mind not to err again, or rather return to the model to redraw that mistaken part so many times that you have it well in your <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "immaginativa"; the mental faculty of forming images</note>. And if you cannot have a flat glass to trace a thing, take a sheet of very thin <term>kidskin parchment</term> <note>original: "carta di capretto"; vellum made from the skin of a young goat</note>, well-oiled and then dried; and when you have used it for one drawing, you can erase it with a sponge and make a second one.

# 70. How the painter is not praiseworthy if he is not universal.

It can be clearly said that some deceive themselves when they call a painter a "good master" who only does a head or a figure well. Certainly, it is no great feat that by studying a single thing for one’s entire life, one should arrive at some perfection in it. But knowing that painting embraces and contains within itself all things produced by nature, as well as the <term>accidental operations</term> <note>original: "accidentale operazione"; this refers to the contingent or non-essential actions and movements of people, as opposed to their fixed anatomy</note> of men, and finally everything that can be perceived by the eyes, it seems to me that he is a poor master who only does one figure well. Now, do you not see how many and what kind of actions are performed by men? Do you not see how many different animals there are, as well as trees, herbs, flowers, and the variety of mountainous and flat sites, springs, rivers, cities, public and private buildings, tools suitable for human use, various clothes, ornaments, and arts? All these things ought to be executed with equal skill and quality by the one you wish to call a good painter.

# 71. On the poor excuses of those who falsely call themselves painters.

There is a certain class of painters who, because of their lack of study, must rely on the beauty of gold and <term>azure</term> <note>original: "azzurro"; specifically referring to expensive pigments like lapis lazuli, which were often used to compensate for poor technique</note>. With extreme foolishness, these men claim they do not produce good work because of poor payment, and that they would know how to do as well as anyone else if they were well paid. Now look at such foolish people! Do these types not know how to keep some good work on hand, saying: "this one is for a high price, this for a medium one, and this for a basic one," and thus show that they have works for every price?

# 72. How the painter should be eager to hear the judgment of everyone while doing the work.

Certainly, while a man is painting, he should not refuse the judgment of anyone; for we clearly know that a man, even if he is not a painter, will have knowledge of the form of another man, and will judge well if he is a hunchback, or if he has one shoulder high or low, or if he has a large mouth or nose, or other defects. If we know that men can truly judge the works of nature, how much more must we admit they can judge our errors? For we know how much a man is deceived in his own works; and if you do not recognize it in yourself, consider it in others, and you will profit from the errors of others. Therefore, be eager to listen patiently to the opinions of others; consider well and think deeply whether the <term>critic</term> <note>original: "biasimatore"; literally "blamer" or "fault-finder"</note> has cause or not to criticize you. If you find that he is right, fix it; and if you find he is not, act as if you did not hear him; or, if he is a man you respect, show him by reasoning that he is mistaken.

<summary>Leonardo argues that a true master must be able to paint everything in the natural world, not just specialized subjects, and encourages artists to embrace public criticism to overcome their own creative biases.</summary>

## 73. How, in works of importance, a man should never trust his memory so much that he fails to draw from life.

A master who believes he can store within himself all the forms and effects of nature strikes me as being cloaked in deep ignorance; this is because the aforementioned effects of nature are infinite, and our memory is not large enough to contain them. Therefore, you, painter, must see to it that the greed for profit does not overcome the honor of your art, for the gain of honor is far greater than the honor of riches. Thus, for these and other reasons that could be mentioned, you should first strive in your drawing to give an illustrative form to the eye, expressing the <term>intention and invention</term> <note>original: "intenzione e la invenzione"; the "intention" is the underlying concept, while the "invention" is the creative composition.</note> first conceived in your <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "immaginativa"; in Leonardo's time, this was viewed as a specific mental faculty that translated sensory data into mental images.</note>. After that, keep removing and adding until you are satisfied. Then, have men—clothed or nude—posed in the manner you have arranged for the work. Ensure that through measurement and scale subjected to <term>perspective</term>, nothing in the work is left without being carefully considered by reason and natural effects. This shall be the path to making yourself honored for your art.

## 74. On those who criticize those who draw on feast days, and who investigate the works of God.

Among the number of fools there is a certain sect called hypocrites, who constantly study how to deceive themselves and others, though others more than themselves; but in truth, they deceive themselves more than the rest. These are the ones who rebuke painters for studying on <term>feast days</term> <note>Religious holidays or Sundays when manual labor was traditionally forbidden.</note> those things pertaining to the true knowledge of all the forms within the works of nature, and who diligently strive to acquire as much knowledge of them as possible. But let such critics be silent! For this is the way to know the Maker of so many wonderful things, and this is the way to love such a great Inventor. Indeed, great love is born of great knowledge of the thing loved; if you do not know it, you can love it little, or not at all. And if you love it only for the benefit you expect from it, and not for its supreme virtue, you are like the dog that wags its tail and celebrates anyone who might give him a bone—whereas if he knew the virtue of such a man, he would love him much more, if that virtue suited his purpose.

## 75. On the variety of figures.

The painter must strive to be universal, because he lacks much dignity if he does one thing well and another poorly. For example, there are many who only study the <term>measured and proportioned nude</term> and do not seek out its variety; for a man can be well-proportioned and yet be fat and short, or long and thin, or average. And anyone who [does not account for] this...

<note>The author is criticizing artists who lack variety in their work.</note> ...one who does not take variety into account always makes his figures according to a single pattern, so that they all appear to be sisters; this is a fault that deserves great reproach.

### 76. On being universal.

It is an easy thing for a man who possesses knowledge to become universal <note>In this context, "universal" refers to the ability to paint all subjects well, rather than specializing in just one.</note>, because all terrestrial animals have a similarity of limbs—that is, muscles, nerves, and bones—and they do not vary at all except in length or thickness, as will be demonstrated in the study of anatomy. Regarding aquatic animals, which are of great variety, and likewise insects, I will not persuade the painter to make a fixed rule for them, because they are of infinite variety.

### 77. On the error of those who use practice without science.

Those who fall in love with practice without science are like pilots who board a ship without a rudder or a compass, who never have certainty of where they are going. Practice must always be built upon sound theory, of which perspective is the guide and the gateway; without this, nothing is done well.

### 78. On imitating painters.

I say to painters that no one should ever imitate the manner of another, because he will be called a grandson and not a son of nature. Since natural things exist in such vast abundance, one should rather have recourse to nature itself than to the masters who have learned from it. I say this not for those who desire to attain wealth through art, but for those who desire fame and honor from such an art.

### 79. The order of learning to draw.

First, copy drawings by a good master that were made based on art and from nature, and not merely from habit <note>original: "di pratica"; referring to rote, unthinking repetition.</note>; then draw from relief <note>Three-dimensional models or sculptures.</note>, in company with a drawing made from that same relief; then draw from a good natural subject, which you must put into practice.

### 80. On drawing from nature.

When you have to draw from nature, stand at a distance three times the size of the object you are drawing.

<summary>Leonardo da Vinci emphasizes that true mastery requires a scientific understanding of anatomy and perspective rather than rote practice, urging artists to study nature directly rather than imitating other painters.</summary>

### 81. On drawing any object.

Ensure that when you draw, or when you begin any line, you look across the entire body you are portraying to see what other parts align with the direction of the line you have started.

Note in your drawing how among the shadows there are "insensible" <note>Subtle or barely perceptible to the eye.</note> shadows of darkness and of shape; and this is proven by the third principle, which states: globular surfaces <note>original: "superficie globulenti" — rounded or spherical forms.</note> possess as many varieties of darkness and light as there are varieties of darkness and light in the objects facing them.

### 82. How high the light should be for drawing from nature.

The light for drawing from nature should be from the north <note>original: "tramontana" — the North Star/North wind; artists prefer north light because it remains consistent throughout the day.</note>, so that it does not change; and if you use a southern light <note>original: "mezzodì" — midday/South.</note>, keep the window covered with a cloth screen, so that the sun, shining all day, does not cause the lighting to shift. The height of the light should be situated in such a way that every body casts a shadow on the ground as long as the body is tall.

### 83. Which lights should be chosen for drawing the figures of bodies.

The figures of any body compel you to adopt the same light in which you imagine those figures to be: that is, if you imagine such figures in the countryside, they are surrounded by a great quantity of light when the sun is not visible; and if the sun sees said figures, their shadows will be very dark compared to the illuminated parts, and they will be shadows with sharp edges <note>original: "termini espediti" — clearly defined boundaries.</note>, both the primary shadows <note>Shadows on the object itself.</note> and the derivative shadows <note>Shadows cast by the object onto another surface.</note>. These shadows will harmonize little with the lights, because from one side the blue of the air illuminates and tints the part it sees with its own color; this is very evident in white objects. That part which is illuminated by the sun will show itself participating in the color of the sun; you will see this very clearly when the sun sinks to the horizon amidst the redness of the clouds, for those clouds are tinted with the color that illuminates them. This redness of the clouds, together with the redness of the sun, makes everything that receives light from them turn reddish; and the part of the bodies that does not see this redness remains the color of the air. Anyone who sees such bodies judges them to be of two colors. You cannot escape this: when showing the cause of such shadows and lights, you must make the shadows and lights participate in the aforementioned causes, otherwise your work is vain and false. 

And if your figure is in a dark house and you view it from outside, such a figure has dark, "smoky" shadows <note>original: "sfumate" — the famous Leonardo technique of soft, blurred transitions.</note> if you are standing in the line of the light; and such a figure has grace and brings honor to its imitator for being of great relief <note>The illusion of three-dimensionality.</note> with soft and smoky shadows, especially in that part where you see the darkness of the dwelling the least, because there the shadows are almost insensible; the reason for this will be stated in its proper place.

### 84. On the quality of light for portraying natural or artificial reliefs.

Light that is separated from shadow with too much harshness is highly criticized by painters. To avoid such a flaw, if you are painting figures in the open countryside, do not represent them as illuminated by direct sunlight. Instead, imagine a certain quality of mist or transparent clouds interposed between the object and the sun. Since the sun's shape is not then clearly defined, the boundaries of the shadows will not be sharply defined against the boundaries of the lights.

### 85. On portraying nudes.

When you portray nudes, ensure that you always sketch them in their entirety first, and then finish whichever limb seems best to you, putting that into practice with the other limbs; otherwise, you would develop the habit of never joining the limbs together properly. Never place the head turned in the same direction as the chest, nor let the arm move in the same way as the leg. If the head turns toward the right shoulder, make its features lower on the left side than on the right; and if you make the chest project forward, ensure that if the head turns to the left side, the parts on the right side are higher than those on the left. <note>Leonardo is describing the principle of *contrapposto*, where the weight shift and rotation of the body create a sense of dynamic balance and naturalism.</note>

### 86. On portraying from artificial or natural relief.

He who portrays from a relief <note>original: "rilievo" — a 3D object or sculpture.</note> must position himself so that the eye of the figure being portrayed is level with his own eye. You should do this with any head you have to portray from life, because generally, the figures or people you encounter in the streets have their eyes at the same height as yours; if you were to make them higher or lower, you would make your portrait look unlike the subject.

### 87. A method for portraying a site with glass.

Take a piece of glass as large as a half-sheet of "royal" paper <note>original: "mezzo foglio reale" — a standard large paper size in the Renaissance.</note>, and fix it firmly before your eyes—that is, between your eye and the thing you wish to portray. Then position your eye at a distance of two-thirds of a "braccio" <note>An Italian unit of measure; two-thirds of a "braccio" is approximately 16 inches or 40 centimeters.</note> from said glass, and steady your head with a device so that you cannot move it at all. Afterward, close or cover one eye, and with a brush or a charcoal pencil, mark on the glass what appears on the other side. Then, trace that glass onto paper, and transfer it <note>original: "spolverizzalo" — refers to "pouncing," a technique where the lines of a drawing are pricked with holes and charcoal dust is rubbed through them to transfer the image to another surface.</note> onto good paper, and paint it if you like, making good use thereafter of **aerial perspective**. <term>Aerial perspective: the technique of representing more distant objects as paler, bluer, and less distinct to mimic the effect of the atmosphere.</term>

<summary>Leonardo advises painters to avoid harsh shadows by mimicking overcast light and provides anatomical rules for posing the human body. He also describes a "perspectograph" device using glass to help artists accurately trace landscapes and figures.</summary>
<keywords>lighting, soft shadows, anatomy, contrapposto, portraiture, eye level, perspective glass, pouncing, aerial perspective, drawing techniques</keywords>
