### 88. Where landscapes should be portrayed.

Landscapes <note>original: "paesi"</note> should be portrayed in such a way that the trees are half-illuminated and half-shaded; but it is better to capture them when the sun is hidden by clouds, for then the trees are illuminated by the universal light of the sky and the universal shadow of the earth; and these are darker in their parts the closer those parts are to the center of the tree and to the ground.

### 89. On portraying the shadows of bodies by the light of a candle or a lamp.

By this light at night, a frame with translucent paper <note>original: "carta lucida"</note> should be interposed—or even without being oiled, just a whole sheet of chancery paper <note>a high-quality, smooth writing paper used in administrative offices</note>; and you will see your shadows become smoky, that is, without sharp edges; and let the light, without the interference of the paper, provide illumination to the paper where you are drawing.

### 90. In what setting a face should be portrayed to give it the grace of shadows and lights.

A very great grace of shadows and lights is added to the faces of those who sit in the doorways of dark dwellings. The eyes of the observer see the shaded part of such faces darkened by the shadows of the aforementioned dwelling, and see added to the illuminated part of the same face the brightness given to it by the splendor of the air. Through this augmentation of shadows and lights, the face gains great relief <note>the illusion of three-dimensionality</note>, with the shadows being almost imperceptible in the illuminated part, and the lights almost imperceptible in the shaded part; and from such a representation and augmentation of shadows and lights, the face acquires much beauty.

### 91. Method of portraying simple and composite shadow.

Do not portray a figure indoors with a specific light <note>a concentrated light source like a lamp or window</note> while pretending it is in the universal light of the countryside without sun; for the countryside creates simple shadow, and the specific light of a window or the sun creates composite shadow, that is, mixed with reflections.

### 92. Of the light where one portrays the flesh tones of faces, or nudes.

This dwelling <note>the studio space</note> should be open to the air, with the walls colored in flesh tones <note>original: "incarnato"</note>, and the portraits should be made in summer when clouds cover the sun; or truly, you shall make the southern wall so high that the rays of the sun do not strike the northern wall, so that its reflected rays do not spoil the shadows.

<summary>Leonardo provides technical advice on achieving "sfumato" and realistic relief by using diffused light, such as cloudy days or doorways, to soften the transition between light and shadow. He warns against mixing different types of light sources which can create confusing reflections on the skin.</summary>

### 93. On portraying figures for narrative paintings.

The painter must always consider, regarding the wall he intends to paint with a narrative <term>istoria: a complex narrative scene or history painting</term>, the height of the location where he wishes to place his figures. Whatever he portrays from nature for this purpose, his eye should be as much lower than the object he is portraying as that object will be placed higher than the eye of the viewer once the work is finished; otherwise, the work will be blameworthy.

### 94. To learn how to correctly execute a pose.

If you wish to accustom yourself to the upright and correct poses of figures, fix a frame or a chassis, squared inside with threads, between your eye and the nude model you are portraying. You shall make those same squares on the paper where you wish to subtly portray said nude. Then, place a small ball of wax on a part of the net to serve as a sight-mark <note>a fixed point of reference for the eye</note>; as you look at the nude, you should always align this mark with the pit of the throat <note>original: "fontanella della gola"</note>, or if the model is turned away, align it with a vertebra of the neck. These threads will teach you all the parts of the body which, in any given action, are found below the pit of the throat, below the angles of the shoulders, below the breasts, the hips, and other parts of the body. The transverse lines of the net will show you how much higher one shoulder is than the other <margin>The Vienna edition proposes the addition: "one of the shoulders."</margin> when posing on one leg, and likewise for the hips, the knees, and the feet.

But always fix the net in a perpendicular line; and in effect, ensure that all the parts you see the nude occupies on the net, your drawn nude occupies on the drawn grid. The drawn squares can be as much smaller than those of the net as you wish your figure to be smaller than life-size. Afterward, keep in mind, in the figures you create, the rule of the correspondence of the limbs as the net showed them to you. The net should be three and a half <term>braccia: an Italian unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 cm</term> high and three wide, at a distance of seven *braccia* from you, and one *braccia* away from the nude model.

### 95. At what time one should study the selection of things.

The winter vigils <note>the long evening hours of winter</note> should be used by young students to study the things prepared during the summer. That is, one should gather together all the nudes drawn in the summer and make a selection of the best limbs and the best bodies, putting them into practice and committing them well to memory.

## 96. On poses.

Then, in the following summer, you should choose someone who is well-built and has not been raised wearing a <term>doublet: a tight-fitting buttoned jacket</term>, so that the body is not marked with creases. You should have this person perform graceful and elegant movements; and if the muscles do not show clearly within the contours of the limbs, it does not matter; it is enough for you to obtain only the good poses from the model, and you can later correct the limbs using the studies you made during the winter <note>Leonardo suggests a seasonal workflow: studying anatomy in the winter when models are clothed, and sketching poses and life movements in the warmth of summer</note>.

## 97. To draw a nude from life or any other thing.

Get into the habit of holding a thread with a hanging lead weight <note>a plumb line</note> in your hand, so that you can see how the different parts of the subject align and intersect.

## 98. Measurements or proportions of the statue.

Divide the head into twelve degrees, and each degree into twelve points, and each point into twelve minutes, and the minutes into <term>minimi</term>, and the <term>minimi</term> into <term>semiminimi</term> <note>These terms, "minimums" and "half-minimums," are borrowed from musical notation to describe extremely fine units of measurement</note>.

## 99. A method for drawing a relief at night.

Ensure that you place a piece of paper that is not too glossy between the relief and the light source, and you will be able to draw well <note>This likely refers to using a paper screen to diffuse harsh candlelight, creating softer shadows on the sculpture being copied</note>.

## 100. How the painter should position himself relative to the light and his relief.

*a b* represents the window, *m* represents the source of light; I say that in whatever position the painter stands, he will be well-placed, provided that his eye is between the shaded part and the illuminated part

---

of the body being drawn: which place you will find by positioning yourself between the point *m* and the division that the shadow makes from the light upon the body being portrayed.

### 101. On the quality of light.

A light that is large, high, and not too powerful will be the one that makes the details of bodies appear most pleasing.

### 102. On the error made in the judgment of limbs.

That painter who has clumsy hands will make them similar in his works, and the same will happen with any other limb, unless long study prevents him from doing so. Therefore, you, painter, look closely at that part of your own person which is most unattractive, and by your study, provide a good remedy for it; because if you are uncouth, your figures will appear the same and lacking in intellect; and likewise, every good or bad quality you have within you will be demonstrated, in part, in your figures. <note>Leonardo is describing a psychological phenomenon where artists unconsciously project their own physical proportions and character onto their work—a concept he often called "every painter paints himself."</note>

### 103. How it is necessary for the painter to know the internal form of man.

That painter who has knowledge of the nature of the nerves, muscles, and <term>lacerti: the fleshy parts or bundles of muscle fibers</term> will know well, when moving a limb, how many and which nerves are the cause of it, and which muscle, by swelling, is the cause of the contraction of that nerve, and which cords, converted into very thin cartilages, surround and involve said muscle. Thus, he will be a varied and universal demonstrator of various muscles through the various actions of the figures, and will not do as many who, in different poses, always make those same things appear in arms, backs, chests, and legs; such things should not be counted among small errors.

### 104. On the defect that masters have of repeating the same poses of faces.

It is a supreme defect in masters to habitually repeat the same movements in the same <term>istoria: a narrative or historical painting</term> near one another, and similarly for the beauty of faces to always be the same. Such repetition is never found in nature; so much so that if all beauties of equal excellence were to come back to life, they would be a greater number of people than are found in our current century; and just as in this century no one precisely resembles another, the same would be true of the aforementioned beauties.

### 105. On the greatest defect of painters.

The greatest defect of painters is to repeat the same movements and the same faces and styles of drapery in a single narrative painting, and to make the majority of the faces resemble their master; a thing which has often caused me wonder, because I have... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence, a common occurrence in Leonardo’s notebooks, where he frequently leaves thoughts unfinished as he moves to a new page or topic.</note>

<summary>Leonardo warns artists against the "mirror defect" of painting figures that resemble themselves or their teachers, emphasizing instead the need for anatomical knowledge and natural variety.</summary>
<keywords>quality of light, anatomical study, muscles, nerves, artistic errors, variety in nature, istoria, physiognomy</keywords>

<header>LEONARDO DA VINCI [§ 105</header>

I have known some who, in all their figures, seemed to have portrayed themselves from life. In these works, one sees the gestures and manners of their creator: if he is quick in speech and movement, his figures possess a similar readiness; if the master is devout, his figures likewise appear with their necks bent <note>A posture often associated with religious humility or "pious" affectation in Renaissance art</note>; if the master is lazy, his figures seem like laziness portrayed from life; if the master is disproportionate, his figures are similar; and if he is mad, it is widely demonstrated in his narrative scenes, which lack any sense of conclusion, where the characters do not attend to their actions, but rather some look here and others look there as if they were dreaming. Thus, every quality in a painting follows the specific quality of the painter.

Having many times considered the cause of such a defect, it seems to me we must judge that the soul which rules and governs each body is that which forms our judgment even before it is our own conscious judgment. Therefore, the soul has constructed the entire figure of a man just as it judged he should be—whether with a long, short, or snub nose—and thus it established his height and form. This judgment is of such power that it moves the painter's arms and makes him replicate himself, for it seems to the soul that this is the true way to represent a man, and that anyone who does not do as it does is in error. And if the soul finds someone who resembles the body it has composed for itself, it loves that person and often falls in love with them. For this reason, many fall in love with and marry women who resemble themselves, and often the children born to them resemble their parents.

---

### 106. **Precept: That the painter should not deceive himself in choosing the figure for which he creates the habit.** <note>Here, "habit" or "abito" refers to the physical constitution, bearing, or habitual appearance of the figure.</note>

The painter must create his figure based on the rule of a natural body, which should generally be of praiseworthy proportion. Beyond this, he must have himself measured to see in what parts his own person varies much or little from the aforementioned praiseworthy standard. Once he has this knowledge, he must strive with all his study to avoid falling into the same defects in the figures he creates that are found in his own person. 

Know that you must fight against this vice with the utmost strength, as it is a failing born together with your judgment; for the soul, the mistress of your body, is that which constitutes your own judgment, and it willingly delights in works similar to that which it performed in composing its own body. From this arises the fact that there is no woman so ugly that she does not find some lover, unless she be truly monstrous. Therefore, remember to understand the defects present in your own person, and guard yourself against them in the figures that you compose.

<summary>Leonardo explains the psychological phenomenon where artists subconsciously project their own physical traits and personality flaws onto their paintings, urging artists to use objective measurements to counteract this bias.</summary>

### 107. The error of painters who depict an object in relief indoors under one light, and then place it in a landscape under another light.

It is a great error for those painters who frequently depict an object in <term>relief: a three-dimensional object or model used for study</term> under a particular light <note>A concentrated light source, such as a single window or candle</note> in their houses, and then place that portrait into a scene under the universal light of the open air in the countryside. In such a landscape, the air surrounds and illuminates all parts of the scene in the same way; thus, these painters create dark shadows where there can be no shadow, or if there is one, it is of such clarity that it is imperceptible <gloss>1</gloss>. Likewise, they create reflections in places where it is impossible for them to have been seen.

### 108. On painting and its divisions.

Painting is divided into two principal parts: the first is figure, that is, the line which distinguishes the shape of bodies and their constituent parts; the second is the color contained within those boundaries.

### 109. Figure and its divisions.

The figure of bodies is divided into two other parts, namely: the proportionality of the parts to one another, which must correspond to the whole, and movement appropriate to the mental state <note>original: "accidente mentale" — Leonardo's term for the outward physical expression of an internal thought or emotion</note> of the living thing that is moving.

### 110. Proportion of limbs.

The proportion of limbs is divided into two other parts: quality and motion <gloss>2</gloss>. By quality is meant—in addition to the measurements corresponding to the whole—that you do not mix the limbs of the young with those of the old, nor those of the fat with those of the thin, nor graceful limbs with clumsy ones; and beyond this, that you do not give feminine limbs to males. By motion is meant that the attitudes or movements of the elderly should not be rendered with that same vivacity that would be appropriate for the young; nor should the movements of a small child be made like those of a young man, nor those of a woman like those of a man. <gloss>3</gloss> Do not create actions that are not suited to the person performing them; that is, let the movements of a man of great health <term>valetudine: physical vigor or robustness</term> manifest his strength, and likewise, let a man of little worth do the same with weak and clumsy movements, which seem to threaten the collapse of the body that generates them.

---

</note>

### 111. On avoiding the slanders of the various judgments held by practitioners of painting.

If you wish to avoid the censures given by practitioners of painting and all those who, in different branches of the art, do not hold opinions conforming with yours, it is necessary to practice the art in diverse manners. In this way, you may conform in some part with every judgment that considers the works of the painter; these parts shall be mentioned below.

### 112. On various movements and actions.

The figures of men should have gestures appropriate to their actions so that, in seeing them, you understand what they are thinking or saying. These gestures will be well learned by one who imitates the motions of the mute, who speak with the movements of their hands, eyes, eyebrows, and their whole person when they wish to express the concept of their mind. Do not laugh at me because I propose to you a teacher without a tongue <note>Leonardo refers here to the deaf and mute as the best models for expressive gesture</note> who must teach you an art he cannot perform himself; for he will teach you better through deeds than all others can with words. Do not despise such advice, for they are the masters of movement and understand from a distance what a person is saying when he matches the motions of his hands with his words. This consideration has many enemies and many defenders. Therefore, you, painter, temper your work with both schools of thought; attend, as the occasion arises, to the qualities of those who speak and to the nature of the subject being discussed.

### 113. Avoid profiles, that is, the sharp outlines of things.

Do not make the boundaries <term>termini: the edges or outlines where one object ends and another begins</term> of your figures a different color than the background against which they end; that is, do not create dark profiles between the background and your figure. <note>This is a foundational principle of Leonardo's "sfumato" technique, where edges are softened to mimic natural vision.</note>

### 114. How errors are not perceived in small things as they are in large ones.

In things of minute form, the quality of their errors cannot be understood as clearly as in large ones. The reason is that if this small thing is made in the likeness of a man or another animal, its parts—due to the immense reduction—cannot be researched and executed with that proper finish by the practitioner as would be appropriate. Thus, it remains unfinished, and not being finished, its errors cannot be perceived. For example: if you look at a man from a distance of three hundred cubits <term>braccia: an Italian measure of length, literally "arms," roughly 23 inches</term>,

And if you wish to see clearly this diminution of the aforementioned man, place a finger a palm's width from your eye, and raise or lower said finger until its upper extremity ends below the feet of the figure you are watching, and you will see an incredible diminution appear; and for this reason, one often doubts the form of a friend seen from afar.

---

### 115. Why painting can never appear as detached <note>original: "spiccata" — meaning standing out in three-dimensional relief</note> as natural things.

Painters often fall into despair regarding their imitation of nature, seeing that their paintings do not have that relief and that vivacity which things seen in a mirror possess, alleging that they have colors which, in brightness and darkness, far surpass the quality of the lights and shadows of the thing seen in the mirror; in this case, they accuse their own ignorance and not the reason, because they do not know it. It is impossible for a painted thing to appear in such relief that it resembles the thing in the mirror, even though both are on a surface, unless it were viewed with a single eye; and the reason is that two eyes see one thing after another, as *a* and *b* see *m* and *n*; *n* cannot entirely occupy <note>original: "occupare" — in this context, to block or hide from view</note> *m*, because the base of the visual lines is so wide that it sees the second body behind the first. But if you close one eye, as *s*, the body *f* will occupy *k*, because the visual line originates in a single point and makes its base on the first body; whereby the second body of equal size will not be seen.

---

### 116. Why tiers of figures one above the other is a work to be avoided.

This universal custom, which is practiced by painters on the walls of chapels, is much to be reasonably blamed, because they make a narrative <term>istoria: a multi-figure narrative or historical scene</term> on one level with its landscape and buildings, then they rise another level and make another narrative, and they change the perspective point from the first, and then a third and a fourth, so that a single wall is seen made with four perspective points, which is the supreme foolishness of such masters. We know that the point is placed at the eye of the viewer of the narrative; and if you were to say: in what way must I make the life of a saint divided into many narratives on the same...

To this part I reply to you that you must place the foreground with the vanishing point at the eye level of the spectators of said narrative <note>original: "istoria" — a complex narrative or historical scene</note>, and on said plane represent the first large narrative; and then, diminishing the figures and buildings little by little upon various hills and plains, you will create the entire setting of that narrative. On the rest of the wall, in its upper part, you will make trees that are large in comparison to the figures, or angels, if they were appropriate to the narrative, or birds, or clouds, or similar things; otherwise do not trouble yourself with it, for all your work will be false.

### 117. Which lighting is better to use to make things appear to stand out.

Figures illuminated by a particular light <note>a focused or directional light source, like a lamp or a sunbeam</note> are those that show more relief than those illuminated by universal light <note>diffuse, ambient light, like an overcast sky</note>, because particular light creates reflected lights, which detach the figures from their backgrounds; these reflections arise from the lights of one figure reflecting into the shadow of the one standing in front of it, illuminating it in part. But a figure placed before a particular light in a large, dark space receives no reflection, and of this figure nothing is seen except the illuminated part: and this is only to be used in the imitation of night, with a small particular light.

### 118. Which is of greater discourse and utility: the lights and shadows of bodies, or their outlines.

The boundaries of bodies are of greater discourse and ingenuity than shadows and lights, for the reason that the outlines of members that are flexible are immutable and are always the same, but the locations, quality, and quantity of shadows are infinite.

### 119. Which is of greater importance: the movement created by the various accidents of the mind in animals, or their shadows and lights.

The most important thing that can be found in the discourses of painting are the movements appropriate to the mental accidents <note>internal emotions or states of mind</note> of each animal, such as desire, contempt, anger, pity, and the like.

### 120. Which is of more importance: that the figure abounds in beauty of colors, or in demonstrations of great relief.

Painting alone renders <gloss>itself a marvelous thing <note>The Vienna edition adds: "cosa maravigliosa" (a marvelous thing).</note></gloss> to its contemplators by making what is not in relief appear to stand out and be detached from the walls; and colors only bring honor to the masters who make them, because in them no other wonder is caused than beauty, which beauty

### 121. Which is more difficult: shadows and lights, or good drawing.

I say that a thing which is constrained by a fixed limit is more difficult than one which is free. Shadows have their limits at certain degrees, and for those who are ignorant of them, their work will lack relief; and this relief is the importance and the soul of painting. Drawing is free, because one will see infinite faces, and all will be different. One will have a long nose, and another a short one. Therefore, the painter can also take this liberty, and where there is liberty, there is no rule.

---

### 122. Precepts for the painter.

O <term>anatomist</term> painter <note>original: "notomista" — one who studies anatomy through dissection</note>, take care that too much knowledge of the bones, cords, and muscles does not cause you to become a "wooden" painter, by wanting your nudes to display all their feelings <note>here meaning the visible tension or "sentiment" of the muscles</note>. Therefore, wishing to remedy this, look at the way the muscles in the elderly or the thin cover or rather clothe their bones. And beyond this, note the rule of how these same muscles fill the surface spaces that are interposed between them, and which are the muscles that are never lost to sight at any degree of fatness; and which are the muscles whose points of contact are lost to sight with even the slightest bit of fat. Many times, several muscles become a single muscle as one grows fat, and many times, in thinning or aging, a single muscle becomes several muscles. Regarding this discourse, all their particulars will be demonstrated in their proper place, and especially in the spaces placed between the joints of each limb.

Furthermore, you shall not fail to observe the variety that the aforementioned muscles make around the joints of the limbs of any animal, by means of the diversity of the movements of each limb; because on some side of these joints, the knowledge of these muscles is entirely lost because of the increase or decrease of the flesh of which such muscles are composed.

---

### 123. A memorandum made by the author.

Describe which are the muscles and which are the cords that, through the various movements of each limb, are revealed, or hidden, or do neither; and remember that such an action is most important and most necessary among painters and sculptors who profess to be masters. You shall do the same for a child, from his birth until the time of his decrepitude through all the stages of his

### 124. Precepts of painting.

The painter who seeks to gain honor through his works must always look for the spontaneity of his figures' actions in the natural movements made by men suddenly and born from a powerful impulse of their emotions. He should make brief records of these in his little notebooks <note>original: "libretti" — Leonardo famously carried small pocket-sized notebooks to capture observations of life as they occurred</note> and then utilize them for his purposes by having a model assume that same pose, in order to see the quality and appearance of the limbs that are utilized in such an action.

### 125. Precepts of painting.

An object, or the figure of an object, will show more distinct and clear boundaries <term>edges</term> <note>original: "termini" — the outlines or limits where one shape ends and another begins</note> the closer it is to the eye. For this reason, you, painter—who under the name of "practical experience" feigns the view of a head seen from a close distance with finished brushstrokes and harsh, crude hatching—know that you are deceiving yourself. No matter at what distance you imagine your figure to be, it is always "finished" to the degree it is actually found, even if at a long distance the knowledge of its boundaries is lost. It does not follow from this that one should not see a smoky finish <note>original: "finito fumoso" — this relates to Leonardo’s famous *sfumato* technique, where edges are softened to blend into the atmosphere</note>, rather than clear and crude boundaries and profiles. 

Therefore, it must be concluded that in a work where the eye of the viewer can come close, all parts of that painting must be finished in their proper degrees with the highest diligence. Beyond this, the foreground elements should be defined by clear and distinct boundaries against their background, while those further away should be well-finished but with "smokier" boundaries—that is, more blurred or less distinct. For those even further away, successively observe what was said above: namely, less distinct boundaries, then the limbs, and finally the whole figure and its color should be less distinct.

### 126. How the first painting began.

The first painting consisted only of a single line, which surrounded the shadow of a man cast by the sun upon a wall.

### 127. How a painting must be seen from a single window.

A painting must be viewed from a single "window" <note>meaning a single, fixed viewpoint or perspective</note>, as is shown by the nature of bodies shaped like this: ○; if you wish to paint a round ball at a certain height, you must make it elongated in this manner, and stand so far back that, through foreshortening <note>original: "scorciando" — the optical illusion that makes an object appear shorter or compressed when viewed from an angle</note>, it appears round.

<summary>Leonardo advises artists to capture spontaneous human emotions in sketchbooks and explains the optical principle of sfumato, where edges soften with distance. He also touches on the legendary origin of painting as a traced shadow and the necessity of a fixed viewpoint for correct perspective.</summary>

<meta>a 132]</meta>

### 128. On the first eight parts into which painting is divided.

Darkness, light, body, figure, color, location, distance, and proximity. To these, two others can be added: namely, motion and rest, because it is necessary to represent these in the movements of the subjects depicted in a painting.

### 129. How painting is divided into five parts.

The parts of painting are five: surface, figure, color, shadow and light, and proximity and distance—otherwise known as "increase and decrease." These last two constitute the two types of perspective: the decrease in the size <note>original: "quantità"</note> of objects, and the decrease in the clarity of information about things seen at great distances. This includes the perspective of colors, identifying which color is the first to fade at equal distances and which one is maintained the longest.

### 130. On the two principal parts into which painting is divided.

There are two principal parts into which painting is divided: first, the lineaments <term>outlines</term> <note>original: "lineamenti" — the contours or boundaries that define a shape</note> that surround the figures of depicted bodies, which are called "drawings." The second is called shadow. But this "drawing" <note>original: "disegno" — in the Italian Renaissance, this term implied both the physical act of drawing and the intellectual concept of design or intent</note> is of such excellence that it not only investigates the works of nature, but many more than those nature actually creates. It commands the sculptor to finish his statues <note>original: "simulacri"</note> with scientific precision, and it teaches every manual art, even if they were infinite, their perfect end. For this reason, we conclude that it is not only a science but should rightfully be called a "deity," a deity that replicates all the visible works created by the Supreme God.

### 131. On linear painting.

The boundaries <term>edges</term> of any body should be considered with the greatest diligence, as well as the way they curve or "snake." One must judge whether these curves partake of circular curvature or angular concavity.

### 132. On painting, that is, on shadows.

In regards to shadows: those which you discern only with difficulty and whose boundaries you cannot easily identify—taking them and transferring them into your work with confused judgment—do not make them sharp or clearly defined. Otherwise, your work will have a wooden <gloss>I</gloss> <note>original: "legnosa" — meaning stiff, rigid, or lacking natural softness</note> result.

---

<note>I In the Roman edition of 1817, the word "wooden" is replaced with "ingenious" <note>original: "ingegnosa"</note>.</note>

<vocab>painting, darkness, light, body, figure, color, site, distance, proximity, motion, rest, perspectives, lineaments, drawings, shadow, statues</vocab>

### 133. On the parts and qualities of painting.

The first part of painting is that the bodies depicted within it should appear in relief <note>meaning they should look three-dimensional or "raised" from the surface</note>, and that the backgrounds surrounding them, with their varying distances, should appear to recede into the wall where such a painting is created. This is achieved through the three perspectives: that is, the diminution <note>the gradual shrinking</note> of the forms of bodies, the diminution of their magnitudes, and the diminution of their colors. Of these three perspectives, the first originates from the eye; the other two are derived from the air interposed between the eye and the objects seen by that eye. The second part of painting consists of appropriate and varied poses in the figures, so that the men do not all look like brothers.

### 134. On the selection of beautiful faces.

It seems to me no small grace in a painter who gives a good air <note>original: "buone arie," referring to a noble or pleasing expression and character</note> to his figures. He who does not possess this grace by nature may acquire it through incidental study in this manner: Look to take the best parts of many beautiful faces, which beautiful parts are confirmed more by public reputation than by your own judgment. For you might deceive yourself by choosing faces that have a similarity to your own; it often seems that such similarities please us, and if you were ugly, you might choose faces that are not beautiful, and you would create ugly faces, as many painters do—for often the figures resemble the master. Therefore, take beauties as I tell you, and fix them in your mind.

### 135. On the selection of the light that gives grace to faces.

If you have a courtyard that you can cover at will with a linen awning, this light will be good. Or, when you wish to portray someone, portray them in bad weather, or at the fall of evening, placing the sitter with their back against one of the walls of that courtyard. Observe in the streets at the fall of evening the faces of men and women when the weather is bad; what grace and sweetness is seen in them! Therefore, you, painter, should have a courtyard arranged with the walls tinted black, with a slight overhang of the roof above the wall; let it be ten cubits <term>braccia: an Italian unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 60 centimeters</term> wide, twenty long, and ten high. When you do not cover it with an awning, use it at the fall of evening to portray a work, or when it is cloudy or misty; and this is perfect light.

### 136. On beauties and ugliness.

Beauties and ugliness appear more powerful when placed beside one another.

### 137. On types of beauty.

The beauties of faces can exist in different people of equal quality, but they are never identical in form; rather, they will possess as many varieties as there are individuals to whom those beauties are joined.

### 138. On the judges of various beauties in different bodies of equal excellence.

Even though various bodies may possess different types of beauty and be equal in grace, different judges of equal intelligence will find great variety among them, each making a different choice from the others.

### 139. How children should be depicted.

Small children <term>putti: young children, usually boys, frequently depicted in Renaissance art to represent innocence or celestial beings</term> should be represented with quick and twisting movements when they are sitting, and when standing, they should be shown with timid and fearful gestures.

### 140. How old men should be depicted.

Old men should be rendered with sluggish and slow movements, with their legs bent at the knees when they stand still, and their feet parallel and set apart from one another. They should be stooped downward, the head leaning forward, and their arms should not be too far extended.

### 141. How women should be depicted.

Women should be represented with modest <note>original: "vergognosi," implying a sense of bashful, virtuous, or shy decorum</note> gestures, their legs held close together, their arms gathered toward themselves, and their heads lowered and tilted to the side.

### 142. How old women should be depicted.

Old women should be represented as bold and quick, with angry movements, in the manner of infernal furies <note>in mythology, the Furies were deities of vengeance known for their wild appearance and rage</note>; their movements should appear quicker in the arms and head than in the legs.

### 143. How a night scene should be depicted.

That which is entirely deprived of light is total darkness. Since night is in such a condition, if you wish to represent a historical scene <note>original: "istoria," referring to a narrative painting</note> within it, you must ensure that, if there is a great fire present, the objects nearest to said fire are most strongly tinted by its color.

because that which is closer to the object participates more in its nature; and if you make the fire lean toward a red color, you shall make all things illuminated by it also appear reddish, and those which are further from said fire should be more tinted by the black color of the night. The figures that are placed in front of the fire should appear dark against the brightness of that fire, because that part of the object which you see is tinted by the darkness of the night and not by the brightness of the fire; and those situated to the sides should be half dark and half reddish; and those that can be seen beyond the edges of the flames will be entirely illuminated by a reddish light against a black field. ### 144. How one should depict a <term>tempest</term> <note>original: "fortuna"; in this context, Leonardo refers to a violent storm or gale at sea and land.</note>.

If you wish to depict a tempest well, consider and arrange its effects carefully: when the wind, blowing over the surface of the sea or the land, removes and carries with it those things that are not firmly fixed to the general mass. And to depict this tempest well, you shall first make the clouds shattered and broken, rushing in the direction of the wind, accompanied by the sandy dust raised from the sea shores; and branches and leaves, lifted by the power of the wind's fury, scattered through the air along with many other light objects. The trees and grasses, bent to the ground, should almost appear to want to follow the course of the winds, with their branches twisted out of their natural growth and with their leaves ruffled and turned upside down. And the men who are found there, some fallen and entangled in their clothes and the dust, almost as if they were unrecognizable; and those who remain standing should be behind some tree, embracing it so that the wind does not drag them away; others with their hands over their eyes because of the dust, stooped toward the ground, with their clothes and hair streaming in the direction of the wind. The sea, troubled and tempestuous, should be full of swirling foam between the high waves, and the wind should cause the finest foam to rise into the embattled air, like a thick and tangled mist. Of the ships that are therein, some should be shown with torn sails, the shreds of which flap in the air along with some broken ropes; some with broken masts fallen, and the ship itself broadside and shattered among the tempestuous waves; and men, crying out, clinging to what remains of the vessel. You shall make the clouds, driven by impetuous winds, beaten against the high peaks of the mountains, and wrapped and swirling among them like waves striking against rocks; the air should be terrifying because of the dark shadows created by the dust, mist, and thick clouds.

## 145. How a battle should be depicted.

You shall first create the smoke of the artillery mixed into the air together with the dust raised by the movement of the horses and the combatants; and you shall use this mixture in this way: the dust, because it is an earthly and heavy thing, although by its fineness it is easily raised and mixed into the air, nevertheless naturally returns downward, and its highest ascent is made by its finest part; therefore, it will be seen the least, and will appear almost the color of the air. The smoke that is mixed into the dusty air, as it rises to a certain height, will appear like dark clouds, and at the summits, the smoke will be seen more clearly than the dust. The smoke will lean toward a somewhat bluish color, and the dust will tend toward its own color. From the side where the light comes, this mixture of air, smoke, and dust will appear much more luminous than from the opposite side. The combatants, the more they are within said turbulence, the less they will be seen, and there will be less difference between their lights and their shadows. You shall make the faces and the persons and the air near the <term>arquebusiers</term> <note>original: "archibusieri"; soldiers armed with an early type of portable long gun.</note> turn red, along with those near them; and this redness, the further it moves from its cause, the more it is lost; and the figures that are between you and the light, being distant, will appear dark against a light field, and their legs, the closer they approach the earth, the less they will be seen; because the dust is thicker and denser there. And if you make horses running outside the crowd, make the little clouds of dust distant from one another by as much as the interval between the jumps made by the horse; and that cloud which is furthest from said horse should be seen the least, rather it should be high, scattered, and thin, and the one closest should be the most evident, smaller, and more dense. Let the air be full of <term>missiles</term> <note>original: "saettume"; a general term for arrows, bolts, or projectiles.</note> of various kinds; some ascending, some descending, and some on a flat line; and the bullets of the musketeers should be accompanied by a bit of smoke behind their flight. And the foremost figures you shall make dusty in their hair and eyebrows and other flat places suited to holding dust. You shall make the victors running with their hair and other light things scattered to the wind, with their eyebrows low, and thrusting forward opposite limbs—that is, if they send the right foot forward, let the left arm also come forward; and if you make someone fallen, you shall give him the marks of sliding through the dust turned into bloody mud; and around the half-liquid earth, you shall show the footprints of men and horses that have passed there. You shall make some horses dragging their dead master, and behind him, leaving in the dust and mud the mark of the dragged body. You shall make the conquered and beaten pale, with their eyebrows raised at their junction <note>meaning the inner corners of the eyebrows near the bridge of the nose, indicating distress.</note>, and the flesh remaining above them should be abundant with sorrowful wrinkles. The sides of the nose should have several wrinkles departing in an arc from the nostrils and ending at the beginning of the eye. The nostrils high, the cause of said folds, and the arched lips should reveal the upper teeth. The teeth parted in the manner of shouting with lamentation. Let one of the hands form a shield for the fearful eyes, turning the palm toward the enemy, while the other stays on the ground to support the raised torso. Others you shall make shouting with their mouths wide open, and fleeing. You shall make many sorts of weapons among the feet of the combatants, such as

### 146. On the method of rendering distant things in painting.

It is clearly seen that there is a <term>thick air</term> <note>original: "aria grossa"; Leonardo's term for the dense, moisture-laden atmosphere near the ground that obscures vision.</note> more than others which borders the flat earth; and the higher it rises, the more subtle and transparent it is. Regarding elevated and large things that are far from you, their lower parts will be little seen, because you see them through a line that passes through the continuous thicker air. The summits of said heights are seen through a line which, although it originates from the side of your eye in the thick air, nevertheless, ending at the highest point of the thing seen, comes to end in air much more subtle than does its base; and for this reason, this line, the further it moves from you point by point, always changes quality from subtle to more subtle air. Therefore you, painter, when you make mountains, see that from hill to hill the bases are always lighter than the summits; and the further you make them from one another, make the bases lighter, and the higher they rise, the more they shall show the truth of their form and color.

Because this air is thick near the earth, and the more it rises the more it thins, when the sun is in the east you shall look toward the west, participating in the midday and...

### 148. How to make figures stand out from their background.

The figures of any body will appear more relieved and detached from their backgrounds when those backgrounds are of light or dark colors with as much variety as possible at the boundaries of the aforementioned figures, as will be demonstrated in its proper place; and in said colors, one must observe the diminution of brightness in the whites and of darkness in the dark colors.

---

### 149. On representing the sizes of painted things.

In the representation of the sizes that things naturally have when placed before the eye, the first figures <note>The "first figures" refers to those in the immediate foreground.</note> must be rendered as finished—even if they are small, like the works of illuminators—as the large works of painters. However, the small works of illuminators must be seen from up close, and those of the painter from afar; in doing so, these figures reach the eye with equal size; and this happens because they arrive with an equal thickness of angle <note>Leonardo is referring to the "visual angle," the angle formed at the eye by the rays coming from the extremities of an object.</note>. This is proven: let the object be *bc*, and the eye be *a*; and let *de* be a sheet of glass through which the images of *bc* penetrate. I say that while the eye *a* remains still, the size of the painting made to imitate *bc* must be a smaller figure in proportion to how much closer the glass *de* is to the eye *a*, and it must be equally finished. And if you represent that figure *bc* on the glass *de*, your figure must be less finished than the figure *bc*, and more finished than the figure *mn* made on the glass *fg*; because if the figure *po* were as finished as the natural *bc*, the perspective of said *op* would be false. For, regarding the reduction of the figure, it would be correct, *bc* being reduced to *po*; but the finish would not agree with the distance. In seeking the perfection of the finish of the natural *bc*, then *bc* would appear to be at the proximity of *op*; but if you wish to seek the reduction of *op*, then *op* appears to be at the distance of *bc*, and in the reduction of the finish at the glass *fg*.

### 1 5 0. On finished things, and those that are blurred.

Things that are finished and distinct should be made close at hand, and those that are blurred—that is, with blurred boundaries—should be depicted in remote areas.

### 1 5 1. On figures that are separate, so that they do not appear joined together.

The colors with which you clothe your figures should be such that they lend grace to one another; and when one color serves as the background for another, it should be such that they do not appear joined and stuck together, even if they were of the same nature of color. Instead, they should vary in brightness, just as is required by the interposition of distance and the thickness of the air that comes between them. By this same rule, the definition of their boundaries should follow—that is, more or less distinct or blurred, according to what their proximity or distance requires.

### 1 5 2. Whether the light should be taken from in front of the figures, or from the side, and which gives more grace.

Light taken from the front of faces placed within side walls that are dark will cause such faces to have great relief <note>In art, "relief" refers to the illusion of three-dimensionality or "popping out" from the flat surface.</note>, especially if the light comes from above. This relief occurs because the front part of such a face is illuminated by the universal light of the air placed before it, whereby that illuminated part has almost imperceptible shadows. After this front part of the face follow the side parts, darkened by the aforementioned side walls of the rooms, which darken the face more the further the face enters between them with its parts. Furthermore, it follows that the light descending from above deprives all those parts of itself which are shielded by the projections of the face—such as the eyebrows, which take the light away from the eye sockets; the nose, which takes it from a large part of the mouth; and the chin from the throat, and other similar projections.

### 1 5 3. On reverberation.

Reverberations <note>Leonardo uses "reverberation" to describe what we now call "reflected light."</note> are caused by bodies of a bright quality, with a flat and semi-dense surface, which, when struck by light, strike it back—similar to the bounce of a ball—onto the first object they face.

### 1 5 4. Where there cannot be luminous reverberation.

All dense bodies are clothed on their surfaces with various qualities of light and shadow. Lights are of two natures: one is called original and the other deri- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; "deri-" likely refers to "derivativo" or derivative light.</note>

...vative. I call "original" that which derives from a flame of fire, or from the light of the sun, or from the air; "derivative light" will be reflected light. But to return to the promised definition, I say that luminous reverberation <term>riverberazione: the bouncing of light from one surface onto another, creating "reflected light"</term> will not come from that part of a body that is turned toward shaded objects, such as dark places, meadows of various heights of grass, or green or dry woods. For although the part of each branch turned toward the original light is clothed in the quality of that light, nonetheless there are so many shadows made by each branch itself, and so many shadows cast by one branch onto another, that in the end such darkness results that the light there counts for nothing; hence such objects cannot give any reflected light to opposing bodies.

# 155. On reflections.

Reflections should partake more or less of the nature of the object where they are generated, and of the object that generates them, in proportion to how much more polished the surface where they are generated is compared to the surface that generates them. <note>Leonardo is explaining that a mirror-like surface reflects the source perfectly, while a dull surface blends its own color with the light it receives.</note>

# 156. On the reflections of lights that surround shadows.

The reflections from illuminated parts that bounce into opposing shadows alleviate their darkness more or less according to whether they are closer or further away, or have more or less brightness. This consideration is put into practice by many, while many others avoid it, and these groups laugh at one another. But you, to avoid the slanders of both, put both into practice where they are necessary; but ensure that their causes are known—that is, that the cause of the reflections and their colors is clearly seen, and likewise the cause of things that do not reflect. By doing so, you will not be entirely blamed nor praised by various judges, who, unless they are entirely ignorant, will necessarily praise you in everything, both one sect and the other.

# 157. Where reflections of lights are of greater or lesser brightness.

Reflections of light are of much less or greater evidence according to whether they are seen against backgrounds of greater or lesser darkness. This happens because if the background is darker than the reflection, then that reflection will be strongly evident because of the great difference between those colors; but if the reflection is seen against a background lighter than itself, then such a reflection will appear dark compared to the whiteness with which it borders, and thus such a reflection will be imperceptible.

### 158. Which part of the reflection will be brightest.

That part of the reflection will be most illuminated which receives light at angles more equal to the light source, much like a physical strike <note>original: "percussione" — Leonardo often compares the behavior of light to the physics of a ball bouncing off a wall.</note>. This is proven: let *n* be the light source, and *a b* be the illuminated part of the body, which reflects throughout the entire opposite concavity, which is in shadow. And let it be that such light, reflecting at *e*, is struck at equal angles; it will not be reflected from a base of equal angles, as shown by angle *e a b* being more obtuse than angle *e b a*. However, the angle *a f b*, even though it is between angles of less equality than angle *e*, has for its base *a b* which has angles more equal than that of angle *e*. Therefore, it will be brighter at *f* than at *e*; and it will also be brighter because it is closer to the thing that illuminates it, according to the sixth proposition which states: that part of the shaded body will be more illuminated which is closer to its light source.

---

### 159. On the reflected colors of flesh.

The reflections of flesh that receive light from other flesh are redder and of a more excellent <term>incarnazione: the artistic technique of rendering the colors and textures of human skin</term> than any other part of the flesh on a person. This occurs because of the third proposition of the second book, which states: the surface of every opaque body partakes of the color of its object; and the more so as that object is closer to it, and less so as it is more remote or larger. Because if the object is large, it blocks the appearances <note>original: "specie" — in Leonardo's optics, these are the "images" or "likenesses" of objects that travel through the air to the eye or other surfaces.</note> of surrounding objects, which are often of various colors that would otherwise corrupt the primary, closer appearances when the bodies are small. Nevertheless, a small nearby colored object will tint a reflection more than a large remote color, according to the sixth proposition of perspective, which says: large things can be at such a distance that they appear much smaller than small things nearby.

---

### 160. Where reflections are most noticeable.

That reflection will be of more distinct evidence which is seen against a field of greater darkness, and that will be less noticeable which is seen against a lighter field. This arises because when things of various darkness are placed in contrast, the less dark one makes the darker one appear even gloomier; likewise, when things of various whiteness are placed in contrast, the whitest one makes the other appear less white than it truly is.

# TREATISE ON PAINTING — PART TWO

## 161. On double and triple reflections.

Double reflections are more powerful than simple reflections, and the shadows that lie between the incident light <note>The primary light source hitting an object.</note> and these reflections have little darkness. Let *a* be the light source; *an* and *as* the direct rays; *sn* are the parts of the bodies that are illuminated; *ob* are the parts of these bodies illuminated by reflections. The reflection *ane* is a simple reflection; *ano* and *aso* is a double reflection. A simple reflection is defined as one seen by only one illuminated body, while a double reflection is seen by two illuminated bodies. The simple reflection *e* is created by the illuminated part *bd*; the double reflection *o* is composed of the illuminated part *bd* and the illuminated part *dr*. Its shadow, which lies between the incident light *n* and the reflected light *no* and *so*, is of little darkness.

---

## 162. How no reflected color is simple, but is mixed with the qualities of other colors.

No color that reflects onto the surface of another body tints that surface with its own color alone, but will be mixed with the meeting of other reflected colors that bounce into the same place. For example, consider the yellow color *a* reflecting onto the part of the sphere *coe*, while the blue color *b* reflects into the same place. I say that because of this mixed reflection of yellow and blue, the impact of their meeting will tint the sphere; if the sphere was white in itself, it will make it green, because it is proven that yellow and blue mixed together compose a most beautiful green.

---

It is very rare that reflections are the same color as the body where they meet. Let

### 164. Where the reflection will be most visible.

Among reflections of the same shape, size, and strength, that part will appear more or less powerful depending on whether it terminates against a more or less dark field <note>The "field" refers to the background or the area surrounding the object.</note>.

### 165. On reflections.

1. The surfaces of bodies take on more of the colors of those objects which reflect their likeness into them at more equal angles <note>Leonardo is referring to the law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. The more direct the alignment, the more vivid the reflected color.</note>.

2. Among the colors of objects reflecting their likenesses onto the surfaces of the bodies placed before them at equal angles, the most powerful will be the one whose reflected ray has the shortest length.

3. Among the colors of objects reflected at equal angles and at an equal distance onto the surface of opposite bodies, the most powerful will be the one that is of a brighter color.

4. That object reflects its color more intensely into the body placed before it when it has no other colors around it except those of its own kind <note>A pure color surrounded by the same hue will not be "polluted" by competing reflections from different colored objects.</note>.

### 166. Reflection.

However, a reflection will be of a more confused color if it is generated by various colors from different objects.

The color that is closest to the reflection will tint that reflection most strongly with its own hue, and vice versa.

Therefore, you, the painter, when working on the reflections in the features of your figures, should apply the color of the parts of the garments that are near the areas of the flesh closest to them; but do not separate them with too much definition <note>original: "pronunziazione"</note> unless there is a specific need.

### 167. On the colors of reflections.

All reflected colors are of less luminosity than direct light <note>original: "lume retto"</note>, and the relationship between the incident light and the reflected light is the same as the relationship between the brightness of their respective sources.

### 168. On the boundaries of reflections within their background.

The boundary of a reflection placed against a background lighter than the reflection itself will result in that reflection terminating in a field darker than itself; then that reflection will be perceptible, and it will become all the more evident as that background is made darker, and vice versa. <note>Leonardo is discussing the principle of contrast: a reflected light is only visible if the surface or background behind it provides enough shadow to make it stand out.</note>

### 169. On the method of learning well how to compose figures together in narrative scenes.

For this reason, when you have learned perspective well and have committed to memory all the parts and bodies of things, you should frequently take pleasure, as you go for walks, in observing and considering the positions and actions of men as they talk, argue, laugh, or come to blows with one another; observe what actions are in them, and what actions are made by the bystanders, the mediators, or the onlookers of these events. Note these down with brief shorthand marks in this manner in a small notebook, which you must always carry with you. It should be of tinted paper <note>Renaissance artists often used paper prepared with a colored wash (tinted paper), which allowed them to use both dark chalk for shadows and white heightening for lights.</note> so that you do not have to erase, but rather move from an old one to a new one; for these are not things to be erased, but rather preserved with the greatest diligence. Indeed, the forms and actions of things are so numerous that the memory is not capable of retaining them; therefore, you shall keep these as your helpers and masters.

### 170. On placing the first figure in a narrative scene.

You shall make the first figure in a narrative scene <note>original: "istoria"—referring to "history painting," the depiction of complex stories from the Bible, mythology, or history.</note> as much smaller than life-size as the number of cubits <note>original: "braccia," a Renaissance unit of measurement approximately 23 inches.</note> you imagine it to be distant from the front line of the picture; then make the others in comparison to that one, following the rule mentioned above.

### 171. On the placement of figures.

Just as much as the side of the nude figure *da* diminishes in order to rest, the opposite side increases; that is, for as much as the side *da* decreases from its measurement, the opposite side grows beyond its measurement. The navel never leaves its height, nor does the male organ. This lowering occurs because when a figure stands upon one foot, that foot becomes the center of the weight placed above it. This being so, the center of the shoulders straightens itself above, moving outside its perpendicular line—the line which passes through the superficial center of the body. This line comes to twist at its upper extremity over the foot that supports the weight; and the transverse lines, forced into equal angles, have their ends lower on that side which is resting, as appears in *abc*. <note>Leonardo is describing the principle of **contrapposto**, the asymmetrical arrangement of the human figure where the weight is shifted onto one leg, causing a counter-positioning of the hips and shoulders to maintain balance.</note>

### 172. Method of composing narrative scenes.

Among the figures that compose <term>narrative scenes</term><note>original: "istorie" — complex multi-figure compositions depicting a historical, biblical, or mythological event</note>, the one that will appear with the greatest <term>relief</term><note>original: "rilievo" — the illusion of three-dimensional depth and solidity on a flat surface</note> is that which is feigned to be closest to the eye. This occurs because of the second principle of the third [book], which states: that color shows itself in greater perfection which has a smaller quantity of intervening air between itself and the eye that judges it. For this reason, the shadows—which show opaque bodies to be in relief—appear even darker up close than from a distance, where they are corrupted by the air interposed between the eye and those shadows. This does not happen in shadows near the eye, where they show the bodies with as much greater relief as they are of greater darkness.

---

### 173. On composing narrative scenes.

Remember, painter, when you create a single figure, to avoid <term>foreshortenings</term><note>original: "scorti" — the visual distortion of an object or body part to show it receding into space</note> of it, both of its parts and of the whole, because you would have to struggle against the ignorance of those unlearned in this art. But in narrative scenes, use them in every way that occurs to you, and especially in battles, where by necessity there occur infinite foreshortenings and bendings of the participants in such discord, or one might say, most beastly madness.

---

### 174. Variety of men in narrative scenes.

In narrative scenes, there ought to be men of various temperaments, ages, complexions, attitudes, thicknesses, and thinness; large, slender, tall, short, fat, lean, fierce, civil, old, young, strong and muscular, weak and with few muscles, cheerful, melancholy, and with hair curly and straight, short and long, movements prompt and languid, and likewise various garments, colors, and whatever else such a scene requires. It is a supreme sin in a painter to make faces that resemble one another, and similarly, the repetition of gestures is a great vice.

---

### 175. On learning the movements of man.

The movements of man should be learned after the knowledge of the limbs and of the whole in all the motions of the limbs and joints. Then, with a brief notation of a few marks, observe the actions of men in their accidental occurrences, without them noticing that you are watching them; because, if they become aware of such observation, their minds will be occupied with you, and they will abandon the ferocity of their action, upon which they were previously intent. For example, when two angry men contend together, and each believes himself to be in the right, they move their eyebrows, arms, and other limbs with great ferocity, with actions appropriate to their intention and their words; which...

### 187. On making colors vivid and beautiful in your paintings.

For those colors that you wish to possess beauty, you should always first prepare a field of the purest white; and I say this regarding colors that are transparent <note>Leonardo refers here to "glazing," a technique where thin, see-through layers of paint are applied over a base</note>, because for those that are not transparent, a light background is of no use. An example of this is taught to us by stained glass; when these are placed between the eye and the luminous air, they show excellent beauty, which they cannot do if they have behind them dark air or other shadows.

### 188. On the colors of shadows of any color.

The color of the shadow of any color always partakes in the color of its object <note>The "object" here refers to the surface or body casting or receiving the shadow</note>, and more or less so depending on how much that object is near to or remote from that shadow, and how much it is more or less luminous.

### 189. On the variations caused by the colors of remote or near things.

Of things darker than the air, that which is more remote will appear less dark; and of things brighter than the air, that which is more remote from the eye will appear less white. Things brighter and darker than the air at a long distance exchange color, because the bright acquires darkness and the dark acquires brightness <note>This is a fundamental principle of "aerial perspective," where atmospheric haze softens contrasts over distance</note>.

### 190. At what distance the colors of things are entirely lost.

The colors of things are entirely lost at a greater or lesser distance depending on whether the eye and the thing seen are at a greater or lesser altitude. This is proven by the seventh [rule] of this [treatise], which says: the air is more or less thick as it is nearer to or further from the earth. Therefore, if the eye and the thing seen by it are near the earth, then the thickness of the air interposed between the eye and the object will be dense and will greatly obstruct the color of the thing seen. But if the eye and the object are remote from the earth, then the air will occupy <note>meaning "interfere with" or "cloud"</note> the color of the aforementioned object very little.

### 191. At what distance the colors of objects are lost to the eye.

There are as many variations in the distances at which the colors of objects are lost as there are variations in the times of day, and as many as there are variations in the thickness or thinness of the air through which the species <note>original: "specie" — a term from medieval optics referring to the visual image or "likeness" of an object traveling through space</note> of the colors of the aforementioned objects penetrate to the eye. And of this, we shall give no other rule for the present.

### 196. Of color that does not change in various thicknesses of air.

A color placed in different thicknesses of air will not change when one is as much more remote from the eye than the other. It is proved thus: if the first low air has four degrees of thickness, and the color is distant one degree from the eye, and the second higher air has three degrees of thickness (having lost one degree), make it so the color acquires one degree of distance; <insert>1</insert> and when the higher air has lost two degrees of thickness, and the color has acquired two degrees of distance, then the first color is the same as the third: and to be brief, if the color rises so much that it enters the air which has lost three degrees of thickness, and the color has moved away three degrees of distance, then you can be certain that the high and remote color has suffered as much loss of color as the low and near color; because if the high air has lost three-quarters of the thickness of the low air, the color in rising has acquired three-quarters of the total distance by which it is remote from the eye. And thus we have proved our intent.

### 197. Whether various colors can appear as a uniform darkness by means of the same shadow.

It is possible that all the varieties of colors under the same shadow appear transformed into the color of that shadow. This is manifested in the darkness of a cloudy night, in which no figure or color of a body is perceived; and because darkness is nothing other than the deprivation of <term>incident light</term> <note>light falling directly onto a surface</note> or reflected light, by means of which all figures and colors of bodies are perceived, it is necessary that, the cause of light being entirely removed, the effect and the knowledge of the colors and figures of the aforementioned bodies should also be missing.

### 198. On the cause of the loss of colors and shapes of bodies through shadows that appear to be, but are not.

There are many places that are in themselves illuminated and bright, yet appear dark and entirely deprived of any variety of colors or shapes of the things found within them. This happens because of the light of the illuminated air that is interposed between the objects seen and the eye, as is seen inside windows that are remote from the eye, in which one perceives only a uniform and quite dark obscurity. Yet, if you then enter into that house, you will see that it is in itself strongly illuminated, and you will be able to readily perceive every smallest part of whatever thing might be found inside such a window. This demonstration arises from a defect of the eye, which, overcome by the excessive light of the air, greatly constricts the size of its pupil, and for this reason loses much of its power; whereas in darker places the pupil dilates, and its power increases as much as it gains in size, as is proven in the second [book] of my <term>perspective</term> <note>Leonardo refers here to his studies on optics and the anatomy of the eye, which he often grouped under the heading of "Perspective."</note>.

### 199. How nothing shows its true color unless it has light from another similar color.

No object will ever show its own proper color unless the light that illuminates it is entirely of that same color. What is said here is manifested in the colors of cloths, of which the illuminated folds, reflecting or giving light to the opposite folds, make them show their true color. Gold leaves do the same in giving light to one another, while the opposite happens when receiving light from another color.

### 200. Of colors that appear to vary from their true being through the comparison of their backgrounds.

No boundary of uniform color will appear equal if it does not end in a background of a color similar to itself. This is clearly seen when black ends against white and white against black, where each color appears more <term>noble</term> <note>original: "nobile" — in this context, it means more intense, vivid, or pure.</note> at the borders of its opposite than it will appear in its center.

### 202. Which part of the same color shows itself most beautiful in painting.

Here it is to be noted which part of the same color shows itself most beautiful in painting: whether it is the part that has the luster, or the part that has the light, or that of the middle shadows, or that of the dark ones, or indeed in transparency. Here one must understand what color is being asked about, because different colors have their beauties in different parts of themselves; and this is shown to us by black, which has its beauty in the shadows; white in the light; blue, green, and <term>tan</term> <note>original: "tanè," a brownish-orange or tawny color</note> in the middle shadows; yellow and red in the lights; gold in the reflections; and <term>lacquer</term> <note>original: "lacca," likely referring to madder lake or a similar transparent red pigment</note> in the middle shadows.

### 203. How every color that does not shine is more beautiful in its luminous parts than in its shadowy ones.

Every color is more beautiful in its illuminated part than in its shadowy part; and this arises because light vivifies and gives true knowledge of the quality of colors, while shadow dampens and obscures that same beauty, and prevents the knowledge of that color; and if, on the contrary, black is more beautiful in the shadows than in the lights, the answer is that black is not a color, nor indeed is white.

### 204. On the evidence of colors.

That thing which is lighter appears more from a distance, and the darker thing does the opposite.

### 205. Which part of the color should reasonably be most beautiful.

If *a* is the light, *b* will be the part illuminated in a straight line by that light; *c*, which cannot see that light, sees only the illuminated part, which part we shall say is red; this being so, the light generated at that part will resemble its cause, and will tinge the face *c* in red; and if *c* is also red itself, you will see it to be much more beautiful than *b*; and if *c* were yellow, you would see a <term>changing color</term> <note>original: "color cangiante," an iridescent or shot-silk effect where the color shifts depending on the light</note> created between yellow and red.

### 206. How the beauty of color must be in the lights.

If we see that the quality of colors is known by means of light, it is to be judged that where there is more light, there the true quality of the illuminated color is most seen, and where there is more darkness, the color is stained with the color of that darkness. Therefore you, painter, remember to show the truth of colors on the illuminated parts.

### 207. Of the green color made from the rust of copper.

Of the green made from copper <note>original: "verde fatto dal rame," referring to verdigris</note>, even though such a color is applied with oil, its beauty vanishes into smoke <note>original: "se ne va in fumo," an idiom meaning it fades or disappears</note> if it is not immediately varnished; and not only does it vanish, but if it is washed with a sponge soaked in simple common water, it will lift off the panel where it is painted, and especially if the weather is humid; and this happens because such <term>verdigris</term> <note>original: "verderame," a green pigment formed by the action of acetic acid on copper plates</note> is made by the force of salt, which salt easily dissolves in rainy weather, and especially when being soaked and washed with the aforementioned sponge.

### 208. Increase of beauty in verdigris.

If <term>aloe caballino</term> <note>original: "aloe camellino," a lower grade of aloe resin used as a transparent glaze</note> is mixed with the verdigris, that verdigris will acquire great beauty, and it would acquire even more with saffron, if it did not vanish into smoke. And the quality of this aloe caballino is known when it dissolves in <term>spirits</term> <note>original: "acquavite," literally "water of life," a high-proof distilled alcohol</note> while it is hot, which dissolves it better than when it is cold. And if you had finished a work with this simple green, and then <gloss>glazed</gloss> it thinly with this aloe dissolved in water, then that work would become a most beautiful color: and also this aloe can be ground in oil by itself, and also together with the verdigris, and with any other color that pleases you.

### 209. Of the mixing of colors with one another, which mixing extends toward infinity.

Even though the mixing of colors with one another extends toward infinity, I will not forbear from making a brief discourse upon it. Setting down first a certain number of simple colors, with each of those I will mix each of the others one by one, and then two by two and three by three, thus continuing until the full number of all the colors. Then I will begin again to mix the colors two with two and three with two, and then four, thus continuing until the end, upon those first two colors. And then I will take three, and with those three I will accompany another three, and then six, and thus I will continue such mixing in all proportions. I call "simple colors" those which are not composed, nor can they be composed by means of mixing other colors. Black,
