### 210. Of the surface of every shaded body.

The surface of every shaded body participates in the color of its object <note>meaning the object reflecting light onto it</note>. Shaded bodies demonstrate this with certainty, seeing as none of the aforementioned bodies show their shape or color if the medium interposed between the body and the light source is not illuminated. We shall say then that if the <term>opaque body</term> is yellow, and the light source is blue; I say that the illuminated part will be green, which green is composed of yellow and blue.

### 211. Which surface is most receptive to colors.

White is more receptive to any color than any other surface of any body that is not mirrored. This is proven by saying that every empty body is capable of receiving what bodies that are not empty cannot receive; we shall say for this reason that white is "empty," or if you prefer, deprived of any color; being illuminated by the color of any light source, it participates more in that light than black would do, which is like a broken vessel that is deprived of any capacity to hold anything.

### 212. Which part of the body will be most tinted by the color of its object.

The surface of every body will participate more intensely in the color of that object which is closest to it. This happens because the nearby object occupies a greater multitude of the varieties of <term>species</term> <note>original: "specie," a philosophical and optical term referring to the "images" or "likenesses" of things that travel through the air to the eye or other surfaces</note>, which, coming to the surface of the bodies, would overwhelm the surface of such an object, which would not happen if such a color were remote: and by occupying such species, that color demonstrates its nature more integrally in that opaque body.

<summary>Leonardo defines eight primary colors, including black and white as the foundations of chiaroscuro, and explains how surfaces take on the hues of nearby objects through reflected light.</summary>

<header>LEONARDO DA VINCI [§ 213</header>

### 213. **Which part of the surface of bodies will show the most beautiful color.**

The surface of an opaque body will display its most perfect color when it has a nearby object of a similar color to its own.

### 214. **Of the flesh tones of faces.**

The color of bodies is better preserved over a long distance when it exists in a greater quantity. This proposition shows us that the face becomes dark at a distance because shadow is the largest part of the face, while the lights are minimal and therefore disappear at a short distance; and their highlights <note>original: "lustri," the sharpest points of reflected light</note> are the smallest of all. This is the reason why, as the darkest part remains, the face becomes or appears dark; and it will seem to lean toward black all the more if that face has something very white on the body or the head.

### 215. **Method for drawing from relief and preparing the paper for this.**

Painters, in order to portray things in relief <note>three-dimensional forms or sculptures</note>, must tint the surface of the paper with a medium darkness, and then apply the darkest shadows, and finally the principal lights in small areas—which are the first things to be lost to the eye at a short distance.

### 216. **Of the variety of a single color at various distances from the eye.**

Among colors of the same nature, the one that changes the least is the one that is moved the least from the eye. This is proven because the air that is interposed between the eye and the thing seen occupies <note>or "veils"</note> the said thing; and if the interposed air is of a great amount, then the thing seen will be strongly tinted with the color of that air, and if such air is of a thin quantity, then the object will be little hindered.

### 217. **Of the greenery seen in the countryside.**

Of the greenery of the countryside of equal quality, that which is in the plants of the trees will appear darker, and that of the meadows will show itself to be lighter.

### 218. **Which greenery will appear to participate more in blue.**

Those green areas will show themselves to participate more in blue <note>original: "azzurro"</note> which have the darkest shadiness; and this is proven by the seventh [rule], which says that blue is composed of light and dark over long distances.

### 219. Which surface demonstrates its true color less than others.

That surface will show its true color the least which is the most polished and clean. We see this in the grass of the meadows and in the leaves of trees which, having a clean and lustrous surface, take on the luster <note>original: "lustro," referring to the specular reflection or highlight</note> in which the sun or the air that illuminates them is mirrored; and thus, in that part of the luster, they are deprived of their natural color.

### 220. Which body will show you its true color more.

That body will most demonstrate its true color whose surface is less clean and smooth. This is seen in linens, and in the leaves of plants and trees that are hairy <note>fuzzy or textured</note>, in which no luster can be generated; wherefore by necessity, being unable to mirror objects, they only return to the eye their true and natural color, that color not being corrupted by any body that illuminates them with an opposing color—such as the redness of the sun when it sets and tints the clouds with its own color.

### 221. Of the brightness of landscapes.

The colors, vibrancy, and brightness of painted landscapes <note>original: "paesi," meaning countrysides or landscapes</note> will never have conformity with natural landscapes illuminated by the sun, unless those painted landscapes are themselves illuminated by that same sun.

### 222. Common perspective, and of the diminution of colors at a long distance.

The air participates so much less in the color blue as it is closer to the horizon, and is so much darker as it is more remote from the horizon. This is proven by the third [proposition] of the ninth [book], which shows that a body will be less illuminated by the sun if it is of a thinner <note>original: "rara," meaning less dense or more rarefied</note> quality. Therefore the fire <note>referring to the Aristotelian "sphere of fire" believed to exist above the atmosphere</note>, the element that clothes the air, because it is thinner and more subtle than the air, occupies the darkness that is above it less than the air does; and consequently the air, a body less thin than fire, is illuminated more by the solar rays that penetrate it, illuminating the infinity of atoms <note>original: "atomi," likely referring to dust motes or particles</note> that are infused through it, and it renders itself bright to our eyes. Wherefore, as the appearance of the aforementioned darkness penetrates through that air, it necessarily causes that whiteness of the air to appear blue to us, as is proven in the third [proposition] of the tenth [book]; and it will appear to us as a brighter blue the greater the thickness of air that is interposed between that darkness and our eyes. As if the eye of the observer were at *p* and looked above itself at the thickness of the air *pr*, then, declining somewhat,

<summary>Leonardo explains how surface texture affects color perception, noting that smooth surfaces reflect light (luster) while textured ones show true color, and provides a physical explanation for why the sky appears blue due to atmospheric density.</summary>

And thus our intent has been proven. <note>Leonardo is using geometry to explain "aerial perspective"—the way the atmosphere scatters light, making distant objects and the low sky appear paler and less blue.</note>

### 223. Of things mirrored in the waters of landscapes, and first of the air.

Only that air will be the one to give an image of itself upon the surface of the water which reflects from the surface of the water to the eye at equal angles; that is, that the angle of incidence be equal to the angle of reflection. <note>This is a fundamental law of optics: light hits and bounces off a surface at the same angle.</note>

### 224. Diminution of colors by the medium interposed between them and the eye.

A visible thing will demonstrate its natural color less in proportion as the medium <note>In this context, "medium" refers to the atmosphere or air between the viewer and the object.</note> interposed between it and the eye is of greater thickness.

### 225. Of the backgrounds that are suitable for shadows and lights.

Regarding the backgrounds that are suitable for the illuminated or shadowed edges of any color, those will create the most separation from one another which are the most varied; that is, a dark color should not end against another dark color, but one that is very different: such as white or participating in white. Similarly, a white color should never end against a white background, but one as dark as possible or drawing toward darkness.

### 226. How one must remedy when white ends in white or dark in dark.

When the color of a white body happens to end against a white background, then either the whites will be equal, or they will not. If they are equal, then the one which is closer to you will become somewhat dark at the edge where it meets that white background. And if such a background is less white than the color which stands out against it, then the foreground color will stand out by itself from its different background without any other help from a dark edge. <note>Leonardo is describing "simultaneous contrast," a technique painters use to define shapes when colors are similar by subtly darkening the edge of the closer object.</note>

### 227. On the nature of the colors of the backgrounds against which white stands out.

A white object will appear whiter if it is against a darker background, and it will appear darker if it is against a whiter background; and this is taught to us by falling snow, which, when we see it against the background of the sky, appears dark to us, and when we see it against the background of an open window, through which one sees the darkness of the shadow of that house, then that snow will appear very white; and the snow nearby appears fast to us, and the remote snow slow; and the nearby snow appears as a continuous quantity, like white cords, and the remote snow appears discontinuous. <note>Leonardo is observing "simultaneous contrast"—how our eyes perceive a color differently based on what surrounds it—and the optical effects of motion parallax and resolution.</note>

### 228. On the backgrounds of figures.

Of things of equal brightness, that one will appear of less brightness which is seen against a background of greater whiteness; and that one will appear whiter which stands out in a darker space; and flesh-tone will appear pale against a red background, and pale flesh will appear reddish when seen against a yellow background; and similarly, colors will be judged as that which they are not by means of the backgrounds that surround them.

### 229. On the backgrounds of painted things.

Of the greatest importance is the discussion of backgrounds, in which opaque bodies <term>opaque bodies: objects that do not let light pass through them</term> stand out, clothed in shadows and lights, because it is appropriate for those to have the illuminated parts against dark backgrounds, and the dark parts against light backgrounds, just as I have demonstrated in part in the margin. <margin>The marginal diagram shows a light block against a dark field and a dark block against a light field to illustrate this principle of contrast.</margin>

### 230. Of those who, in a landscape, pretend that the more remote thing becomes darker.

There are many who, in an open landscape, make the figures darker the more remote they are from the eye; which is the opposite, unless the thing imitated were white, because then that which is proposed below would happen.

### 231. On the colors of things remote from the eye.

The air tints the objects it separates from the eye with its own color more in proportion to its greater thickness. Therefore, the air having divided a dark object with a thickness of two miles, it tints it more than that which has a thickness of one mile. Here the adversary responds and says that in landscapes, the trees of a... <note>Leonardo is beginning a rebuttal to those who do not understand how the blue/gray "veil" of the atmosphere lightens dark objects in the distance.</note>

plants of the same species appear darker from a distance than from nearby. This is not true if the plants are of equal size and separated by spaces; but it will indeed be true if the first trees are sparse, allowing the brightness of the meadows dividing them to be seen, while the furthest trees are dense, as happens on the banks and vicinities of rivers. In that case, one does not see the spaces of the bright meadows, but all the trees joined together, casting shadows upon one another. Furthermore, it happens that the shadowed part of the plants is much larger than the luminous part; because of the "species" <note>original: "specie"—In Leonardo's time, this referred to the visual images or "simulacra" that objects were thought to emit through the air to reach the eye.</note> that the plant sends to the eye, they mingle at a long distance, and the dark color, which is present in greater quantity, maintains its "species" more than the less dark part; and thus this mixture carries with it the more powerful part over a longer distance.

### 232. Degrees of painting.

That which is beautiful is not always good; and I say this for those painters who love the beauty of colors so much that, not without a great lack of conscience, they give them very weak and almost insensible shadows, disregarding their relief <note>relief: the three-dimensional quality or "pop" of a figure on a flat surface</note>. In this error are those who are beautiful speakers without any substance.

### 233. On the reflection and color of sea water seen from different aspects.

The waving sea has no universal color, but he who sees it from the mainland sees it as a dark color, and so much darker as it is closer to the horizon, though he sees there some brightness or luster that moves slowly, like white sheep in a flock. And he who sees the sea while being out on the high seas sees it as blue. This happens because from the land the sea appears dark because you see in it the waves reflecting the darkness of the earth, and from the high sea they appear blue because you see in the waves the blue air reflected by such waves.

### 234. On the nature of comparisons.

Black garments make the flesh of human figures appear whiter than they are, and white garments make the flesh appear dark, and yellow garments make them appear colorful, while red garments show them to be pale.

### 235. On the color of the shadow of any body.

The color of the shadow of any body will never be its true or proper shadow unless the object that casts the shadow is the same color as the body being shadowed. Let us say, for example, that I have a dwelling where the walls are green; I say:

if in such a place blue is seen, being illuminated by the brightness of the blue of the air, then that illuminated wall will be of a most beautiful blue, and the shadow will be ugly, and not a true shadow of such beauty of blue, because it is corrupted by the green that reflects into it; and it would be worse if such a wall were of tawny <note>original: "tanè"—a brownish-orange or dark yellowish-tan color</note> color.

### 236. On the perspective of colors in dark places.

In luminous places that are uniformly varied down to total darkness, that color will appear darker which is more remote from the eye itself.

### 237. Perspective of colors.

The primary colors ought to be simple, and the degrees of their diminution must agree with the degrees of their distances; that is, the sizes of things will participate more in the nature of the point <note>the "point" refers to the vanishing point in linear perspective</note> the closer they are to it, and colors must participate more in the color of their horizon the closer they are to it.

### 238. On colors.

The color found between the shadowed part and the illuminated part of shadowed bodies will be of less beauty than that which is entirely illuminated; therefore, the primary beauty of colors will be found in the principal lights.

### 239. From what the blue of the air arises.

The blue of the air arises from the thickness of the body of illuminated air interposed between the darkness above and the earth. The air in itself has no quality of smell, or taste, or color, but in itself it takes on the likenesses of the things placed behind it; and it will be of a more beautiful blue the greater the darkness behind it, provided that the air is not of too great a space, nor of too great a thickness of moisture. And one sees in mountains that have more shadows that there is a more beautiful blue at long distances; and likewise, where it is more illuminated, it shows more the color of the mountain than of the blue attached to it by the air that interposes itself between the mountain and the eye.

### 240. On colors.

Among colors that are not blue, that which is closer to black will participate more in blue at a long distance; and conversely, that which is most dissimilar to the said black will maintain its own proper color over a long distance.

Therefore, the green of the countryside will transform more into blue than will yellow or white; and conversely, yellow and white will transform less than green and red.

### 241. On colors.

Colors placed in shadows will participate more or less in their natural beauty according to whether they are in greater or lesser darkness. But if colors are situated in a luminous space, then they will show themselves with much greater beauty as the light is of greater splendor. — **Opponent:** There are as many varieties of colors in shadows as there are varieties of colors in the things being shaded. — **Response:** Colors placed in shadows will show among themselves much less variety as the shadows situated there are darker; of this, those who look from the public squares into the doorways of shaded temples are witnesses, where paintings dressed in various colors appear even now to be dressed in darkness.

### 242. On the backgrounds of the figures of painted bodies.

The background <note>original: "campo"—the field or area surrounding a subject</note> that surrounds the figures of any painted thing must be darker than the illuminated part of those figures, and lighter than their shadowed part.

### 243. Why white is not a color.

White is not a color, but is in a state of potential receptivity to every color. When it is in a high countryside, all its shadows are blue; and this arises from the fourth [rule], which says: the surface of every opaque body participates in the color of its object <note>meaning the object or environment facing it</note>. Therefore, such white being deprived of the light of the sun by the interposition of some object placed between the sun and that white, all the white remains—which sees the sun and the air—participating in the color of the sun and the air; and that part which is not seen by the sun <insert>original: "which is not of the sun"</insert> remains in shadow, participating in the color of the air. And if such white did not see the greenery of the countryside all the way to the horizon, nor see the whiteness of that horizon, without doubt that white would appear to be of the simple color which the air shows itself to be.

The light of fire tinges everything in yellow; but this will not appear to be true except by comparison with things illuminated by the air; and this comparison can be seen

### 247. On things placed against a light background, and why such a practice is useful in painting.

When a shaded body ends against a field of light and illuminated color, it will necessarily appear detached and distant from that field. This occurs because bodies with curved surfaces necessarily become shaded on the opposite side from where they are struck by light rays, as that area is deprived of such rays; for

which reason it varies greatly from the background; and the illuminated part of said body never ends against that illuminated background with its primary brightness; rather, between the background and the primary light of the body, a boundary of the body is interposed which is darker than either the background or the respective light of the body. <note>Leonardo is describing the "edge effect" or "contour," noting that even the bright side of an object usually has a subtle transition that separates it from a bright background.</note>

### 248. On backgrounds.

Regarding the backgrounds of figures—that is, the light figure in a dark field, and the dark figure in a light field—the white with the black, or black with the white, each appears more powerful because of the other; and thus, opposites always show themselves more powerfully through one another. <note>This is the principle of simultaneous contrast, a cornerstone of Renaissance "chiaroscuro" (light-dark) painting.</note>

### 249. On colors.

The colors that suit one another are green with red, or purple <note>original: "paonazzo," a deep violet or peacock-colored purple</note>, or dark mauve <note>original: "biffa," a specific Renaissance term for a reddish-purple or mulberry hue</note>, and yellow with blue.

### 250. On colors resulting from the mixture of other colors, which are called the second species.

The simple colors are six, of which the first is white, although some philosophers do not accept either white or black in the number of colors, because one is the cause of colors and the other is their deprivation. But nevertheless, because the painter cannot do without these, we will place them in the number of the others, and we shall say that white, in this order, is the first among the simple colors, yellow the second, green the third, blue the

### 251. On colors.

Blue and green are not simple in themselves, because blue is composed of light and darkness, such as that of the air—that is, a most perfect black and a most brilliant white. <note>Leonardo believed the blue of the sky was not an inherent color but the result of white light from the sun illuminating the "darkness" of space through the atmosphere.</note> Green is composed of a simple and a composite color; that is, it is composed of blue and yellow.

### 252. On colors reflected upon lustrous things of various colors.

The reflected thing always participates in the color of the body that reflects it. The mirror is partially tinted by the color it reflects, and each participates in the other more or less according to whether the thing being reflected is more or less powerful than the color of the mirror. And that thing will appear to be of a more powerful color in the mirror which most participates in the color of that mirror.

### 253. On the colors of the body.

Among the colors of a body, that which is of a more splendid whiteness will be seen at a greater distance. Therefore, that which is of a greater darkness will be seen at a lesser distance.

Among bodies of equal whiteness and distance from the eye, that which is surrounded by greater darkness will appear more brilliant; and conversely, that darkness will appear more shadowy which is seen against a more brilliant whiteness.

## PART THREE.

### *ON THE VARIOUS ACCIDENTS AND MOVEMENTS OF MAN AND THE PROPORTION OF LIMBS.*

259. On the changes in human measurements caused by the movement of limbs in various positions.

The measurements of a man vary in every limb as they are bent more or less, and according to different perspectives; they diminish or increase more or less on one side, just as they increase or diminish on the opposite side. <note>Leonardo is describing the principle of "contrapposto" and how muscles contract and expand: as one side of a joint compresses, the other must stretch.</note>

260. On the changes in human measurements from birth to full growth.

A man in his early infancy has a shoulder width equal to the length of his face, and to the space from the shoulder to the elbow when the arm is extended; it is also equal to the space from the thumb of the hand to the said elbow when bent, and equal to the space from the base of the penis <note>original: "nascimento della verga"</note> to the middle of the knee, and equal to the space from that same knee joint to the ankle joint. But when a man has reached his final height, every aforementioned space doubles its length, except for the length of the face, which, together with the size of the entire head, undergoes little change; and for this reason, the man who has completed his growth... <note>The text cuts off here, noting that while the body grows significantly, the head remains relatively stable in size, leading to the different proportions seen in adults versus children.</note>

...who is well-proportioned, is ten of his own faces in height, and the width of the shoulders is two of those faces: and likewise all the other aforementioned lengths are two of those faces; and the rest will be discussed in the universal measurement of man.

### 261. How infants have joints that are the opposite of men in their thickness.

Small children <note>original: "putti piccoli"</note> all have slender joints, while the spaces located between one joint and another are thick; and this happens because the skin over the joints is alone, without any other flesh than that of a nerve-like nature <note>Leonardo uses "nervo" to refer to tendons or ligaments</note>, which surrounds and binds the bones together, and the moist fleshiness is found between one joint and another, enclosed between the skin and the bone; but because the bones are thicker at the joints than between the joints, the flesh, as a man grows, comes to lose that superfluity that stayed between the skin and the bone, whereby the skin draws closer to the bone and makes the limbs appear more slender; since there is nothing over the joints but the cartilaginous and nervous skin, it cannot dry out, and not drying out, it does not diminish; for these reasons infants are slender at the joints and thick between the joints themselves, as one sees the joints of the fingers, arms, and shoulders are slender and with hollowed pits <margin>1 In the Roman edition, 1817: "and concave"; perhaps: "and hollowed out".</margin>; and men, on the contrary, are thick in all the joints, fingers, arms, and legs; and where infants have a hollow <margin>2 In the manuscript: "outward".</margin>, men have a protrusion.

### 262. Of the different measurements that exist between children and men.

Between men and small children I find a great difference in the lengths from one joint to another, because a man has from the shoulder joint to the elbow, and from the elbow to the tip of the thumb, and from one shoulder blade to the other, two heads per section, and the child has one, because nature composes the size of the house of the intellect <note>The skull/head</note> before that of the vital spirits <note>The torso and limbs, associated in Renaissance thought with the heart and lungs</note>.

### 263. Of the joints of the fingers.

The fingers of the hand thicken at their joints from all views when they bend, and they thicken the more they bend, and likewise they diminish the more the fingers are straightened; the same happens with the toes, and they will vary all the more as they are more fleshy.

facing the same direction, figure *a* having turned its feet toward that direction when it twists, and moves away from it toward the opposite side—where it prepares the arrangement of its power—it then returns with speed and ease to the position where it lets the weight fly from its hands. But in this same case, figure *b*, having the tips of its feet turned in the opposite direction to the place where it wishes to throw its weight, twists toward that place with great discomfort; consequently, the effect is weak, and the motion partakes of its cause. This is because the preparation of force in every movement requires twists and bends of great violence <note>Leonardo uses "violence" here to mean physical tension or potential energy, like a coiled spring.</note>, so that the return may be with ease and comfort, and thus the action has a good effect. For the crossbow that has no "violent" arrangement will produce a short motion, or none at all, in the object it moves; because where there is no release of tension, there is no motion, and where there is no tension, it cannot be destroyed. For this reason, the bow that has no tension cannot create motion unless it acquires that tension, and in acquiring it, it does not yet cast it away. Thus, the man who does not twist or bend has not acquired power. Therefore, when he has thrown his dart, he will find himself twisted and weak in the direction toward which he threw the object, having acquired a power which is only useful for returning in the opposite direction.

### 276. On the attitude and movements of the limbs.

Let not the same movements be repeated in the limbs, or hands, or fingers of a single figure; nor should the same attitudes be repeated in a narrative painting <term>istoria: a complex narrative or historical scene</term>; and if the scene should be very large, such as a fray or slaughter of soldiers, where there are only three ways of striking—namely a thrust, a backhand, and a downward cut <note>original: "una punta, un rovescio e un fendente"</note>—in this case you must strive so that all the downward cuts are shown from various views: for example, some seen from behind, some from the side, and some from the front. Thus, all other views of these same three movements should participate in these three simple motions; and for this reason, we shall call all others participants of one of these. <gloss>1</gloss> But compound motions in battles are of great artifice and of great vivacity and movement; those are called compound where a single figure shows you the legs from the front, <gloss>2</gloss> and part of the profile of the shoulder. And of these compound motions, we shall speak in another place.

### 277. On the joints of the limbs.

Regarding the joints of the limbs and the variety of their bends, one must consider how the flesh increases on one side and diminishes on the other; and this must be researched in the necks of animals, because their motions are of three natures, of which—

two of them are simple and one is composite, which partakes of both simple ones; of which simple motions, one is when it bends toward one or the other shoulder, or when it raises or lowers the head that rests upon it. The second is when the neck itself twists to the right or to the left without curving—rather, it remains straight, but the face will be turned toward one of the shoulders. The third motion, which is called composite, is when its twisting is added to its bending, as when the ear inclines toward one of the shoulders and the face turns toward that same side, or toward the opposite shoulder with the face turned toward the sky.

### 278. On the formation of the limbs of man.

Measure within yourself the proportion of your own limb formation <note>Leonardo uses the term "membrificazione" to describe the structural assembly and proportions of the body parts.</note>, and if you find it discordant in any part, take note of it, and take great care not to use it in the figures that you compose; for it is a common vice of painters to make things similar to themselves. <note>Leonardo frequently warned that artists tend to paint their own physical likeness or defects into their subjects unless they study objective proportions.</note>

### 279. On the limbs.

Let all the limbs perform that office for which they were intended. In the dead or the sleeping, let no limb appear alive or awake. The foot, which receives the weight of the man, should be flattened and not with playful toes, unless it is resting only upon the heel.

### 280. On the formation of the limbs of animals.

Let the limbs of animals be made suitable to their qualities. I say that you should not take a leg of a graceful creature, or an arm, or other limbs, and attach them to one with a thick chest or neck. And do not mix the limbs of the young with those of the old; nor powerful and muscular limbs with those that are graceful and feeble, nor those of males with those of females.

### 281. On the motions of the parts of the face.

The motions of the parts of the face, caused by mental accidents <note>The term "accidenti mentali" refers to "passions of the soul" or emotional states that manifest physically.</note>, are many; of which the principal ones are laughing, crying, shouting, singing in various high and low voices: admiration, anger, joy, melancholy, fear, the pain of martyrdom and the like, of which mention will be made. And first of laughter and weeping, which are very similar in the mouth and the cheeks and the closing of the eyes, but vary only in the eyebrows and the space between them; and all of this we shall discuss in its place—that is, the variations that the face, the hands, and the whole person take on for each of these "accidents," of which knowledge is necessary for you, the painter; otherwise, your art will truly show bodies that are twice dead. And further, I remind you that the movements should not be so exaggerated and so agitated,

...so that a scene of peace does not look like a battle or a drunken Moorish dance <note>original: "moresca d'ubriachi"; a lively, often chaotic folk dance</note>, and above all, that those present at the event for which the story is made are intent upon that event with actions that show admiration, reverence, sorrow, suspicion, fear, or joy, according as the event requires for which the assembly or gathering of your figures is made. And ensure that your narrative scenes are not placed one above the other on the same wall with different horizons, so that it does not look like a merchant's shop with its boxes arranged in little squares.

### 282. On the movements of the human face.

Mental states <term>accidenti mentali: the internal emotions or "accidents" of the mind that manifest physically</term> move the face of man in various ways, of which some laugh, some weep, others rejoice, others are saddened, some show anger, others pity, some are filled with wonder, others are terrified, others appear foolish, others thoughtful and speculative. And these mental states must be accompanied by the hands and the face, and likewise the whole person.

### 283. Quality of the character of faces.

Ensure that the faces are not all of the same character <note>original: "aria"; referring to the general look, air, or "vibe" of a person</note>, as one sees most painters do; but create diverse characters according to their ages and temperaments <term>complessioni: the "complexion" or physical makeup believed to be determined by the four humors</term>, and their natures, whether wicked or good.

### 284. On the limbs and the description of features.

The parts that flank the bridge of the nose vary in eight ways:
1st: they are either equally straight, equally concave, or equally convex; 2nd: or they are unequally straight, concave, and convex; 3rd: or they are straight in the upper parts and concave below; 4th: or straight above and convex below; 5th: or concave above and straight below; 6th: or concave above and convex below; 7th: or convex above and straight below; 8th: or convex above and concave below.

The junction of the nose with the brow is of two types: it is either concave or it is straight.

The forehead has three varieties: it is either flat, or it is concave, or it is full <note>meaning rounded or bulging</note>; the flat forehead is divided into two parts: it is either convex in the upper part, or in the lower part, or else flat both above and below.

### 285. On making a human likeness in profile after having looked at it only once.

In this case, you must commit to memory the varieties of the four different features in profile, which would be the nose, mouth, chin, and forehead. We shall speak first of noses, which—

# LEONARDO DA VINCI [§ 288]

### 288. On Physiognomy and Palmistry.

I will not dwell upon the fallacious sciences of physiognomy <note>The practice of judging character from facial features.</note> and palmistry, because there is no truth in them; this is evident because such chimeras lack scientific foundations. It is true, however, that facial markings show, in part, the nature of men, their vices, and temperaments. In the face, the lines that separate the cheeks from the lips of the mouth, the nostrils, and the sockets of the eyes are prominent in men who are cheerful and laugh often. Those who have these lines only faintly marked are men given to deep thought. Those whose facial features have great relief and depth are bestial and prone to anger, possessing little reason. Those who have the vertical lines between the eyebrows strongly marked are also prone to anger, and those who have the horizontal lines of the forehead deeply etched are men full of lamentations, both hidden and overt. One can say the same for many other parts of the body. But regarding the hand, you will find that great armies have died by the sword in the same hour, yet no two signs on their hands were alike; the same can be seen in a shipwreck.

### 289. On the Placement of Limbs.

You should make the limbs that are undergoing exertion muscular, and those that are not being used you should make without muscles and soft.

### 290. On the Actions of Figures.

You must depict figures in such an action as is sufficient to demonstrate what the figure has in its mind; otherwise, your art will not be praiseworthy.

### 291. On Attitude.

The "little fountain" <note>original: "fontanella"; refers to the pit of the throat or the jugular notch.</note> of the throat falls directly over the foot [of support]; if one arm is thrown forward, this point moves off that foot; and if the leg is thrown backward, the point moves forward, and thus it changes with every attitude.

### 292. On the Movements of Limbs: Ensuring They Are Appropriate Actions When Depicting Man.

That figure whose movement does not correspond to the emotion <note>original: "accidente"; here meaning a mental state or internal event.</note> feigned to be in its mind, shows that its limbs are not obedient to its own judgment, and that the judgment of the artist is of little value <term>valetudine: strength or capability</term>.

<summary>Leonardo dismisses palmistry as unscientific while acknowledging that facial expressions leave physical traces of a person's character, and he emphasizes that a figure's physical posture must accurately reflect its internal thoughts.</summary>

### 298. On the articulation of limbs in nudes and their actions.

The limbs of nude figures must show their muscles more or less clearly depending on the greater or lesser exertion of said limbs.

### 299. On the revealing or concealing of muscles in each limb during the movements of animals.

I remind you, painter, that in the movements you depict your figures making, you should only reveal those muscles which are actually employed in the motion and action of your figure. The muscle that is most used in such a case should be most manifest; that which is less used should be less defined; and that which is not used at all should remain relaxed, soft, and with little definition. For this reason, I urge you to understand the <term>anatomy</term> <note>original: "notomia"; Leonardo refers here to the structural study of the body for artistic purposes</note> of muscles, tendons, and bones, without which knowledge you will achieve little. If you draw from life, perhaps the model you choose will lack well-defined muscles in the specific pose you want them to take; furthermore, you will not always have access to good nude models, nor will you always be able to draw them. It is better and more useful for you to have such variety practiced and committed to memory.

### 300. On the movements of man and other animals.

The movements of animals are of two kinds: <term>local motion</term> <note>movement from one place to another</note> and <term>actional motion</term> <note>movement within the body itself while staying in one spot</note>. Local motion occurs when the animal moves from place to place; actional motion is the movement the animal makes within itself without changing location. Local motion is of three types: ascending, descending, and traveling across a level surface. To these three, two more are added—slow and fast—and two others—straight and winding—and one more besides: jumping. However, actional motion is infinite, along with the infinite tasks which man often pursues, not without harm to himself. Movements are of three types: local, simple actional, and the third is a compound motion of actional with local. Slowness and speed should not be counted as types of local motion, but as qualities of those motions. Compound motions are infinite, for among them are dancing, fencing, juggling, sowing, plowing, and rowing; however, this rowing consists of simple actional movements, because the actional motion performed by the man in rowing is not mixed with local motion through the man's own movement, but through the movement of the boat.

### 301. On the motion and running of man and other animals.

When a man or other animal moves with speed or slowness, the part of the body above the leg that supports the weight will always be lower than the opposite side.

# LEONARDO DA VINCI [§ 306

### 306. On the man who carries a weight upon his shoulders.

The shoulder of the man who supports a weight is always higher than the shoulder without the weight; and this is demonstrated in the figure placed in the margin, through which passes the central line of the entire weight of the man and the weight carried by him. If this combined weight were not divided in equal measure over the center of the leg that rests on the ground, it would be necessary for the entire composition to collapse. But necessity provides that as much of the man's natural weight is thrown to one side as there is <term>accidental weight</term><note>Leonardo uses "accidental weight" to refer to an external load added to the body, as opposed to "natural weight" which is the body itself.</note> added to the opposite side. This cannot be done unless the man bends and lowers himself on his lighter side with enough of a lean that it partakes in the accidental weight he carries; and this cannot be done unless the shoulder carrying the weight rises and the light shoulder lowers. This is the means that ingenious necessity has found for such an action.

### 307. On the balancing of a man upon his feet.

The weight of a man who rests upon a single leg will always be divided with an equal opposite part over the center of gravity that he supports.

### 308. On the man who moves.

The man who moves will have his center of gravity over the center of the leg that is placed on the ground.

### 309. On the balancing of the weight of any animal standing still upon its legs.

The lack of motion in any animal which rests upon its feet arises from the lack of inequality between the opposite weights supported upon their feet. <note>In other words, if the weights on either side of the center of gravity are perfectly balanced, the body remains stationary.</note>

### 310. On the bendings and turnings of the man.

A man decreases as much in the bending of one of his sides as he increases in his other opposite side; and such a fold will ultimately be <term>subdouble</term><note>A mathematical term meaning one-half (1:2 ratio).</note> to the part that extends. And of this, a particular treatise shall be made.

### 315. On the <term>equilibrium</term> <note>original: "bilico"; refers to the balance or center of gravity of a body</note> of figures.

If the figure rests upon one of its feet, the shoulder of that side which rests will always be lower than the other, and the <term>pit of the throat</term> <note>original: "fontanella della gola"; the hollow at the base of the neck between the collarbones</note> will be positioned over the middle of the leg that supports the weight. The same will occur from whichever line we view the figure, provided it is without arms extending far out from the body, or without a weight on its back, in its hand, or on its shoulder, and without the non-supporting leg extending forward or backward.

### 316. On the grace of the limbs.

The limbs and the body must be arranged with grace according to the purpose of the action you wish the figure to perform; and if you wish to create a figure that shows elegance in itself, you must make the limbs delicate and extended, without showing too many muscles. Those few muscles that you do show for the purpose, make them soft—that is, with little prominence and with shadows that are not harsh. The limbs, and especially the arms, should be "un-knotted"—that is, no limb should be in a straight line with the limb that joins it. And if the hip, which is the pole of the man, is positioned such that the right side is higher than the left due to the stance, you shall make the <term>joint</term> <note>original: "giuntura"</note> of the upper shoulder fall in a perpendicular line over the most prominent part of the hip; and let this right shoulder be lower than the left, and the pit of the throat must always be above the middle of the <term>joint</term> of the supporting foot. The leg that does not support the weight should have its knee lower than the other and close to the other leg.

The poses of the head and arms are infinite, therefore I will not expand upon giving any specific rule for them. Nevertheless, I will say that they should be easy and pleasing, with various twists and turns, and that the joints should be united with the mind <note>meaning: with careful thought and observation</note> so that they do not appear like pieces of wood.

### 317. On the natural ease of the limbs.

Regarding the ease of these limbs, you must consider that when you want to depict someone who, for some reason, has to turn backward or to the side, you should not make the feet and all the limbs move in the same direction as the head. Instead, you shall create the action by distributing that twist across four <term>joints</term>: namely, those of the foot, the knee, the hip, and the neck. If the figure rests on the right leg, you shall make the left knee bend inward, and its foot should be slightly raised on the outside; the left shoulder should be somewhat lower than the right, and the nape of the neck should align with the same place where the outer <term>ankle-bone</term> <note>original: "noce"; literally "nut," referring here to the lateral malleolus of the ankle</note> of the left foot is turned, and the left shoulder will be over the tip of the right foot in a perpendicular line. And always

And if you depict a man sitting, and his arms must in some way be used for something across him, make the chest turn above the hip joint.

## 318. On a single figure outside of a narrative scene.

Furthermore, do not repeat the limbs in the same motion in a figure which you represent as being alone; that is, if the figure is shown running alone, do not make both hands forward, but one forward and the other backward, because otherwise it cannot run; and if the right foot is forward, let the right arm be backward and the left forward; because without such an arrangement one cannot run well. And if you depict one who saws, <note>The original manuscript says "sega" (saws). The Vienna edition suggests "segga" (sits), while the 1817 Roman edition has "lo seguiti" (follows him).</note> let him have one leg that is thrown somewhat forward, and make the other return under the head, and the upper arm should exchange the motion and go forward; and so of this it will be spoken of fully in the book of movements.

## 319. What are the principal matters of importance belonging to the figure.

Among the principal important things required in the representation of animals <note>Leonardo often uses "animals" to refer to all living beings, including humans, in a biological sense.</note> is to situate the head well upon the shoulders, the torso upon the hips, and the hips and the shoulders above the feet.

## 320. On balancing the weight around the center of gravity of bodies.

A figure that sustains itself upon its feet without motion will provide equal opposite weights around the center of its support. I say that if the figure without motion is placed upon its feet, if it throws an arm forward in front of its chest, it must throw as much natural weight backward as it throws of natural and <term>accidental weight</term> <note>Weight added by an external object or the momentum of a limb.</note> forward. And I say the same of every part that projects out from its whole beyond the usual.

## 321. On figures that have to handle or carry weights.

A man will never lift or carry a weight without sending out from himself more than as much weight as that which he wishes to lift, and he carries it on the opposite side to that from which he lifts the said weight.

<note><sup>I</sup> Thus the codex. The Vienna edition proposes to say: "one who sits"; the Roman edition, 1817, has: "one who follows him".</note>

### 322. On the attitudes of men.

Let the attitudes of men be arranged with their limbs in such a way that, through them, the intention of their soul is demonstrated. <note>This is Leonardo's famous concept of "moti mentali" (mental motions), where physical gesture must reveal internal thought.</note>

### 323. Variety of attitudes.

Let the actions of men be expressed according to their age and dignity, and let them vary according to their kind—that is, between males and females.

### 324. On the attitudes of figures.

I say that the painter must observe in men the attitudes and movements born immediately from any sudden event; let them be noted or committed to memory, and do not wait for the act of weeping to be performed by someone as a trial without a great cause for crying, and then portray it; because such an act, not being born from a true case, will be neither prompt nor natural. However, it is very good to have first noted it from a natural occurrence, and then have someone remain in that pose to observe some specific part for the purpose, and then portray it.

### 325. On the attention of bystanders to a noteworthy event.

All the bystanders of any event worthy of being noted stand with various admiring gestures to consider that act—as when justice punishes wrongdoers. And if the event is of a devout nature, all the bystanders should direct their eyes with various acts of devotion toward that event, such as the showing of the Host during the Sacrifice <note>Referring to the elevation of the bread during the Catholic Mass.</note>, and the like. And if it is an event worthy of laughter or weeping, in this it is not necessary that all the bystanders turn their eyes toward the event, but rather they should show various movements, and a large part of them should rejoice or grieve together. And if the event is fearful, the frightened faces of those who flee should make a great demonstration of fear and flight, with various movements, as will be discussed in the fourth book on movements.

### 326. Quality of nudes.

Never make a figure that is slender with muscles of too much relief; for slender men never have too much flesh over their bones, but are slender due to a lack of flesh, and where there is little flesh there cannot be thickness of muscles. <note>Leonardo warns against "anatomical exaggeration," a critique he often leveled at Michelangelo's muscular style.</note>

<summary>Leonardo explains how a painter must capture authentic human emotion and social reactions by observing real-life events rather than staged poses. He emphasizes that physical gestures must reveal the "intention of the soul" and adhere to the subject's age, gender, and anatomy.</summary>

<header>TREATISE ON PAINTING — PART THREE</header>

### 327. How muscular men are short and thick.

Muscular men have thick bones and are thick and short men, and they have a scarcity of fat, because the fleshiness of the muscles, through their growth, draw together, and the fat that is usually interspersed between them has no place; and the muscles in such lean men, being in tight contact with one another and unable to expand <insert>outwardly</insert>, grow in thickness, and they grow most in that part which is furthest from their ends—that is, toward the middle of their width and length.

### 328. How fat men do not have large muscles.

Even though fat men are in themselves short and thick, like the aforementioned muscular ones, they have thin muscles, but their skin covers much spongy and empty fat—that is, full of air; and therefore these fat men stay afloat on water better than muscular men do, who have solid skin and a smaller quantity of air within it.

### 329. Which muscles disappear in the various movements of man.

In the raising and lowering of the arms, the breasts <note>original: "poppe"; here referring to the pectoral muscles</note> disappear, or they become more prominent; the same happens to the curves of the flanks when bending outward or inward at the hips; and the shoulders show more variety, as do the hips and the neck, than any other joint, because they have more variable movements; and of this a specific book will be made.

### 330. On muscles.

The limbs in youth should not have a pronounced definition of muscles, because that is a sign of aged strength, and in youths it is neither the time nor the season for mature strength. Let the <term>sentimenti</term> <note>In Renaissance art theory, "sentimenti" refers to the visible "feel" or anatomical definition of the muscles and joints.</note> of the limbs be pronounced more or less evidently, according to whether they are more or less exerted. The muscles of those limbs that are exercised with greater labor will always be more evident. Those muscles will be less sculpted in the limbs that are exercised with less labor. The internal central lines of limbs that bend never remain at their natural length. Let thick and wide muscles be made for powerful men, with limbs corresponding to such a disposition.

### 331. On not showing all the muscles in figures, unless they are under great exertion.

Do not wish to make all the muscles evident in your figures, because even though they are in their proper places, they do not show great prominence unless the limbs where they are located...

<summary>Leonardo explains the anatomical differences between muscular and fat physiques, noting how muscle definition changes with movement and age. He cautions painters against over-defining muscles in youth or in figures not undergoing physical strain.</summary>

<meta>[§ 331]</meta>

situated are not in great force or under strain, and the limbs that remain without exercise should be without the demonstration of muscles. And if you do otherwise, you will have imitated a sack of walnuts rather than a human figure. <note>Leonardo uses the "sack of walnuts" metaphor to criticize artists who over-emphasize every muscle regardless of the body's pose, making the skin look lumpy and unnatural.</note>

### 332. On the muscles of animals.

The hollows placed between the muscles must not be of such a quality that the skin appears to clothe two sticks placed in mutual contact; nor should they appear like two sticks somewhat removed from such contact, where the skin hangs in vain with a long curve like *f*. Instead, it should be as it is at *i*, resting upon the spongy fat <term>spongy fat: Leonardo's term for adipose tissue that fills the gaps between muscle groups</term> placed in the corners, such as the angle *mno*. This angle arises from the end of the contact between muscles; and because the skin cannot descend into such an angle, Nature has filled that angle with a small quantity of spongy or, one might say, vesicular fat, with minute vesicles full of air, which condenses or rarefies within itself according to the increase or thinning of the substance of the muscles. <margin>A note in the manuscript warns that "the end is missing" from this paragraph.</margin>

### 333. That a nude figure depicted with great prominence of muscles will be without motion.

A nude figure depicted with great prominence of all its muscles will be without motion, because it cannot move unless one part of the muscles relaxes while the opposing muscles pull. Those muscles that relax lose their definition, and those that pull reveal themselves strongly and become evident. <note>This is a fundamental principle of Leonardo's "dynamic anatomy": for one muscle to contract (agonist), the opposite must relax (antagonist).</note>

### 334. That nude figures should not have their muscles entirely emphasized.

Nude figures should not be rendered entirely with all their muscles emphasized, because they turn out labored and ungraceful. You must understand all the muscles of man, but pronounce them with little evidence where the man is not exerting himself in those parts. That limb which is most exerted will be the one that most demonstrates its muscles. In whatever direction the limb turns for its operation, in that same direction its muscles will be most frequently pronounced. The muscle itself often pronounces its individual parts through the action, in such a way that without such action they were not demonstrated in it before.

### 335. That those who develop fatness increase greatly in strength after their early youth.

Those who develop fatness increase greatly in strength after their early youth, because the skin always remains pulled tight over the muscles. However, these individuals are not very dexterous or agile in their movements; and because such skin remains taut, they possess a great universal power infused through all their limbs. From this it follows that those who lack the arrangement of the aforementioned skin help themselves by wearing their clothes tight over their limbs and binding themselves with various ties, so that during the contraction of the muscles, the muscles have something to push against and lean upon. But when fat people happen to grow thin, they become very weak, because the deflated skin remains flabby and wrinkled; and the muscles, finding nothing to lean upon, cannot contract nor become hard, whereby they remain of little power. Moderate fatness that is never deflated by any illness ensures that the skin remains pulled tight over the muscles, and these show few <note>original: "sentimenti" — in this context, Leonardo refers to the visible "expressions" or outlines of the muscles beneath the surface</note> details on the surface of their bodies.

### 336. How nature intends to hide the bones in animals as much as the necessity of their limbs allows.

Nature intends to hide the bones in animals as much as the necessity of their limbs allows, and this she does more in one body than in another. She will do so more in bodies where she is not hindered than where she is hindered. Therefore, in the flower of youth, the skin is pulled and stretched as much as it can be, given the height of bodies that are not meant to be fat or corpulent; later, through the movement of the limbs, the skin grows over the folds of the joints, and thus when the limbs are extended, the skin that grew over the joints becomes wrinkled. Later, as one grows in age, the muscles thin out, and the skin that clothes them grows and fills with wrinkles, falling away and separating from the muscles due to the fluids interposed between the muscles and the skin. The branching of the nerves, which connect the skin to the muscles and give it sensation, become stripped of the parts of the muscles that clothed them, and in place of those muscles, they are surrounded by poor fluids; because of this, they are poorly and scantily nourished. Wherefore such <term>membrification</term> <note>The structural formation or arrangement of the limbs and their components.</note>, due both to the continuous weight of the skin and the great amount of fluid, causes the skin to lengthen and distance itself from the muscles and bones, forming various bags full of folds and wrinkles.

### 337. How it is necessary for the painter to know anatomy.

It is a necessary thing for the painter, in order to be a good <term>membrificator</term> <note>One who depicts the structure and proportions of the limbs.</note> in the attitudes and gestures that can be made by nude figures, to know the <term>anatomy</term> <note>original: "notomia" — Leonardo's term for the study of internal structure through dissection.</note> of nerves, bones, and muscles.

<summary>Leonardo explains how skin tension affects physical strength and how aging causes the skin to sag and wrinkle as muscles thin and fluids accumulate. He concludes by emphasizing that a painter must master anatomy to correctly depict the human form in motion.</summary>
<keywords>anatomy, skin tension, aging, muscle contraction, membrification, youth vs age, physical strength</keywords>

and tendons, in order to know in various movements and forces which nerve or muscle is the cause of such movement; and only make those evident and those enlarged, and not the others throughout, as many do, who, to appear as great draftsmen, make their nudes woody and without grace, so that to look at them they seem like a sack of walnuts rather than a human surface, or rather a bundle of radishes, instead of muscular nudes. <note>Leonardo famously criticized Michelangelo and his followers for over-emphasizing musculature, which he felt looked unnatural.</note>

### 338. **On the widening and shortening of the muscles.**

The muscle of the back of the thigh shows greater variety in its extension and contraction than any other muscle in man; the second is that which composes the buttock; the third is that of the back; the fourth is that of the throat; the fifth is that of the shoulders; the sixth is that of the stomach, which originates under the <term>pomegranate apple</term> <note>original: "pomo granato" — the xiphoid process at the base of the breastbone</note> and ends in the <term>pubic bone</term> <note>original: "pettignone" — the pubic region</note>, as will be said of all of them.

### 339. **Where a cord is found in men without muscles.**

Where the arm ends with the palm of the hand, about four fingers away, there is a cord <note>Leonardo uses "corda" to refer to tendons or ligaments</note>, the largest in man, which is without muscle, and originates in the middle of one of the <term>arm-focils</term> <note>original: "fucili del braccio" — the radius and ulna bones of the forearm</note>, and ends in the middle of the other bone, and has a square shape, and is about three fingers wide and half a finger thick; and this serves only to hold the two said bones of the arm tightly together, so that they do not spread apart.

### 340. **Of the eight pieces that originate in the middle of the cords in various joints of man.**

There originate in the joints of man certain pieces of bone, which are stable in the middle of the cords that bind certain joints, such as the kneecaps and those of the shoulders, and the tops of the feet, which are eight in total, for there is one for each shoulder and one for each knee, and two for each foot under the first joint of the big toes toward the heel; and these become very hard toward a man's old age. <note>These are the sesamoid bones, which Leonardo correctly identifies as hardening with age.</note>

### 341. **Of the muscle that is between the pomegranate apple and the pubic bone.**

A muscle originates near the <term>pomegranate apple</term> and ends in the <term>pubic bone</term>, which muscle is of three powers, because it is divided in its length by three cords; that is, first the upper muscle, then a cord as wide as the muscle itself, then follows the second muscle lower than this, to which the second cord is joined; finally follows the third muscle with the third cord, which cord is joined to the pubic bone; and these three stages of three muscles with three cords are made by nature

### 361. On the quality of limbs according to age.

In young people, you should not seek out defined muscles or <term>lacerti<note>From the Latin 'lacertus', referring to the bundles of muscle fibers that give a lean, powerful appearance.</note></term>, but rather a soft fleshiness with simple folds and rounded limbs.

### 362. On the variety of faces.

The expression of faces should be varied according to the circumstances of the person: in fatigue, at rest, in weeping, in laughter, in shouting, in fear, and similar states; and furthermore, the limbs of the person, together with their entire posture, must correspond to the altered expression of the face.

### 363. On the structure of the limbs of animals.

All parts of any animal must correspond to the age of the whole; that is, the limbs of the young should not be rendered with pronounced muscles, tendons, or veins, as some do who—wishing to show off a skillful and grand style of drawing—ruin the whole by using mismatched limbs. Others do the same when, through a lack of drawing skill, they give the limbs of youth to the elderly.

### 364. How a figure is not praiseworthy if it does not show the passion of the soul.

That figure will not be praiseworthy if it does not, as much as possible, express the passion of its soul through its actions.

### 365. How the hands and arms in all their operations must demonstrate the intention of their mover as much as possible.

The hands and arms in all their operations must demonstrate the intention of their mover <note>The 'mover' refers to the mind or soul directing the body's actions.</note> as much as possible, because with these, anyone of refined judgment accompanies their mental intentions in all their movements. Great orators, whenever they wish to persuade their audience of something, always accompany their words with their hands and arms, though some foolish men do not care for such adornment and appear on their rostrums like wooden statues, through whose mouths the voice of some hidden man passes as if through a tube. This habit is a great defect in the living, and much more so in painted figures; if these are not aided by their creator with prompt gestures suited to the intention you imagine to be in such a figure, then that figure will be judged twice dead: dead because it is not alive, and dead in its action. But to return to our purpose, here...

<summary>Leonardo emphasizes that physical anatomy must match a subject's age and that a figure's posture and gestures must vividly express their internal emotions and intentions.</summary>

### 370. On the movement of animals.

Every two-footed animal, in its motion, lowers that part which is above the lifting foot more than the part above the foot resting on the ground; and its uppermost part does the opposite. This is visible in the hips and shoulders of a man when he walks, and likewise in birds with their heads and their rumps. <note>Leonardo is describing the counter-balancing shift of the center of gravity during locomotion.</note>

### 371. That every limb should be proportioned to its whole body.

Ensure that every part of a whole is proportioned to its entirety: for example, if a man is of a thick and short stature, ensure that every one of his limbs is the same—that is, short and thick arms, wide, thick, and short hands, and fingers with joints in the aforementioned manner, and so with the rest. And I intend the same to be said of all animals and plants, whether in diminishing the proportions of their thickness or in increasing them.

### 372. That if figures do not express the mind, they are twice dead.

If figures do not perform prompt actions which express the concept of their minds through their limbs, those figures are twice dead: they are dead primarily because painting in itself is not alive, but rather an expresser of living things without life; and if the vivacity of action is not added to them, the work remains dead a second time. Therefore, delight yourselves studiously in observing those who speak, along with the movements of their hands—if you can approach them and hear them—to see what cause makes them perform such movements. The nuances of particular actions will be very well observed among the mute <note>original: "mutoli," referring to those who cannot speak and must rely entirely on gesture.</note>, who do not know how to draw, although there are few who do not help themselves and illustrate with drawing. Learn, therefore, from the mute to make the movements of the limbs that express the concept of the speakers' minds. Consider those who laugh and those who weep; look at those who shout with anger, and likewise all the accidents <term>accidents: in Renaissance philosophy, these are the outward manifestations or changing states of the internal mind</term> of our minds. Observe decorum <note>original: "decoro," the artistic principle of appropriateness and suitability.</note>, and consider that it is not fitting, neither by location nor by action, for a master to act like a servant, nor an infant like an adolescent, but rather like an old man who can hardly support himself. Do not give a peasant the action that belongs to a noble and well-bred man, nor the strong man the action of the weak, nor the actions of harlots those of honest women, nor those of males those of females.

### 373. On the observance of decorum.

Observe decorum—that is, the suitability of action, clothing, setting, and the circumstances of the dignity or lowliness of the things you wish to represent; that is, that a king be of beard, air, and... <note>The text breaks off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

<summary>Leonardo explains the mechanics of walking and emphasizes that a painting is "twice dead" if it fails to use physical gestures to reveal the internal thoughts and social status of the subjects.</summary>

## 377. How an angry figure should be depicted.

For an angry figure, you should show him holding someone by the hair with their head twisted toward the ground, pressing one of his knees into the victim's ribs, and raising his right fist high in the air. This man should have his hair standing up, his brows low and knit together, his teeth clenched, and the two corners of his mouth arched downward. His neck should be thick and, because he is leaning over his enemy, the front of it should be full of wrinkles.

## 378. How a desperate man is depicted.

For a man in despair, you should show him turning a knife upon himself, having torn his clothes with his hands; let one of those hands be in the act of tearing at his own wound. You should depict him with his feet spread apart, his legs somewhat bent, and his body likewise inclined toward the ground, with his hair torn and disheveled.

## 379. On the suitability of the limbs.

I remind you also to take great care when assigning limbs to your figures; ensure that, besides being proportionate to the size of the body, they also correspond to its age. That is: youths should have few visible muscles in their limbs, with veins appearing delicately on the surface, and rounded limbs of a pleasing color. Men should be sinewy and full of muscles. Old men should have surfaces with rough wrinkles and prominent veins, with the tendons <term>nervi</term> <note>Leonardo often uses "nervi" to refer to tendons or sinews rather than nerves in the modern neurological sense.</note> very evident.

## 380. On laughing and crying and the difference between them.

Between one who laughs and one who weeps, there is no variation in the eyes, nor the mouth, nor the cheeks, except for the rigidity of the eyebrows, which is added to the one who weeps and lifted in the one who laughs. To the one who weeps is also added the act of tearing at clothes and hair with the hands, and scratching the skin of the face with the fingernails—which does not happen to the one who laughs. You should not make the face of one who weeps with the same movements as one who laughs, because they often resemble one another; the true method is to vary them just as the cause <term>accidente</term> <note>Literally "accident," referring here to the external cause or the specific emotional state triggering the physical reaction.</note> of weeping is varied from the cause of laughter. Indeed, in weeping, the brows and the mouth vary according to the different causes of the tears: for some weep with anger, some with fear, some out of tenderness and joy, some out of suspicion, some from pain and torment, and some out of pity and grief for lost relatives or friends. Among these mourners, some appear desperate, some moderate; some scream, some stand with their faces toward heaven and their hands held low, with their fingers woven together; others, fearful, have their shoulders raised to their ears; and so they follow according to the aforementioned causes. That which...

->TREATISE ON PAINTING — PART THREE<-

The compound balance is understood to be that which a man maintains when supporting a weight upon himself through various movements; as in the depiction of Hercules crushing Antaeus <note>In Greek mythology, Hercules defeated the giant Antaeus by lifting him off the ground, as Antaeus drew strength from his mother, the Earth.</note>. In this case, as Hercules suspends him from the ground between his chest and arms, you must place Hercules's own figure as far behind the central line of his feet as Antaeus has his center of gravity in front of those same feet.

### 389. Of the man who rests upon his two feet, giving more of his weight to one than the other.

When a man has tired the leg he is standing on due to long standing, he shifts part of the weight onto the other leg; but this type of posture should only be used for decrepit old age, or for infancy, or indeed for someone exhausted, because it demonstrates weariness or a lack of strength in the limbs. Therefore, one always sees a young man, who is healthy and vigorous, resting upon one of his legs; and if he gives some weight to the other leg, he does so only when he wishes to begin a necessary movement—without which all motion is denied, because motion is generated from inequality <note>Leonardo views "inequality" or imbalance as the fundamental spark of all physical movement.</note>.

### 390. Of the poses of figures.

Figures that are at rest must always vary their limbs; that is, if one arm moves forward, the other should remain still or move backward. If the figure rests upon one leg, the shoulder above that leg should be lower than the other. This is practiced by men of good sense <note>Meaning artists with keen observation and judgment.</note>, who always naturally attend to balancing the man over his feet so that he does not collapse. Because, when resting on one foot, the opposite leg—being bent—does not support the man, acting as if it were dead; hence, necessity dictates that the weight from the legs upward must send its center of gravity over the joint of the leg that supports it.

### 391. Of the <term>ponderation</term> <note>From the Latin 'ponderare' (to weigh); the distribution of weight in a figure to achieve balance.</note> of a man when standing still upon his feet.

A man who stands still upon his feet will either load himself with equal weight upon each foot, or he will load himself with unequal weights. If he loads himself equally upon these feet, he will be loaded with <term>natural weight</term> <note>The weight of the body itself.</note> mixed with <term>accidental weight</term> <note>External weight, such as an object being carried.</note>, or he will be loaded with simple natural weight. If he is loaded with natural weight mixed with accidental weight, then the opposite ends of the limbs will not be equally distant from the poles of the joints of the feet; but if he is loaded with simple natural weight, then such ends of opposite limbs will be equally distant from the joint of the foot. And thus, a specific book shall be made regarding this ponderation.

<summary>Leonardo explains the mechanics of balance and weight distribution in the human body, distinguishing between the postures of the young and the infirm, and defining how "accidental" weights affect a figure's center of gravity.</summary>
<keywords>balance, Hercules and Antaeus, center of gravity, posture, movement, ponderation, natural weight, accidental weight</keywords>

### 392. On local motion, more or less fast.

Local motion <note>The physical movement of a body from one place to another.</note> performed by a man or another animal will be of greater or lesser speed depending on whether their center of gravity is further from or closer to the center of the foot where they are supported.

### 393. On four-footed animals, and how they move.

The maximum height of four-footed animals varies more in animals that are walking than in those that stand still; and this varies more or less according to whether the animals are of greater or lesser size. This is caused by the slant of the legs that touch the ground, which raise the body of the animal when those legs lose their slant as they are placed perpendicular to the earth.

### 394. On the correspondences that one half of a man has with the other half.

One half of the thickness and width of a man will never be equal to the other, unless the limbs joined to it perform equal and similar movements.

### 395. How three motions are found in a man jumping upward.

When a man jumps upward, the head is three times faster than the heel of the foot before the tip of the toe leaves the ground, and twice as fast as the hips. This happens because three angles are straightened at the same time: the first is where the torso joins the thighs at the front; the second is where the thighs join the legs at the back; the third is where the leg at the front joins the bone of the foot.

### 396. That it is impossible for a memory to retain all the aspects and changes of the limbs.

It is impossible for any memory to retain all the aspects or changes of any limb of any animal whatsoever. We shall exemplify this case with the demonstration of a hand. And because every continuous quantity is infinitely divisible, the motion of the eye that looks at the hand, and moves from *a* to *b*, moves through a space *ab*, which is also a continuous quantity, and consequently infinitely divisible; and in every part of that motion, the aspect and the figure of the hand varies in the...
