his vision, and he will do the same moving through the entire circle; and the same will be done by the hand that rises in its motion, that is, it will pass through space, which is a quantity. <note>Leonardo is explaining that movement is continuous and geometric, making it impossible for a painter to memorize every single point of a motion without scientific understanding.</note>

### 397. On the first four parts required for the figure.

Attitude <note>The "attitude" (attitudine) refers to the pose or posture of a figure and how it expresses an internal state or action.</note> is the first and most noble part of the figure; not that a good figure painted in a poor attitude lacks grace, but even a living person of the highest beauty loses reputation when their actions are not suited to the task they must perform. Without any doubt, this attitude requires greater intellectual speculation than the inherent quality of the painted figure itself; for such quality of the figure can be achieved by imitating life, but the movement of such a figure must be born from a great discernment of the mind. The second noble part is having relief <note>The illusion of three-dimensionality and depth.</note>; the third is good design; the fourth is beautiful coloring.

### 398. A discourse on the practical.

And you, painter, strive to make your works such that they draw their viewers to them, and hold them with great admiration and delight; do not attract them and then drive them away, as the air does to one who, in the night, leaps naked from bed to contemplate the quality of that air, whether cloudy or serene—who, immediately driven away by the cold, returns to the bed from which he first rose. Instead, make your works like that air which, in warm weather, draws men from their beds and keeps them there with delight to take in the summer coolness. Do not wish to be a practitioner before you are a scholar, nor let greed overcome the glory that is deservedly acquired from such an art.

Do you not see that among human beauties, it is the most beautiful face that stops wayfarers, and not their rich ornaments? And this I say to you who adorn your figures with gold or other rich decorations. Do you not see the radiant beauties of youth diminish in their excellence because of excessive and overly labored ornaments? Have you not seen mountain women wrapped in unrefined and poor clothes acquire greater beauty than those who are adorned? 

Do not use affected hairstyles or arrangements of heads, where—among those with dull wits—if a single hair is placed more to one side than the other, the one who wears it fears great infamy, believing that those around them will abandon every other thought and only speak of that hair and only criticize that. Such people always have the mirror and the comb as their counselor, and the wind is their capital enemy, the spoiler of groomed hair. You, therefore, should make the hair on your heads play together with an imaginary wind around youthful faces, and adorn them gracefully with diverse turns. Do not do as those who plaster them with glues <note>original: "colle"</note>, making the faces look as if they were glazed; human follies are increasing, for which it is not enough for sailors to bring gum arabic <term>Gum arabic: A natural gum made of hardened sap from acacia trees, used historically as a hair fixative and an adhesive in pigments.</term> from Eastern parts to prevent the wind from altering the uniformity of their locks—they go on investigating even more.

<header>LEONARDO DA VINCI</header>
<meta>[§ 399</meta>

### 399. On the practice sought with great diligence by the painter.

And you, painter, who desire the greatest mastery, must understand that if you do not build it upon the firm foundation of natural things, you will produce many works with little honor and less profit; but if you build it well, your works will be many and good, bringing you great honor and much utility.

---

### 400. On the painter judging his own works and those of others.

When a work stands equal to the artist's judgment, that is a poor sign for such judgment; and when the work exceeds the judgment, that is the worst case, as happens to one who marvels at having performed so well; but when the judgment exceeds the work, that is a perfect sign. If a young man finds himself in such a state, he will without doubt become an excellent practitioner, though he will be a composer of few works—works of such quality that they will stop men in admiration to contemplate their perfections. <note>Leonardo suggests that a healthy dissatisfaction with one's work is the engine of genius; if you think your painting is perfect, you have stopped growing.</note>

---

### 401. On the painter judging his own painting.

We know that errors are recognized more easily in the works of others than in our own, and often, while reproving the small errors of others, you will fail to see your own great ones. To escape such ignorance, see that you first become a master of <term>perspective</term> <note>The mathematical science of representing three-dimensional space on a flat surface.</note>, and then that you have a complete knowledge of the measurements of man and other animals. Furthermore, ensure you are a good <term>architect</term> <note>Here meaning a designer of forms and structures.</note>, at least regarding the form of buildings and other things upon the earth, which are of infinite shapes; the more knowledge you have of these, the more your work will be praised, and in those things where you lack practice, do not refuse to draw them from nature. 

But to return to the promise made above, I say that while painting you should hold a flat mirror and often look at your work within it. There, the work will be seen in reverse, and it will seem to you to be by the hand of another master; thus you will judge your errors better than otherwise. It is also good to rise often and take some recreation, because upon returning, your judgment will be improved; staying fixed upon the work will lead you into great deception. It is also good to move some distance away, because the work appears smaller and more of it is grasped in a single glance, allowing the discordant and disproportionate limbs or colors to be better recognized than when viewed from up close.

---

### 402. How the mirror is the master of painters.

When you wish to see if your painting as a whole conforms to the thing portrayed from nature, take a mirror and reflect the living object within it; then compare the reflected object with your painting, and consider well if the subject...

<page-num>135</page-num>
<header>TREATISE ON PAINTING — PART THREE</header>
<meta>a 404]</meta>

...so that both likenesses may conform to one another. Above all, the mirror should be taken as your master—I mean the flat mirror—because upon its surface, things have a likeness to painting in many ways. That is, you see a painting made upon a flat surface demonstrating things that appear in <term>relief</term> <note>The illusion of three-dimensionality or "popping out" from the surface.</note>, and the mirror on a flat surface does the same. The painting is a single surface, and the mirror is the same. The painting is impalpable, in that what appears round and distinct cannot be grasped by the hands, and the mirror does the same. The mirror and the painting show the likeness of things surrounded by shadow and light, and both appear to exist far beyond their actual surface. And if you recognize that the mirror, by means of outlines, shadows, and lights, makes things appear to stand out, and since you have among your colors shadows and lights more powerful than those of the mirror, certainly, if you know how to compose them well together, your painting will also appear like a natural thing seen in a large mirror.

### *403. How one should recognize a good painting and what qualities it must have to be good.*

The first thing to be judged in order to recognize a good painting is whether the motion is appropriate to the mind of the mover <note>The "mover" refers to the soul or will of the figure; the physical action must reflect the character's internal intent.</note>; second, that the greater or lesser relief of the shadowed things is adjusted according to their distances; third, that the proportions of the limbs correspond to the proportionality of their whole; fourth, that the <term>decorum</term> <note>The suitability or appropriateness of a setting to the subject matter.</note> of the site corresponds to the decorum of the actions; fifth, that the <term>membrifications</term> <note>The anatomical structure and shaping of the limbs.</note> are suited to the condition of the subjects—that is, to the refined, refined limbs; to the coarse, coarse limbs; and to the fat, fat limbs likewise.

### *404. How true painting resides in the surface of the flat mirror.*

The mirror with a flat surface contains within itself true painting upon that surface; and a perfect painting, made upon the surface of any flat material, is similar to the surface of the mirror. And you, painters, find your master in the surface of flat mirrors, which teach you the <term>chiaroscuro</term> <note>original: "il chiaro e l' oscuro"; the treatment of light and shade in drawing and painting.</note> and the <term>foreshortening</term> <note>original: "lo scorto"; the visual effect that causes an object to appear shorter than it actually is when angled toward the viewer.</note> of any object. Your colors include one that is brighter than the illuminated parts of the <term>simulacrum</term> <note>The reflected image or likeness.</note> of such an object, and similarly among those colors one finds some darker than any darkness of that object. From this it follows that you, painter, will make your paintings similar to those of such a mirror when it is viewed with a single eye; for two eyes encompass an object that is smaller than the eye itself.

<summary>Leonardo argues that the flat mirror is the painter's best teacher because it translates 3D reality onto a 2D plane, and he lists five criteria for judging artistic quality, including anatomical appropriateness and the "motion of the mind."</summary>
<keywords>mirror, relief, chiaroscuro, foreshortening, anatomy, decorum, proportions, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

### 405. Which painting is most praiseworthy.

That painting is most praiseworthy which has the most conformity with the thing imitated. I propose this to the confusion of those painters who wish to "improve" upon the things of nature, such as those who imitate a small child of one year, whose head fits five times into his height, and they make it fit eight times; and while the width of the shoulders is equal to the head, they make it double; and thus they go about reducing a small child of one year to the proportions of a man of thirty years. They have used and seen this error used so many times that they have turned it into a custom, which custom has so deeply penetrated and established itself in their corrupt judgment that they make themselves believe that nature—or whoever imitates nature—commits a very great error by not doing as they do.

### 406. What is the primary intentional objective of the painter.

The first intention of the painter is to make a flat surface demonstrate a body in <term>relief</term> <note>The illusion of three-dimensionality.</note> and standing out from that plane; and he who exceeds others in such an art deserves the greatest praise. This investigation—or rather, the crown of this science—is born from shadows and lights, or what you might call <term>chiaroscuro</term> <note>original: "chiaro e scuro"; the technique of using strong contrasts between light and dark to model three-dimensional forms.</note>. Therefore, he who flees from shadows flees from the glory of the art among noble minds, and acquires it among the ignorant common folk, who desire nothing more than the beauty of colors, entirely forgetting the beauty and wonder of showing a flat thing in relief.

### 407. Which is more important in painting: the shadows or their outlines.

Shadows in painting require much greater investigation and speculation than their outlines. The proof of this is taught by the fact that outlines can be traced <note>original: "lucidare"; literally to "clear" or "trace through."</note> using veils or flat glass placed between the eye and the thing to be traced; but shadows are not captured by such a rule, because of the <term>insensibility</term> <note>The lack of a sharp, perceptible edge.</note> of their boundaries, which are most often blurred, as is demonstrated in the *Book of Shadows and Lights*.

### 408. How light should be given to figures.

Light must be used according to the natural site where you imagine your figure to be; that is, if you imagine it in the sun, make the shadows dark and the areas of light large, and stamp the shadows of all surrounding bodies upon the ground. And if the figure is in gloomy weather, make little difference between the lights and the shadows, and without giving it any shadow at its feet.

<summary>Leonardo argues that the highest goal of painting is the realistic imitation of nature through the mastery of relief and chiaroscuro, criticizing those who use artificial proportions or prioritize bright colors over the subtle science of shadows.</summary>
<keywords>imitation of nature, proportions of children, relief, chiaroscuro, light and shadow, outlines, environmental lighting, artistic judgment</keywords>

and if the figure is indoors, make a great difference between the lights and the shadows, and the shadow on the ground; and if you depict a window covered with cloth <note>original: "impannata"; windows in Leonardo's time were often covered with oiled cloth or paper rather than clear glass, creating a soft, diffused light.</note> and a white dwelling, make little difference between the lights and the shadows; and if it is illuminated by fire, make the lights reddish and powerful, and the shadows dark, and the cast of the shadows against the walls or on the ground should be sharp; and the further the shadow moves from the body, the wider and larger it should become; and if said figure were illuminated partly by fire and partly by the air, make the light caused by the air more powerful, and that of the fire almost red, in the likeness of fire. And above all, ensure that your painted figures have a large light from above—that is, the living model you portray—because the people you see in the streets all have the light from above; and know that there is no great acquaintance of yours who, if given light from below, you would not struggle to recognize.

### 409. Where the viewer of the painting should stand.

Let us suppose that *a b* is the painting being viewed, and that *d* is the light. I say that if you place yourself between *c* and *e*, you will perceive the painting poorly, and especially if it is done in oil, or truly varnished, because it will have a <term>glare</term> <note>original: "lustro"; the specular reflection or "shine" on a surface that obscures the image.</note>, and will be almost like a mirror; and for this reason, the closer you approach point *c*, the less you will see, because there the rays of light sent from the window to the painting bounce back; and if you place yourself between *e* and *d*, there your vision will be well-served, and especially the more you approach point *d*, because that place participates less in said percussion of reflected rays.

### 410. How high the point should be placed.

The <term>vanishing point</term> <note>original: "il punto"; the central point in a perspective construction.</note> must be at the eye level of an average man, and the furthest horizon of the plain that borders the sky must be made at the height of that boundary where the flat earth meets the sky, except for the mountains, which are free.

### 411. That small figures should not, by reason, be finished.

I say that if things appear minute in form, this arises from said things being far from the eye; this being so, it is necessary that much air exists between the eye and the object, and much air hinders the clarity of the form of these objects, whereby the minute particles of these bodies will be indiscernible and unrecognizable. Therefore you, painter, shall make small figures only suggested and not finished, and if you do otherwise, it will be against the effects of nature, your mistress. The object remains small because of the great distance between the eye and the object; the great distance encloses within itself much air; much air creates in itself a thick body, which hinders and takes away the minute particles of the objects from the eye.

### 412. What background the painter should use for his works.

Since experience shows that all bodies are surrounded by shadow and light, I want you, painter, to arrange the part that is illuminated so that it ends against a dark object, and likewise the shadowed part of the body should end against a light object. And this rule will be of great help in giving <term>relief</term> <note>original: "rilevare"; the illusion of three-dimensionality or "popping out" from the flat surface.</note> to your figures.

### 413. A precept of painting.

Where the shadow borders the light, pay attention to where it is lighter or darker and where it is more or less <term>smoky</term> <note>original: "sfumosa"; referring to Leonardo's famous "sfumato" technique of soft, blurred transitions.</note> toward the light. And above all, I remind you that in young people you should not make the shadows as defined as those of stone, because flesh has a bit of transparency, as can be seen by looking at a hand placed between the eye and the sun, which is seen to redden and appear luminously transparent; and if you want to see what kind of shadow is required for your flesh, cast a shadow upon it with your finger, and according to whether you want it lighter or darker, hold your finger closer or further from your painting and imitate that.

### 414. On depicting a wild place.

Trees and grasses that are more branched with thin twigs should have less darkness in their shadows, and those trees and grasses that have larger leaves will be the cause of greater shadow.

### 415. How you must make a fictional animal appear natural.

You know that it is impossible to create any animal which does not have its own limbs, and that each limb by itself must bear a resemblance to that of some other animal. Therefore, if you want to make a fictional animal appear natural—let us say, for example, a serpent—for the head take that of a mastiff or a hound, and give it the eyes of a cat, the ears of a porcupine, the nose of a greyhound, the eyebrows of a lion, the temples of an old rooster, and the neck of a <term>water turtle</term> <note>original: "testuggine d’acqua"; likely referring to a pond turtle or terrapin.</note>.

### 416. Of the sites that should be chosen to create things that have graceful relief.

In streets facing west, when the sun is at midday, let the walls be so high that the one facing the sun does not reflect onto the shadowed bodies; and the air without glare would be good; then the sides of the faces will be seen part—

the observer that it is not a man who appears to want to enter therein. We have seen porticos laden with men, where the columns supporting them were held in the fist of a man who leaned against one of them as if it were a slender walking stick; and such similar things are greatly to be avoided. <note>Leonardo is criticizing artists who fail to maintain consistent scale, making buildings look like toys compared to the figures.</note>

### 420. Bodies should correspond, both in size and function, to the subject matter.

This proposition is defined before it is proposed; therefore, you shall read above. <note>A cross-reference likely added by the original compiler of the Codex Urbinas.</note>

### 421. On the boundaries of bodies called lineaments, or contours.

The boundaries of bodies are of such minimal visibility that at even a small distance between the object and the eye, the eye cannot perceive the features of a friend or relative; one recognizes them only by their clothing, and thus the mind receives knowledge of the whole through the combination of the whole and its parts. <term>Lineaments</term> <note>From the Latin 'lineamentum', referring here to the precise outlines or facial features that define an individual's likeness.</note>

### 422. On the superficial qualities that are first lost due to distance.

The first things lost when moving away from shaded bodies are their boundaries; secondly, at a greater distance, the shadows that divide the parts of bodies that touch each other are lost; thirdly, the thickness of the legs at the feet, and so on successively the smaller parts are lost, so that at a long distance there remains only an oval mass of confused shape.

### 423. On the superficial qualities that are first lost when moving away from shaded bodies.

The first thing among colors to be lost at a distance is the luster <note>The 'lustro' refers to the specular highlight or the brightest point of reflection on a surface.</note>, their smallest part and the light of lights; the second is the light, because it is smaller than the shadow; the third are the principal shadows; and in the end, there remains a mediocre, confused darkness.

### 424. On the nature of the boundaries of bodies against other bodies.

When bodies with a convex surface end against other bodies of the same color, the boundary of the convex part will appear darker than the body against which that convex boundary ends. The boundary of horizontal rods will appear very dark against a white background, and against a dark background, they will appear brighter than any other part of themselves, even if the light descending upon the rods is of equal brightness across them.

Suppose you had made the first shadow using three degrees of darkness and one degree of lightness—that is, three level spoonfuls, like the measures used for grain. If these three spoonfuls were of simple black and one spoonful was of white lead <term>white lead: a heavy, opaque white pigment (biacca) used in Renaissance painting</term>, you would have created a composition of a certain, definite quality without any doubt. Now, imagine you have made one wall white and one dark, and you must place a blue object between them. You want this object to have the true shadow and light that befits such a blue. Therefore, place on one side that blue which you wish to remain without shadow, and place the black beside it. Then take three spoonfuls of black and mix it with one spoonful of luminous blue, and apply the darkest shadow with this mixture. Having done this, observe if the object is spherical, columnar, square, or whatever it may be. If it is spherical, draw lines from the edges of the dark wall to the center of said spherical object; where these lines intersect the surface of the object, there the greatest shadows terminate within equal angles. Then begin to lighten the color, as it would be at *no*, which retains as much darkness as it receives from the upper wall *ad*; you will mix this color with the first shadow of *ab* using the same proportions.

### 429. On the movement and speed of animals.

That figure will demonstrate the greatest speed which appears most ready to fall forward. <note>Leonardo observes that rapid forward motion requires a shift in the center of gravity, making the body appear to be in a state of "controlled falling."</note>

### 430. On bodies that move by themselves, either fast or slow.

A body that moves by its own power will be faster the further the center of its gravity is from the center of its support. This is said regarding the flight of birds, which move themselves without the beating of wings or the favor of the wind. This happens when the center of their gravity is outside the center of their support—that is, outside the middle of the resistance of their wings. For if the middle of the wings is further back than the middle, or center, of the gravity of the whole bird, then that bird will move forward and downward. It will move more or less forward than downward depending on how far or near the center of gravity is to the middle of its wings; specifically, a center of gravity far from the middle of the wings makes the bird’s descent very oblique <note>meaning a long, shallow glide</note>, and if the center is near the middle of the wings, the descent of such a bird will have little obliquity <note>meaning a steeper drop</note>.

## 431. How to create a figure that appears to be forty cubits high within a space of twenty cubits, with corresponding limbs, and standing upright.¹ <note>original: "braccia" (arms). A Florentine measure of length, roughly 23 inches or 58 centimeters.</note>

In this and every other case, the painter should not be troubled by the orientation of the wall or surface where he is painting, especially if the eye of the viewer is to see such a painting from a window or other opening. This is because the eye should not attend to the <term>planarity</term> <note>original: "planizie" — the flat surface of the wall</note> or the curvature of those walls, but only to the things that are meant to be shown beyond such a wall across various parts of the simulated landscape. However, such a figure would be better made on the curve *frg*, because there are no angles in it.

## 432. How to make a figure on a wall twelve cubits high that appears to be twenty-four cubits in height.

If you wish to make a figure or another object that appears to be twenty-four cubits high, you shall do it in this manner: first, represent on the wall *mn* half of the man you wish to create; then, you shall create the other half on the vault *mr*. But before making the figure on the vault, create on the floor of a hall the shape of the wall and the vault where you are to make your figure. Then, behind that wall, create the figure drawn in profile at whatever size you please, and draw all its lines to the point *t*; and in the way that these lines intersect the wall *rn*, so you shall represent it on the actual wall (which is similar to your drawing), and you will have all the heights and projections of the figure. As for the widths or thicknesses found on the straight wall *mn*, you shall make them in their proper form, because as the wall <term>recedes</term> <note>original: "fuggir" — literally "flees." Refers to the way a surface slants away from the viewer's eye.</note>, the figure diminishes by itself. The figure that goes—

### 433. Painting: its members and components.

Light, darkness, color, body, figure, location, distance, proximity, motion, and rest. Of these ten functions of the eye, painting possesses seven. The first of these are light, darkness, color, figure, location, distance, and proximity. I exclude body, motion, and rest. Thus, there remain light and darkness—which is to say shadow and light, or if you prefer, <term>chiaroscuro</term> <note>original: "chiaro e scuro" (clear and dark). The technique of using strong contrasts between light and dark to give the illusion of three-dimensional volume.</note>—and color. I do not include "body" because painting is, in itself, a superficial thing <note>Existing only on a surface.</note>, and a surface has no body, as defined in geometry. To put it better, whatever is visible is included within the science of painting. Therefore, the ten "predicaments" of the eye mentioned above are reasonably the ten books into which I divide my painting. However, light and darkness constitute a single book, which treats light and shadow; they are made into the same book because shadow is surrounded by, or rather in contact with, light. The same happens with light and shadow: they always mix together at their boundaries.

And the "derivative shadow" <note>The shadow cast into the air or onto another surface, as opposed to the "attached shadow" on the object itself.</note> mixes with the light all the more as it is more distant from the shaded body. But color will never be seen in its simple state. This is proven by the ninth proposition, which says: the surface of every body participates in the color of its object <note>The object reflecting light onto it.</note>, even if it is the surface of a transparent body, such as air, water, and the like. This is because the air takes its light from the sun, and darkness is born from the deprivation of that sun. Therefore, the air is tinged with as many various colors as there are things placed between it and the eye. Air in itself has no more color than water, but the moisture that mixes with it from the middle region downward is what thickens it; as it thickens, the solar rays that strike it illuminate it. The air from said middle region upward remains dark. Because light and darkness together compose the color blue, this is the blue with which the air is tinged—with more or less darkness as the air is mixed with less or more moisture.

---

### 434. Painting and its definition.

Painting is a composition of light and darkness, mixed together with the diverse qualities of all simple and compound colors.

---

### 435. Painting in universal light.

In crowds of men and animals, always make the parts of their figures or bodies darker as they are lower down and as they...

are closer to the middle of their multitude, even though they are in themselves of uniform color; and this is necessary because a smaller quantity of the sky, the illuminator of bodies, is seen in the low spaces interposed between the said animals than in the upper parts of the same spaces. This is proven by the figure placed here, where *a b c d* represents the arc of the sky, the universal illuminator of the bodies within it; *n m* are the bodies that terminate the space *s f r h* interposed between them, in which space it is clearly seen that the site *t* (being illuminated only by the part of the sky *c d*) is illuminated by a smaller part of the sky than the site *e*, which is seen by the part of the sky *a b* that is three times larger than the sky *c d*; therefore, it will be three times more illuminated in *e* than in *t*.

### 436. On backgrounds proportioned to the bodies that stand out against them, and first regarding flat surfaces of uniform color.

The backgrounds of any flat surface of uniform color and light will not appear separated from that surface if they are of the same color and light. Therefore, conversely, they will appear separated if the opposite conclusion follows.

### 437. Painting: on figure and body.

Regular bodies are of two kinds: one is clothed in a curved surface, oval or spherical; the other is surrounded by a faceted surface, whether regular or irregular. Spherical or oval bodies always appear separated from their backgrounds, even if the body is the same color as its background, and the same will happen with faceted bodies; and this happens because they are disposed to the generation of shadows on some of their sides, which cannot happen on flat surfaces.

### 438. Painting: the part of a body that is of smaller quantity will be the first to lose its definition.

Of the parts of those bodies that move away from the eye, that which is of smaller shape will be the first to lose its definition <note>original: "notizia" (notice/knowledge). Leonardo uses this to mean the point at which the eye can no longer distinguish a specific detail.</note>; it follows that the part of greater quantity will be the last to lose its definition. Therefore, you, painter, do not finish the small members of those things that are very remote from the eye, but follow the rule given in the sixth <note>Likely referring to the sixth book or section of his notes on perspective.</note>.

How many are those who, in depicting cities and other things remote from the eye, make the outlines of buildings as distinct as if they were in the closest proximity...

proximity; and this is impossible in nature, because no sight, however powerful, is able to see the aforementioned boundaries with true certainty at such close proximity. This is because the boundaries of these bodies are the boundaries of their surfaces, and the boundaries of surfaces are lines, which lines are not any part of the quantity of that surface, nor even of the air that clothes such a surface. Therefore, that which is not part of any thing is invisible, as is proven in geometry <note>Leonardo frequently applies Euclidean geometry to art, arguing that since a mathematical line has no thickness, it cannot be seen by the eye.</note>. And if you, the painter, make these boundaries sharp and distinct, as is the custom, you will not represent a remote distance, for by such a defect <gloss>I</gloss> it will appear very close. Furthermore, the corners of buildings are things that should not be depicted in distant cities, because it is impossible to see them from nearby; for these corners are the meeting of two lines in a point, and the point has no part, therefore it is invisible.

### 439. Why the same countryside appears at times larger or smaller than it actually is.

Countrysides appear at times larger or smaller than they are due to the interposition of air that is thicker or thinner than usual, which is placed between the horizon and the eye that sees it. Between horizons of equal distance from the eye, that one will appear more remote which is seen through thicker air, and that one will appear closer which is seen in thinner air. The same object, seen at equal distances, will appear larger or smaller in proportion to whether the air interposed between the eye and the object is thicker or thinner. And if the object is seen at a distance of one hundred miles, which miles consist of uniform and thin air, and the same object is seen at the same distance of one hundred miles of uniform and thick air—with a thickness four times that of the aforementioned air—without doubt the same things seen first in the thin air, and then in the thick, will appear four times larger than in the thin.

Unequal things seen at equal distances will appear equal if the thickness of the air interposed between the eye and those things is unequal—that is, the thick air is placed before the smaller object. This is proven by means of the <term>perspective of colors</term> <note>Also known as aerial or atmospheric perspective, where the atmosphere changes the appearance of objects as they recede.</note>, which causes a great mountain, appearing small by measurement, to seem larger than a small thing near the eye; just as it is often seen that a finger near the eye covers a great mountain far from the eye.

### 440. Painting.

Among things of equal darkness, magnitude, shape, and distance from the eye, that one will appear smaller which is seen against a field of greater brightness or whiteness.

This is taught to us by the sun when seen behind trees without leaves: all their branches that are positioned against the solar body are so diminished that they remain invisible. A similar effect will be produced by a rod placed between the eye and the solar body.

Parallel bodies positioned vertically, when seen through mist, must appear thicker at the top than at the bottom. This is proven by the ninth [proposition], which says: mist or thick air penetrated by solar rays will appear whiter the lower it is.

Things seen from a distance are disproportionate, and this arises because the lighter part sends its <term>simulacrum</term> <note>original: "simulacro"; in Leonardo's optics, this refers to the "species" or visual image of an object traveling through the air to the eye.</note> to the eye with a more vigorous ray than its dark part does. And I saw a woman dressed in black with a white cloth on her head, which appeared twice as large as the thickness of her shoulders, which were dressed in black.

## 441. Of cities and other things seen in thick air.

The buildings of cities seen below the eye in times of mist and air thickened by the smoke of their fires, or other vapors, will always be less distinct the lower they are in height; and conversely, they will be clearer and more distinct the higher they are seen. This is proven by the fourth [proposition] of this [treatise], which says: the air is thicker the lower it is, and thinner the higher it is. And this is demonstrated by that same fourth proposition placed in the margin; and we shall say the tower *af* is seen by the eye *n* in thick air, which is divided into four degrees, each thicker the lower they are.

The smaller the quantity of air interposed between the eye and the thing seen, the less the color of that thing will participate in the color of such air. It follows that the greater the quantity of air interposed between the eye and the thing seen, the more the thing will participate in the color of the interposed air. It is demonstrated thus: the eye being *n*, to which the five species of the five parts of the tower *af* converge—namely *a b c d e f*—I say that if the air were of uniform thickness, the proportion of the color of the air acquired by the foot of the tower, *f*, would be to the color of the air acquired by the part of the tower *b*, as the proportion of the length of line *fm* is to line *bs*. But by the previous [proposition], which proves that air is not uniform in its thickness, but thicker the lower it is, it is necessary that the proportion of colors with which the air tints the parts of the tower *b* and *f* be of a greater proportion than the aforementioned proportion; because the line *mf*, besides being longer than the line *sb*, passes through air that has a <term>uniformly varying</term> <note>original: "uniformemente disforme"; a scholastic term used by Leonardo to describe a gradient that changes at a constant rate.</note> thickness.

### 442. Of solar rays that penetrate the openings of clouds.

<insert>Clouds that obstruct the sun</insert>

The solar rays penetrating the openings <note>original: "spiracoli"; literally "breathing holes," referring to gaps or vents in the cloud cover.</note> interspersed between the various densities and rounded shapes of the clouds, illuminate all the sites where they intersect; they also illuminate the darkness and tint all the dark places that lie behind them with their own color, which obscurities are revealed within the intervals between these solar rays.

---

### 443. Of things that the eye sees below itself mixed within mist and thick air.

The closer the air is to the water or the earth, the thicker it will become. This is proven by the nineteenth [proposition] of the second [book], which says: that thing which has in itself greater weight will rise less; it follows that the lighter thing rises higher than the heavy one; therefore, our proposition is concluded.

---

### 444. Of buildings seen in thick air.

That part of the building will be less evident which is seen in air of greater thickness; and conversely, that which is seen in thinner air will be more noticeable. Therefore, the eye <term>n</term> <note>Referring to the observer's position in the accompanying diagram.</note>, seeing the tower <term>a d</term>, will see in every degree of lowliness a part that is less noticeable and lighter in color, and in every degree of height a part that is more noticeable and less light.

---

### 445. Of the object that shows itself from a distance.

That dark object will appear lighter which is more remote from the eye. It follows conversely that the dark object will show itself with greater darkness the closer it is found to the eye. Therefore, the lower parts of any object placed in thick air will seem more remote from the feet than at their summits; and for this reason, the nearby base of a mountain will appear further away than the peak of the same mountain, which in itself is actually more remote. <note>Leonardo is describing an optical illusion where the dense haze at the base of a mountain makes it appear more "faded" and thus more distant than the clearer peak above.</note>

### 446. Of the view of a city in thick air.

The eye that sees a city below itself in thick air <note>original: "aria grossa"; refers to air filled with moisture, dust, or haze which creates atmospheric perspective.</note> sees the tops of the buildings as darker and more distinct than their bases; it sees these summits against a light background because it views them against the low, thick air. This occurs for the reasons previously stated.

### 447. Of the lower boundaries of remote objects.

The lower boundaries of remote objects will be less perceptible than their upper boundaries. This happens frequently with mountains and hills, the peaks of which are set against the sides of other mountains situated behind them. In these cases, the upper edges are seen more clearly than their bases, because the upper edge is darker, being less obscured by the thick air that settles in low places. It is this thick air that confuses the boundaries of the bases of the hills. The same occurs with trees, buildings, and other things that rise up through the air. From this it arises that tall towers seen at a great distance often appear thick at the top and thin at the bottom; this is because the upper part reveals the angles of the sides where they meet the front, as the thin air does not hide them from you as the thick air does to those at the base. 

This happens according to the seventh [proposition] of the first [book], which says: where thick air is interposed between the eye and the sun, it is brighter at the bottom than at the top. Where the air is whiter, it obscures dark objects from the eye more than if such air were blue. This is seen at a long distance when the battlements <term>merli</term> <note>The rectangular teeth-like structures atop a fortress wall.</note> of fortresses have gaps equal to the width of the battlements themselves; the gap appears much larger than the battlement, and at a more remote distance, the gap occupies and covers the entire battlement, so that the fortress shows only a straight wall without any battlements at all.

### 448. Of things seen from afar.

The boundaries of an object will be less distinct the greater the distance at which they are seen.

### 449. Of the blue color shown by distant landscapes.

Of remote objects seen by the eye, whatever their color may be, that which is of the greatest darkness—whether natural or accidental—will appear to be the most blue. Natural darkness is that which is dark in itself; accidental darkness is that which is darkened by the shadow cast upon it by other objects.

### 450. Which parts of bodies are the first to be lost to sight due to distance.

Those parts of bodies that are smaller in size will be the first of which we lose visual knowledge <note>original: "notizia"; in this context, it refers to the visual information or perception of a detail.</note> over a long distance. This happens because the visual images <note>original: "specie"; a term from medieval and Renaissance optics referring to the "species" or likeness of an object that travels through the air to the eye.</note> of smaller things, at an equal distance, reach the eye at a smaller angle than larger things; and the recognition of remote things is diminished in proportion to their smaller size. It follows, therefore, that when a larger mass at a great distance reaches the eye at a minimal angle and is almost lost to perception, a smaller mass will lose its visibility entirely.

### 451. Why things are less recognizable the further they are removed from the eye.

An object will be less recognizable the more remote it is from the eye. This happens because the smallest parts are lost first, and the second-smallest parts are lost at a greater distance; and so continuing step by step, as the parts are consumed, the knowledge of the remote object is consumed, so that in the end all the parts are lost along with the whole. Furthermore, the color fails because of the thickness of the air that is interposed between the eye and the thing seen.

### 452. Why parallel towers appear narrower at the bottom than at the top in the mist.

Parallel towers in the mist appear at a long distance to be thinner at the base than at the top. This is because the mist, which serves as their background, is thicker and whiter at the bottom than at the top; therefore, by the third [proposition] of this [treatise] which says: a dark object placed against a white background appears smaller to the eye, and the converse which says: a white object placed against a dark background appears thicker than against a light background, it follows that the lower part of the dark tower, having the whiteness of the low and thick mist as its background, causes that mist to appear to grow over the lower boundaries of said tower and diminish them. This the mist cannot do to the upper boundaries of the tower, where the mist is thinner.

### 453. Why faces appear dark from a distance.

We see clearly that all the likenesses <note>original: "similitudini"; similar to "specie," the visual representations of objects.</note> of evident things that are before us as objects, both large and small, enter the senses through the small light <note>original: "luce dell' occhio"; Leonardo often uses "light" to refer to the pupil or the visual opening of the eye.</note> of the eye. If through such a small entrance passes the likeness of the greatness of the heaven and the earth,

than the first; and if a third object is of equal size to the second and the first before it, and is as far from the second as the second is from the first, it will appear to be one-third the size of the first. Thus, step by step, at equal distances, they will always decrease proportionately from the first, provided that the interval does not exceed the number of twenty <term>braccia</term> <note>A "braccio" (plural "braccia") was a Florentine unit of measurement roughly equal to 23 inches or 58 centimeters, based on the length of an arm.</note>. Within these twenty braccia, a figure similar to your own will lose two-quarters of its size; within forty, it will lose three-quarters; and then five-sixths at sixty braccia. So, little by little, it will continue its diminution, provided the vertical plane <note>The "parete" or "wall" refers to the imaginary transparent plane used in perspective drawing.</note> is distant from you by twice your own height; for placing it at only one height's distance creates too great a difference between the first braccia and the second.

# 457. On bodies seen in the fog.

Those things seen in the fog will appear much larger than their true size. This happens because the <term>perspective of the medium</term> <note>The "medium" refers to the air or atmosphere between the eye and the object.</note> interposed between the eye and such an object does not harmonize its color with the magnitude of that object. This is because such fog is similar to the hazy air placed between the eye and the horizon in clear weather; thus, a body near the eye seen through nearby fog appears to be at the distance of the horizon, where a massive tower would appear smaller than the aforementioned man standing close by.

# 458. On the heights of buildings seen in the fog.

That part of a nearby building appears more blurred which is more remote from the ground; this happens because there is more fog between the eye and the top of the building than there is between the eye and its base. A parallel tower seen at a long distance through the fog will appear thinner the closer it is to its base. This arises from the previous rule, which states: fog appears whiter and thicker the closer it is to the earth; and from the second rule of this [treatise], which states: a dark object will appear to be of a smaller shape the more it is seen against a field of more powerful whiteness. Therefore, since the fog is whiter at the foot than at the top, it is necessary that the darkness of such a tower appears narrower at the foot than at the top.

# 459. On cities and other buildings seen in the evening or morning in the fog.

In buildings seen at a long distance in the evening or morning in fog or thick air, only the brightness of their parts illuminated by the sun (which is near the horizon) is visible; the parts of said buildings not seen by the sun remain almost the color of the medium darkness of the fog.

# 460. Why higher objects placed in the distance are darker than lower ones, even if the fog is uniform in thickness.

Of objects placed in fog, or other thick air—whether by vapor, smoke, or distance—that which is higher will be more recognizable; and of objects of equal height, that which is seen through a deeper layer of fog will appear darker. This is seen at the eye *h*, which, looking at towers *a b c* of equal height to one another, sees *c* (the top of the first tower) at *r*, a depth of two degrees of thickness in the fog, and sees the top of the middle tower *b* through only one degree of fog. Therefore, the summit *c* shows itself to be darker than the summit of tower *b*.

# 461. On the patches of shadows that appear on bodies from a distance.

The throat, or any other vertical surface that has a projection above it, will always be darker than the vertical face of that projection itself. It follows that a body will appear more illuminated when it is seen by a greater portion of the same light source. See at *a* <note>Referring to the diagram of the human profile</note> that no part of the sky *f k* illuminates it; at *b*, the sky *i k* illuminates it; at *c*, the sky *h k*; at *d*, the sky *g k*; and at *e*, the sky *f k* illuminates it entirely. Therefore, the chest will be of equal brightness to the forehead, nose, and chin. 

But what I must remind you regarding faces is that you should consider how, at various distances, different qualities of shadows are lost, and only those primary patches remain—namely, the hollow of the eye and other similar features. Ultimately, the face remains dark because the highlights are consumed <note>Leonardo uses "consumano" (consumed/worn away) to describe how light diminishes over distance until it is overwhelmed by shadow.</note>, being small in comparison to the middle shadows. For this reason, over a long distance, the quality and quantity of the principal lights and shadows are consumed, and every quality is blended into a middle shadow. 

This is the reason why trees and every body at a certain distance appear to become darker in themselves than when those same objects are near the eye. This darkness, caused by the air interposed between the eye and the object, makes the object brighten and lean toward blue; however, it turns blue more in the shadows than in the luminous parts, where the truth of the colors is more apparent.

### 462. Why at the approach of evening the shadows of bodies produced on a white wall are blue.

The shadows of bodies produced by the redness of the sun near the horizon will always be blue; and this arises from the eleventh principle, which states: the surface of every opaque body partakes of the color of its object <note>In Leonardo's optics, "object" refers to whatever source of light or color is facing the surface.</note>. Therefore, the whiteness of the wall being entirely deprived of any color of its own, it becomes tinged by the color of its objects, which in this case are the sun and the sky. Because the sun turns reddish toward evening, and the sky appears blue; and where there is shadow, the sun does not see <note>Leonardo frequently personifies light sources, saying they "see" the surfaces they illuminate.</note>, according to the eighth principle of shadows, which says: the luminous source never sees the shadows it creates; <margin>1</margin> and where the sun does not see on such a wall, it is seen by the sky. Therefore, by the said eleventh principle, the derivative shadow <term>derivative shadow: the shadow cast by an object onto another surface, as opposed to the "primary shadow" on the object itself</term> striking the white wall will be blue in color, and the field of that shadow, seen by the redness of the sun, will partake of the red color.

### 463. Where smoke is brightest.

Smoke seen between the sun and the eye will be brighter and more lucid than any other part of the landscape where it originates; the same is true of dust and mist, which, if you are instead between the sun and them, will appear dark to you.

### 464. Regarding dust.

Dust that is raised by the running of any animal: the higher it rises, the brighter it is; and likewise, it is darker the less it rises, provided it is between the sun and the eye.

### 465. Regarding smoke.

Smoke is more transparent and dark toward the edges of its billows <note>original: "globulenze"</note> than toward their centers.

Smoke moves with greater obliquity <note>i.e., at a sharper angle or more horizontally</note> the more powerful the wind that moves it is.

Smokes are of as many various colors as there are varieties of things that generate them.

Smokes do not create sharp shadows, and their boundaries are less discernible the further they are from their source; and the things placed behind them are so much <note>The sentence breaks off here, continuing on the next page.</note>

# LEONARDO DA VINCI

<meta>[§ 468]</meta>

Distant things appear with confused and uncertain edges for two different reasons. The first is that they reach the eye at such a small angle that they diminish so much they function like tiny objects; even if these were close to the eye, the eye could not comprehend what shape such a body might be, such as the fingernails on the legs of ants and similar things. The second is that between the eye and distant things, so much air is interposed that it becomes thick and dense; because of its whiteness <note>Leonardo often refers to the "whiteness" of the atmosphere as the way it scatters light, creating a veil over distant objects.</note>, it tints the shadows and veils them with its brightness, making them dark with a color that is between black and white, which is blue.

Although through long distances the knowledge of the true nature of many things is lost, nonetheless those that are illuminated by the sun will present themselves with more certain clarity, while the others will appear wrapped in confused mists.

Because at every lower level the air acquires a degree of thickness, things that are lower down will appear more confused, and vice versa.

When the sun makes the clouds on the horizon turn red, those things which by distance were clothed in blue will participate in that redness; thus a mixture will be made between blue and red, which will make the countryside very cheerful and joyful. All those things illuminated by such redness that are dense will be very evident and will turn red; and the air, being transparent, will have that redness infused throughout it, whereby it will appear the color of the lily flower <note>likely referring to the *Lilium martagon* or a similar reddish-purple lily common in Italy</note>.

That air which stays between the sun and the earth, when it rises or sets, will always obscure the things behind it more than any other part of the air; and this arises from it being more whitish.

### 469. On the edges of white objects.

No outlines should be made at the edges of a body that stands out against another; rather, the body should stand out by itself.

If the edge of a white object meets another white object, if it is curved, it will naturally create a dark edge, and it will be the darkest part of the illuminated side; but if it stands out against a dark place, that edge will appear as the lightest part of the illuminated side.

That object will appear more remote and detached from another if it stands out against a background more varied from itself.

At great distances, the edges of bodies that have similar colors are lost first, especially when the edge of one is against the other, such as the edge of an oak tree against another similar oak. Secondly, at a greater distance, the edges of bodies of medium colors meeting one another will be lost, such as green—that is, trees, plowed ground, walls, or other ruins of mountains or rocks. Finally, the edges of bodies where light meets dark and dark meets light will be lost.

<summary>Leonardo explains the principles of aerial perspective, describing how the density of the atmosphere turns distant shadows blue and how light conditions, such as sunset, affect the clarity and color of the landscape. He also provides technical advice for painters on how to render edges and contrast to create a sense of depth without using artificial outlines.</summary>

# TREATISE ON PAINTING — PART THREE

### 480. Painting.

The blue of the atmosphere is a color composed of light and darkness; by light, I mean the air illuminated within the particles of moisture infused within said air; by darkness, I mean the pure air, which is not divided into atoms—that is, particles of moisture—upon which the solar rays might strike. An example of this is seen in the air that lies between the eye and shaded mountains, darkened by the great abundance of trees found upon them, or shaded in those parts not struck by the sun's rays. This air becomes blue, but it does not become blue in its luminous parts, and even less so in parts covered with snow.

Among objects equally dark and at an equal distance, that which is set against a whiter field will appear darker, and vice versa.

An object painted in white and black will appear to have better <term>relief</term> <note>The illusion of three-dimensional depth and volume on a flat surface</note> than any other. Therefore, remember, painter, to dress your figures in the lightest colors you can: for if you make them of dark color, they will have little relief and little visibility from a distance. This is because the shadows of all things are dark; if you make a garment dark, there will be little variation between the light and the shadows, whereas in light colors there will be a great difference.

---

### 481. Why, of two things of equal size, the painted one will appear larger than the one in relief.

This reasoning is not as easy to demonstrate as many others, but I will nonetheless strive to satisfy the inquiry, if not entirely, at least as much as I am able. Diminishing perspective shows us by logic that things diminish the further they are from the eye, and these reasons are well confirmed by experience. Therefore, the visual lines located between the object and the eye, when they extend to the surface of a painting, are all cut at the same boundary <note>Meaning the flat plane of the canvas or panel</note>; however, the lines located between the eye and a sculpture have various boundaries and lengths. That line is longer which extends to a limb further away than the others, and therefore that limb appears smaller. Because there are many parts further away than others, and being further away, they must necessarily appear smaller; appearing smaller, they cause the entire sum of the object to appear smaller through their diminution. This does not happen in painting. Because the lines terminate at one and the same distance, they must be without diminution; therefore, the parts that do not diminish do not decrease the sum of the object. For this reason, a painting does not diminish in size as a sculpture does.

## 489. On representing the four seasons of the year, or their characteristics.

In autumn, you shall depict things according to the age of that season; that is, at the beginning, the leaves of the trees start to turn pale on the oldest branches, more or less depending on whether the plant is in a sterile or fertile location. They appear even paler and more reddish on those species of trees which were the first to produce their fruit. Do not do as many painters do, making all sorts of trees—even if they are at an equal distance from you—the same quality of green. The same applies to meadows, plants, and different types of soil and stones, as well as the <term>pedals</term> <note>The lower part of the trunk or the base of the tree</note> of the aforementioned plants: always vary them, because nature is infinitely variable. Not only in different species, but within the same plants one will find various colors; for instance, on the <term>osiers</term> <note>original: "vimene" - species of willow used in basketry</note> the leaves are more beautiful and larger than on the other branches. Nature is so delightful and abundant in variation that among trees of the same kind, one would not find a single plant that closely resembles another; and not just the plants, but among the branches, leaves, or fruits, one will not find one that precisely resembles another. Therefore, pay close attention and vary your work as much as you can.

## 490. On painting the wind.

In the representation of wind, besides the bending of branches and the turning over of leaves toward the direction the wind is coming from, one must depict the swirling clouds of fine dust mixed with the turbid air.

## 491. On the beginning of a rainstorm.

Rain falls through the air, darkening it with a leaden tint, catching the light of the sun on one side and casting a shadow on the opposite side, just as is seen with mists. The earth is darkened where the splendor of the sun is taken away by such rain. Objects seen beyond the rain have confused and unintelligible outlines, while those closer to the eye will be more distinct. Furthermore, things seen within the shaded part of the rain will be more distinct than those seen in the illuminated rain. This happens because objects seen in the shaded rain lose only their primary highlights; however, objects seen in the luminous rain lose both light and shadow, because their bright parts blend with the brightness of the illuminated air, and their shaded parts are brightened by that same clarity of the said illuminated air.<note>I</note>

---

### 492. On the arrangement of a storm of winds and rain.

One sees the air tinted with dark cloudiness in the preparation of tempests, or <term>fortunes</term> <note>original: "fortune" - a term used historically to describe violent sea storms or gales</note> of the sea, which are mixtures of rains and winds with the serpent-like movements of the twisting paths of threatening celestial lightnings. The plants are bent to the ground with their leaves overturned above the declining branches, appearing as if they wish to flee from their places, as if terrified by the strikes of the horrible and frightening flights of the winds. Amidst these are infused the swirling paths of the turbulent dust and sand from the sea shores. The dark horizon of the sky becomes a field of smoky clouds which, struck by the solar rays penetrating through the opposite breaks in the clouds, strike the earth, illuminating it beneath their impact. The winds, persecutors of the dust, lift it with clustered globes high into the air with an <term>ash-blue</term> <note>original: "cineruleo" - a grayish-blue color characteristic of stormy skies</note> color mixed with the reddening solar rays penetrating through it. The animals, terrified and without guidance, run in circles through various places; the thunders created in the globular clouds cast out from themselves the infuriated lightning bolts, the light of which illuminates the shadowy countrysides in various locations.

---

### 493. On the shadows made by bridges upon their water.

The shadows of bridges will never be seen upon their waters unless the water first loses its function of mirroring because of <term>turbidity</term> <note>muddiness or cloudiness caused by suspended sediment</note>. And this is proven because clear water has a lustrous and polished surface, and it mirrors the bridge in all the places interposed within equal angles between the eye and the bridge; it mirrors the air under the bridge, where the shadow of such a bridge ought to be. This the turbid water cannot do, because it does not mirror, but indeed receives the shadow, just as a dusty road would.

---

### 494. On the clear or dark images that are imprinted upon the shadowy and illuminated places positioned between the surface and the bottom of clear waters.

When the <term>simulacra</term> <note>original: "simulacri" - images, reflections, or visual representations of objects</note> of dark or luminous objects are imprinted upon the dark or illuminated parts of bodies interposed between the bottom of the waters and the surface, then the shadowy parts of those bodies will become darker where they are covered by the shadowy images; and their luminous parts will do the same. But if the luminous images are imprinted upon the shadowy and luminous parts, then the illuminated parts of the aforementioned bodies will become of greater brightness, and their shadows will lose their great darkness; and such bodies will show themselves with less <term>relief</term> <note>the three-dimensional quality or "popping out" effect in a painting</note> than the bodies struck by dark images. And this happens because, as it is said, the images...

dark objects increase the shadows of shadowy bodies, which, even though they are seen by the sun that penetrates the surface of the water and are made strongly different from their highlights by their shadows, have added to them the shadow of the dark <term>image</term> <note>original: "simulacro" - Leonardo uses this to mean the reflected image or visual representation of an object on a surface</note> that is mirrored in the skin of the water; and thus the shadow of these bodies is increased, becoming darker. And even though such a dark image tints the illuminated parts of such submerged bodies, it does not lack the clarity given to it by the percussion of the solar rays, which, although somewhat altered by that dark image, does little harm; this is because the benefit it gives to the shadowy parts is so great that the submerged bodies have much more <term>relief</term> <note>the illusion of three-dimensionality and depth in painting</note> than those altered by a luminous image. The latter, although it brightens their illuminated parts as well as the shadowy ones, causes such clarity in those shadowy parts that such submerged bodies in that location show little relief. Suppose that the sea $n m t v$ has gravel, or weeds, or other dark bodies at the bottom of its clear water, which takes its light from the solar rays coming from the sun $d$, and that one part of the gravel has above it the image which is mirrored in the surface of such water, and that another part of the gravel has above it the image of the air $b c s m$; I say that the gravel covered by the dark image will be more visible than the gravel covered by the brightness of the clear image. And the reason is that the part struck by the dark image is more visible than that struck by the illuminated image, because the <term>visual power</term> <note>original: "virtù visiva" - the Renaissance concept of the eye's active ability to perceive light and form</note> is overcome and offended by the illuminated part of the water due to the air mirrored in it, and thus such visual power is increased by the darkened part of said water; and in this case the pupil of the eye is not of uniform power, because on one side it is offended by too much light and on the other increased by the dark.

Therefore, what is said above arises only from causes remote from such waters and such images, because such a thing arises only from the eye, which is offended by the splendor of the image of the air, and is enhanced on the other side by the dark image.

### 495. On clear water, the bottom is transparent beyond the surface.

In water where the bottom is seen through its transparency, that bottom will be demonstrated more clearly the slower the water's motion; and this happens because waters in slow motion have a surface without waves; through its level surface, the true shapes of the gravel and sand placed at the bottom of such waters are seen. This cannot happen in fast-moving water because of the waves generated on the surface; as the images of the various shapes of the gravel must pass through these waves, they cannot carry them to the eye, because the

### 496. On the foam of the water.

The foam of the water will appear less white the further it is from the surface of the water. This is proven by the fourth [rule] of this [treatise], which says: the natural color of a submerged thing will transform more into the green color of the water when it has a greater quantity of water above it.

### 497. Precept of painting.

Perspective is the bridle and the rudder of painting.
The size of a painted figure should show at what distance it is being seen.
If you see a figure that is life-sized, know that it is shown to be close to the eye.

### 498. Precept.

The navel is always on the central line of the weight that is from that navel upward; thus, take into account the accidental weight of a man as well as his natural weight. This is demonstrated in the extending of the arm, where the fist placed at its extremity performs the same function seen in the counterweight placed at the end of a <term>steelyard</term> <note>a portable balance scale with a sliding weight</note>; wherefore, by necessity, as much weight is thrown on the other side of the navel as the accidental weight of the fist; and the heel on that side must be raised.

### 499. On the ten functions of the eye, all belonging to painting.

Painting extends to all ten functions of the eye, namely: darkness, light, body, color, shape, location, distance, proximity, motion, and rest. My little work will be woven from these functions, reminding the painter with what rule and method he must imitate with his art all these things—the work of nature and the ornament of the world.

# 500. On the statue.

If you wish to make a figure of marble, first make one of clay. Once you have finished it and it is dry, place it in a crate that is large enough—after the figure is removed from that place—to receive the marble in which you wish to carve the figure in the likeness of the one in clay. Then, having placed the clay figure inside this crate, take small rods that fit exactly through holes in the crate, and push them into each hole until each white rod touches the figure in various places. Dye the part of these rods that remains outside the crate black, and mark each rod and its corresponding hole so that they can be matched at your will. Then you shall remove the clay figure from the crate and put in your piece of marble, and take away so much from the marble that all your rods are hidden up to their marks in said holes. To be able to do this better, arrange it so that the entire crate can be lifted up, while the bottom of said crate remains always under the marble; in this way, you will be able to remove the stone with your tools with great ease. <note>Leonardo is describing a "pointing machine," a mechanical aid used to accurately copy a model into stone by measuring depths.</note>

# 501. To make a painting with eternal varnish.

Paint your picture upon paper stretched on a frame, well-outlined <insert>In the codex: "delicate"</insert> and flat; then apply a good, thick priming of pitch and well-crushed brick. After that, apply a priming of <term>white lead</term> <note>biacca: a common white pigment in the Renaissance</note> and <term>yellow-tin</term> <note>giallorino: a lead-tin yellow pigment</note>. Then color it, and varnish it with clear, thick old oil, and fix it to the glass very flatly. But it will be better to make a panel of well-glazed and very flat clay, and then apply the priming of white lead and yellow-tin over that glaze; then color and varnish it. Next, attach the crystalline glass to it with a very clear varnish; but first, let that coloring dry well in a dark stove, and then varnish it with walnut oil and amber, or walnut oil thickened in the sun. If you wish to make thin and flat glass, blow the glass bulbs between two polished plates of bronze or marble, and blow them so much that you burst them with your breath; they will be flat and so thin that you can bend the glass, which will then be attached with the varnish to the painting. Because this glass is thin, it will not break from any blow. One can also stretch a heated plate long and wide over a heated furnace.

# 502. Method of coloring on canvas.

Put your canvas in a frame, and give it a weak glue size, and let it dry. Draw your design, and apply the <term>flesh tones</term> <note>incarnazioni: the colors used to represent human skin</note> with bristle brushes, and while it is still fresh, you shall make the <term>sfumato</term> <note>the "smoky" blending of tones for which Leonardo is famous</note> shadows in your own manner. The flesh tone will be white lead, <term>lacquer</term> <note>lacca: a red pigment derived from organic matter</note>, and yellow-tin; and the shadow will be black and...

### 503. On the smoke of cities.

Smoke is seen better and more clearly in eastern parts than in western parts when the sun is in the east; and this arises from two causes:

The first is that the sun shines with its rays through the particles of such smoke, brightening them and making them evident;

The second is that the roofs of the houses seen to the east at such a time are in shadow, because their slant cannot be illuminated by the sun.

And the same happens with dust; both are more luminous the denser they are, and they are densest toward the middle.

---

### 504. On smoke and dust.

When the sun is in the east, the smoke of cities will not be seen to the west, because it is neither seen penetrated by the solar rays, nor seen against a dark background; this is because the roofs of the houses show the eye the same side that is shown to the sun, and against this light background such smoke is hardly visible.

But dust in a similar aspect appears darker than smoke, because it consists of denser matter than smoke, which is a moist matter.

---

### 505. A precept of perspective in painting.

When you do not perceive a variety of brightness or darkness within the air, then the perspective of shadows will be excluded from your imitation; you must then rely only on the perspective of the diminution of bodies, the perspective of the fading of colors, and the loss of definition of things placed before the eye. This process makes the same object appear more remote—that is, the loss of the knowledge of the shape of any object.

The eye, through linear perspective alone and without its own movement, will never have knowledge of—

### 506. The eye placed on high seeing low objects.

When the eye placed in a high position sees the high summits of mountains together with their bases, then the colors of the mountain summits will appear more distant than the colors of their bases. This is proved by the fourth [rule] of this [treatise], which says: among colors of equal nature, the most remote is tinged more by the color of the medium interposed between it and the eye that sees it. It follows that, the bases of the mountains being seen through <term>thicker air</term> <note>original: "più grossa aria"; denser atmosphere near the ground, filled with moisture and dust</note> than their summits, these bases will appear more remote from the eye than those summits, which are seen by the same eye through <term>thinner air</term> <note>original: "aria più sottile"; clearer, less dense atmosphere at higher altitudes</note>. Let the eye therefore be placed at height $a$, which sees the summit of the mountain $b$ after the interposition of the air $ab$, and sees the base $d$ of the same mountain after the air $ad$, a shorter space than $ab$; because this air $ad$ is thicker than the air $ab$, the base of the mountain, as was said, will appear more distant than its summit.

---

### 507. The eye placed below seeing low and high objects.

But when the eye placed in a low position sees the bases of mountains and their summits, then the colors of that mountain will be much less distinct than those of the preceding [example]; and this happens because such a summit and base of the mountain are seen through so much greater thickness than the aforementioned ones, as the eye that sees them is situated in a lower place. Let this eye be $n$, and the summit and the base of the mountain be $oc$. Therefore, the <term>visual line</term> <note>original: "linea visuale"; the straight line of sight from the eye to the object</note> $cn$ in the second figure being lower than the visual line of the first figure $da$, it is necessary that the color of the base in the second demonstration be more changed from its natural color than that of the base in the first demonstration, and the same is understood to have been said of the summits of the mountains.

---

### 508. Why the convergence of all the species that come to the eye occurs at a single point.

Of things of equal size situated at various distances, the most remote will be seen under a smaller angle; $bd$ is equal to $ce$, but $ce$ comes to the eye through an angle so much smaller than $bd$, as it is more remote from point $a$, as shown by the angle $cae$ in respect to the angle $bad$.

<note>original vocabulary: perspective of colors, low objects, mountain summits, visual line, convergence of all species, thin air, thick air</note>
