# 509. Of things mirrored in water.

Of things mirrored in water, that one will be most similar in color to the object mirrored which is reflected in the clearest water.

# 510. Of things mirrored in turbid water.

Things mirrored in turbid water always partake of the color of that substance which makes such water turbid.

# 511. Of things mirrored in running water.

Of things mirrored in running water, the <term>image</term> <note>original: "simulacro"; a technical term for the visual representation or "likeness" of an object as it appears in a reflection</note> of that thing will appear longer and with more confused outlines the faster the water flows.

# 512. Of the nature of the medium interposed between the eye and the object.

The medium interposed between the eye and the object is of two kinds: either it has a surface, such as water, crystal, or another transparent substance; or it is without a common surface, such as the air that rests against the surface of the bodies enclosed within it, which air has no continuous surface in itself except at its lower and upper boundaries.

# 513. Effects of the medium surrounded by a common surface.

A medium surrounded by a common surface never returns the object behind it to the eye in its true position. This is proved: let there be a crystal with parallel surfaces *o r*, through which the eye *a* sees half of the object *n g* which stands behind it—that is, *n m*—through the part of the crystal *b o*; and it sees the remainder of the object, *m g*, through the air that stands below the crystal. According to the seventh [rule] of the fourth [book], the line of the upper part of the object *n* bends at the entry into the crystal and forms the line *n b a*; and the line of the lower part *m g* is seen in its true position according to the seventh of the fourth, as shown in the lines that pass through the air below the crystal in *m g a*. Therefore, one half of the object *n m* <term>increases</term> <note>original: "cresce"; refers to the visual displacement or magnification caused by refraction</note> in the crystal *b o* and the other half <term>decreases</term> <note>original: "diminuisce"</note> in the air that stands below the crystal in *o p*.

### 514. Of objects.

That part of the object will be more illuminated which is closer to the light source that illuminates it.

The <term>likeness</term> <note>original: "similitudine"; in Leonardo's optics, this refers to the "species" or visual information traveling from an object to the eye</note> and the substance of things lose their degrees of power at every stage of distance; that is, the more remote a thing is from the eye, the less its likeness will be able to penetrate through the air.

### 515. Of the diminution of colors and bodies.

Let the diminution of the quality of colors be observed together with the diminution of the bodies <note>i.e., the physical size or scale of the objects</note> to which they are applied.

### 516. Of the interposition of transparent bodies between the eye and the object.

The greater the transparent interposition between the eye and the object, the more the color of the object will be transformed into the color of the interposed transparent medium.

When the object is placed between the eye and the light, along the central line that extends between the center of the light and the eye, then such an object will be totally deprived of light <note>This describes the effect of a silhouette, where the object appears as a dark shape against a bright background</note>.

<margin>
**Vocabulary:**
object, near, likeness, interpositions, transparent, optics, light, shadow
</margin>

He also notes that an object positioned directly between a light source and the eye results in a total loss of visible surface illumination.</summary>

# PART FOUR.

## OF DRAPERY AND THE MANNER OF CLOTHING FIGURES WITH GRACE, AND OF THE GARMENTS AND NATURE OF FABRICS.

517. Of the drapery that clothes figures.

The <term>DRAPERY</term> <note>original: "panni"; refers generally to any cloth, fabric, or garments used in a composition</note> that clothes figures must show that it is inhabited by those figures. With a brief circumference, it should show the attitude and motion of such figures and avoid the confusion of many folds, especially over the highlights <note>original: "rilievi"; the raised or illuminated parts of the form</note>, so that the forms may be clearly recognized.

518. Of the broken or solid manners of drapery that clothes figures.

The drapery that clothes figures should have <term>solid</term> or <term>broken</term> <note>Leonardo distinguishes between "salde" (smooth, continuous folds typical of heavy cloth) and "rotte" (sharp, angular, or fragmented folds typical of thin or stiff fabric)</note> folds according to the quality of the thin or thick cloth you wish to represent; and you may use both types in the composition of your <term>narrative paintings</term> <note>original: "istorie"; large-scale historical, biblical, or mythological scenes</note> to satisfy different artistic judgments.

519. Of clothing figures with grace.

Ensure in your drapery that the part which surrounds the figure shows the manner of that figure's attitude, and those parts that remain outside of that form, adorn them in a flying and scattered manner, as will be described.

<margin>
**Vocabulary:**
drapery, clothing, figures, grace, garments, natures, attitude, motion, folds, highlights, broken manners, solid manners, narrative paintings
</margin>

<summary>Leonardo provides instructions on how to depict drapery so that it reveals the underlying human form and motion, advising artists to vary fold styles based on fabric thickness. He emphasizes using "flying" or loose fabric to add grace and decorative flair to a figure's silhouette.</summary>
<keywords>drapery, anatomy in art, folds, fabric texture, artistic grace, composition, Renaissance painting techniques</keywords>

# TREATISE ON PAINTING — PART FOUR

If the fabric is of medium thickness and dense, it will form folds that face each other with small angles; and above all, remember with every quality of cloth to make the folds between one break and the next thick in the middle and thin at the sides, and the smallest thickness of that fold should be in the middle of the rounded angle of the fold.

### 523. On flying or stable drapery.

The fabrics with which figures are dressed are of three kinds: thin, thick, and medium. Thin fabrics are more agile and suited to movement; therefore, when a figure runs, consider the motions of that figure, because it bends now to the right, now to the left. As the right leg is planted, the cloth on that side rises from the foot, reflecting the impact of its wave; and at that time, the leg left behind does the same with the cloth that rests upon it from above. The front part rests against the chest, body, thighs, and legs with various folds, while at the back, it all moves away, except for the leg that remains behind. Medium fabrics make smaller movements, and thick ones almost none, unless the wind helps to move them.

The edges of the garments, whether high or low, [should vary] according to the bends, and should draw close to the feet according to the planting, bending, twisting, or the striking of the legs within them; they should draw near or move away from the joints according to the step, run, or jump, or even if the wind itself strikes them without any other motion of the figure; and let the folds be adapted to the qualities of the fabrics, whether transparent or opaque.

### 524. Operations of fabrics and their folds, which are of three natures.

There are many who love the folds of the skirts of garments with sharp, raw, and brisk angles; others with angles that are almost imperceptible; others without any angle at all, but in place of them make curves. Of these three kinds, some want thick cloth and few folds, others thin cloth and a great number of folds, and others take the middle ground. You should follow the opinions of all three, putting each kind into your <term>history painting<note>original: "istoria" — a term used in the Renaissance to describe a complex narrative painting featuring multiple figures and a moral or historical theme.</note></term>, adding those that appear old and patched, and new ones abundant with cloth, and some miserable ones, according to the status of those you dress; and do the same with their colors.

### 525. On the natures of the folds of fabrics.

That part of the fold which is found furthest from its constrained ends will return most to its original nature. Naturally, everything desires to maintain itself in its [original state]...

<summary>Leonardo da Vinci provides technical instructions on how to paint drapery, emphasizing how different fabric weights react to the movement of the human body and the wind. He advises artists to vary the style and condition of clothing to match the character and narrative context of their paintings.</summary>

...being; cloth, because it is of equal density and thickness on its reverse side as on its right <gloss>front</gloss> side, desires to remain flat. Therefore, when it is forced by some fold or pleat to leave that flatness, it observes the nature of the force in that part of itself where it is most constrained; and you will find that the part furthest from those constraints returns most to its original nature—that is, staying spread out and wide. Example: let *abc* be the fold of the cloth mentioned above; let *ac* be the place where said cloth is folded and constrained. I proposed to you that the part of the cloth furthest from the constrained ends would return most to its original nature; therefore, *c* being further from *ab*, the fold will be wider at *b* than in any other of its places.

### 526. How folds should be given to fabrics.

One should not give a cloth a confusion of many folds; rather, make them only where they are held by the hands or arms, and let the rest be left to fall simply where its nature pulls it. The figure should not be crossed by too many lines or breakages of folds.

Fabrics must be portrayed from life; that is, if you want to make woolen cloth, use folds according to that, and if it is silk, or fine cloth, or peasant's cloth, or linen, or a veil, go about diversifying the folds for each one. Do not make clothing as many do over models covered in paper or thin leather <note>Leonardo warns against using stiff, artificial models which do not mimic the fluid drape of real textiles</note>, for you would be greatly deceived.

### 527. On having few folds in fabrics.

Figures dressed in a mantle <note>a loose, sleeveless cloak</note> should not show so much of the nude form that the mantle appears to be directly upon the flesh, unless you actually intended for the mantle to be against the skin. You must consider that between the mantle and the flesh there are other garments which prevent the shape of the limbs from being revealed through the mantle. That shape of the limbs which you do allow to be seen, make it thick enough so that other garments appear to be under the mantle. You should only allow the nearly true thickness of the limbs to be revealed in a nymph or an angel, who are depicted dressed in thin garments, pushed or pressed by the blowing of the winds; in these and similar cases, one may very well allow the form of the limbs to be revealed.

### 528. On the folds of fabrics in foreshortening.

Where the figure is foreshortened <term>foreshortening: a technique used to create the illusion of an object receding strongly into the distance</term>, show a greater number of folds than where it is not foreshortened; and let its limbs be surrounded by thick folds that wind around...

# 531. On the folds of drapery.

The folds of drapery <note>original: "panni," referring to cloth or garments</note> situated upon any action of the figures must, with their outlines, demonstrate the action of such a figure in a way that they do not create ambiguity or confusion regarding the true posture to those who observe them. No fold, through the shadow of its depth, should appear to "cut" through any limb; that is, the depth of the fold must not seem to penetrate deeper than the surface of the clothed limb itself. 

Furthermore, if you represent figures wearing multiple layers of clothing, it must not appear as though the outermost garment encloses merely the bare bones of the figure, but rather the flesh along with them. The garments covering the flesh should possess a thickness consistent with the multiplication of their various layers.

The folds of the drapery that surround the limbs should diminish in their thickness toward the extremities of the part they encircle.

# 532. On the folds.

The length of the folds that are pulled tightest against the limbs must wrinkle on that side where the limb contracts <note>literally "diminishes" due to bending</note> and stretch out on the opposite side of that bend.

# PART FIVE.

## *ON SHADOW AND LIGHT, AND ON PERSPECTIVE.*

### 533. What shadow is.

**SHADOW**, named by its own proper term, is to be called the alleviation of light applied to the surface of bodies, of which the beginning is at the end of light, and the end is in darkness. <note>Leonardo defines shadow not as an entity, but as a gradual reduction of light intensity.</note>

### 534. What the difference is between shadow and darkness.

The difference that exists between shadow and darkness <note>original: "tenebre," referring to total absence of light</note> is this: that shadow is an alleviation of light, and darkness is the integral deprivation of that light.

### 535. From what shadow derives.

Shadow derives from two things dissimilar to one another, because one is corporeal and the other is spiritual: the corporeal is the shadowy body <note>the physical object blocking the light</note>, and the spiritual is the light; therefore, light and body are the cause of shadow.

### 536. On the being of shadow in itself.

Shadow is of the nature of universal things, which are all more powerful at their beginning and weaken toward their end: I say at the beginning of every form and quality <note>Leonardo suggests that shadow is darkest at its point of origin, where the light is first obstructed, and softens as it spreads.</note>

<term>alleviazione</term> <note>alleviation or mitigation; used here to describe the softening or lessening of light intensity.</note>
<term>tenebre</term> <note>darkness or gloom; specifically the total absence of light as opposed to the partial light of a shadow.</term>

<summary>Leonardo da Vinci defines the scientific nature of shadow as a mitigation of light caused by the interaction of a physical body and "spiritual" light. He distinguishes between partial shadow and total darkness, noting that shadow is strongest at its point of origin.</summary>
<keywords>shadow, light, perspective, optics, darkness, corporeal, spiritual, Leonardo da Vinci, art theory</keywords>

evident and non-evident, and not of those things led from a small beginning to a great increase by time, such as a great oak tree which has a weak beginning from a small acorn; rather, I would say the oak is most powerful at its birth, which it makes from the earth, that is, in its greatest thickness; therefore, darkness is the first degree of shadow, and light is the last. Therefore you, the painter, shall make the shadow darkest near its cause, and the end such that it converts into light, that is, so that it appears without an end. <note>Leonardo advises painters to avoid hard edges on shadows, suggesting they should fade imperceptibly into the light.</note>

### 537. What shadow and light are, and which is of greater power.

Shadow is the privation of light, and only the opposition of dense bodies placed against luminous rays; shadow is of the nature of darkness, light is of the nature of brightness; one hides and the other demonstrates; they are always in company joined to bodies; and shadow is of greater power than light, because it prohibits and entirely deprives bodies of light, and light can never entirely drive shadow away from bodies, that is, from dense bodies.

### 538. What shadow and darkness are.

Shadow is the diminution of light; darkness <note>original: "tenebre"</note> is the privation of light.

### 539. Into how many parts shadow is divided.

Shadow is divided into two parts, of which the first is called the primary shadow <note>original: "ombra primitiva"</note>, and the second the derivative shadow <note>original: "ombra derivativa"</note>.

### 540. On shadow and its division.

Shadows on bodies are generated by dark objects placed before those bodies, and they are divided into two parts, of which one is called primary, the other derivative.

### 541. On two species of shadows and into how many parts they are divided.

The species of shadows are divided into two parts, one of which is called simple and the other composite: simple is that which is caused by a single light and a single body; composite is that which is generated by multiple lights upon the same body, or by multiple lights upon multiple bodies. Simple shadow is divided into two parts, namely primary and derivative: primary is that which is joined to the surfaces of the shaded body; derivative is that shadow which departs from the aforementioned body and travels through the air, and if it finds resistance, it stops at the place where it strikes with the shape of its own base; and the same is said of composite shadows.

The primary shadow always forms the base of the derivative shadow.

## 549. How the primary and derivative shadows are joined.

The <term>primary shadow</term><note>original: "ombra primitiva"; the shadow on the object itself</note> will always be joined with the <term>derivative shadow</term><note>original: "ombra derivativa"; the shadow cast into the air or onto another surface</note>; this conclusion is self-evident, because the primary shadow forms the base of the derivative one. They differ only in that the primary shadow stains the body to which it is joined, while the derivative shadow pours through all the air it penetrates. This is proven: let the luminous body be $f$, and the shaded body be $aobc$. The primary shadow joined to such a shaded body is the part $abc$, and the derivative shadow $abcd$ is born together with the primary; and such a shadow is called <term>simple</term><note>original: "ombra semplice"; a total shadow or umbra where no light reaches</note>, in which no part of the light source can be seen.

## 550. How the simple shadow joins with the composite shadow.

The simple shadow will always be joined with the <term>composite shadow</term><note>original: "ombra composta"; a partial shadow or penumbra where some light still reaches</note>; this is proven by the previous statement, which says the primary shadow forms the base of the derivative shadow. And because the simple and composite shadows are born in the same body joined to one another, it is necessary that the effect participates in the cause. Because the composite shadow is in itself nothing other than a diminution of light, beginning at the edge of the luminous body and ending with the limit of that same light, it follows that such a shadow is generated in the middle between the simple shadow and the simple light. This is proven: let the light be $abc$ and the shaded object $de$. Let the simple derivative shadow be $def$, and the composite derivative shadow be $f e k$. The simple derivative shadow sees no part of the luminous body; but the composite derivative shadow always sees a part of the light, greater or smaller, according to the greater or lesser distance its parts have from the simple derivative shadow. This is proven: let such a shadow be $efk$, which with half of its thickness $fk$ (that is $ik$) sees half of the light $ab$ (which is $ac$); and this is the brightest part of that composite shadow. The other, darker half of the same composite shadow (which is $fi$) sees $cb$, the second half of that light; and thus we have determined the two parts of the composite derivative shadow, one being brighter or less dark than the other.

## 551. Of the simple and composite primary shadow.

The simple and composite shadows are proportioned among themselves in the primary shadows joined to shaded bodies just as they are in the derivative shadows separated from those same shaded bodies. This is proven because the simple and composite derivatives are joined to one another without any interruption, just as if they were the primary origins of those derivative shadows.

<summary>Leonardo explains the geometric relationship between primary shadows (on the object), derivative shadows (cast in space), and the transition from total shadow (simple) to partial shadow (composite/penumbra).</summary>

### 552. On the boundaries of the <term>composite shadow</term>.

The derivative <term>composite shadow</term><note>The penumbra, or the partial shadow where only a portion of the light source is obscured.</note> is of infinite length, because it is pyramidal, originating from a pyramid at its point; and this is proven because, no matter where that pyramidal length is cut, its angle will never be destroyed, as happens in the derivative <term>simple shadow</term><note>The umbra, or total shadow.</note>.

### 553. On the boundary of the <term>simple shadow</term>.

The <term>simple derivative shadow</term> is of short duration compared to the composite derivative, because the composite, as stated, originates from its angle <note>The point where the penumbra begins to spread outward.</note>, while this one has its origin from its base; and this is evident because in whatever part that pyramid is cut by a <term>shaded body</term><note>original: "corpo ombroso"; an opaque object that blocks light.</note>, that division never destroys its base.

### 554. What shadow is made by a light equal to the shaded body in the shape of its shadows.

If the shaded body is equal in size to the luminous body, then the <term>simple shadow</term> will be parallel and infinite in length; but the shadow and the composite light will be pyramidal, with the angle facing toward the luminous body.

### 555. What shadow is made by a shaded body larger than the luminous body.

If the shaded body is larger than its light source, then the simple derivative shadow will have its sides converging toward a potential angle beyond the luminous body; and the angles of the shadow and composite light will face the entire luminous body.

### 556. How many types of shadows there are.

There are three types of shadows: the first arises from a <term>particular light</term><note>A point source or concentrated light.</note>, such as the sun, moon, or a flame; the second is that which derives from a door, window, or other opening through which a large part of the sky is seen; the third is that which arises from <term>universal light</term><note>Ambient or diffused light.</note>, such as the light of our hemisphere when the sun is not present.

### 557. How many species of shadows there are.

The species of shadows are of two kinds: one is called <term>primitive</term><note>The shadow on the object itself.</note>, the other <term>derivative</term><note>The shadow cast away from the object.</note>. The primitive is that which is joined to the <term>shaded body</term>; the derivative is that which derives from the primitive.

<note>The following terms are defined by Leonardo's usage in this text:
- **Composite shadow**: Penumbra (partial shadow).
- **Simple shadow**: Umbra (total shadow).
- **Primitive shadow**: The shadow attached to the object's surface.
- **Derivative shadow**: The shadow projected into space or onto another surface.
- **Shaded body**: An opaque object.
- **Luminous body**: A light source.
- **Universal light**: Diffused light (e.g., an overcast sky).
- **Particular light**: A specific, directed light source.
- **Pyramidal**: Tapering like a pyramid or cone.</note>

He also categorizes shadows into three types based on their light source and two species based on their location.</summary>

### 558. Of how many kinds is the <term>primitive shadow</term>.

The <term>primitive shadow</term><note>The shadow that exists directly on the surface of the opaque object itself, as opposed to the shadow cast onto another surface.</note> is one and unique and never varies; its boundaries perceive the boundary of the luminous body and the boundaries of the illuminated part of the body to which it is joined.

---

### 559. In how many ways the <term>primitive shadow</term> varies.

The primitive shadow varies in two ways, the first of which is simple, and the second is composite. Simple is that which faces a dark place, and for this reason such a shadow is gloomy; composite is that which faces a place illuminated with various colors, for then such a shadow will mix with the qualities of the colors of the opposing objects.

---

### 560. What variety the <term>derivative shadow</term> has.

The varieties of the <term>derivative shadow</term><note>The shadow cast by an object onto the air or onto another surface.</note> are of two kinds: one is mixed with the air that stands opposite the primitive shadow; the other is that which strikes the object that intersects said derivative shadow.

---

### 561. Of how many shapes is the <term>derivative shadow</term>.

There are three shapes of the derivative shadow: the first is pyramidal, born from a shaded body smaller than the light source; the second is parallel, born from a shaded body equal to the light source; the third is infinitely divergent. The columnar shadow is infinite, and the pyramidal is infinite, because after the first pyramid it creates an intersection, and generates an infinite pyramid opposite the finite pyramid, finding infinite space. And these three kinds of derivative shadows will be fully discussed.

---

### 562. Of the shadow that moves with greater speed than its shaded body.

It is possible for the derivative shadow to be many times faster than its primitive shadow. This is proven: let *a* be the light source, and let *b* be the shaded body, which moves from *b* to *c* along the line *bd*; and in the same time, the derivative shadow of body *b* moves across the entire space *be*, which space can contain within itself thousands of times the space *bc*.

## 568. Whether the primary shadow is more powerful than the derivative shadow.

The primary shadow <note>original: "ombra primitiva"; the shadow on the object itself</note>, being simple, will be of equal darkness to the simple derivative shadow <note>original: "ombra derivativa"; the shadow cast by the object onto another surface</note>. This is proven: let the simple primary shadow be *de*, and the simple derivative be *fg*; I say, according to the fourth [proposition] of this [treatise], which states: darkness is the deprivation of light. Therefore, a simple shadow is that which receives no illuminated reflection, and for this reason remains dark. Just as *de* does not see the light *a*, neither does the simple derivative shadow *fg* see it; and therefore, these shadows are of equal darkness to one another, because both are deprived of light and luminous reflection.

## 569. On the motions of shadows.

The motions of shadows are of five natures. We shall say the first is that which moves the derivative shadow together with its shaded body, while the light source causing that shadow remains immobile. The second is that in which the shadow and the light move, but the shaded body is immobile. The third is that in which the shaded body and the luminous body move, but the luminous body moves more slowly than the shaded one. In the fourth motion of said shadow, the shaded body moves faster than the luminous body,¹ and in the fifth, the motions of the shaded and luminous bodies are equal to each other. And this shall be treated distinctly in its proper place.

## 570. The striking of the derivative shadow and its conditions.

The striking <note>original: "percussione"; the point where a cast shadow hits a surface</note> of the derivative shadow will never be similar to the primary shadow unless it meets certain conditions: first, that the shaded body has no angles, nor is it perforated or jagged <note>original: "frappato"; likely referring to a fringed or irregular edge</note>; second, that the shape of the luminous body is similar to the shape of the shaded body; third, that the size of the luminous body is equal to the size of the shaded body; fourth, that the surface of the shaded ray is of equal length on every side; fifth, that the striking of the derivative shadow is created between equal angles; sixth, that such a striking is made upon a wall that is flat and uniform.

---

¹ The Vienna edition proposes: "the luminous body moves faster than the shaded body."

which at every degree of distance beyond the width of its origin acquires degrees of width.

### 576. Variety of each of the three aforementioned derivative shadows.

Of the <term>derivative shadow</term> <note>The "derivative shadow" refers to the cone or volume of darkness cast into the air by an object, as opposed to the "attached shadow" on the object itself.</note> born from a shaded body smaller than the body that illuminates it, that one will be pyramidal, and it will be shorter the closer it is to the luminous body; but the parallel shadow in such a case does not vary; but the dilating shadow widens more the closer it approaches its light source.

### 577. That derivative shadows are of three natures.

Derivative shadows are of three natures, of which one is dilating, the other column-like <note>cylindrical</note>, and the third converging toward the point of the intersection of its sides; which, after such intersection, are of infinite width or straightness. And if you were to say that such a shadow is terminated at the angle of the junction of its sides and passes no further, this is denied; because in the first principles of shadows it is proven that a thing is entirely terminated when no part of it exceeds its boundaries; whereas here, in such a shadow, the contrary is seen. For as soon as such a derivative shadow is born, there is clearly born the figure of two shaded pyramids <note>cones</note> which are joined at their angles <note>vertices</note>. Therefore, if according to the opponent the first shaded pyramid terminates the derivative shadow with its angle, from where does the second shaded pyramid arise? The opponent says it is caused by the angle and not by the shaded body; but this is denied with the help of the second [proposition] of this [treatise], which says that shadow is an <term>accident</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property that does not exist by itself but only within a subject—here, shadow exists only because of the light and the object.</note> created by shaded bodies interposed between the site of said shadow and the luminous body. And because of this, it is clear that the shadow is not generated by the angle of the derivative shadow, but only by the shaded body.

### 578. That derivative shadows are of three species.

Derivative shadows are of three species: that is, either the <term>section</term> <note>original: "tagliamento"; refers to the shadow cast onto a surface like a wall.</note> of the shadow on the wall where it strikes will be larger than its base <note>the object itself</note>, or the shadow will be smaller than said base, or it will be equal. And if it is larger, it is a sign that the light illuminating the shaded body is smaller than said body; and if it is smaller, the light is larger than the body; and if it is equal, the light is equal to said body.

<summary>Leonardo classifies the three types of shadows cast by objects (converging, parallel, and diverging) based on the relative size of the light source and the object. He argues against the idea that a shadow ends at its point of intersection, suggesting instead a geometric continuity of two opposing cones.</summary>

### 579. Qualities of shadows.

Among equal reductions of light, the proportion between the darkness of the generated shadows will be the same as the proportion between the darkness of the colors where those shadows are joined <note>Leonardo is observing that the perceived darkness of a shadow depends on the underlying color of the surface it falls upon.</note>.

### 580. On the movement of the shadow.

The movement of a shadow is always faster than the movement of the body that generates it, provided the light source is stationary. This is proven: let the light source be *a*, the shaded body *b*, and the shadow *d*; I say that in the same time that the shaded body *b* moves to *c*, the shadow *d* moves to *e*. The proportion of the speeds achieved in the same duration is equal to the proportion of the length of one movement to the length of the other. Therefore, the proportion that the length of the movement made by the body from *b* to *c* has to the length of the movement made by the shadow from *d* to *e*, is the same as the proportion between their respective speeds. 

But if the light source moves at a speed equal to the movement of the shaded body, then the shadow and the shaded body will be equal to each other in their movements. And if the light source is faster than the shaded body, then the movement of the shadow will be slower than the movement of the shaded body. But if the light source is slower than the shaded body, then the shadow will be faster than the shaded body.

### 581. On the pyramidal shadow.

The <term>pyramidal shadow</term> <note>A cone-shaped shadow that tapers to a point.</note> generated by a parallel-sided body will be narrower than the shaded body in proportion to how far the <term>simple derivative shadow</term> is cut <note>intersected by a surface</note> from its shaded body.

### 582. On the simple derivative shadow.

The simple derivative shadow is of three kinds: one finite in length and two infinite. The finite one is pyramidal; of the infinite ones, one is <term>columnar</term> <note>cylindrical</note> and the other is <term>dilating</term> <note>expanding</note>. All three have straight sides. The converging shadow—that is, the pyramidal one—arises from a shaded body smaller than the light source; the columnar arises from a shaded body equal to the light source; and the dilating arises from a shaded body larger than the light source.

### 583. On the composite derivative shadow.

The <term>composite derivative shadow</term> <note>Shadows formed by multiple light sources or complex light environments.</note> is of two kinds: namely, columnar and dilating.

### 596. How every opaque body generates as many shadows as there are luminous parts surrounding it.

Opaque bodies <note>original: "corpi ombrosi" – literally "shadowy bodies," referring to objects that block light</note> generate as many kinds of shadows around their base, and of as many colors, as there are opposing illuminated colors surrounding them; but one will be so much more powerful than the other as the opposing light is of greater splendor, and this is taught to us by various lights placed around the same opaque body.

### 597. Of the various darknesses of the shadows surrounding the same opaque body.

Of the shadows surrounding the same opaque body, that one will be darkest which is generated by the most powerful light source.

### 598. Of the shadow made by a body between two equal lights.

That body which finds itself placed between two equal lights will cast from itself two shadows, which will direct themselves in a line toward the two lights; and if you move said body and place it closer to one of the lights than the other, the shadow directed toward the nearer light will be of less darkness than the one directed toward the more distant light. <note>Leonardo observes that the closer light "washes out" the shadow cast by the distant light.</note>

### 599. That the body which is closer to the light makes a larger shadow, and why.

If an object placed before a specific light is in close proximity, you will see it cast a very large shadow on the opposite wall; and the further you move said object from the light, the more the form of that shadow will diminish.

### 600. Why a shadow larger than its cause is made of discordant proportion.

The discordance in the proportion of a shadow larger than its cause <note>the "cause" is the object casting the shadow</note> arises because the light, being smaller than the object, cannot be at an equal distance from the extremities of that object; and that part which is closer increases more than the distant parts, and therefore it grows larger. <term>Discordant proportion: the distortion that occurs when a shadow does not perfectly mirror the shape of the object due to the angle of light.</term>

### 601. Why a shadow larger than its cause has blurred edges.

That air which circumscribes the light is almost of the nature of that light in its clarity and color, and the further it recedes, the more it loses its resemblance; and the thing... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence at the end of the page.</note>

### 602. How the detached shadow will never be equal in size to its cause.

If the luminous rays are, as experience confirms, caused by a single point, and in a circular course from its point go on dispersing and spreading through the air, the further they move away, the more they widen; and always the thing placed between the light and the wall is conveyed as a larger shadow, because the rays that touch it, once their convergence reaches the wall, are made wider.

### 603. What difference there is between a shadow joined to bodies and a detached shadow.

<term>Joined shadow</term> <note>original: "ombra congiunta" – also known as "attached shadow," the dark side of the object itself</note> is that which never departs from the illuminated bodies, such as would be a ball, which, standing in the light, always has a part of itself occupied by shadow, which never divides itself by any change of position made by said ball. <term>Detached shadow</term> <note>original: "ombra separata" – also known as "cast shadow," the shadow thrown onto another surface</note> can be and not be created by the body; let us suppose that said ball is distant from a wall by one cubit <note>original: "braccio" – a historical unit of measurement roughly the length of an arm</note>, and on the opposite side is the light; the said light will send onto said wall exactly as much expansion of shadow as that which is found on the part of the ball that is turned toward said wall. That part of the detached shadow which does not appear will be when the light is beneath the ball, so that its shadow goes toward the sky, and finding no resistance along the path, it is lost.

### 604. Nature of the <term>derivative shadow</term>.

The <term>derivative shadow</term> <note>The "derivative shadow" refers to the cone of darkness traveling through the air between the object and the surface it falls upon.</note> increases and decreases according to the increase or decrease of its <term>primitive shadow</term> <note>The "primitive shadow" is the initial shadow on the object itself.</note>.

### 605. Of the shapes of shadows.

Never will the <term>derivative shadow</term> be entirely similar to the shadowy body that generates it if the light which surrounds the boundaries of such a body with its rays is not of the same shape as that body.

### 613. On light that turns into shadow.

A spot illuminated by the air <note>ambient or diffused light</note> will appear shadowy if it is surrounded by the striking of solar rays; and this arises because the greater light makes the light of lesser brightness appear dark.

### 614. On the derivative shadow created by a light of long shape, which strikes an object similar to itself.

When light passing through an opening <term>spiracolo; a small aperture or vent</term> of a long and narrow shape strikes a shadowy object of a shape and position similar to itself, then the shadow will take the shape of the shadowy object. This is proven: let the opening where the light penetrates into the dark place be *ab*, and let the columnar object <note>original: "obietto colonnale"</note> of equal and similar shape to the shape of the opening be *cd*, and let *ef* be the striking of the shadowy ray of the said object *cd*; I say such a shadow cannot be larger, nor yet smaller than that opening at any distance, the light being conditioned in the aforementioned way. And this remains proven by the fourth [proposition] of this [treatise], which says that all shadowy and luminous rays are rectilinear <note>traveling in straight lines</note>.

### 615. That shadows must always participate in the color of the shadowy body.

Nothing appears in its natural whiteness, because the places in which it is seen render it to the eye as much more or less white as that place is more or less dark; and the moon teaches us this, which by day shows itself in the sky with little clarity and at night with such splendor that it renders to us the image of the sun and of the day by its chasing away of the darkness. And this arises from two things: the first is comparison, which by its nature shows things to be more perfect in the types of their colors the more they are dissimilar; the second is that the pupil is larger at night than during the day, as is proven; and a larger pupil sees a luminous body in greater quantity and with more excellent splendor than a smaller pupil, as is proven by one who looks at the stars through a small hole made in paper.

### 616. On white things remote from the eye.

A white thing removed from the eye, the further it is removed, the more it loses its whiteness, and all the more so when the sun illuminates it, because it participates in the color of the sun mixed with the color of the air that is interposed between the eye and the white object. The

The shadows of remote things will participate so much more in the color of blue as they are in themselves darker and more remote; and this happens because of the interposition of the brightness of the air which places itself between the darkness of the shadowy bodies positioned between the sun and the eye that sees them; but if the eye turns opposite to the sun, it will not see such a blue.

### 618. On shadows, and which are those primary shadows that will be darkest upon their body.

The primary shadows <term>ombre primitive; the shadow on the object itself, rather than the shadow it casts</term> will become darker when they are generated on the surface of a denser body, and conversely lighter on the surfaces of rarer <note>less dense or more porous</note> bodies; this is manifest because the images <note>original: "specie"; the visual information or "species" of an object</note> of those objects which tint the opposing bodies with their colors are imprinted with greater vigor when they find a denser and cleaner surface upon those bodies. ### 619. Which part of the surface of a body is best imprinted with the color of its object.

That part of the surface of a dense body participates most intensely in the color of its object which is least seen by other objects of other colors. Therefore, we shall use the same figure for our purpose; and let it be that the surface of the aforementioned body *crd* is not seen by the darkness *op*, it will be entirely deprived of shadow, and similarly if the surface *asb* is not seen by the luminous [object] *nm*, it will be entirely deprived of light.

# TREATISE ON PAINTING — PART FIVE

### 629. On the shadow of the greenery of meadows.

The greenery of meadows has minimal, or rather almost imperceptible shadow, especially where the grasses are small and have thin leaves; for this reason, shadows cannot be generated, because the great hemisphere <note>The "hemisphere" refers to the entire visible sky acting as a broad, diffuse light source.</note> surrounds the tiny stalks in a circle, and unless there is a clump of wide leaves, the shadows of the grasses are of little evidence.

### 630. Precept of painting.

In universal light <note>Diffuse light coming from all directions, such as an overcast sky.</note>, shadows occupy little space on the surfaces of bodies; and this arises because the great sum of light from our hemisphere surrounds even the lowest parts of shaded bodies, unless it is obstructed by its horizon, and especially if the body is suspended above the ground. Let *f* be the shaded body, *e* the earth; *a b c d* is our hemisphere, *a d* is the horizon of said hemisphere. From this, even though the darkness of the earth *u x* obscures as much of the shaded body as it "sees," the horizon that sees those same parts illuminates those same places and confuses the shaded qualities of the aforementioned earth—which was in a position to make such shadows dark on the underside of the object, if it had not been prevented.

### 631. On shadows that do not match the illuminated part.

Very rare are those shadows of opaque bodies that are the true shadows of their illuminated parts. This is proven by the seventh [rule] of the fourth [book], which says that the surface of every shaded body participates in the color of its object <note>The "object" here refers to any surrounding surface or environment facing the body.</note>. Therefore, the illuminated color of faces, having a black color as their object, will participate in black shadows; and it will do the same with yellow, green, and blue, and every other color placed opposite to it. This happens because every body sends its likeness through all its surrounding air, as is proven in perspective; and as is seen by the experience of the sun, from which all objects placed before it participate in its light and reflect it to other objects—as is seen with the moon and the other stars, which reflect to us the light given to them by the sun. And darkness does the same, since it clothes with its own obscurity whatever is enclosed within it.

### 632. On the light of shaded bodies, which are almost never the true color of the illuminated body.

We can say it is almost never the case that the surface of illuminated bodies is the true color of those bodies.

### 634. On the width of shadows and primary lights.

The expansion and retraction of shadows—that is, the greater or lesser width of shadows and lights upon opaque bodies—will be found in the greater or lesser curvature of the parts of the bodies where they are generated.

### 635. On the greater or lesser darkness of shadows.

The greater or lesser darkness of shadows is generated in the most curved parts of the limbs, and the least dark will be found in the widest <note>Meaning the flatter or more gradual</note> parts.

### 636. Where shadows deceive the judgment that gives sentence on their greater or lesser darkness.

Among shadows of equal darkness, that one will appear less dark which is surrounded by lights of lesser power, such as the shadows generated between reflected lights; therefore you, painter, take care not to deceive yourself by varying such a shadow <note>Leonardo warns that the surrounding environment changes our perception of a shadow's depth, even if the physical darkness is the same.</note>.

### 637. Where lights deceive the judgment of the painter.

Among lights of equal brightness, that one will seem more powerful which is smaller and surrounded by a darker field.

### 641. On lights and shadows, and their colors.

No body will ever show itself entirely in its natural color. That part of the body would show its natural color which was illuminated by a light source without color, and which in such illumination sees no other object than the aforementioned light: this can never be seen except in the color deep blue <note>original: "turchino"</note> placed on a flat surface facing the sky on a very high mountain, so that in such a place it cannot see any other object, and the sun is blocked, at its setting, by low clouds, and the cloth is the color of the air. ## 652. On shadow and light.

Darkness is the deprivation of light, and light is the deprivation of darkness; shadow is the mixture of darkness with light, and it will be of greater or lesser obscurity depending on whether the light mixed with it is of lesser or greater power.

## 653. On shadow and light.

That object will have the boundaries of its shadows and lights most imperceptible <note>meaning the transitions are soft or blurred</note> when it is placed between larger dark and light objects of continuous quantity. This is proven: let the object be *o*, which is placed between the dark area *nm* and the light area *rs*; I say that the dark object surrounds almost the entire object with its pyramid *nam*, and the same is done on the opposite side by the pyramid of the light area *rcs*; and by the eighth [proposition] of the fifth [book] <note>Leonardo frequently references Euclidean geometry or his own planned treatises by book and proposition number</note> the proposition is concluded, which says that the part of the sphere will be darker which sees more of the darkness placed before it; it follows that *c* is darker than any other part of that sphere; and the second figure proves it: *bac* sees all the darkness *egf*; such darkness is not impressed upon *bac* with equal power, because it is not impressed with uniform quantity, since *a*, which sees all the darkness *ef*, is much darker than *b*, which sees only half of it *eg*; and the same happens at *c*, which is seen by the shadow *gf*.

## 654. Of lights and shadows.

Every part of the body and every tiny particle that possesses any amount of relief <term>relief: the quality of standing out from a surface, creating a three-dimensional effect</term>, I remind you to be careful to give them their primary shadows and lights.

## 655. On shadow and light.

Every part of the surface surrounding bodies is transformed in part by the color of that thing which is placed before it as an object.

### 657. On shadows and lights.

You, who draw from the works of nature, see the quantities and qualities and the shapes of lights and shadows of each muscle, and note in the lengths of their shape toward which muscle they are directed with the straightness of their central lines.

### 658. Of lights within shadows.

When you draw any body, remember, when you make a comparison of the power of the lights of its illuminated parts, that the eye is often deceived, appearing to it clearer that which is less clear; and the cause arises through the comparisons of the parts that border them, because if you have two parts of unequal brightness, and the less bright one borders dark parts, and the brighter one borders bright parts, such as the sky or similar brightnesses, then that which is less bright—or let us say luminous—will appear more luminous, and the brighter one will appear darker. <note>Leonardo is describing the phenomenon of simultaneous contrast, where the background significantly alters our perception of a value.</note>

### 659. Of light and dark.

Light and dark <note>original: "chiaro e scuro"</note> together with foreshortenings <term>foreshortening: the technique of depicting an object or figure in a picture or relief as shorter than it is in reality to create an illusion of depth</term> is the excellence of the science of painting.

### 660. Of light and dark.

Light and dark, that is, light and shadows, have a middle ground, which can be named neither light nor dark, but equally participating in both light and dark; and it is sometimes equally distant from the light and from the dark, and sometimes closer to one than to the other.

### 661. Of the four things that must be considered principally in shadows and in lights.

There are four principal parts which must be considered in painting, namely quality, quantity, location, and shape: by quality is meant what kind of shadow, and which part of the shadow is more or less dark; quantity, that is, how great is the size of such a shadow compared to the others nearby; location, that is, in what way they should be situated, and upon what part of the limb where it rests; shape, that is, what the shape of that shadow is, as if to say whether it is triangular, or participates in the round, or the square, etc.

# LEONARDO DA VINCI [§ 661

The aspect <note>In this context, "aspect" refers to the orientation or directional alignment of a shape.</note> is also to be counted among the parts of shadows; that is, if the shadow has length, observe toward which aspect the sum of that length is directed. If the shadow of an eyebrow is directed toward the ear, or if the lower shadow of the eye socket is directed toward the nostrils, and thus with similar comparisons of various aspects, situate these shadows; therefore, the aspect is to be prioritized over the location.

### 662. On the nature of the light illuminating shaded bodies.

Universal light <note>original: "lume universale" — referring to diffused or ambient light, like an overcast sky.</note> surrounds the part of the shaded body seen by it, and illuminates it, and varies the illumination of that body with greater or lesser clarity, according to whether the illuminated parts of such a body are seen by a greater or lesser quantity of that universal light.

### 663. On universal lights upon polished bodies.

Universal lights surrounding polished bodies will provide a universal clarity on the surfaces of such bodies.

### 664. On shaded bodies which are polished and lustrous.

In shaded bodies which have a polished and lustrous surface, those that have a particular light <note>original: "lume particolare" — referring to a specific, directional light source like the sun or a lamp.</note> vary their shadows and highlights <note>original: "lustri"</note> in as many different locations as there are changes in the light of the eye that sees them.

In this case, the particular light can be immobile and the eye mobile, and vice versa, which is the same thing regarding the changes of the highlights and shadows on the surfaces of these bodies.

### 665. How bodies surrounded by universal light generate particular lights in many of their parts.

Particular lights are generated on the surfaces of shaded bodies, even though their entirety is surrounded from above by the universal light of the sky without the sun—as it is when some dark cloud takes it from us and occupies it. This arises from the inequality of the surfaces of these bodies, by means of the limbs joined to them, which, interposing themselves between that light and the shaded body, deprive that body of a great quantity of universal light; hence the light that penetrates between the limbs and the body will be a particular light, that is, a part of the whole light which encompasses the exterior parts of each limb of the body.

### 666. On the shadows and lights with which natural things are imitated.

There are some who wish to see dark shadows in all of their works, and thus they criticize those who do not do as they do. These people can be satisfied in part by using both dark shadows and light shadows; the dark ones in dark places, and the light ones in landscapes under universal lights <note>diffused, ambient light such as an overcast sky</note>.

### 667. On shadows, and in which bodies they cannot have great power of darkness, and likewise the lights.

Where shadows of great darkness are not generated, lights of great brightness cannot be generated either. And this happens in trees with sparse and narrow leaves, such as willows, broom plants, junipers and the like, and also in transparent fabrics, such as <term>zendadi</term> <note>a thin, light silk fabric common in the Renaissance</note>, veils and the like, as well as in frizzy and scattered hair. This occurs because the entirety of each of the aforementioned types does not create highlights <note>original: "lustri"</note> in its individual parts, and if they do exist, they are imperceptible, and their appearance is hardly removed from the place where they are generated. The same happens with the shaded parts of such particles; the whole sum does not generate a dark shadow because the air penetrates and illuminates them, both the parts near the middle and those on the outside. If there is variety, it is almost imperceptible, and thus the illuminated parts of that whole cannot be too different from the shaded parts. Because the luminous air penetrates, as was said, through all the particles, the illuminated parts are so close to the shaded particles that the images they send to the eye create a confused mixture, composed of tiny lights and darks, so that in such a mixture nothing is discerned but a confusion like a mist. The same happens in veils, spiderwebs, and the like.

### 668. On the particular light of the sun or another luminous body.

That part of the illuminated body will be of more intense brightness which is struck by the luminous ray at more similar angles <note>meaning angles closer to perpendicular (90 degrees)</note>; and the least illuminated will be that which is found at more dissimilar angles of those luminous rays.

The angle <term>n</term> on the side facing the sun, because it is struck by that sun at equal angles, will be illuminated with a greater power of rays than any other part of that illuminated body; and the point <term>c</term> will be less illuminated than any other part, because that point is struck by the solar body at more dissimilar angles than any other part of the <term>planizie</term> <note>the flat surface or plane</note> where such solar rays extend; and let the larger of the two angles be—

<summary>Leonardo explains why certain materials like thin silk or sparse foliage do not produce high-contrast shadows and uses geometry to demonstrate how the angle of light rays determines the intensity of brightness on a surface.</summary>

### 669. On the universal light of the air where the sun does not strike.

That object will appear more illuminated which is seen by a greater quantity of the luminous source; according to what has been said, *e* will be more illuminated than *a*, because *e* sees a greater portion of the sky, seeing *rs*, whereas *a* does not, seeing only the sky *bcd*.

### 670. On universal illumination mixed with the particular light of the sun or other lights.

Without doubt, that part of the shaded body which is seen by a smaller quantity of the universal and particular body <note>meaning the ambient sky and the specific sun</note> will be the least illuminated. This is proven: let *a* be the body of the sun placed in the sky *nam*; I say that point *o* of the shaded body will be more illuminated by the universal light than point *r*, because *o* sees and is seen by the entire part of the universal light *nam*, while point *r* is seen only by the part of the sky *me*. Furthermore, *o* is seen by the entire mass of the sun that is turned toward it, and *r* does not see any part of that sun.

### 671. On the middle shadow, which is interposed between the illuminated and the shaded part of bodies.

Between the illuminated part and the shaded part of bodies, the middle shadow <note>often referred to in art as the "half-tone"</note> is interposed, which varies its boundaries significantly; for where it ends with the shadow it turns into shadow, and where it ends with the illuminated part it takes on the brightness of that illumination. And if the primary light is a particular one <note>a direct, concentrated source like a lamp or the sun</note>, then there will be highlights <note>original: "lustri"</note>, which are as clearly defined boundaries of the middle shadow as the shaded part itself.

### 672. Whether a large light of little power is worth as much as a small light of great power.

The shadow generated by a small and powerful light is darker than the shadow born from a larger light of lesser power.

### 673. On the medium included between the lights and the primary shadows.

The middle shadow <note>original: "ombra mezzana"; the transitional tone between light and dark</note> will appear in greater quantity the more the eye that sees it is aligned with the center of its magnitude. Middle shadow is the name given to that which tints the surface of shaded bodies after the primary shadow, and within it is contained the reflection; it becomes darker or lighter as it is closer to or more remote from the primary shadow. Let *mn* be the darkest shadow; the rest will always brighten until point *o*. The rest of the figure is not relevant to the current proposition but will serve the one following.

### 674. On the position of the eye which sees more or less shadow according to the movement it makes around the shaded body.

The proportions of the quantities held between the shaded and illuminated parts of shaded bodies vary as much as the varieties of the positions of the eye that sees them. This is proven: let *amno* be the shaded body, and let *p* be the luminous source that embraces it; with its rays *pr* and *ps* it illuminates the part *mdn*, and the remainder *nom* remains dark. Let the eye that sees such a body be *q*, which with its visual rays embraces this shaded body and sees the whole of *dmo*. In this view, it sees *dm*, an illuminated part much smaller than *mo*, the shaded part, as is proven in the pyramid <note>a "pyramid" in Leonardo's optics refers to the cone of light or vision</note> *dqo*, cut at *kh*, equally distant to its base divided at point *c*. And thus, similarly, the quantity of light and dark to the eye that sees it will vary in as many ways as there are varieties of positions of the aforementioned eye.

### 675. Which position is that from which shadow is never seen on shaded spheres.

The eye that is situated within the reflected pyramid of the illuminated species <note>original: "specie illuminate"; the visual information or "images" of the light</note> of shaded bodies will never see any shaded part of that body. Let the reflected pyramid of the illuminated species be *abc*, and let the illuminated part of the shaded body be the part *bcd*; let the eye that stands within such a pyramid be *e*, to which all the illuminated species *bcd* can never converge unless it finds itself at the luminous point *a*, from which no shadow is ever seen, because it immediately destroys it. It follows, therefore, that *e*, seeing nothing but the illuminated part *odp*, is more deprived of seeing the boundaries of the shadow *bc* than is *a*, which is so much more remote.

### 676. Which position or distance around a spherical body is such that it is never deprived of shadow.

When the eye is further distant from the shaded sphere than the body which illuminates it, then it is impossible to find a position where the eye is entirely deprived of the shaded qualities of such a body. This is proven: let *b n c* be the shaded body, let *a* be the luminous body; *b n c* is its shaded part and *b s c* will be illuminated; let *o* be the eye further removed from the shaded body than the light *a*. This eye sees the entire shadow *b d c e*; and if this eye moves circularly around this body at the same distance, it is impossible that it ever entirely loses all of the aforementioned shadow; because, if by its motion it loses a part of that shadow on one side, by that same motion it acquires more from the other.

### 677. Which light makes the shadows of bodies most different from their lights.

That body will produce shadows of greater darkness which is illuminated by a light of greater splendor. Point *a* is illuminated by the sun, and point *b* is illuminated by the air <note>ambient light from the sky</note> illuminated by the sun; and such proportion will exist from the illuminated *a* to the illuminated *b*, as is the proportion that the light of the sun has with that of the air.

### 678. Of various nearby objects seen at a long distance.

When objects that are near to one another and small are seen at a long distance, in such a way that the knowledge of their shapes is lost, then a mixture of their species <note>original: "specie"; in Renaissance optics, the 'species' are the visual images or qualities emitted by an object</note> is caused, which will participate most in that color which clothes the greatest sum of the said objects.

### 679. Of the position where the object shows itself with greater darkness.

That object shows itself darker at an equal distance from the eye which is seen in a higher position; and this happens because the air is thinner the higher it rises, and it obstructs the object less than its thickness <note>referring to the denser air at lower altitudes</note>; and from this it arises that the peaks of hills which stand out against the slopes of mountains always show themselves to be darker than the bases of those same hills.

<summary>Leonardo explains the geometric persistence of shadow on a sphere and how atmospheric density affects the perceived darkness of objects at different altitudes.</summary>

### 680. Where and in which color shadows most lose the natural color of the shaded object.

White, which sees neither incident light <note>direct light hitting a surface</note> nor any sort of reflected light, is that which first loses its own natural color entirely in its shadow—if indeed white can be called a color. But black increases its color in the shadows and loses it in its illuminated parts; and it loses it all the more as the illuminated part is seen by a light of greater power. And green and blue increase their color in the middle shadows; and red and yellow gain color in their illuminated parts; white does the same, and mixed colors participate in the nature of the colors that compose such a mixture; that is, black mixed with white makes ash-gray <note>original: "berettino"; a dull, leaden, or bluish-gray color</note>, which is not beautiful in the deepest shadows as simple black is, and is not beautiful in the highlights as simple white is, but its supreme beauty is found between light and shadow.

### 681. Which color of a body will make a shadow most different from the light, that is, which will be darkest.

That body will have its shaded parts furthest removed from brightness in respect to its illuminated parts which is of a color closest to white. <note>Leonardo observes that the contrast between light and shadow is most extreme on white objects because the shadow appears much darker by comparison.</note>

### 682. Which part of a body will be most illuminated by a light of the same quality.

That part of a body which is illuminated by a luminous quality will be of more intense brightness than that which is struck by a wider luminous angle. <note>Leonardo is discussing the concentration of light rays.</note> It is proven: let the hemisphere be *rmc*, which illuminates the house *klof*; I say that the part of the house which is struck by a wider angle born from the same luminous quality will be more illuminated. Therefore at *f*, where the angle *nfc* strikes, there will be a more intense brightness of light than where the angle *edc* strikes, and the proportion of the lights will be the same as that of the angles, and the proportion of the angles will be the same as that of their bases *nc* and *ec*, of which the larger exceeds the smaller by the whole part *ne*; and thus at *a*, under the eaves of the roof of such a house, there will be as much less light than at *d* as the base *bc* of such an angle *bac* is smaller than the base *ec*; and so it always follows proportionately, the light being of one and the same quality. And the same which is said above is confirmed in any body illuminated by our hemisphere; and here it...

The shadow that remains under the overhangs of building roofs, which is created by the sun, acquires darkness at every degree of height <note>Leonardo is noting that shadows deepen in intensity as they recede further under an architectural projection.</note>.

That portion of reflected light which partially coats the surface of bodies will be as much less bright than the part illuminated by the air as it [the reflection] is less bright than the air itself.

And you, painter, who practice <term>history painting</term> <note>original: "istorie"; the genre of painting depicting narrative scenes from the Bible, mythology, or history, considered the highest form of art</note>, ensure that your figures have as many varieties of lights and shadows as there are varieties of objects that created them, and do not adopt a generalized manner <note>A warning against "mannerism" or using a repetitive, formulaic lighting style instead of observing nature.</note>.

The part of the surface of every body participates in as many various colors as there are objects standing before it.

The countryside illuminated by the sun will have shadows of great darkness, and to one who views it from the side opposite to where the sun sees it <note>Meaning the side in shadow, looking toward the light.</note>, it will appear extremely dark and remote objects will seem close.

But when you view things along the same line as the sun sees them, they will appear to you without shadows, and nearby things will seem remote and of unrecognizable shape.

An object that is illuminated by the air <note>Ambient or atmospheric light, rather than direct sunlight.</note> without the sun will have its darkest part where it sees the least amount of air, and it will be darker in proportion to the amount of dark surroundings it faces.

Things seen in the countryside have little difference between their shadows and their lights, and the shadows will be almost imperceptible and without any clear termination <note>Leonardo uses "termination" to mean a sharp edge or boundary.</note>; rather, like smoke, they will go on losing themselves toward the luminous parts, and will only be darker where they are deprived of the object of the air <note>Where the ambient light of the sky is blocked.</note>.

An object seen in dimly lit places, or at the onset of night, will also have little difference between its lights and shadows; and if it is full night, the difference between lights and shadows to the human eye is so imperceptible that the shape is lost entirely and is only revealed to the keen sight of nocturnal animals.

Things at a distance appear ambiguous and doubtful to you; make them with such confusion, otherwise they will not seem to be at the same distance; do not finish their boundaries with a certain termination, because boundaries are lines or angles, and being the very smallest parts of things, they are invisible not only from afar, but even from nearby.

If the line and likewise the mathematical point are invisible things, the boundaries of objects—being themselves lines—are invisible even when close; therefore, you, painter, shall not terminate things remote from the eye, at which distances not only those boundaries, but even the parts of the bodies are imperceptible.

All illuminated things participate in the color of their illuminant.

Shaded things retain the color of the object that casts the shadow.

The greater the light of the illuminated object, the darker the shaded body that stands out against it appears.

### 683. Equality of shadows in similar shaded and luminous bodies at different distances.

It is possible for the same shaded body to receive an equal shadow from light sources of various sizes. *f o g r* is a shaded body, of which the shadow is *f g o*, generated by the deprivation of the sight of the light source *d e* at the true distance, and by the light source *b c* at the remote distance; and this arises because both light sources are equally deprived of the shaded aspect *f o g* by means of the straightness of the lines *a b* and *p c*. We shall say the same of two light sources at various distances from a shaded body.

### 684. Which luminous body is that which will never see more than half of the shaded sphere.

When the <term>shaded sphere</term><note>A non-luminous, opaque ball or globe.</note> is illuminated by a <term>luminous sphere</term><note>A light source in the shape of a ball, like a sun or a lamp globe.</note> of equal size to the shaded sphere, then the shaded part and the luminous part of that shaded body will be equal to each other. Let *a b c d* be the shaded sphere equal to the luminous sphere *e f*; I say the shaded part *a b c* of the shaded sphere is equal to the luminous part *a b d*. And it is proved thus: the parallel lines *e f s t* are <term>contingent</term><note>Touching at a single point; tangent.</note> to the fronts of the diameter *a b*, that is, the diameter of the shaded sphere, which diameter passes through the center of said sphere; which, being divided at the said diameter, will be divided into equal parts, and one part will be entirely shaded and the other will be entirely luminous.

### 685. Whether it is possible that at any distance a luminous body can illuminate only half of a shaded body smaller than itself.

It is impossible that at any distance a luminous body larger than a shaded body can illuminate exactly half of that shaded body.

What has been said is proved by parallel lines, which are caused by being equidistant from each other; and between equidistant lines, nothing is included except spherical bodies of that same diameter; therefore, the extremes of two unequal spheres will not be contingent to two parallel lines. <note>Leonardo is arguing that if the light source is larger than the object, the light rays will converge behind the object, illuminating more than half of it.</note>

### 686. Of the various darknesses of the shadows of bodies represented in painting.

The surface of every <term>opaque body</term><note>A solid object that does not allow light to pass through it.</note> participates in the color of its <term>object</term><note>In this context, "object" refers to a nearby thing that reflects its color onto the surface being studied.</note>, and more or less so as the object is nearer or more remote.

The first part is proved: let *g b c* be the surface of the opaque body, which we shall assume is of a white surface, and let the object *r s* be black, and the object *n m* be also white; and by the ninth [proposition] of this [treatise], which proves that every body fills the surrounding air with the <term>species</term><note>original: "specie". A technical term in Renaissance optics referring to the "likeness" or "image" of an object's color and form traveling through space.</note> of its color and the likeness of the colored body, *r s*, the black object, will fill the air that stands before it with a dark color, which will terminate on *v g b*, part of the opaque body *g b c*, which part will be tinted in the same color as its object *r s*; and the white body of the other object *n m* will whiten the whole part of the opaque body in *g b c*; therefore, in the opaque body, all of *g v* will be found in simple participa-

### 687. Which colors create the greatest variety from lights to shadows.

Among colors, there will be a greater difference between their shadows and their lights in those which are most similar to whiteness; because white has brighter illumination and darker shadow than any other color, although neither white nor black are numbered among the colors <note>Leonardo often argued that white and black were the "extremes" of light and dark rather than true colors like red or blue.</note>.

### 688. All colors in distant shadows are unknown and indiscernible.

All colors from a distance will be unknown in the shadows, because a thing that is not touched by the principal light is not powerful enough to send its <term>similitude</term><note>The "species" or visual image of an object that Leonardo believed traveled through the air to the eye.</note> to the eye through the more luminous air, because the lesser light is overcome by the greater.

Example: we see, being inside a house, that all the colors on the walls are seen clearly and distinctly when the windows of said dwelling are open; but if we go outside that house and look from a little distance through said windows at the paintings made on those walls, in place of those paintings we will see a continuous darkness.

### 689. Of the colors of the species of objects that tint the surfaces of opaque bodies with themselves.

Many are the times that the surfaces of opaque bodies, in being tinted by the colors of their objects, take on colors that are not in those objects. ### 690. On the false color of the shadows of opaque bodies.

When an opaque body casts its shadow upon the surface of another opaque body which is illuminated by two different light sources, then such a shadow will not appear to belong to that same opaque body, but to something else.

It is proved thus: let $nde$ be the opaque body, white in itself, and let it be illuminated by the air $ab$ <note>Representing natural daylight or the blue of the sky.</note> and by the fire $cg$. Then, let the object $op$ be placed between the fire and the opaque body, the shadow of which will be cut into the surface at $dn$. Now, in this area $dn$, the redness of the fire no longer illuminates, but rather the blue of the air; hence, $dn$ will participate in blue, while at $nf$ it sees the fire. Therefore, the blue shadow ends below with the redness of the fire upon such an opaque body, and above it ends with the color of violet—that is, at $de$ it is illuminated by a mixture composed of the blue of the air $ab$ and the redness of the fire $de$, which is almost the color of violet. Thus we have proved such a shadow to be "false," meaning it is neither the shadow of the white, nor even of the redness that surrounds it.

### 691. What is in itself the true shadow of the colors of bodies.

The shadow of bodies should not participate in any color other than that of the body to which it is applied. Therefore, since black is not counted among the number of colors, the shadows of all the colors of bodies are derived from it with more or less darkness, as is required in its place, never entirely losing the color of said body except in the darkness enclosed within the boundaries of the opaque body.

Therefore you, painter, who wish to portray [from life], tint the walls of your studio somewhat with white mixed with black, because white and black are not colors.

### 692. Which object tints the white surfaces of opaque bodies more with its likeness.

That object will tint the surfaces of white opaque bodies more with its likeness which is by nature most remote from white. That which is demonstrated here...
