# LEONARDO DA VINCI [§ 697

697. Which objects acting upon the flesh cause it to show shadows that harmonize with the lights.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Light passing through flesh-colored glass, or a room painted in that same flesh-tone, as well as garments of that color, will make a face appear with its true lights and shadows in harmony with its skin. This method is extremely useful for making the flesh appear most beautiful; however, such a rule is contrary to the rules for figures placed in an open landscape surrounded by diverse colors. If a figure were placed in such a landscape <note>literally "campagna," referring to the open countryside or background environment</note>, it would contradict the third rule of the ninth book of this work.

698. Concerning the shadows of faces which, when passing through damp streets, do not appear to harmonize with their flesh tones.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The phenomenon in question occurs when a face is often colored or white while the shadows appear yellowish. This happens because wet streets are more yellow than dry ones, and the parts of the face turned toward such streets are tinted by the yellowness and darkness of the streets that stand before them as an object <note>Leonardo is describing how reflected light from the ground influences the color of shadows on the skin</note>.

699. Concerning the quality of the air in relation to shadows and lights.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;That body will show the greatest difference between shadows and lights which is seen under the strongest light, such as sunlight or, at night, the light of a fire. This should be used sparingly in painting, because the works remain harsh and without grace.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In a body found in moderate light, there will be little difference between the lights and the shadows; this occurs toward evening, or when it is cloudy. Such works are soft, and every kind of face possesses grace under these conditions. Thus, in everything, the extremes are flawed: too much light makes a work harsh; too much darkness prevents one from seeing; the middle ground is good.

700. Concerning small lights.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Furthermore, lights created by small windows produce a great difference between lights and shadows, especially if the room illuminated by them is large; and this is not good to use.

701. Which surface shows the least difference between light and dark.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;A black surface—and those which partake most of that blackness <term>nigredine: a Latinate term for absolute blackness or the quality of being black</term>—shows less difference between its shaded and luminous parts than any other, because the...

<summary>Leonardo discusses how environmental reflections and light sources—such as colored glass, wet streets, or small windows—affect the appearance of flesh tones and the "grace" of a painting. He advocates for moderate, soft lighting (like twilight or overcast skies) over harsh, direct light to avoid unappealing contrasts.</summary>

### 702. Where there is greater variety between shadows and lights, whether in near or remote things.

That shaded body will have less difference between its lights and shadows the further it is from the eye; and conversely, being near to said eye, [the difference is greater] because of the clarity of the luminous air which interposes itself with greater thickness between the eye and that shaded body when it is remote than when it is near. <note>Leonardo is describing atmospheric perspective: as an object moves further away, the "thickness" of the air between the viewer and the object softens the contrast between light and dark.</note>

### 703. Which body of equal color and distance from the eye varies its lights from its shadows the least.

That body will show less difference from its shadows to its lights which is in air of greater darkness; and conversely, being in air of greater splendor [the difference is greater], as is shown to us by things placed in the dark, which cannot be recognized, and things placed before the splendor of the sun, where the shadows appear dark compared to the parts struck by the solar rays.

### 704. Why the true figures of any body, clothed and defined in its surfaces, are recognized.

Shadows and lights are the most certain cause for making the figures <note>meaning the three-dimensional forms or shapes</note> of any body known, because a color of equal brightness or darkness cannot demonstrate its relief <term>relief: the illusion of three-dimensionality on a flat surface</term>, but performs the office of a flat surface, which with equal distance in all its parts is equally distant from the splendor that illuminates it.

### 705. Concerning the discernment of shadows of locations and the things placed within them.

If the sun is in the east and you look toward the west, you will see all illuminated things to be entirely deprived of shadow, because you see what the sun sees; and if you look to the south or north, you will see all bodies to be surrounded by shadow and light, because you see what the sun sees and what it does not see; and if you look toward the path of the sun <note>looking toward the east in this example</note>, all bodies will show you their shaded part, because that part which you see cannot be seen by the sun.

### 708. On the removal and proximity of a man as he moves away from or approaches the same light, and on the variety of his shadows.

The shadows and lights on a body of the same shape and size vary as much as the variations in the approach or removal made by the man before that light. This is proven: let the man be *bc*, who, having the light from *a*, creates his shadow *bcf*; then the man moves from *c* to *e*, and the light, which remains stationary, varies the shadow in shape and size, which is the second shadow *deg*.

### 709. On the variations created by a stationary light in the shadows generated by bodies that bend, lower, or raise themselves without moving their feet.

This is proven: let the stationary light be *f* and the man, stationary in his stance <note>literally "stationary of plants/soles," referring to the feet remaining fixed on the ground</note>, be *ab*, who bows to *cb*; I say the shadow varies infinitely from *a* to *c* because the movement is made in space, and space is a continuous quantity, and consequently divisible to infinity; therefore the shadows are varied infinitely, that is, from the first shadow *aob* to the second shadow *bcr*; and thus our proposition is concluded.

### 711. Which body is it that, the closer it approaches the light, the more its shaded part diminishes.

When the luminous body is larger than the body it illuminates, the shadow on the illuminated body will diminish more as it moves closer to that light source. Let *a b* be the luminous body, larger than the shaded body *x y r h*, which, by approaching the light at *f e c d*, diminishes its shadow; this occurs because it is embraced further beyond its center by the luminous rays when standing near the body that illuminates it than when it was more remote.

### 712. Which shaded body is it that neither increases nor diminishes its shaded or luminous parts regardless of any distance or proximity to the body that illuminates it.

When the shaded body and the luminous body are of equal size to one another, then no distance or proximity placed between them will have the power to diminish or increase their shaded or illuminated parts. Let *n m* be the shaded body, which, when moved to the position *c d* closer to the light source *a b*, has not increased or diminished the quantity of its shadow; and this happens because the luminous rays that embrace it are parallel to one another.

### 714. Those scattered bodies situated in a room illuminated by a single window will produce a derivative shadow that is more or less short, according to whether it is more or less directly opposite that window.

### 720. For every shadow with all its varieties which, due to distance, grows in width more than its cause, its exterior lines join together between the light and the shaded body.

This proposition clearly appears and is confirmed by experience; for if *ab* is a window without any crossbar, the luminous air that is on the right at *a* is seen from the left at *d*, and the air that is on the left at *b* illuminates from the right at point *c*, and these lines intersect at point *m*.

<note>Leonardo is describing how light rays crossing through a narrow opening invert their positions—light from the right side of the sky hits the left side of the room, and vice versa.</note>

### 721. Every shaded body is located between two pyramids, one dark and the other luminous; one is seen and the other is not, and this only happens when the light enters through a window.

Imagine that *ab* is the window and that *r* is the shaded body; the right light *3* passes the body from the left side of the shaded body at *g* and goes to *p*; the left light *k* passes said body on the right side at *i* and goes to *m*, and those two lines intersect at *c* and there they form a pyramid; then *ab* touches the shaded body at *ig* and forms its pyramid at *fig*; *f* will be dark, because the light *abig* can never see there; *c* will always be luminous, because it sees the light there.

<note>The "pyramid" is Leonardo's term for a cone of light or shadow. The "dark pyramid" is the actual shadow cast behind the object, while the "luminous pyramid" is the triangular area of light created by the crossing rays in front of the object.</note>

### 733. When the angles made by the <term>incident lines</term> <note>lines of light striking a surface</note> are more equal, there will be more light in that place; and where they are more unequal, there will be more darkness.

Since it has been proven that every finite light originates, or appears to be born, from a single point, that part illuminated by it will have its brightest portion where the <term>radiant line</term> falls between two equal angles, as shown above in line *ag*, and likewise in *ah* and similarly in *al*; and that portion of the illuminated part will be less bright where the <term>incident line</term> strikes between two [unequal] angles, as appears in *bcd*; and by this same method you can also recognize the parts deprived of light, as appears in *mk*.

### 734. How bodies accompanied by shadow and light always vary their boundaries according to the color and light of the object bordering their surface.

If you see a body where the illuminated part stands out and ends against a dark background, the part of that light which will appear to have the greatest brightness will be the one that ends against the dark at *d*; and if said illuminated part borders a light background, the boundary

### 736. The manner in which shadows made by objects must terminate.

### 737. Which part of a sphere is least illuminated.

That part of the shaded body will be least illuminated which is seen by the smallest part of the luminous body. But *r*, seen by the smaller arc *odf*, receives less light; and *p*, which only sees *df* (which is smaller than *edf*), remains for this reason less luminous; and even less luminous remains *q*, which only sees the edge of the horizon *f*.

## 739. Which part of the spherical opaque body is least illuminated.

That part of the spherical <term>opaque body</term> <note>original: "opaco sferico"</note> will be of the darkest shadow which is seen by the smallest sum of luminous rays. Although this has great similarity with the first [proposition] above, I shall not refrain from proving it, because the proof varies somewhat; and let the shaded body be *f n o*, and the hemisphere be *a b c*, and the darkness of the earth be the line *a c*; I say first that the upper part of the sphere *f p n* will be equally illuminated by the entire hemisphere *a b c*, and I demonstrate it thus by the three given equal portions, namely *a r e* which illuminates point *f*, and *r b s* which illuminates *p*, and *g s c* which illuminates *n*; therefore, by the seventh [proposition] of the ninth [book] <note>Leonardo frequently references his own organized books of theorems on optics and geometry</note> it is concluded that *f p n*, the upper part of the sphere, is of equal brightness; which seventh of the ninth says that all those parts of bodies which are illuminated from an equal distance by equal and similar lights will always of necessity be of equal brightness, and such a condition occurs at *f p n*. 

The second demonstration follows: let *a b c* be the spherical shaded body; let *d f e* be the illuminating hemisphere; *d e* is the earth which here causes the shadow; I say that the entire part of the sphere *a n b*, by the preceding [rule], is deprived of shadow, because it is not seen by the darkness of the earth, and all the remainder of the surface of such a sphere is shaded with more or less darkness, according as a greater or lesser sum of the darkness of the earth is accompanied by a smaller or greater quantity of the light of the hemisphere. Therefore point *c*, which sees the smallest sum of such a hemisphere and the greatest sum of the earth, will be more darkened than any other part of the shadow, that is, it sees nothing but *r d* and *s e* of the hemisphere, and sees the entire earth *d e*; and the brightest part will be *a b*, because it sees nothing but the extremities of the earth *d e*.

That part of any spherical body which is illuminated will be smaller in proportion as the part of the luminous body that sees it is smaller. It is proven: let *a h* be the shaded body, let *c i e* be our hemisphere; it follows that *a*, a part of the shaded body, will be less illuminated because it is seen by a smaller part of the luminous body, that is, by a smaller part of the daylight of our hemisphere, as the two parts *b c* and *d e* show us.

Therefore, that part of the sphere which is illuminated will be of a larger shape when it is illuminated by a greater sum of the luminous [source]. It is proven by the converse of the antecedent: if the smallest light *b c*, *d e* of our hemisphere illuminates a very small part of the sphere *a h*, the maximum light of that hemisphere will illuminate the maximum part of such a spherical body; that is, if *b c*, *d f* of the following figure illuminates only the part *n m r*,

### 740. Of the proportion that the luminous parts of bodies have with their reflections.

Such proportion as the part illuminated by the <term>incident light</term> <note>Direct light hitting a surface</note> has to that which is illuminated by the <term>reflected light</term>, the incident light itself has to that reflected light. It is proven: let *ab* be the incident light that illuminates the spherical body *cd* at *cnd*, and passes with its rays to the object *ef*, and from there is reflected into *cmd*; I say that if the light *ab* has two degrees of power and *ef* has one (which is half of two), then the reflected light *cmd* will be half the power of the light *cnd*.

### 741. Of the darkest part of the shadow in spherical or columnar bodies.

The part of the shadow of spherical or columnar bodies will be interposed between its incident light and the reflected light. <note>This refers to the "core shadow," which is darkest because it receives neither direct light nor reflected light from the surrounding environment.</note>

### 742. How shadows made by particular lights should be avoided, because their ends are similar to their beginnings.

Shadows made by the sun or other <term>particular lights</term> <note>Point sources of light, like a lamp or the sun, as opposed to the "universal light" of a cloudy sky</note> are without grace for the body they accompany, because they leave parts of the body confused with an evident boundary between shadow and light, and the shadows are of equal power at the end as they are at the beginning.

### 743. Of giving the proper lights to illuminated things according to their locations.

Great respect must be paid to the lights suited to the things illuminated by them, since in one and the same <term>history</term> <note>original: "istoria" — a narrative painting or composition</note> there occur parts that are in the countryside under the universal light of the air, and others that are in porticos, which are lights mixed of particular and universal, and others under particular lights, that is, in dwellings that take the...

## 749. On surrounding bodies with various outlines of shadow.

Ensure that the shadows cast upon the surfaces of bodies by various objects always tend to undulate with various twists, according to the variety of the limbs <note>In this context, Leonardo refers to the projecting parts of an object</note> that create the shadows and the nature of the object that receives said shadow.

## 750. A method for giving figures a shadow that matches the light and the body.

When you are painting a figure and you wish to see if the shadow is a proper companion to the light—ensuring it is not more red or yellow than the natural character of the color you wish to shade—do as follows: cast a shadow with your finger over the illuminated part of your work. If the accidental shadow <term>accidental shadow: a shadow cast by an external object onto a surface</term> made by you is similar to the natural shadow made by the finger upon your work, then it is correct. By moving your finger closer or further away, you can create darker or lighter shadows, which you should always compare with your own painted shadows.

## 751. On the positions of lights and shadows of things seen in the countryside.

When the eye sees all the parts of bodies that are seen by the sun, it will see all those bodies without shadow. This is proven by the ninth proposition, which says: the surface of every opaque body partakes of the color of its object. Therefore, the sun being the "object" of all those parts of the surfaces of bodies that "see" it, those parts of the surface partake of the brightness of the sun that illuminates them. The eye will look at these bodies, and it is impossible for it to see any part of such bodies other than that which is seen by the sun. Therefore, it will see neither the primary shadow <term>primary shadow: the shadow on the side of the object not facing the light source</term> nor the derivative shadow <term>derivative shadow: the shadow cast by the object onto the ground or another surface</term> of any of the aforementioned bodies.

## 752. If the sun is in the east and the eye is to the north or the south.

When the sun is in the east and the eye is to the north or the south, then the eye will see the primary shadows of the eastern bodies and the lights of the western bodies, and the eye itself will be exactly in the middle of the lights and the shadows of those bodies.

## 753. Of the sun and the eye both placed in the east.

When both the sun and the eye are in the east, then all the parts of the surfaces that "see" the sun will appear illuminated to the eye, according to the ninth proposition of this treatise.

### 762. How the luster generated on a white field is of little power.

Of lusters of equal power, the one that will appear of lesser brilliance is that which is generated on a whiter surface. <note>Leonardo observes that contrast is key to brightness; a highlight stands out less against a white background than against a dark one.</note>

### 763. On the sizes of lusters upon polished bodies.

Of lusters generated upon spherical bodies equally distant from the eye, the one that will be of smaller shape is that which is generated upon a sphere of smaller size. This can be seen in the tiny grains of quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury</note>, which are of almost imperceptible quantity; their lusters appear equal to the size of the grains themselves. This occurs because the visual power of the pupil is larger than the tiny grain, and therefore surrounds it as has been stated.

### 764. What difference there is between luster and light.

The difference between luster <term>lustro: a specular highlight or reflection of the light source</term> and light <term>lume: the general illumination or diffuse light on a surface</term> is that luster is always more powerful than light, and light is of greater quantity than luster. Furthermore, the luster moves along with the eye, or with its source, or with both; but the light remains fixed in its determined place, provided the source that generates it does not move.

### 765. Of light and luster.

The lights that are generated on the polished surfaces of opaque bodies will remain immobile on immobile bodies even if the eye of the viewer moves; but the lusters on those same bodies will appear in as many places on their surface as there are positions to which the eye moves.

### 766. Which bodies are those that have light without luster.

Opaque bodies that have a dense and rough surface never generate luster in any part of their illuminated side.

### 767. Which bodies are those that have luster and no luminous part.

Dense opaque bodies with a polished <insert>polished</insert> <note>The original manuscript says "dense" here, but the context implies "polished" or "smooth."</note> surface are those that have all their luster in as many places on the illuminated part as there are positions that can receive the angle of incidence of the light and the eye; but because such a surface mirrors everything...

## 768. On Luster.

The <term>luster</term> <note>lustro: a specular highlight or the direct reflection of a light source on a surface</note> partakes much more of the color of the light that illuminates the body than of the color of the body itself; and this occurs on dense surfaces. <margin>In the Vienna edition: "polished".</margin>

The <term>luster</term> of many dark bodies is entirely the color of the illuminated body <note>meaning the light source</note>, such as that of burnished gold, silver, and other metals and similar bodies.

The <term>luster</term> of leaves, glass, and jewels partakes little of the color of the body where it originates, and much of the color of the body that illuminates it.

The <term>luster</term> created in the depths of dense transparent objects is of the highest degree of beauty for such a color, as is seen inside the ruby, the <term>balas ruby</term> <note>balascio: a rose-red variety of spinel, often mistaken for a true ruby in the Renaissance</note>, glass, and similar things; this happens because between the eye and that luster, the entire natural color of the transparent body is interposed.

The reflected lights of dense and lustrous bodies are of much greater beauty than the natural color of those bodies, as is seen in the opening folds of spun gold and in other similar bodies, where one surface reflects into the other opposite to it, and the other reflects back into the first, and so they continue successively to infinity.

No <term>lustrous</term> and transparent body can show upon itself a shadow received from any object, as is seen in the shadows of river bridges, which are never seen except upon turbid waters; in clear waters, they do not appear.

The <term>luster</term> will be found upon objects in as many different sites as there are different places from which it is viewed.

If the eye and the object remain motionless, the <term>luster</term> will move across the object along with the light that causes it; if the light and the object remain motionless, the <term>luster</term> will move across the object along with the movement of the eye that sees it.

<term>Luster</term> originates on the polished surfaces of any body; those that are denser and more polished will take on more light.

## 769. On the shadow interposed between incident light and reflected light.

The shadow that is interposed between the <term>incident light</term> <note>lume incidente: the primary light hitting a surface directly from the source</note> and the <term>reflected light</term> <note>lume riflesso: light bounced onto a surface from another object</note> will be of great darkness, and will appear darker than it actually is because of the comparison with the <term>incident light</term> that borders it.

### 775. On the eye that is in the light and sees a dark place.

In darkness, no secondary color <note>meaning a color further away in the distance</note> is of the same clarity as the first, even if they are inherently similar. This is proven by the fourth [proposition] of this [treatise] which says: the surface of a body will be tinted more by the transparent medium interposed between the eye and that body when that interposed medium is of greater thickness. Therefore, it is concluded that the secondary color, placed in the midst of a dark transparency, will have more darkness interposed between itself and the eye than the first color, which is closer to the same eye; and the proportion between the darkness of these colors will be the same as the proportion between the quantities of the dark medium that tints them.

### 776. On the eye that sees things in a bright place.

In illuminated air, no secondary color will be as dark as the same color that is closer. This is proven by the preceding [proposition], because a greater thickness of the air's brightness remains interposed between the eye and the second color than between the eye and the first color; and consequently, the proportion of the variations of such colors will be similar to the proportions of those quantities of air interposed between the eye and the said colors. <note>Leonardo is describing "aerial perspective," where the atmosphere makes distant objects appear lighter or bluer.</note>

### 777. On the shadows and lights of cities.

When the sun is in the east and the eye is positioned above the center of a city, that eye will see the southern part of that city having roofs that are half-shadowed and half-lit, and the same for the northern part; the eastern side will be entirely in shadow, and the western side will be entirely illuminated.

### 778. On the illumination of the lower parts of bodies crowded together, such as men in battle.

The parts of men and horses struggling in battle will be darker the closer they are to the earth that supports them; and this is proven by the walls of wells, which become darker the deeper they go. This arises because the deepest part of the well sees and is seen by a smaller portion of the luminous air than any other part; and the floors of the same color as the...

### 780. Common perspective.

Of things with equal movement, that which is more distant from the eye will appear slower, whether at the same time equal lengths of motion are made at various distances, which are from *a* to *f* and from *g* to *k*, and likewise from *l* to *m*; I say that such a proportion will appear from velocity to velocity and from length of motion to length of motion, as is the distance to distance of the moving thing seen to the eye that sees it. And let *lm* therefore be in triple proportion of distance from the eye *o* compared with the distance *af* from the same *o*; I say that the motion *lm* will appear in velocity and length to be triple to the motion from *a* to *b* <gloss>2</gloss> <note>The text likely means 'a' to 'f' based on the context of the diagram</note> made in the same time and motion. This is proven because at the distance *af* from the eye *o*, it is shown that *lm* has moved only the space *cd*, when *a* has moved to *f*, and thus the space *cd* will be found to fit three times into the space *af*; therefore, that space *af* is triple the space *cd*, and because both one motion and the other are made in the same time, the motion *af* appears three times faster than the motion *cd*. Which is what was to be proven.

### 786. On the painter's deception regarding the size of trees and other bodies in the countryside.

<margin>to 787]</margin>
Judge well, O painter or illuminator <note>A "miniatore" or illuminator specialized in the fine, detailed work of manuscript decoration</note>, how far your painting must be seen from the eye, and imagine that at such a distance an opening is seen—be it a hole or a window—through which the objects placed before it may reach your eye. Truly, you will judge the things seen to be so tiny that not only the limbs, but the whole will seem almost impossible to depict. For example, if the eye were *o* and the hole—measuring a quarter of a braccio <note>A "braccio" (arm) was a common Italian unit of measurement, roughly 23 inches or 58 cm</note>, equal to your painted panel—were *ab*, placed half a braccio from the eye; then you would see through that space all the things that can be seen within the length of a horizon of a hundred miles. They would be in such confused diminution that not only could you not depict any part of them that has a distinct shape, but you could hardly place a brush point so small that it would not be larger than any house located ten miles away.

---

### 787. Why mountains at a great distance appear darker at the summit than at the base.

The air, which acquires degrees of thickness <note>Leonardo uses "grossezza" (thickness/density) to describe the haze or atmospheric moisture that obscures distant objects</note> at every degree of its lowliness and its distance, is the reason why the peaks of mountains that rise higher show more of their natural darkness. This is because they are less hindered by the thickness of the air at the summit than at their base, or in proximity rather than in remoteness. It is proven: *op*, *ds*, *cr*, *ak* are degrees of the air that always become thinner the higher they rise; *af*, *fh*, *hk* are the other transverse degrees where the air acquires thinness the closer it approaches. It follows that the summit of mountain *e* is darker at the top than at the base because, as stated, the air is thicker below than above. Furthermore, mountain *e* is darker than mountain *g* because there is less thickness of air between *ce* than between *dg*. And the summit *g*, being higher than its base, behaves similarly to mountain *e*, becoming darker the higher it rises. At an equal distance, such as *yg*, it would appear darker than summit *e* because it reaches into air that hinders less by being thinner. Thus, it does not follow that the proportion of the darkness of mountains is the same as that of their proximity—which would follow if the mountain peaks were of equal height; but *g*, by rising higher, does not observe this, because it penetrates into thinner air.

<summary>Leonardo explains the optical challenges of painting vast landscapes within small panels and details how atmospheric density causes mountain peaks to appear darker than their bases.</summary>
<keywords>aerial perspective, atmospheric density, landscape painting, optical illusion, mountain peaks, scale and distance, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

### 788. Why mountains appear to have darker summits than bases at a long distance.

The density of the air possesses as many varieties of thinness as there are varieties of height that its parts have from the water and the earth; it is found to be thinner and colder the further it is removed from the said earth. For the first reason, mountain *p* will appear lighter than mountain *o*, because there is more air between the eye *a* and mountain *p* than between the eye *a* and mountain *o*; and thus mountain *q* will be lighter than mountain *p*. However, such lightness will not have the same proportion to the lightness of *p* as the distances have, because *q* is located in thinner air than *p*, and therefore it appears darker than the proportion of the distance requires. <note>Leonardo is observing that while distance usually makes things lighter due to atmospheric haze, the fact that mountain peaks sit in "thinner" (less dense) air at higher altitudes means they lose some of that lightening effect, making them appear darker than expected.</note>

### 789. Why one must not depict mountains as blue in winter as in summer.

Landscapes created in a depiction of winter should not show their mountains as blue as one sees mountains in the summer; and this is proven by the fourth [rule] of this [treatise] which says: among mountains seen at a long distance, that one will appear more blue which is in itself darker. Therefore, since plants are stripped of their leaves, they appear a grayish-brown color <term>berettino: a dull, brownish-gray or ash color common in Renaissance descriptions of undyed wool or winter landscapes</term>; when they have leaves, they are green. And just as green is darker than grayish-brown, so the green will appear more blue than the grayish-brown, according to the fifth [rule] of this [treatise]. The shadows of plants clothed in leaves are as much darker than the shadows of those plants stripped of leaves as the leafy plants are less sparse than those without leaves. And thus we have proven our intent.

The definition of the blue color of the air gives the verdict as to why landscapes are bluer in summer than in winter. <note>Leonardo correctly identifies that the "blue" we see in the distance is a result of light scattering through the atmosphere; because summer foliage is darker and denser than bare winter branches, it provides a darker "backdrop" that makes the atmospheric blue appear more vivid.</note>

### 790. How mountains shaded by clouds participate in the color blue.

Mountains shaded by clouds participate in the color blue when the weather is clear around said cloud; and this is caused because the air illuminated by the sun is of great brightness, and the likeness of such darkness of a mountain shaded by a cloud, passing to the eye through the aforementioned brightness of the air, becomes blue in color, as was proven in the fifth [rule] of the second [book].

# TREATISE ON PAINTING — PART FIVE

## 791. On the air that is seen between mountains.

The air appears more luminous and clear toward the direction of the sun than in the opposite directions.

## 792. On mountains and their division in painting.

I say that the air interposed between the eye and the mountain appears clearer at *p* than at *a*; and this can happen for several reasons, the first of which is that the air interposed between the eye and *p* is a greater total amount than that which is interposed between the eye and *a*, and consequently it is clearer. The second is that the air is thicker <note>meaning denser or more filled with moisture and dust</note> in the valley at *p* than at the mountain at *a*.

## 793. Painting that shows the necessary formation of the Alps, mountains, and hills.

The shapes of the mountains, called the chain of the world, are generated by the courses of rivers born from rain, snow, hail, and ice melted by the solar rays of summer. This melting is the generation of waters gathered from many small streams flowing from various aspects to the larger rivers; they grow in magnitude as they gain momentum, until they assemble at the great ocean sea, always taking from one of the banks and giving to the other, until they seek the full width of their valleys. And not content with that, they consume the roots of the lateral mountains, which, collapsing upon these rivers, close the valleys; and, as if they wished to avenge themselves, they prohibit the course of such a river and convert it into a lake, where the water with very slow motion appears humbled, until the generated blockage of the ruined mountain is again consumed by the course of the aforementioned water.

Therefore, we shall say that the water found in the narrowest and shortest path consumes the place where it passes the least, and conversely consumes more where it is widest and deepest. It follows from this that the highest ridges of the mountains, being for most of the time clothed in snow, and the rains striking them for only a short time, and the rivers not being there—until the few drops of rain left over from the absorption of the arid summit begin to generate the tiniest branches of very slow motion—these have no power to become turbid with any particle of earth moved by them, owing to the old roots of the tiny grasses. For this reason, such ridges of the mountains have more eternity in their surfaces than in their roots <note>the base of the mountain</note>, where the furious courses of the gathered waters, continually active and not content with the carried earth, remove the hills...

## 794. Painting, and how the mountains grow.

By what has been concluded behind this <note>referring to the previous arguments on erosion</note>, it is necessary to concede that the bases of the mountains and hills are continually narrowing. This being so, it cannot be denied that the valleys are widening; and because the width of the river cannot then occupy the full width of its increased valley, <gloss>I</gloss> <note>original: "della cresciuta sua valle"</note> rather, it continually changes its position, leaving its course from that place where it has deposited more material. This material, eroding and removing the gravelly banks until such time as, having carried away all the previously deposited material, it reacquires its ancient bed, from which it does not depart until another similar accident removes it from the aforementioned site; and thus from rain to rain, occurring from time to time, each valley is discharged of material and weight.

## 795. Painting in depicting the qualities and members of mountainous landscapes.

Those grasses and plants will be of a color so much paler as the soil that nourishes them is leaner and more lacking in moisture. The soil is leaner and more lacking above the stones of which the mountains are composed. And the trees will be so much smaller and thinner as they get closer to the summits of the mountains; and the soil is so much leaner as it approaches the aforementioned summits of the mountains; and the soil is so much more abundant in richness as it is closer to the hollows of the valleys. Therefore you, painter, shall show on the summits of the mountains the stones of which they are composed, largely uncovered by soil, and the grasses that grow there minute and lean and largely paled and dried by lack of moisture; and let the sandy and lean earth be seen showing through between the pale grasses, and the minute plants stunted and aged in minimal size with short and thick branching and with few leaves, discovering in large part the rusty and arid roots woven with the layers and fractures of the rusty crags, born from stumps mangled by men and by the winds; and in many parts let the crags be seen rising above the hills of the high mountains clothed in thin and pale rust <note>likely referring to lichen or oxidation</note>; and in some parts show their true colors, uncovered by the striking of the lightning bolts of heaven, whose course, not without vengeance upon such crags, is often impeded. And the further you descend to the roots of the mountains, the plants will be more vigorous and thick with branches and leaves, and their greenery of as many varieties as there are species of plants of which such forests are composed; of which the branchings have different orders, and different thicknesses of branches and leaves, and different shapes and heights, and some with narrow branchings, like the cypress, and...

### 796. On mountains.

The summits of hills and mountains are much more discernible at various distances than anything else upon them. And this happens because in every degree of distance from the eye toward the east <note>Leonardo often uses "the east" or "the horizon" to discuss the source of light and atmospheric depth</note>, one acquires degrees of loss and clarity of air, or rather whiteness; and from $f$ to $b$ it is twice as clear as from $f$ to $a$.

### 797. On mountains.

The summits of mountains and hills will appear darker because a greater quantity of trees meet one another, and their flat interval—which is lighter—is not seen, as is seen on the slopes; and it is that same reason that darkens the countryside in the middle of its heights.

### 798. Precept.

Lights and shadows are as varied as the variety of the sites where they are found. When the shadowy part of bodies is increased by a dark object, that shadow will become so much darker than before, as much as such an increase is less clear than the air. The percussion <note>The "percussion" refers to the point where a shadow falls upon a surface</note> of the derivative shadow <term>derivative shadow: the shadow cast by an object onto another surface, as opposed to the "primitive" shadow on the object itself</term> will never be of its primitive origin, if the primitive light is not of a similar shape to the body that makes the shadows.

### 799. Of the luminous body that turns around without changing its site and receives the same light from different sides and varies infinitely.

The shadows which, in company with the lights, clothe an irregular body will be of as many various darknesses and as many shapes as there are varieties made by that body in the...

## 802. Those boundaries of shadows will be more imperceptible which arise from a greater quantity of light.

The reflections, or rather the shadows that are enclosed between the incident light <note>Light falling directly onto a surface</note> and the reflected light, will be of greater darkness in the same location when they are of greater quantity. This happens because, when they are of greater quantity, according to the seventh [proposition] of the ninth [book], they have the two lights—that is, the reflected and the incident—more remote, whereby the shadow is less obstructed.

## 803. Which shadow is darker.

That part of the shadow will be darker which is closer to its origin.

## 804. Of light.

That light will be of greater quantity which is generated upon a body of lesser curvature, provided such light is produced by the same cause.

Those bodies that are illuminated by the air without the sun generate shadows without perceptible boundaries. Those bodies that are illuminated by the air with the sun make shadows with boundaries of excessive perceptibility. <note>original: "soperchia sensibilità di termini." The Roman edition of 1817 reads: "make shadows with excessive perceptibility of boundaries."</note>

## 805. Precept.

Bodies illuminated by different qualities of colored lights do not have the illuminated parts of their surfaces matching the colors of their shaded parts.

It is very rare that the colors of the surfaces of opaque bodies have the proper colors of shadows corresponding to the colors of their illuminated parts.

What is proposed arises because the objects that cast the shadow upon such bodies are not of the natural color of those bodies, nor of the same natural color as the source illuminating that body.

## 806. Precept.

The true color of the shadows and lights of any body is achieved when the walls of the room where such a body is located are of the same color as the body enclosed within them.

### 807. Of the boundaries of bodies by means of the backgrounds.

The boundaries <note>original: "termini" — the edges or outlines where an object meets its background</note> of bodies seen against backgrounds <note>original: "campi" — the fields or areas of color behind a subject</note> always appear varied with more darkness or lightness than the rest of their surface. This occurs because of the seventh [proposition] of this [treatise], which proves that the boundaries of white things appear lighter the more they border on darker boundaries, and the boundaries of shaded things appear darker the more they border on a whiter thing. The primary example is shown in a white object seen partly in the sun: the illuminated part appears whiter in comparison to the shadow, and the shadow darker in comparison to the light; and this is clearly seen on the faces of walls and in other flat bodies.

### 808. Precept of shadows.

The shadows of distant bodies ought to be made under the same light; for if you were to make your mixture <note>original: "mistione" — the blending of pigments</note> of colors in the sun to imitate things seen in the sun, and then you made the mixture of the shadows of bodies in the shade to imitate things that are not seen in the sun, and you then placed everything in the shade, you would not achieve a true likeness. This is because you must consider that a single quality of color placed in the shade will be the true shadow of that which is placed in the sun; and if you then applied sunlight to the shaded part as you did to the illuminated part, you would see that the imitated shadow and light were made of the very same color.

### 809. Of the imitation of colors at any distance.

When you wish to counterfeit a color, take care that, while staying in a shaded spot, you do not try to imitate a luminous spot, because you would deceive yourself with such an imitation. What you must do in such a case, if you wish to work with the certainty required by mathematical demonstrations, is to compare the imitating color with the imitated color under the very same light for all the colors you must replicate, and ensure that your color is adjacent <note>original: "conterminale" — sharing a boundary or being in the same line of sight</note> to the visual line of the natural color.

Let us say you wish to imitate a mountain in the part seen by the sun. Place your colors in the sun, and according to that view, make your mixture of imitable colors, and compare them under the same solar light, holding your color up against the color being imitated; as if to say: I have the sun at noon, and I am portraying the mountain at

# PART SIX.

## CONCERNING TREES AND VEGETATION.

812. Discourse on the qualities of flowers in the branching of plants.

**Regarding the flowers** that grow upon the branching of plants <note>original: "erbe" - here referring to herbaceous plants or flora in general</note>, some bloom first at the highest points of those branches, while others open their first flower at the lowest base of their stem.

813. Concerning the branching of plants.

First: every branch of any plant that is not overcome by its own weight curves upward, lifting its tip toward the sky. Second: the small shoots <term>ramiculi: small or secondary branches</term> of tree branches that grow from underneath are larger than those that grow from above. Third: all small shoots born toward the center of the tree are consumed in a short time due to excessive shade. Fourth: those branchings of plants will be more vigorous and favored which are closer to the upper extremities of said plants, because of the air and the sun. Fifth: the angles of the divisions of the branchings of trees are equal among themselves. Sixth: but those angles become more obtuse <note>wider than 90 degrees</note> as the branches on their sides grow older. Seventh: the side of that angle becomes more oblique <note>slanted</note> when it is made of a thinner branch. Eighth: every bifurcation of branches joined together restores the thickness of the branch with which it connects: as if to say *a* and *b* joined together make *e*; *c* and *d* joined together <note>The text ends mid-sentence, referring to the accompanying diagram of branching proportions</note>

[The foliage] appears at a long distance, but up close one then sees the highlights <note>original: "lustri"</note> upon each leaf; and in the lower part of such branching, the leaves hang obliquely below their point of origin, casting shadows one upon the other onto those below. ---

### 817. On the proportion that the branches of plants have between one another.

The thickness of the branches of any plant born in the same year maintains the same proportion to their primary stem as do the preceding and succeeding branches of all other past and future years. That is, every year the branches that each plant has acquired, when they have finished growing—their thicknesses being calculated and joined together—are equal to the branch born the previous year which produced them. This continues forward and will be found so in future times; for example, the branches *ad* and *bd*, the last of the plant, being joined together, will be equal to the branch *dc* which produced them.

---

### 818. On the branching of trees.

The branches of trees, when burdened with fruit and leaves, change the position they held during the winter. The thickness of the branches that bifurcate <note>split into two</note> never varies from branch to branch, except almost imperceptibly; and if one were to put back the small branchlets that grow between the main branches, it would restore the thickness to be exactly equal throughout.

---

### 819. The bark of a young tree does not crack.

The branches of plants are situated in two ways: either they are opposite one another, or they are not. If they are not opposite, the central stem will bend now toward one branch, now toward the other; and if they are opposite, the central tree <insert>stem</insert> will be straight.

# TREATISE ON PAINTING — PART SIX

The southern part of plants shows greater youth and vigor than the northern parts. The oldest part of the bark of the tree is always that which cracks first. That part of the tree will have rougher and thicker bark which is of greater age. The circles of the branches of sawn trees <note>tree rings</note> show the number of their years, and which were more humid or drier, according to their greater or lesser thickness. And so they show the directions of the world toward which they were turned; because they are thicker to the north than to the south; and thus the center of the tree for this reason is closer to its southern bark than to the northern bark; and although this is of no use to painting, nevertheless I will write it down to leave behind fewer things about trees that are possible for my knowledge. Those tips of the trees will make greater growth which are closer to the master branch of their tree. The leaves that are born first, and that fall latest, are those that are born in the master tips of the trees. That tree which grows older admits fewer branches. That branch which extends in more continuous thickness and more straightly is the one which generates fewer <term>ramiculi</term> <note>original: "ramiculi"; small secondary branches or twigs</note> around itself.

---

### 821. On the ramifications of plants.

Plants that spread out extensively have the angles of the partitions that separate their ramifications more obtuse the lower their birth is—that is, the closer to the thickest and oldest part of the tree. Therefore, in the younger part of the tree, the angles of its ramifications are more acute.

---

### 822. On the birth of leaves upon the branches.

The thickness of any branch never diminishes in the space from leaf to leaf, except by as much as the thickness of the <term>eye</term> <note>original: "occhio"; a botanical bud</note> which is upon that leaf, which thickness is missing from the branch that follows until the next leaf. Nature has placed the leaves of the last branches of many plants so that the sixth leaf is always above the first, and so it follows successively, if the rule is not impeded; and this she has done for two benefits to these plants: the first is because, as the branch and the fruit are born in the following year from the <term>twin vein</term> <note>original: "gemella vena"; likely referring to the axillary bud or vascular connection</note> of the eye which is above in contact with the attachment of the leaf, the water that wets such a branch can descend to nourish that twin by the drop stopping in the concavity of the birth of that leaf; and the second benefit is that, when such branches are born the following year, one does not cover the other, because the five branches are born facing five directions, and the sixth is born above the first, quite far removed.

### 823. On the ramifications of plants with their leaves.

The ramifications of plants, some, like the elm, are wide and thin like an open hand seen in perspective <note>original: "in iscorto"; foreshortened</note>, and these show themselves in their total masses; from below they are seen from their upper side; and those that are higher are seen from below, and those in the middle partly from below and partly from above; and the upper part is at the very end of said ramification: and this middle part is more foreshortened than any other of those that are turned with their tips toward you, and of those middle parts of the height of the plant, the longest will be toward the ends of those trees, and these ramifications act like the leaves of the wild fern that grows along the banks of rivers. Other ramifications are round, like those of trees that put forth <term>ramiculi</term> <note>small twigs or secondary branches</note> and leaves such that the sixth is above the first; and others are sparse and transparent, like the willow and the like. The ends of the ramifications of plants, if they are not overcome by the weight of the fruit, turn toward the sky as much as possible. The upper surfaces of their leaves stay turned toward the sky to receive the nourishment of the dew that falls at night. The sun gives spirit and life to plants; and the earth with its moisture nourishes them. Regarding this case, I once tried leaving only a tiny root on a gourd, and that I kept nourished with water; and such a gourd brought to perfection all the fruits it could generate, which were about sixty gourds of the wide variety. And I applied my mind diligently to such a life, and I recognized that the dew of the night was that which, with its moisture, penetrated abundantly through the attachment of its large leaves for the nourishment of that plant with its offspring.

As a rule, the leaves born on the last branch of the year will be in contrary motion on the two sibling branches—that is, as the birth of the leaves turns around their branch, in such a way that the sixth leaf above is born above the sixth below, the motion of their turning is such that if one turns toward its companion to the right, the other turns to the left. The leaf is the teat or breast of the branch or fruit that is born in the coming year.

### 824. On the birth of branches in plants.

The birth of the ramifications of plants upon their principal branches is the same as the birth of the leaves, which leaves have four ways of proceeding one higher than the other. The first, most universal, is that the sixth above is always born above the sixth below; the second is that the two-thirds above are over the two-thirds below, and the third way is that the third above is over the third below. <note>Leonardo is describing phyllotaxis, the mathematical arrangement of leaves around a stem.</note>

He also recounts a botanical experiment with a gourd to prove that leaves absorb nighttime dew for nourishment.</summary>

### **829. Concerning the branching that grows in one year from the ends of cut branches.**

The quantity of the small shoot that grows back upon a cut branch, compared with the quantity of small shoots that the same cut branch should have produced in that same year, is proportional to the quantity of the <term>cambium</term><note>original: "camicia" (shirt); Leonardo uses this to describe the thin layer of living tissue between the bark and the wood</note> that lies between the bark and the wood—that is, its circumferential line made upon the cut of the branch compared with the length of the diameter of such a small shoot. This happens because the nourishment that passes through such a diameter, which used to pass through there to rise up and nourish the branches of that same year, finding them gone, stops to nourish that branch which is born at the edge of the bark and cambium. 

But this rule seems to suffer an exception; for if all the branches produced that year from all the nourishment coming with it were to remake such a quantity of branches that, being recomposed and united together, their thicknesses equaled the thickness of the cut branch; then, if the entire edge of the bark and cambium of the cut plant were to recompose in the whole lips of its cut a united circle of a continuous branch that embraced the whole circumference of the wood, it would remake in that same year as much thickness of wood as the thickness of the branch it embraces. This seems impossible, even if the air, rain, and dew assisted it; since the circumference of all the final branchings joined together, which the plant would have generated that year had it not been cut, is much greater than the circumference extended across the entire edge of the cut bark; and consequently, it draws more nourishment, because the life of the plant resides in such bark and cambium. But the conclusion of this will not be treated in this place, because it is reserved for elsewhere, and is not necessary for painting.

### **830. On the proportion of branches in relation to the proportion of their nourishment.**

The proportion that all the branchings of the same year have in their combined thicknesses compared to the thickness of their trunk, is the same as the proportion of the nourishment of that trunk to the nourishment of the aforesaid branches; that is, the thing nourished is equal to its nourishment. For if a branch of a plant is cut, and one of its own small shoots is grafted or inserted upon it, that small shoot will in time become much thicker than the branch that nourishes it; and this is because the nourishment or <term>vital spirits</term><note>In Renaissance science, "spiriti vitali" were believed to be the subtle fluids or forces that carried life and growth through an organism.</note> rush to the injured place. In <term>shield budding</term><note>original: "inserire a scudo"; a grafting technique where a bud is inserted into a T-shaped slit in the bark.</note>, many eyes <note>buds</note> of plants placed in a circle on a cut trunk will produce in the same year a greater quantity of thickness than the face of that cut trunk.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the botanical mechanics of how trees heal and regrow after being pruned, noting that nutrients (vital spirits) concentrate at the site of an injury to produce rapid growth. He concludes that while these mathematical proportions are vital for science, they are not strictly necessary for the art of painting.</summary>
<keywords>botany, tree growth, grafting, cambium, nourishment, vital spirits, proportions, Leonardo da Vinci, plant physiology</keywords>

<header>a 834] TREATISE ON PAINTING — PART SIX</header>
<page-num>267</page-num>

### 831. Concerning the growth of trees and in which direction they grow most.

The branching of the larger limbs does not grow toward the center of their parent plant; and this occurs because every branch naturally seeks the air and flees the shade. Furthermore, shadows are more powerful on the lower part of the branches that face the earth than on the part that turns toward the sky; on this upper side, the flow of rainwater and the dew that multiplies at night always settles, keeping this lower part more moist than the upper. For this reason, the branches have more abundant nourishment in that area, and consequently, they grow more there.

### 832. Which branches of the trees are those that grow most in a year.

The largest ramifications of the primary limbs are always those born from the side of the branch facing the earth, while the smaller ones are born from the side above that primary limb. This greater size of the lower branch occurs because the moisture of the limb—when not struck by the heat of the sun—always falls to the underside of its branch; therefore, the moisture provides more nourishment where it is in greater abundance. Because of this, a branch always has thicker bark on the bottom than on the top. This is the primary reason why the <term>shootlets</term><note>original: "ramiculi"; small or secondary shoots</note> of that branch are much larger below than above. Consequently, trees put out many branches downwards, which is the reason why the branch succeeding it from below does not put out large shootlets against the branch situated above it. In this way, plants do not become entangled, nor do they take the air from one another despite the proximity of so many ramifications, because they give place to one another; and if that branch, as stated, grows significantly downwards, the one growing toward it grows very little upwards.

### 833. Concerning the bark of trees.

The increase in the thickness of plants is caused by the <term>sap</term><note>original: "sugo" (juice/sap)</note>, which is generated in the month of April between the <term>cambium</term><note>original: "camicia" (shirt); the living layer under the bark</note> and the wood of that tree. At that time, this cambium is converted into bark, and the bark acquires new cracks within the depths of the existing cracks.

### 834. Concerning the northern side of the trunks of trees.

The northern side of old trees always clothes the bark of its <term>trunk</term><note>original: "pedale"; the base or main stem of the tree</note> with a greenish mossiness <note>original: "piumosità" (plumage/fuzziness); Leonardo refers to the growth of moss or lichen which thrives in the shade of the north side</note>.

<summary>Leonardo explains how gravity and moisture cause branches to grow thicker on their undersides and how trees naturally organize their growth to avoid overcrowding. He also identifies the cambium layer as the source of new bark and notes that moss grows primarily on the northern side of trunks.</summary>

<keywords>botany, tree growth, sap, cambium, phototropism, bark, moss, moisture, Leonardo da Vinci</keywords>

### 835. Concerning the bark of plants.

The bark of plants always has larger cracks on the side facing south than on the northern side. <note>Leonardo observed that the sun's heat causes the bark to expand and dry more rapidly on the southern side, leading to deeper fissures.</note>

### 836. Concerning the diversity found in the branching of trees.

There are three ways in which trees branch. One way is to put out branches in two opposite directions—one toward the east and the other toward the west—and they are not directly across from one another, but placed in the middle of the opposite space. <note>This describes an alternating arrangement where branches do not sprout from the same height on the trunk.</note> The second way puts them out two by two, directly across from one another; but if two are facing east and west, the next two will face south and north. The third way always has the sixth branch positioned directly above the first in succession. <note>Leonardo is describing phyllotaxis, the mathematical arrangement of leaves and branches; here he identifies a spiral pattern where the cycle repeats every six branches.</note>

### 837. Concerning the branching of plants that put out branches directly across from one another.

All plants that put out branches in tiers, one directly across from the other with equal thickness, will always be straight like the fir tree *ab*. This straightness arises because the opposite parts, being equal in thickness, draw an equal amount of <term>humor</term><note>original: "umore"; the fluid or sap within a plant believed to carry nutrients</note>—or I should say nourishment—and create branches of equal weight. From this it follows that equal causes produce equal effects, and such equality preserves the equal straightness of that plant.

### 838. Concerning the accidents that bend the aforementioned plants.

But when the aforementioned plants put out branches that are unequal in thickness, then such a plant will not maintain its straightness, but will bend in the direction opposite to the thicker branch. This happens because necessity forces such a plant to exist in a state of balance between equal weights; without this, <insert>if it were not so</insert><margin>In the codex: "if not that."</margin> it would soon collapse from a slight wind blowing along the line where the thicker branch grows. <note>Leonardo applies the laws of mechanics to biology, arguing that a tree must grow "crooked" to counterbalance the weight of its own heavy limbs and remain upright.</note>

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the physical symmetry of trees, explaining how the distribution of sap and the weight of branches dictate whether a trunk grows straight or curved. He also identifies specific mathematical patterns in how branches sprout around a stem.</summary>
<keywords>bark, branching patterns, phyllotaxis, fir tree, humor, botanical balance, plant physiology</keywords>

# 839. Concerning the optical effects of the branching of plants.

The four <term>accidents</term><note>original: "accidenti"; in Renaissance philosophy, these are non-essential qualities or appearances, such as how light hits a surface</note> of the branching of plants are these: luster, light, transparency, and shadow. If the eye looks upon such branching from above, the illuminated part will appear greater in quantity than the shadowed part. This happens because the illuminated portion is larger than the shadowed one, since it contains within it the light, the luster, and the transparency. For the moment, I shall set aside transparency and describe the demonstration of the illuminated part. This is categorized as the fourth part of the qualities of colors that vary on the surfaces of bodies—namely, the "middle quality," which means it is not the primary light but a medium one. Then follows the other middle fourth part, which means it is not the primary shadow, but a medium one. This illuminated middle quality is positioned between the luster and the shadowed middle quality; this shadowed middle quality is, in turn, positioned between the illuminated middle quality and the primary shadows. The third part, which is transparency, occurs only in transparent things and not in opaque bodies. But speaking now of the leaves of trees, it is necessary to describe this second accident, which is of great importance for the depiction of plants, although before me it has not been used, nor has there been any knowledge of it. This is situated as will be stated below.

# 840. Concerning the transparency of leaves.

When the light is in the east and the eye views the plant from below looking toward the north, it will see the eastern part of the tree as largely transparent, except for those leaves that are blocked by the shadow of other leaves. The western part of the tree will be dark, because it receives upon itself the shadow of the branching—that is, the part that is turned toward the east.

# 841. Concerning the center of trees within their thickness.

The center of plants, at the division of their branches, will never be in the middle of the thickness of those branches. This happens because more <term>humor</term><note>original: "umore"; sap or vital fluid</note> exists on the inner side of the tree's branching than on the outside. For example, at *c*, which is the junction of branches *ac* and *ce*, the wood grows more from the center of the branches *bd* <note>toward the interior junction</note> than from those centers *bd* toward the outer extremities *ae*.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes the optical properties of foliage—luster, light, transparency, and shadow—and observes that branches grow thicker on their inner sides due to a higher concentration of sap.</summary>

### 842. Which plant grows in the forests with the most consistent thickness and to the greatest height.

That plant will grow with the most consistent and greatest length which is born in the lowest and narrowest valley, and in the thickest forest, and furthest from the edges of said forest. <note>Leonardo observes that trees in dense, sheltered areas must grow straight and tall to reach the sunlight, whereas those on the edges are more exposed to wind and varied light.</note>

### 843. Which plant is of the most irregular thickness, of lesser height, and harder.

That plant will be more irregular in its thickness which is born in a higher location, in a thinner forest, and further from the center of it.

### 844. Concerning plants and sawn timber which will never warp on their own.

When you wish for a cut tree not to warp from its straightness, saw it in half along the direction of its length, and turn the divided parts opposite to one another—that is, take the part that was at the foot and place it at the head, and turn the head part to the foot—and then rejoin them together; such a connection never warps. <note>This is an early description of "book-matching" or laminating wood to counteract the natural internal stresses that cause timber to bend as it seasons.</note>

### 845. Concerning the rods that best maintain their straightness.

The rod that is made from that part of the tree which faces most toward the <term>north</term><note>original: "tramontana"; the north wind or the northern direction</note> will be the one that warps less than the others and best maintains its natural straightness. And this is because in that part the sun sees little, and little moves the <term>humor</term><note>original: "umore"; the sap or internal moisture of the plant</note> of the tree; this does not happen to the southern part, because it is seen by the sun all day, which moves the humor in that part of the plant from its eastern side to the western side along with its course.

### 846. Concerning the cracks in wood when it dries.

Of the cracks that wood makes during its drying, that plant will make them the straightest which is furthest from the edges of its forest; and those will be more twisted which were born closer to the edges of said forest.

### 847. Concerning wood that does not split while drying.

When you wish for wood not to make any cracks while drying, boil it for a long time in common water, or keep it for a long time at the bottom of a river, until it consumes its natural vigor. <note>Leonardo suggests that leaching out the sap (the "natural vigor") prevents the uneven shrinking that causes splitting.</note>

<summary>Leonardo analyzes how a tree's environment—such as its position in a forest or its exposure to the sun—affects the quality of its timber, and provides practical engineering advice for preventing wood from warping or cracking.</summary>

# TREATISE ON PAINTING — PART SIX

### 854. On the variety of shadows on trees under the same light, in the same landscape, under a specific light source.

When the sun is in the east, the trees to your east have large shadows, those to the south are half-shaded, and those to the west are fully illuminated. However, these three aspects are not sufficient, because it is more accurate to say that the entire eastern tree will be in shadow; the tree to the southeast <note>original: "scirocco," the Mediterranean wind from the southeast</note> will be three-quarters in shadow; the shadow of the southern tree occupies half of the tree; one-quarter of the tree to the southwest <note>original: "libeccio," the wind from the southwest</note> will be in shadow; and the western tree shows no shadow at all.

### 855. On the lights of the branching of trees.

Following what was stated above, regarding the clusters of illuminated branches: even though each leaf is separated from the others by a shaded space, it happens that at a distance the shaded part, being minute, is lost. This occurs because, as has been said, it is overtaken and overwhelmed by the luminous part, which does not diminish across distance as much as the shaded part does. Consequently, the total mass of leaves on a single branch appears at a certain distance to be almost of a single color. Even if a person with good eyesight can discern something of the shadows in those shaded intervals between the leaves, they do not appear with their proper darkness. This arises from two causes: first, the thickness of the air <note>A reference to "aerial perspective," where the atmosphere softens colors and contrasts over distance</note> that is interposed between the eye and the shaded object; second, because at such a great distance, the small shapes mix somewhat at their edges and blur their definition. Since the illuminated part remains more noticeable than the shaded part, the shadows appear to have little darkness.

### 856. On the shape that plants take where they join with their roots.

The trunks <term>pedali: the lower part of the trunk near the ground</term> of plants do not maintain a perfectly round thickness as they approach the origin of the branches or their roots. This happens because these upper and lower branchings are the members through which the plants are nourished; that is, in the summer they are nourished from above by dew and rain through the leaves, and in the winter from below through the contact the earth has with their roots.

### 857. On shadows and lights and their sizes on leaves.

The branchings of plants are seen from below, or from above, or from the middle. If they are seen from below, then, if the light is universal <note>meaning diffused light, such as an overcast sky, rather than direct sunlight</note>, the larger part is...

...more shadowed than illuminated. And if they are seen from above, the illuminated part will be greater than the shadowed part. And if they are seen from the middle, the illuminated part will be equal to that of the shadows.

### 858. On the illumination of plants.

From the position of the eye, which sees that part of the plants illuminated by the light source, one plant will never be seen illuminated in the same way as another.
This is proven: let the eye be *c*, which sees the two plants *b* and *d*, which are illuminated by the sun *a*; I say that such an eye *c* will not see the lights in the same proportion to their shadow in one tree as in the other, because the tree that is closer to the sun will appear so much more shadowed than the one that is more remote, as the one tree is closer to the convergence of the solar rays coming to the eye than the other. You see that of tree *d*, nothing is seen by eye *c* but the shadow, and from the same eye *c*, tree *b* is seen half-illuminated and half-shadowed.

### 859. A reminder for the painter regarding plants.

Remember, O painter, that the darkness of shadows in the same species of plants varies as much as the rarity or density of their branching varies.

### 860. On the universal light illuminating plants.

That part of the plant will appear clothed in shadows of lesser darkness which is more remote from the earth. This is proven: let *np* be the plant, and *nbc* be the illuminated hemisphere <note>The "illuminated hemisphere" refers to the open sky providing ambient light from all directions</note>; the lower part of the tree sees the earth *pc*—that is, part *o*—and sees a little of the hemisphere at *cd*; but the highest part in the concavity *a* is seen by a greater sum of the hemisphere, namely *bc*; and for this reason, because it does not see the darkness of the earth, it remains more illuminated. But if the tree is thick with leaves, such as the laurel, the fir, and the boxwood, then it varies; because, even though *a* does not see the earth, it sees the darkness of the leaves divided by many shadows, which darkness reflects upwards onto the undersides of the leaves placed above; and such trees have shadows that are darker the closer they are to the center of the tree.

<summary>Leonardo explains how the viewer's perspective and the ambient light from the sky (the "hemisphere") versus the dark ground determine the shading of trees, noting that denser foliage creates darker internal shadows.</summary>

### 875. Concerning the luminous parts of the greenery of plants.

The luminous parts of the greenery of plants, in the proximity they have to the eye, appear to that eye to be brighter than those of remote plants, and their shaded parts appear darker than those of said remote plants. Remote plants show their luminous parts darker than those of nearby plants, and their shaded parts appear brighter than the shaded parts of those nearby plants; and this arises because the convergence of the <term>species</term> <note>Leonardo uses "species" (specie) to refer to the visual images or "simulacra" that travel from an object to the eye</note> of these shaded and luminous plants blur and mix together due to the great distances they have from the eye that sees them.

### 876. Concerning plants that are between the eye and the light.

Of the plants that are between the eye and the light, the front part will be bright, which brightness will be a mixture of branches of transparent leaves seen from the reverse, along with lustrous leaves seen from the front; and their background below and behind will be of dark greenery, being shaded by the front part of said plant; and this happens in plants higher than the eye.

### 877. Concerning the accidental color of trees.

The <term>accidental colors</term> <note>In Renaissance art theory, "accidental" colors are those caused by external factors like light and shadow, as opposed to the "natural" or inherent color of the object</note> of the foliage of trees are four: namely **shadow**, **light**, **luster**, and **transparency**.

### 878. Concerning the demonstration of accidents.

From the accidental parts of the leaves of plants at a long distance, a mixture will be made, which will partake most of that "accident" which is of the greatest shape.

### 879. Which boundaries are shown by remote plants against the air that forms their background.

The boundaries that the branches of trees have against the illuminated air, the more remote they are, the more they take on a shape tending toward the spherical; and the closer they are, the less they demonstrate such a
