Every shaded body, of whatever shape it may be, appears to be spherical at a long distance. This occurs because, if it is a square body, its angles are lost at a very short distance, and a little further on, the smaller remaining sides are lost <margin>In the manuscript: "a little more is lost more of sides" <note>original: "poco più si perde più di lati"</note></margin>; and so, before the whole is lost, the parts are lost because they are smaller than the whole. Just as a man in such a view first loses his legs, arms, and head before his torso; then he loses the extremes of length before those of width, and when they are made equal, it would be a square if the angles remained; but since they do not remain, it is round.

### 880. Concerning the shadows of plants.

The shadows of plants placed in landscapes do not appear to clothe themselves in the same position on the right-hand plants as on the left-hand ones, especially when the sun is to the right or to the left. This is proven by the fourth [rule] which says: opaque bodies placed between the light and the eye appear entirely shaded; and by the fifth: the eye placed between the opaque body and the light sees the opaque body entirely illuminated; and by the sixth: the eye and the opaque body placed between the darkness and the light will be seen half shaded and half luminous.

### 881. Concerning the shadows and transparencies of leaves.

Because the leaves of plants are transparent, they do not cast total darkness upon the leaves they shade, but cast shadows of slight obscurity that acquire a beauty of green; and the third leaves placed beneath the first take on a double obscurity compared to the obscurity of the second leaf, because two leaves shade it; and thus the third and then the fourth, they always go on multiplying in obscurity, and so they would go on to infinity. And therefore you, painter, when you make the clusters of large leafy branches, make them more illuminated than the part toward the center of the tree; and the clusters of branches closer to the light even more illuminated, and the clusters of those clusters more still, and the final leaves most of all, and especially the outermost parts of the leaves turned toward the light. All the grasses and leaves of the tree placed between the eye and the sun are seen through transparency aided by the light of the sun; this transparency is at its highest degree of beauty of green, and it has more power from the solar rays that illuminate it from the opposite side than from its natural color.

### 882. Concerning the shadows of transparent leaves.

The shadows found in transparent leaves, when viewed from the underside, are the very same shadows that exist on the front side of those leaves; these show through the underside along with the luminous part, except for <gloss>I</gloss> the luster <note>term: "lustro" (luster) refers to the specular reflection or the bright "glint" on a shiny surface</note> which can never show through. When one mass of greenery is behind another, the lusters of the leaves and their transparencies appear with greater intensity than those that border the brightness of the air. And if the sun illuminates leaves that are positioned between it and the eye, without the eye seeing the sun directly, then the lusters of the leaves and their transparencies are excessive. It is very useful to create some low-lying branches that are dark and stand out against illuminated greenery that is somewhat distant from the first.

Regarding dark greenery viewed from below, that part is darkest which is closest to the eye—that is, which is furthest from the luminous air.

### 883. On never feigning transparent leaves in the sun.

Never depict leaves as transparent in the sun because they are confusing; this happens because upon the transparency of one leaf, the shadow of another leaf above it will be imprinted. This shadow has sharp edges and a definite darkness, and sometimes it covers a half or a third of the leaf that is being shaded; thus, such branching is confused, and its imitation should be avoided. The upper small shoots of the lateral branches of plants draw closer to their master branch than those below them do. That leaf is less transparent which receives the light at more unequal angles. The lowest branches of plants that produce large leaves and heavy fruits, such as walnuts, figs, and the like, always direct themselves toward the earth.

### 884. Concerning the shadow of the leaf.

Sometimes a leaf has three qualities: namely, shadow, luster, and transparency. For example, if the light were at *n* relative to the leaf *s*, and the eye at *m*, it will see *a* illuminated, *b* shaded, and *c* transparent. A leaf with a concave surface viewed from the underside looking up will sometimes show itself half-shadowed and half-transparent; for example: let *po* be the leaf, the light *m*, and the eye *n*, which will see *o* in shadow because the light does not strike it at equal angles, neither from the front nor the back, and *p* will be the transparent light on its underside.

### 889. On the shadows of trees.

When the sun is in the east, the trees to the west of the eye will appear with very little relief <note>Relief refers to the three-dimensional quality or "pop" of an object</note> and will be almost imperceptible if the air interposed between the eye and those plants is very misty; according to the seventh [rule] of this [treatise], they are deprived of shadow. Although shadow exists in every division of the branches, it happens that the images <note>original: "similitudini," referring to the visual species or rays reaching the eye</note> of shadow and light reaching the eye are confused and mixed together, and because of their small scale, they cannot be discerned. The principal lights are in the middle of the plants, and the shadows are toward the edges; their separations are divided by the shadows of the intervals between these plants when the woods are thick with trees, whereas in sparse woods the boundaries are hardly seen.

### 890. On eastern trees.

When the sun is in the east, trees viewed toward that eastern direction will have light surrounding their shadows, except toward the ground—unless the tree had been pruned the year before <note>Pruning would thin the branches, altering how light passes through to the ground</note>. The southern and northern trees will be half in shadow and half in light, being more or less shaded or luminous depending on whether they are positioned more toward the east or the west.

The eye, whether positioned high or low, varies the shadows and lights in trees; for the high eye sees the trees with few shadows, and the low eye sees them with many shadows.

The greens of plants are as varied as their species are varied.

When the sun is in the east, the trees there are dark toward the center, and their extremities are luminous.

### 891. On the shadows of eastern plants.

The shadows of eastern plants occupy a large part of the plant, and they are darker in proportion to how thick the trees are with leaves.

### 892. On southern plants.

When the sun is in the east, the southern and northern plants have almost as much light as shadow; however, they possess a greater total of light the more they are toward the west, and a greater total of shadow the more they are toward the east.

<summary>Leonardo analyzes how the sun's eastern position affects the visual relief and shading of trees located in different cardinal directions relative to the observer. He notes that atmospheric mist and the observer's viewing height significantly alter the perception of light and shadow within foliage.</summary>

### 893. On meadows.

When the sun is in the east, the greens of the meadows and other small plants are of a most beautiful green because they are transparent to the sun <note>Leonardo is describing the "backlighting" effect where light passes through thin leaves, making them appear vibrant</note>; this does not happen in western meadows. The southern and northern grasses are of a mediocre beauty in their greenery.

### 894. On the grasses of the meadows.

Of the grasses that catch the shadow of the plants growing among them, those that are on this side of the shadow have their stalks <term>festuche: the stems or blades of grass</term> illuminated against a shadowy field, and the grasses that are shaded have their stalks dark against a light field—that is, against the field that lies beyond the shadow.

### 895. On the shadow of greenery.

The shadows of greenery always participate in blue <note>original: "azzurro"</note>, as does every shadow of every other thing; and the shadow takes on more of this blue the further it is from the eye, and less as it is closer. <note>This is a key observation of "atmospheric perspective," where the air between the object and the viewer adds a blue tint to distant shadows.</note>

### 896. On landscapes in painting.

The trees and the mountains of landscapes <term>paesi: literally "countries," but used here to mean landscape paintings</term> made in painting must show their shadows on that side from which the light comes, and they must show the illuminated parts on that side from which the shadows come; and let them show the light and the shadows in those things that the eye sees where it sees the light and the shadows; this is proven by the figure in the margin.

The illuminated part of the branches of trees at a great distance confuses the shadowy parts that are found between the illuminated particles of those branches. ### 898. Which part of the branch of the plant will be darkest.

That part of the branch of the plant will be darkest which is most remote from its extremities, provided the tree has a uniform distribution of branching. <note>Leonardo observes that the interior of a tree is darker because the density of outer leaves blocks the light from reaching the center.</note>

### 899. On the view of trees.

Among the plants that are on the banks of roads, you shall make their solar shadows entirely discontinuous, in the likeness of the positions of the foliage from which they derive.

### 900. On landscapes.

Landscapes <term>paesi: landscape paintings or vistas</term> are light at the beginning <note>meaning in the foreground or near distance</note>, because you see between the tops of the trees and meadows and other spaces and intervals of the plants. But when you begin to lose those intervals due to distance, you see only the branching of the trees, which—even though they are of the same color as the meadows—take on more shadow toward the center of the tree than the meadow does, because of their thickness and the diminution <insert>of light</insert>; hence, because of this, such darkness occurs, which then itself lightens through distance and is converted into the color of the horizon.

### 901. Painting of the fog that covers landscapes.

The fogs that mix through the air, the more they descend, the more they thicken, so that the solar rays shine more within them when the fog is interposed between the sun and the eye; but if the eye is placed between the sun and the fog, that fog appears dark. This darkness is more powerful the lower the fog is, as has been proven; and both types of fog remain dark like a cloud when that cloud is interposed between the sun and the fog. 

But the fog placed between the sun and the eye, removed by some space from the eye, participates greatly in the splendor of the sun, and all the more so the closer it is to the solar body; and the buildings of cities will show themselves in such a case to be darker the more they are placed in brighter fog, because they will then be closer to the sun. And because it is said that this fog is of a "uniformly variegated" thickness—that is, it is thicker the closer it gets to the earth, and takes on greater splendor from the sun the lower it is—for this reason, parallel buildings, such as towers and bell towers found within it, appear less thick <note>meaning they appear narrower or less substantial</note> the closer they are to their base; and

### 902. On landscapes.

The shadowy parts of remote <term>landscapes: "paesi," referring to both natural vistas and their painted representations</term> participate more in the color <term>blue: "azzurro," often referring to the atmospheric blue caused by the scattering of light</term> than the illuminated parts. This is proven by the definition of the blue with which the air—deprived of color—is tinged; which, if it did not have darkness above it, would remain white, because in itself the blue of the air is composed of light and darkness. <note>Leonardo correctly intuited that the blue sky is a result of light interacting with the "darkness" of the vacuum of space through the medium of the atmosphere.</note>

### 903. On landscapes in fogs or at the rising or setting of the sun.

I speak of landscapes that are to the east of your eye; at the rising of the sun, or with <term>fogs: "nebbie," including mist and atmospheric haze</term> or other thick vapors interposed between the sun and the eye, I say that they will be much brighter toward the sun and less splendid in the opposite parts, that is, the west;

but if it is without fog or vapors, the eastern part, or rather that part which is interposed between the sun and the eye, will be so much darker as it is closer to the eye; and such an occurrence will happen in that part which is closest to the sun, that is, which appears most directly under the sun; and in the opposite parts it will do the contrary in clear weather, and in cloudy weather it will do the opposite of what it does in fair weather.

## 905. Description of the elm.

This branching of the elm has its largest branch at its front, and the smallest are the first and the penultimate, when the main stem is straight. The birth <note>original: "nascimento," referring to the point where the leaf emerges from the stem</note> from one leaf to another is half of the greatest length of the leaf, or slightly less, because the leaves create an interval which is about a third of the width of such a leaf. The elm has its leaves closer to the tip of its branch than to its base, and their widths vary little when viewed from the same aspect. In the compositions of leafy trees, be careful not to repeat the same color of one plant too many times where it stands out against the same color of another plant, but vary them with foliage that is lighter, or darker, or a different shade of green.

The leaf always turns its right side <note>the upper surface of the leaf</note> toward the sky, so that it can better receive with its entire surface the dew that descends with slow motion from the air; and such leaves are distributed over their branches in such a way that one occupies the other as little as possible, by intertwining one above the other, as is seen in the ivy that covers walls; and such intertwining serves two purposes: first, to leave intervals so that the air and the sun can penetrate between them; the second, so that the drops that fall from the first leaf can also fall upon the fourth and the sixth of the other branches.

## 906. Of the leaves of the walnut.

The leaves of the walnut are distributed throughout the small shoot of that year, and they are more distant from one another and greater in number the younger the branch is from which that shoot is born; and they are closer at their births and fewer in number the more the shoot on which they are born originated from an older branch. Its fruits are born at the extreme end of its shoot, and the larger branches are below their parent branch; and this happens because the weight of its sap <note>original: "umore," literally "humor" or fluid</note> is more inclined to descend than to rise, and for this reason the branches born above them, which go toward the sky, are small and thin; and when the shoot looks toward the sky, its leaves spread out from its end with equal partitions at their tips; and if the shoot looks toward the horizon, the leaves remain flattened; and this arises because leaves universally keep their underside turned toward the earth.

### 907. On the appearance of landscapes.

When the sun is in the east, all the illuminated parts of the plants are of a most beautiful green; and this happens because the leaves illuminated by the sun within the half of the horizon—that is, the eastern half—are transparent. And within the western semicircle, the greenery has a dismal color in the humid and turbid air of a dark ashen hue, because it is not transparent like the eastern side, which is luminous, and all the more so the more humid it is.

### 908. On the visual transparency of plants within themselves.

The transparency <term>trasforazione: literally "boring through," referring to the gaps or openings in foliage that allow light or background to show through</term> of the air through the bodies of plants, and the transparency of plants against the air at a long distance, are not apparent to the eye; for where the whole is perceived with effort, the parts are recognized with difficulty. Instead, a confused mixture is created, which partakes most of that which is the greater sum. The openings of the tree consist of particles of illuminated air, which are much smaller than the plant, and therefore they are lost to our notice sooner than the plant itself; but this does not mean they are not there. Thus, by necessity, a mixture is made of the air and the darkness of the shaded tree, which together reach the eye of the beholder.

### 909. On trees that block each other's transparency.

That part of the tree will be less transparent where a greater mass of another tree is positioned behind it, between the tree and the air. For example, in tree *a* the transparency is not blocked, nor in *b*, because there are no trees behind them; but in *c* it is only half transparent; that is, *co* is blocked by tree *d*, which is blocked by tree *e*; <gloss>I</gloss> and a little further on, all the physical transparency of the trees is lost.

The eye positioned behind the flight of the wind <note>meaning the observer is looking in the same direction the wind is blowing</note> will never see any leaf of any plant except from its underside, save for those branches which, under the wind, look back toward that wind, or the leaves of laurels or other plants that have a strong attachment.

### 916. Precept for imitating the color of leaves.

Those who do not wish to trust entirely to their own judgment when imitating the true colors of leaves should take a leaf from the very tree they wish to represent and create their mixtures <note>The term "mistioni" refers to the physical blending of pigments on the palette.</note> directly upon it. When the mixture can no longer be distinguished from the color of that leaf, then you will be certain that the color is a perfect imitation of the leaf; and you may do the same for any other things you wish to imitate.

# PART SEVEN.

## *ON CLOUDS.*

### 917. On clouds.

Clouds are mists drawn upward by the heat of the sun, and their elevation <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: "e la loro elevazione..." This sentence is grammatically incomplete in the original manuscript.</note> where their acquired weight becomes equal in power to its motor <note>The "motor" refers to the upward force of heat; Leonardo views this as a mechanical balance of forces.</note>; and this acquired weight arises from their condensation, and condensation has its origin in the heat infused within them, which flees from the outer edges that are penetrated by the cold of the middle region of the air. The moisture follows the heat that carried it up there, to whatever part that heat flees; and because it flees toward the center of each globosity <note>A term used by Leonardo to describe the rounded, spherical shapes of cumulus clouds.</note> of the clouds, these globosities condense with defined surfaces like dense mountains, and they take on shadows by means of the solar rays that strike them up there.

Clouds are sometimes seen to receive the solar rays and illuminate themselves in the manner of dense mountains, and at other times the same clouds remain very dark, without any part of that darkness varying; and this arises from the shadows cast upon them by other clouds, which take the solar rays away from them by interposing themselves between the sun and those darkened clouds.

---

### 918. On the redness of clouds.

That redness with which clouds are tinted occurs with more or less intensity when the sun is at the horizons in the evening or morning. This happens because a body that possesses some transparency is somewhat penetrated by the solar rays when the sun appears at evening or morning; and because those parts of the clouds which are toward the edges of their globosities <note>Leonardo uses "globosità" to describe the rounded, bulbous forms of clouds.</note> are thinner in thickness than in the middle of said globosity, the solar rays penetrate them with a more brilliant redness than those thick parts, which remain dark because they are impenetrable by such solar rays. Clouds are always thinner at the contact points of their globosities than in the middle, as is proven here above; and for this reason, the redness of clouds consists of various qualities of red.

I say that the eye positioned between the globosities of the clouds and the body of the sun will see the centers of those globosities to be of greater brilliance than in any other part; but if the eye is to the side, such that the lines coming from the globosities to the eye and from the sun to the same eye form a junction less than a right angle, then the maximum light of such cloud globulences <note>original: "globulenze." A technical term Leonardo uses for the spherical clusters within a cloud mass.</note> will be at the edges of those globulences.

What is discussed here regarding the redness of clouds is understood to be when the sun is behind the clouds; but if the sun is in front of the same clouds, then their globosities will be of greater brilliance than in their intervals—that is, in the middle of the globosities and concavities—but not at the sides, which see the darkness of the sky and the earth.

### 919. On the creation of clouds.

Clouds are created by moisture infused through the air, which gathers together by means of the cold that is transported through the air by various winds; and such clouds generate winds in their creation, just as in their destruction. In their creation, winds are generated because the scattered and evaporated moisture, in rushing toward the creation of the clouds, leaves a vacuum in the place from which it fled; and because nature does not allow a vacuum <note>A reference to the Aristotelian principle "horror vacui" (nature abhors a vacuum), which Leonardo accepted as a physical law.</note>, it is necessary that the parts of the air surrounding the flight of the moisture fill the incipient vacuum with themselves: and this such motion is called wind. But when, by means of the heat of the sun, such clouds are dissolved into air, then a contrary wind is generated, created by the destruction and evaporation of the cloud compound; and both occurrences, as stated, are caused by wind. <margin>I</margin> And such winds are generated in every part of the air that is altered by heat or cold, and their motion is straight and not curved, as the adversary <note>Leonardo often frames his arguments against a hypothetical "adversary" or traditional scholastic views he intends to debunk.</note> claims; because, if it were curved, it would not be necessary to raise or

---

### 920. On clouds and their gravity and lightness.

A cloud is lighter than the air that is below it, and it is heavier than the air that is above it.

### 921. Why clouds are made from mist.

Mist, when struck by various currents of wind, condenses and becomes a cloud with various globulences <note>original: "globulenze." Leonardo’s term for the rounded, cauliflower-like clusters that form a cloud mass.</note>.

### 922. On the entirely cloudy air.

The entirely cloudy air renders the countryside below it lighter or darker according to the lesser or greater thickness of the clouds that are interposed between the sun and said countryside. When the thickened air that is interposed between the sun and the earth is of uniform thickness, you will see little difference between the illuminated and shaded parts of any body.

### 923. On the shadow of clouds.

Let the shadows of the clouds be made upon the earth with intervals struck by the solar rays, with greater or lesser splendor according to the greater or lesser transparency of those clouds. Clouds are of a much greater redness the closer they are to the horizon, and they are of much less redness the more remote they are from that horizon.

### 925. On clouds beneath the moon.

The cloud that is found beneath the moon is darker than any other, and those more remote are lighter; and the part of the cloud that is transparent within and between the edges of said cloud appears lighter than any other similar part found in the transparencies of more remote clouds; because at every degree of distance the middle of the clouds becomes lighter, and their light parts become more opaque, reddening with a dull redness; and the edges of their darkness entering into their transparent lightness have smoky and confused boundaries; and the same occurs with the edges of their light parts where they end against the air. And clouds of little thickness are entirely transparent, and more so toward the middle than at the edges, which is a dull color reddening into a coarse and confused color. And the further the clouds are from the moon, the whiter their light is, which spreads around the shadowiness of the cloud, and especially toward the moon; and that which is thin has no blackness <note>original: "nigredine"</note> and little whiteness <note>original: "albore"</note>, because the darkness of the night that shows through the air penetrates it.

### 926. On clouds.

Ensure that the clouds cast their shadows upon the earth, and make the clouds with a greater redness the closer they are to the horizon.

# PART EIGHT.

## ON THE HORIZON.

927. What the true location of the horizon is.

**Horizons** are at various distances from the eye, since that is called the horizon where the clarity of the air ends with the boundary of the earth; and it is seen in as many locations along a single perpendicular line above the center of the world <note>The "center of the world" refers to the center of the Earth in the Aristotelian/Ptolemaic sense common in Leonardo's time.</note> as there are heights of the eye that sees it. For the eye, placed at the surface <note>original: "pelle," literally "skin"</note> of a calm sea, sees that horizon about half a mile away; and if a man raises his eye to his usual height, the horizon is seen seven miles remote from him. Thus, at every degree of height, he discovers a more remote horizon. From this it happens that those who are on the summits of high mountains near the sea see the circle of the horizon very remote from them. However, those who are inland do not have a horizon at an equal distance, because the surface of the earth is not equally distant from the center of the world, and therefore it is not of perfect sphericity like the surface of the water; and this is the cause of such variety of distances between the eye and the horizon.

The horizon of the sphere of water will never be higher than the soles of the feet of the one who sees it, while standing in contact with those soles at the point where the boundary of the sea meets the boundary of the land uncovered by the waters.

The horizon of the sky is sometimes very near, especially to one who finds himself beside the summits of mountains, seeing it generated at the edge of that summit; and turning back toward the horizon of the sea, he will see it as extremely remote.

<term>horizon</term> <note>The boundary where the sky appears to meet the earth or sea.</note>, <term>sphericity</term> <note>The quality of being a sphere; Leonardo notes that the sea is more perfectly round than the uneven land.</note>, <term>height of the eye</term> <note>The altitude of the observer's viewpoint, which dictates how far they can see.</note>, <term>center of the world</term> <note>The Earth's center.</note>

<summary>Leonardo explains that the distance to the horizon depends on the observer's height and the Earth's curvature, noting that the sea provides a more consistent horizon than the irregular land.</summary>
<keywords>horizon, perspective, geometry of the earth, atmospheric optics, sea level, mountain heights</keywords>

# LEONARDO DA VINCI [§ 927

The horizon seen from the coast of the Egyptian sea is very distant; looking along the course of the Nile toward Ethiopia with its lateral plains, one sees the horizon confused, or rather unknown, because there are three thousand miles of plain that constantly rises along with the height of the river. So much thickness of air is interposed between the eye and the Ethiopian horizon that everything becomes white; and thus, such a horizon is lost to our knowledge. These types of horizons are very beautiful to see in a painting. It is true that one must create some lateral mountains with diminished degrees of colors, as required by the order of the diminution of colors over long distances <note>Leonardo is describing "aerial perspective," where the atmosphere makes distant objects appear paler and bluer.</note>.

But to demonstrate that the <term>pyramid of perspective</term> <note>A geometric concept where lines of sight converge from the object to the eye, forming a pyramid shape.</note> embraces infinite space, we will imagine *a b* as the eye, which cuts the degrees of an infinite distance *d n m o p*, and cuts them with the visual lines on the wall <note>original: "parete," referring to the picture plane or a vertical surface.</note> *c d*. These visual lines, at every degree of distance from their origin, acquire height on this wall *c d*, yet they will never reach the height of the eye; and because *c d* is a wall of a continuous quantity, it is infinitely divisible and will never be filled by the visual lines, even though the length of such a final line were infinite; nor will you ever reach it with a parallel line, even if the space *b s* were infinite.

Figures that diminish little are only slightly remote from the eye; wherefore, by necessity, the natural boundary of the horizon always meets the eye of the portrayed figure, as is the case with figure *a t* which sees figure *r u* near to itself in the outermost part of the pyramid *a t b*—that is, *r u* is smaller than *a t*. But this specific pyramid is not the one required by perspective; for that one is not used in practice because it has infinite space from its base to its point, while the one mentioned above has seven miles from its base to said point.

### 928. On the horizon.

The horizon of the sky and of the earth ends in one and the same line. This is proven: let the sphere of the earth be *d n m*, and the sphere of the air be *a r p*, and let the eye of the viewer of the earth's horizon be *b*. Then *f* is the said horizon of the earth, in which the view of the air ends, and it appears that *a*, the air, is joined with *f*, the earth.

### 929. On the true horizon.

The true horizon must be the boundary of the sphere of water, which should be immobile, because such immobility establishes a surface equidistant to the center of the world, as will be proven in its proper place. If the sky and the earth were of a flat surface <unclear>...</unclear>

with the interposition of equidistant space, the horizon of perspective would undoubtedly be at the height of the eye that sees it; but it would be necessary for such parallel spaces to be at an infinite distance if they were to appear to the eye to converge in a line, that is, in contact; and this contact would be at the height of the eye of that observer. However, because the earth would have a smaller quantity of plane than that of the sky, it would happen that when the <term>plain</term> <note>original: "planizie," referring to a flat expanse or level surface.</note> of the sky had its final boundary descended to the level of the eye, the horizon of the earth would be raised to the navel of that same observer, and for this reason they do not converge at the same eye. But because such sky and earth are not divided by a space of parallel, or I should say equidistant, planes, but by a space that is convex on the side of the sky and concave on the side that clothes the earth, it happens that every part of the earth's surface can be a horizon. This could not happen if the sky and earth were flat, as shown in the sky *ab* and in the earth *fe*, with the eye being at *g* and the wall <note>original: "parete," the vertical picture plane used in perspective geometry.</note> being *cd*, where the horizons *af* of the flat sky and earth intersect at points *nm*.

### 930. On the horizon.

The horizon will never be equal to the height of the eye that sees it. That figure which is closer to the horizon will have that horizon closer to its feet while you stand still watching it. That thing is higher which is more distant from the center of the world <note>Leonardo refers to the "center of the world" as the center of the Earth's gravity/sphere.</note>.

Therefore, a straight <term>equi-lying</term> <note>original: "equigiacente," meaning a horizontal line parallel to the ground.</note> line is not of equal height, and consequently, it is not equi-lying; hence, if you speak of a line of equal height, it will not be understood as anything other than a curve. If *ab* are two men, the horizon *n* will come to the level of their height.

### 931. On the horizon.

If the earth is spherical, the horizon will never reach the height of the eye that is higher than the surface of the earth. # TREATISE ON PAINTING — PART EIGHT

### 935. Why the dense air near the horizon turns red.

The air turns red at both the eastern and western horizons when it is dense <note>Leonardo uses "grossa" (thick/dense) to describe air filled with moisture or particulate matter</note>, and this redness is generated between the eye and the sun. However, the redness of the celestial bow <note>The rainbow</note> is generated when the eye is positioned between the rain and the sun. The cause of the former is the sun and the humidity of the air; but the causes of the redness of the bow are the sun, the rain, and the eye that perceives it. This redness, along with the other colors, will be of much greater excellence <note>Vibrancy or saturation</note> as the rain is composed of larger droplets. And as these droplets become smaller, those colors become more dull; and if the rain is of the nature of mist, then the bow will be entirely white and colorless; but the eye must be between the mist and the sun.

<term>aria grossa: dense air</term> <term>orizzonte: horizon</term> <term>rossore: redness</term> <term>arco celeste: celestial bow (rainbow)</term> <term>pioggia: rain</term> <term>nebbia: mist or fog</term> <term>ottica: optics</term>

<meta>This page provides a detailed list of the illustrations and engravings included in the volume, identifying their sources, the artists involved in the reproductions, and the specific subjects depicted by Leonardo da Vinci and his school.</meta>

The engravings that adorn this volume have been taken from the Album entitled: *Drawings by Leonardo da Vinci engraved from the originals by* CARLO GIUSEPPE GERLI, *reproduced with illustrative notes by* GIUSEPPE VALLARDI (Milan, 1830). Those on the pediments (in woodcut <term>xilografia: a relief printing technique where an image is carved into the surface of a block of wood</term>) are reductions engraved by Mr. G. STELLUTI of Rome; the others (in photo-zincotype <term>fotozincotipia: an early process for reproducing drawings using light-sensitive chemicals on zinc plates</term>) are the work of the FRATELLI TREVES ESTABLISHMENT in Milan, where the illustrations for the text were also executed. The reproduction (in halftone typo-photography <term>tipofotografia a mezza tinta: a mechanical printing process that simulates continuous tones using dots of varying sizes</term>) of the painting of the *Dispute* by Leonardo comes from the DANESI ESTABLISHMENT in Rome and was reduced from a steel engraving by G. Carrelli.

In the present list, the indications given by Vallardi are followed.
